CHAPTER 1 HISTORY OF FIRE SPRINKLERS Fire sprinklers have a long and successful history of protecting lives and property from fire. The chronological history of automatic fire sprinklers began a few centuries ago, This chapter will detail the people involved and the technological advances that have taken place to arrive at the systems that are installed today, The first records of any type of fixed fire protection system appear in 1723. Ambrose Godfrey used a stationary cask of water with a pewter chamber of gunpowder attached. The chamber was attached to a system of fuses stretched throughout the room, When a fire occurred, the hope was that it would ignite one of the fuses and burn towards the gunpowder. The gunpowder would then explode, breaking the cask open and distributing thé water around the room. Similar to Godfrey's invention, Figure 1-1 shows another water-based fire protection system idea of the early 18th Century, a barrel filled with water that also has a fuse and gunpowder attached. In the event of a fire, the fuse could be lit and rolled toward the fire. The fuse will burn to the gunpowder, explode and distribute the water directly on the fire, assuming that the barrel roll could be timed correctly. It is clear to see why these devices did not catch on and gain widespread public acceptance. In the years that followed the technology improved and inventors continued to come up with original ideas for protecting people and property from fire. Some of the major developments in the 1800s include perforated pipes fusible cords and fusible -caps.- In the early 19th Century, John Carey developed a system of pipes with holes in them that came to be known as a perforated pipe system, The pipes were connected to a water supply on the roof of the building. A series of ropes attached to Figure '1-1: Rolling a cask of water into the weights were scattered around the building and fire to distribute water at the source. 1

If a fire occuLTed, it would bum through the rope, causing the weight attached to the rope to fall and pull the stopper out of the tank. The water would then be released to flow through the pipes and out of the holes. Carey's system had the advantage of being automatic and having relatively reliable (and non-explosive) parts. Since all of the holes were open, the water would be distributed everywhere, similar to what is now a deluge system, but potentially wasting the water on locations nowhere near the fire. The names of those who designed the perforated pipe systems in Figure 1-4(b) may seem familiar, The Grinnell Company has merged with many other firrns to become one of the largest providers of fire protection in the world today. Also, Factory Mutual has been an insurance company that has promoted fixed fire protection systems for the properties that they insure and sponsored fire research to improve those systems for over 130 years now. Other advancements that were made during the 1800' s include fantail deflectors, a rotating pipe system, a steam system and improyements on the perforated piping systems. The fantail deflectors were one of the early steps to creating a spray pattern that had a planned distribution pattem of the water on the hazard. The rotating pipe system was also an improvement that aimed to get water spread farther in the building by spinning the pipe and in turn, throwing the water. The changes to the perforated pipe system included making the automatic function more reliable, removing the need for manual intervention. While the system shown in Figure 1.2 developed by Carey was automatic, it was impractical given the ropes involved and the need to burn through before starting the water flow, so most early perforated pipe systems were manual as shown in Figure 1-3. In the late developed a pelforated pipe system with fusible links spaced along the ropes (as shown in Figure 1-5) that melt when they reach a specific temperature. The weights that are attached to the rope then fall, pulling the valve open and allowing water to flow into the pipe and onto the fire. The advantage to Pratt's design was that the links melted much sooner than waiting for the whole rope to burn through. ieue•u .18.72 MAGS, Figure '1-5: Pratt's system with valve oper- ated by weights. Perhaps the most important technological advance of the 18001s was the development of the automatic sprinkler that improved fire protection in two respects. First, it could hold back water within the pipe until such time that the sprinkler was activated by the heat from the fire, allowing the water to be distributed only near the fire. Second, the sprinkler broke the water streams into droplets where the surface area of the droplet increased the efficiency of water delivery and its cooling capabilities, According to Nash and Young, Major A, Stewart Harrison invented the first automatic sprinkler in 1864 in London. This design consisted of a spherical brass shell with an orifice plugged by a rubber valve and attached to a string, when the string bumed it released the valve allowing water to flow. The need for this type of device was not readily seen by the public and Harrison's invention was not widely used. But it remains as the first known design of a device that could be described as a "fire sprinkler" Henry Parmalee is credited with developing the first "widely used" sprinkler in 1874. Parmalee was the President of the Mathusek Piano Works, (that continues today as the 3

## Page 10

Baldwin Piano Company), which suffered a fire in t.heir piano factory in New Haven, CT. Parmalee then set out to rebuild and find a way to prevent a loss of the same scale in his factory, After several designs, Parmalee developed a perforated shell covered by a brass cap soldered to a heavy base. The solder melted at 1600F and the water pressure forced the cap off to permit flowing water. In 1878 he improved the distribution characteristics of the sprinkler by installing a small rotating turbine. Parmalee met up with Frederick Grinnell, owner of the Providence •Steam and Gas Pipe Company. As an installer of pipe for gas and steam systems, Grinnell was familiar with putting pipe together, and had installed several pelforated pipe fire protection systems. Grimell agreed to install fire sprinkler systems using Parmalee's sprinklers. By the 1880's, Grinnell staffed to develop his own sprinklers. Examples of early sprinklers are displayed in Figures 1-6. On the left is an early Grinnell model, developed by Frederick Grinnell, and on the right is a Parmalee sprinkler, which is also called a saltshaker sprinkler due to its shape and size. Figure 1-7 is a cross section of a Parmalee sprinkler showing where the cap is soldered to the sprinkler and that the entire cap will fall away when the sprinkler is activated. Figure 1-6: Grinnell (left) and Parmalee (right) sprin- kiers were two of the first models developed for auto- Figure 4-7: Section view of a Par- malee sprinkler. This cleariy shows In the early 1900' s glass bulbs were placed in sprinklers as another type of link, However, this development did not catch on in the United States as installers were leery of the new technology, Frederick Grinnell met with Sir William Mather of England and, since the glass bulb technology was not catching on in the United States, gave him the rights to produce glass bulb sprinklers in•Europe where they proved to be much more popular. Matherts company, Mather & Platte, manufactured sprinklers for years in Europe. They were bought out by Wormald, and in the 198(Ys Tyco (the parent company of Grinnell) bought Wormald. It took about 100 years for Grinnell to again hold the patent on the glass bulb sprinkler that they developed. In the 1980's glass bulbs started to make a comeback in the United States, and their use continues to be on the rise, It should be noted that today the majority of the glass bulbs used for sprinklers are made in Germany by the Job company. 4

Figures 1-8 and 1-9 show a type of sprinkler called a ' 'link and lever sprinkler". These models are no longer produced, but the concept of a lever, keeping the sprinkler link under stress and, once activated, sweeping away the pieces of the link so that the orifice will be clear of obstructions for water distribution, is still used today. The design of early .sprinklers shows that from the beginning, consideration has been given to making sure that water is distributed in all directions from the sprinkler. With the specific design shown in Figure 1-10, there are many small holes allowing water to spray in many directions. These holes could easily get plugged from pipe scale and sediment that may build up with time and effect the flow of water from the sprinkler. With time the concern over corrosion lead to sprinklers having larger orifices. With the developments and advancements of the automatic sprinkler it becaine possible to design the piping system differently than the open perforated pipe systems. The assumption that only one floor would be involved should a fire start, and the ability to control water flowing by activating only those devices in the area of the fire, allowed designers to supply the entire-system with a single riser, and still mind the owner's desire to place water only where the fire is located. On these risers was the early form of an alarm check valve. It was installed and attached through a bell or whistle by using a lever extending through the valve casing to signal thé flow of water, The practice of using the hot water or steam pipes used for heating the building as piping for the sprinlder systems also became popular in the late 1800's. From this early time, it was recognized that some buildings could take advantage of the efficiency in using water distribution piping in buildings for multiple purposes. These systems became the circulating closed loop systems in use today, Because of the climate in the New England area where sprinkler systems first gained popularity, it became apparent that the freezing of piping would cause problems in fire sprinlder systems. steam through the piping to keep the water in the pipe from freezing and also heat the building. The sprinklers were attached to inverted U pipes that trapped enough water not to heat the sprinkler link and result in false operation. Prior to the development of dry-pipe valves, Osmund Williams patented an antifreeze solution to be used for sprinkler systems. The first actual mechanically operated dry valve was attached to a cord that would melt at temperatures between 900 and 1200F. The fusing of the cord released a hammer mechanism that Opened a valve on the sprinkler supply piping. In 1885 Grinnell patented the bellows differential dry valve that utilized air pressure to hold back the water below the clapper and its subsequent improvements are the forerunners of today's dry-pipe valves. By the late 1800's, fire sprinkler systems were so popular and reliable, that most insurance companies were offering significant discounts for owners of warehouses and factories that would install the systems. Unfortunately, each insurance company had its own mles for the installation of fire sprinkler systems, leading to confusion in the industry and concern over the lack of standardization for manufacturers and installers. In the 1890's, members of the fire sprinkler industry joined with members of the insurance community and the fire service to forni the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). One of the first tasks of the NFPA was to produce a document to standardize the installation of fire sprinkler systems, This first edition of NFPA 13, Standard for the Installation of Automatic Sprinkler Systems was published in 1896, The committee that wrote the first edition of NFPA 13 included Frederick Grinnell, Everett Hugh Crosby (with one of the stock insurance companies), Uberto C. Crosby (also with one of the stock insurance companies), W.H. Stratton of the FIA (an insurance industry association), John R. Freeman of Factory Mutual and Elliott Cabot of the Boston Board of Fire Underwriters. Prior to NFPA 13, there were some manufacturer installation guidelines such as the one published by James Francis for perforated pipe systems and one written by Frederick Grinnell for installing Pannalee sprinkler systems in accordance with a pipe schedule, But after NFPA 13 was issued in 1896, most insurance companies and manufacturers dropped their special rules and adopted the NFPA standard. The early 1900's saw many developments in the sprinkler industry. With the introduction of different fusible links, Grinnell and Globe were able to make sprinklers more sensitive, decreasing the time for them to react to the heat of a fire. The Grinnell Duraspeed was, and is still is, one of the fastest responding standard spray sprinklers in use, Preaction valves, which along with deluge valves had been used since the early 1900's were developed in 1933 when modifications to the valves allowed for a supervisory alarm when the piping had been damaged or the air pressure had been released, "Conventional" or "old-style" sprinklers, shown in Figure were used exclusively prior to 1955. These sprinklers sprayed approximately 50 to 70 percent of their discharge down towards the floors and the rest up against the ceiling to help cool the 6

## Page 13

building's structural members. In 1955, as a result of extensive research at Factory Mutual, the sprinkler underwent a drastic modification to the deflector. These modifications provided a more finely dispersed and more uniform downward pattem to the sprinkler's discharge. The new sprinklers produced smaller water droplets that stayed near the ceiling and absorbed the heat from a fire and protected the structure, while also producing medium and large water droplets to cool the surface of the fuel and pre-wet adjacent combustibles. These new sprinklers became known as the "standard spray sprinklers" (see Figure I-I I(a))and quickly replaced the older models in the United States. Testing has shown that as long as the standard spray sprinkler is within 12 inches of the ceiling there is enough cooling from the presence of water to prevent fire spread along the ceiling. By the latter half of the 20th century, fire sprinklers had gained widespread acceptance for use in factory, industrial, warehouse and commercial occupancies. But concem over extensive water damage kept sprinklers from being installed in some occupancies that were sensitive-to. the excess flow of water. To eliminate the concem over excess water damage, a cycling valve with a heat detector activated control valve was developed in 1967, and the on-off sprinkler was developed in 1972. After the residential sprinkler was developed, the fast acting link was placed in the standard spray sprinkler in order to create a commercial sprinkler that was faster to respond to fire than the sprinklers that were then on the market, This sprinkler came to be known as the Quick Response (QR) sprinkler. The first sprinkler to obtain the QR listing was the Grinnell F931 sprinkler. These sprinklers have the same deflector as the standard spray sprinkler, and are considered as a special type of standard spray sprinkler, It is just their activation link that is different, having a faster response characteristic. Figure 1-14: Prototype Early Suppression Fast Response sprinkler. Another significant change in 1972 occurred with the listing of the first extended coverage sprinklers. This listing resulted in a change in the 1973 edition of NFPA 13, allowing for larger coverage areas in accordance with the sprinklers listing up to 400 ft2. This category now contains over 100 different listed sprinklers that can be used to cover greater areas than the standard spray sprinkler limits in NFPA 13. In order to protect the growing number of large warehouses that could generate large fires a research program was initiated at Factory Mutual Research Corp. in the 1980's to improve the sprinkler discharge penetration of 8

the fire plume. The result wag the large drop sprinkler. This, sprinkler, with its larger droplet spray, is able to deliver more water to the seat of the fire. The next step in the development of sprinklers for warehouse occupancies was to improve the mass and velocity of the water droplets so that the sprinkler would be ablve to suppress a fire, not just control it. In 1983, Factory Mutual introduced the concept of the Early Suppression Fast Response (ESFR) sprinkler. In 1989, UL and FM listed the first two available ESFR sprinklers. CHAPTER 2 THE ROLE OF THE FIRE SPRINKLER TEC}NICIAN The Fire Sprinkler Technician is a critical member of a fire sprinkler contractor's or- ganization that includes sales, fabrication, installation, supervision, administration and manage- ment. Each of these functions is interdependent on the others, and without full communication and cooperation it is difficult, if not impossible, to bring a project to successful, profitable com- pletion. The job title is something that bears discussion. Over the years, the people who lay out sprinkler systems have been called designers, engineers, sprinkler designers, technicians, and a long list of combinations of these words. The department they work in has been called Engi- neering or Design. It is now a reality that the Professional Engineering community has taken an adversarial position on the use of the words design and engineering unless a person is registered as a Professional Engineer. That doesn't mean the individuals who layout sprinkler systems are any less talented or knowledgeable, It means that there is a legally recognized definition of the practice of engineering and engineering technicians play a vital and important role in the design process. The technician performs his or her job following recognized standards and is subject to being under the supervision of a design professional. We could go on with this topic for many hours, but suffice it to say that urdess you are a registered professional engineer, when you per- form layout and produce shop drawings you are doing technicians work. The correct job title for you would be as stated in the title of this section, Fire Sprinkler Design Technician or Fire Protection Engineering Technician (FPET). The goal of the FPET is to produce unambiguous plans that result in the lowest installed cost of a fire sprinkler system consistent with project specifications, applicable requirements of codes and standards, and quality for the customer. There are a number of job responsibilities and activities that allow this to happen: Examination of sales estimate compared to specifications and conformance to codes and standards. Consider alternate system layouts to produce the most efficient installation. Factors include building structure, type of materials, expertise of installation personnel, and coordination with other trades, 11

## Page 18

Make the shop drawings a communication channel, A shop drawing is a just another communication device that issues instructions on how to assemble a system. Shop drawings must be complete and independent so that each person who views them does not have to use multiple sources to complete their job. The installer needs to know how and where to hang and join pipe, AHJ's need to be able to understand the system fea- tures, spacing, devices and calculations, other trades must know where the sprinkler piping is being run. Establish contact with the fire/code official before layout begins to verify specification requirements. Maintain the contact and be available to answer questions during the ap- proval process. Field-check all project segments before stock listing and fabrication. Maintain continual communication with the field and prepare as-built drawings as the system is being installed. Maintain records and files for the project including updated contract drawings, change order requests, field changes, and shop drawings from other trades that were used for coordination. The above description is not complete as each project and company is organized differ- ently. The Fire Protection Engineering Technician can expect added responsibilities to be as- signed as he or she gains experience and knowledge. However, the items listed above are cen- tral to helping a FPET meet the goal of being a valued member of the contracting team. 12

CHAPTER 3 INTRODUCTION TO NFSA, NICET AND OTHER ORGANIZATIONS This text will make specific reference to a number of different organizations that are somehow involved with the fire sprinkler industry. Some of these organizations directly affect the industry by writing rules that are adopted into laws in many jurisdictions. Other organizations represent different elements of the fire sprinkler industry or provide some service to the industry. A basic description of each organization is included here along with a Sholt history of how that organization became involved in fire protection and the fire sprinkler industry. National Fire Sprinlder Association (NFSA) Organized in 1905, the National Fire Sprinkler Association (NFSA) is a trade association representing all of the elements of the fire sprinkler industry including manufacturers, contractors (union and non-union), suppliers, professionals (engineers and architects) and authorities (fire, building and insurance) that wish to stay informed on the progress of the fire sprinkler industry. The Mission Statement of the NFSA is to "Support the widespread acceptance of competently installed fire sprinkler systems in all buildings from homes to high-rise." In order to complete this mission statement, the NFSA provides services to its members in four distinct areas: engineering, training and education, labor relations and marketing. The engineering functions of the NFSA include representing the membership on the various committees of the organizations that write codes and standards such as the NFPA and the ICC. Some of the organizations that write model codes do not allow the NFSA to have a vote on their committees because they only want public officials to have a say in the language of their codes. In these cases, the NFSA remains active in the process by submitting proposals and comments and by working with the public officials that do get to vote so that they understand the concerns of the fire sprinkler industry. Another function of the engineering depattment is to offer interpretations of the standards and codes, acting as an impartial third party that can settle disputes between contractors and local authorities. Many times, the NFSA staff, being involved in the development of codes and 13

## Page 20

standards is in a position to give deeper understanding to the requirements of the codes and standards, With this deeper understanding, disputes over the application of specific rules can be settled to everyone's satisfaction. The advantage of this approach to clarifying the codes and standards is that it can usually be completed in a single business day rather than waiting several months for the code making body to issue a Fomal Interpretation, The training and education functions of the NFSA focus on keeping the members up-to-date on the changes in the fire sprinkler industry. Every diree years, a new set of codes and standards is released with many technical changes. In addition, new products are always, being developed with their own special installation instructions. The members of the NFSA rely on the association to keep abreast of the most recent rules in our fast-changing industry. In addition, the training and education department helps to train the plan review officials that are responsible for ultimately deciding whether or not fire sprinkler plans get approved. Lastly, the training and education department maintains a series of seminars for training and upgrading the skills of technicians in the industry so that the members always have an appropriate pool of skilled workers to meet the demand. The labor relations function of the NFSA allows the union contractors to negotiate with the sprinkler fitter locals in a collective bargaining fashion. By bargaining as a unit, the industry remains stable with uniform wage rates in any area regardless of the company selected for a specific job. Non-union contractors benefit from this collective bargaining because it stabilizes the wage rates in any area as well as creating a distinct classification for individuals installing sprinkler systems. Without the labor unions recognizing sprinkler installation as a separate and unique function of construction, sprinkler work would be absorbed as just another type of mechanical work or plumbing work and non-union contractors would lose their identity as well. Even though the non-union members benefit from the NFSA labor relations functions, they do not pay för these ftnctions. The dues of the NFSA are structured so that union contractors pay for the labor relations activities and that none of the dues from non-union members go to this ftnction. From a marketing perspective, the NFSA spends a great deal of time trying to get the public to understand how fire sprinklers work and get them to expect sprinklers everywhere they live, work and play, While the concept of sprinkler protection in high-rise buildings is generally accepted by the public, the expectation of fire sprinklers in low-rise residential construction and other occupancies is not as high as the NFSA would hope. The marketing ftnction of the NFSA is directed at raising the expectations of the public so that they choose to live in sprinklered homes, work in sprinklered properties, and recreate in sprinklered amusement halls and assembly buildings. National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) Because their names are very similar, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) is often confused with the NFSA, but the two organizations are very different and operate independently. 14

## Page 21

The NFPA was organized in 1896 for the purpose of developing a single consensus standard for the installation of fire sprinkler systems and a unified national electrical code. Prior to the development of the NFPA, individual insurance companies and other authorities were writing their own standards for both fire sprinklers and electrical installations. The need for clear, consensus documents on these two subjects led to the formation of the NFPA and remains the focus of the organization to this day. The NFPA has branched out well beyond just fire sprinklers and electricity, but these two documents remain the two most popular they produce. The Mission Statement of the NFPA is to "reduce the worldwide burden of fire and other hazards on the quality of life by providing and advocating scientifically-based consensus codes and standards, research, training, and education." In working to fulfill its mission, the NFPA has established a large staff to meet the needs of its 70,000 members worldwide. One of the most important functions of the NFPA is to develop over 300 codes, standards and recommended practices regarding the installation of fire protection systems in buildings and the construction requirements for those buildings. Since the mission of the NFPA and the mission of the NFSA overlap where it comes to fire sprinkler systems, the two organizations work together on a number of projects including the development of textbooks and training materials. Many NFSA staff and members sit on NFPA technical committees helping to write the codes, standards and recommended practices that affect the fire sprinkler industry. Having NFSA staff and members sit on NFPA committees often leads to confusion and people thinking that the organizations are linked some how (or even the same), but they are completely independent. More information on the NFPA can be found in Chapter 4 of this text titled Rules Governing Installation, National Institute for Certification in Engineering Technologies (NICET) Organized in 1961, the National Institute for Celtification in Engineering Technologies (NICET) is a branch of the National Society of Professional Engineers (NSPE). The purpose of the NICET organization is to recognize technicians that are capable of performing layout and detail work on building and structure plans under the supervision of a Professional Engineer. Note that the teclmician is not required or expected to be an engineer. Instead, the technician is the individual that interprets the engineer's design and applies the design concepts by preparing working drawings. Technically, this is not the practice of engineering and can be performed by an individual (technician) that is not a Professional Engineer, but still needs to be performed by a knowledgeable individual. NICET offers a way of identifying these knowledgeable individuals. Certification by NICET is obtained through passing a series of examinations and providing proof of work experience. NICET breaks the material that the technician needs to know down into discrete subject categories called "Work Elements", Each Work Element represents an area of knowledge that the technician will need to prove that they know something about. A short exam Will need to be passed for each Work Element, In addition to passing the exam, the candidate needs to provide proof to NICET that they actually work in the field, performing the 15

## Page 22

tasks described in the Work Element. Only after passing the exam, and verifying the work experience, will NICET provide credit to the candidate for passing the Work Element. NICET certification is available in 30 categories of technology including Geotechnical Engineering Technology and Transportation Engineering Technology. NICET did not always certify people in the field of fire protection. In fact, for the first 100 years of the fire sprinkler industry, it was not necessary to certify individuals in the area of preparing fire sprinkler drawings. Instead, the general public relied on the insurance authorities to approve the plans for fire sprinkler systems because the insurance authorities were responsible for the sprinklers being required in the building, or were expected to give some reduction In insurance for the system. So, the insurance authority had the most direct concerns about the sprinkler system being installed corectly. With this third party review, sprinkler contractors were forced to draw (and many times redraw) plans to make the insurance company happy, Most of the insurance companies did not perform the review of the sprinkler plans themselves; they relied on the Insurance Services Office (ISO) to review and approve the plans for them. In 1975, ISO announced that it would no longer approve plans for fire sprinkler systems. ISO agreed to continue to review plans to determine insurance credits for sprinkler systems, but would no longer determine if those systems complied with NFPA 13. There were a number of reasons for ISO's decision, but a few of the reasons had to do with the large number of sprinkler systems being installed (ISO could not hire enough engineers to review the plans) and the fact that sprinklers were being mandated more by codes that were outside the jurisdiction of the insurance industry. With ISO backing out of the process of approving plans, many local authorities went looking for methods of protecting the public by making sure that individuals preparing working plans for sprinkler systems had the knowledge to do so. While it is true that the plans would have to be submitted for plan review in the local jurisdiction, but the problem was that most of the plan reviewers did not know as much about sprinkler systems and they needed to know to perform a complete review. Many plan review authorities looked to the sprinkler industry to develop a plan for identifying knowledgeable and competent individuals. The NFSA responded by working with NICET to develop the certification programs. Of most direct interest to those individuals in the fire sprinkler industry are the four categories (subfields) in which NICET ceftifies Fire Protection Engineering Technicians: 1) Automatic Sprinkler System Layout and Detail 2) Fire Alarm Systems 3) Special Hazard Systems 4) Inspection and Testing of Water-B ased Systems Most of the NICET subfields have four different levels of certification. Level I (Student Technician) certification is intended to be an entry level for people just getting started in the field, Typically, Level I technicians perform their work under supervision of higher-level 16

## Page 23

technicians. To achieve Level I certification, the candidate needs to pass a few basic Work Elements demonstrating that they know a little bit about the fire sprinkler business. Level II is considered the Associate Engineering Technician level and demonstrates a basic understanding of the subject material. Level II technicians can work on simple systems. In the Automatic Sprinkler Layout and Detail certification program, Level II technicians are considered the minimum level to work on residential sprinkler systems on their own and supervision is still needed for Level II technicians to work on commercial systems. In the Inspection and Testing program, Level II is considered the minimum level of certification for an individual to inspect or test basic fire protection systems on their own. Level II certification generally requires two years of work experience along with passing the Work Element tests. Level III certification is for the Engineering Technician. In the Automatic Sprinkler System Layout and Detail program, the Level III technician can work on their own on commercial systems. Level III is the highest level of certification available in the Inspection and Testing program, being designated for senior inspectors that have knowledge of complex systems. Level III certification generally requires five years of work experience along with passing the requisite Work Elements. Level IV ceftification is for Senior Engineering Technicians and is available for all of the fire protection subfields of celtification except the Inspection and Testing program. In addition to the testing and experience, the technician wishing a Level IV certification in Automatic Sprinkler Layout and Detailing needs to document a project where they are in responsible charge of fire protection system layout and detail from initial working plan preparation through final installation and acceptance testing. Level IV certification generally requires ten years of work experience along with passing the requisite Work Elements. For more information on NICET, visit the NICET website at www.nicetaoro. To determine which elements need to be passed in order to achieve any specific level of certification, download the Program Detail Manual for the subfield in question from the NICET website. The Program Detail Manual will explain which Work Elements are required and which choices the candidate has to achieve certification at each level in the program. The International Code Council (ICC) The ICC is the newest of the organizations discussed here, but its roots go back almost 100 years. While the NFPA developed standards flu•oughout the century dealing with the installation of fire protection systems and electrical systems, other organizations were writing building codes, fire codes} mechanical codes and plumbing codes, Although many different organizations wrote building and fire codes during the 20th Century, by the 1980's tlu•ee organizations pretty much dominated the code arena: 1) Building Officials and Code Administrators (BOCA) 2) International Conference of Building Officials (ICBO) 3) Southern Standard Building Code Congress International (SBCCI) 17

## Page 24

Each of the three different code organizations discussed above was used in a specific region of the country. As such, the early version of their codes tended to focus on different building problems related to their region. The BOCA Codes were primarily used in the Midwest and Atlantic regions of the United States (Illinois, Ohio, Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey and New England) and focused on issues like snow loads common to these regions, although they certainly covered other requirements for buildings. The ICBO Codes were used mostly west of the Mississippi River and focused on seismic issues. Even though many of the states that used the ICBO Codes were not in active seismic zones, the state of California was one of the prime movers in the ICBO code development process and made sure that the seismic provisions in that code were as comprehensive as possible although they certainly covered other requirements for buildings. The SBCCI Codes were used primarily tlroughout the southeast portion of the United States (North Caroline through Florida). Not surprisingly, these codes focused on the need to design buildings to withstand significant wind forces in order to minimize damage from hurricanes, although they certainly covered other requirements for buildings. Toward the end of the Century, it became clear that the three different sets of Codes had each expanded to the point where all of the different subjects were being handled comprehensively in all of the Codes. At that point, some forward-thinking individuals proposed that the three code organizations should merge and develop a single set of codes and the ICC was born. Each of the individual code organizations agreed to stop developing their own codes and participate in the development of the ICC codes instead. Today, the ICC publishes the International Building Code, International Fire Code, International Mechanical Code and International Plumbing Code. Plans are underway for an International Existing Buildings Code and an International Performance-Based Code as well. A deeper discussion of building codes is found in Chapter 4 of this text, Rules Governing Installation. Summary Engineering technicians will encounter many different organizations throughout their careers. Each organization fills a different role in the fire protection community. While some organizations write the codes and standards that are adopted by law, others work to insure that the industry is represented and that the public can identify knowledgeable individuals. The National Fire Sprinkler Association (NFSA) and the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) are different organizations. Even though their names are the same, and they have a similar goal of reducing the damage done by fire, they are completely separate companies. In the interest of conserving resources and saving money, the two organizations work closely together on many different projects. Members and staff of the NFSA frequently sit on the committees established by the NFPA to write codes and standards. While sitting on these committees, the members and staff of the NFSA are not acting as agents of the NFPA. Rather, they are representing the interests of the NFSA membership in establishing the rules that will eventually be adopted into law. 18

CHAPTER 4 RULES GOVERNING INSTALLATION As you have read in previous chapters, there are many different people or bodies that will review or approve the work you do. There are municipal or governmental authorities, such as Fire Departments and Building Departments. There are project authorities, such as the owner, the architect} the engineer, the builder and the insurance company. There are authorities within your own organization, such as the design manager, the general manager and the company owner. Any of these authorities that have jurisdiction over your company's work may be called an Authority Having Jurisdiction or, more simply, the must follow when detailing a sprinkler system can be found in a wide variety of sources, Learning how to apply these rules Can be a daunting task for the new design technician. Let's hope this chapter helps you understand what some of these mles are and how you might apply them. Here is a brief list of the types of rules you will be expected to follow: Building Codes (C Installation Standards Local Ordinances Insurance Requirements Product Listings & Approvals Project Specifications Federal Government Recommended Practices Manuals & Guides 21

## Page 28

Codes and Standards There are two very different types of documents that will generally guide your design work: standards and codes. The NFPA defines them this way: Standard "A document, the main text of which contains only mandatory provisions using the word "shall" to indicate requirements and which is in afonn generally suitable for mandatory reference by another standard or code or for adoption i.nlo law. Non-ntandatory provisions shall be located in an appendix, footnote, or fine- print note and are not to be considered a part of the requirements ofa standard. "l Code — "14 standard that is an extensive compilation of provisions covering broad subject matter or that is suitable for adoption into law independently of other codes and standards. " 2 Not everyone takes the same opinion about the distinction between codes and standards as the NFPA. Since both Codes and Standards contain mandatory requirements that are written in a form that can be legally adopted and enforced, it is difficult to tell the difference between the two. For many of the code-writing organizations, a code is a document that determines what kind of systems and equipment need to be inst.alled in any given type of building. A standard generally informs the user on how to arrange the equipment required by a code, For example, a building code or fire code might state that all hospitals are required to have a fire sprinkler system. But the fire code should not contain requirements on how far apart the sprinklers need to be installed or how much water needs to discharge from the sprinklers if there is a fire, A standard should cover the concepts of sprinkler spacing and required discharge. Codes generally include references to standards, interlocking their requirements and making standards a subset of the rules expressly written in the codes. Unfortunately, the line between codes and standards isn't as clean as described above. Building codes and fire codes have taken issue with some of the rules in standards and gotten into the business of determining how to install some systems. On the other hand, some' standards have taken to calling themselves "Codes" because of the name recognition that goes along with the marketing of such documents, For example, NFPA 72 is a standard that describes how to install fire alarm and detection systems. But the document has been titled the National Fire Alarm Code for many years now because the NFPA feels that it is easier to market the document under this kind of title. Codeg and Standards must be written in language that is legally enforceable, without any ambiguity in the text. Lawyers have determined that the word "shall" needs to be used to make sure that the requirement is clear. Words like "should" "can" and 'Cmay" are not allowed to be used in the body of the text because they have multiple meanings and can be taken different ways when trying to enforce the rules, There is a difference between saying, "the maximum distance between sprinklers shall be 10 ft" and "the maximum distance between sprinklers should be 10 ft." The first statement is much more enforceable than the second. 22

## Page 29

The Building Codes According to the International Code Council (ICC), Building Codes provide comprehensive and compatible regulatory system for the built environment, through consistent petfomance-based regulations that are effective, efficient and meet government, industry and public needs," The ICC oversees the development of a ' 'model building code" (the International Building Code) that, by itself, has no force and effect in law. In other words, there is no requirement for anybody to follow a model code just because it has been produced by the •ICC. However, Federal, State and Local Authorities adopt building codes by passing laws that architects and engineers must then follow when they design a building. Rather than write their own code from scratch, the state or the municipality usually adopts one of the "model') building codes as law, They often amend that model code to better reflect local practices$ traditions, and political environments. The ICC's International Building Code is the most predominant code being used today. Before the ICC was formed, there were three different organizations that were writing model building codes and fire prevention, mechanical and plumbing codes to go with them. The ün•ee model code organizations were: Building Officials and Code Administrators International (BOCA), responsible for the National Building Code and before that, the Basic Building Code. These codes were used extensively throughout the Midwest and Northeast portions of the United States, International Conference of Building Officials (ICBO), responsible for the Uniform Building Code, used mostly west of the Mississippi River. Southern Building Code Congress International (SBCCI), responsible for the Standard Building Code, used throughout the Southeast portion of the United States. Each of the regional model code organizations was formed to deal with specific problems in their respective regions. The initial focus of the Uniform Building Code was to protect structures from damage due to earthquake. The initial focus of the Standard Building Code was the wind loads associated hurricanes. initial focus of the National Building Code (and its predecessor, the Basic Building Code) was snow loads, Over time, these codes grew to handle all of the structural and life safety concerns necessary for a building. Each code expanded to adequately handle earthquakes, snow loads, wind •loads and all of the other issues necessary for a building. As the codes started to address all of the same issues, some forward-thinking individuals got together and laid out plans for merging the organizations. In 1997, the three model building code developing bodies began an effort to consolidate the model building codes. The combined committees developed and produced the 2000 edition of the International Building Code (IBC), and they stopped producing their own codes. By 2005, some form of the IBC has been adopted in at least 45 states in 23

## Page 30

the USA. The older model codes are now referred to as the ' 'legacy codes" and are still being .enforced in some portions of the United States that have not yet adopted a new code since 2000, The building code is generally the document that mandates what kind of fire protection system is required in a building, The building codes are often the original source for determining when a fire sprinkler system is required in the built environment. "Trade-ups" in the built environment (alternative Lilles for other fire protection features when sprinklers are installed in the building) may bé allowed when a fire sprinkler system is installed, The building codes recognize that a fire sprinkler system dramatically increases life safety in a building, So when an owner or architect installs fire sprinklers in a building, the building code allows them to build larger, taller buildings of different types of construction. The code committees understand that life safety is not compromised in larger, taller buildings when fire sprinkler systems are present, Another organization that creates model codes is the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). The NFPA is an international nonprofit organization with more than 75,000 members from around the world and at least 80 national trade and professional organizations. The NFPA's stated mission is "to reduce the worldwide burden of fire and other hazards on the quality of life by providing and advocating scientifically-based consensus codes and standards, research, training and education." See Chapter 1 of this text for more infomation on the founding of the NFPA and the role that fire sprinklers played in helping to form this organization. For more than 50 years, the NFPA has written the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101). This document is not a building code and does not have requirements for structural loads. The Life Safety Code actually started out as the Building Exits Code and focused on safe egress systems for buildings, making sure that everyone that was in a building could get out safely in case of fire or other emergency. Over the years, requirements for other life safety systems were added to the Building Exits Code and its name was changed to the Life Safety Code, Although the Life Safety Code is not a building code, it is used by many jurisdictions as a basis for writing their own building code or it is incorporated into a fire prevention code. Federal govemment agencies have adopted the Life Safety Code as a minimum level of performance for buildings. The General Services Administration (GSA) asks that office buildings that are purchased or leased for federal employees meet the Life Safety Code. And the federal agency responsible for Medicare and Medicaid requires that hospitals and health-care facilities that want to be reimbursed by these programs must comply with the Life Safety Code, At the beginning of the 218t century, the NFPA decided that they wanted to include a building code in their set of codes and standards. Using the Life Safety Code as a base, and then adding the other necessary structural and other issues that a building code has to cover, the NFPA created NFPA 5000, the Building Construction and Safety Code. The first edition of NFPA 5000 was published in 2003 and an update was published in 2006, Since the Life Safety Code is still used by many agencies and jurisdictions, the decision was made to continue to produce the Life Safety Code in addition to NFPA 5000. 24

The NFPA Standards As stated earlier, standards generally tell us how to fulfill the requirements mandated by the Codes. The standards most often used in the fire sprinkler industry are created and published by the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). The following NFPA Standards are used frequently in the work you will be doing as a layout technician: NFPA 13, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems NFPA 13D, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systerns in One- and Two- Family Dwellings and Manufactured Homes NFPA 13R, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems in Residential Occupancies up to and Including Four Stories in Height NFPA 14, Standard for the Installation of Standpipe and Hose Systems NFPA 15, Standard for Water Spray Fixed Systems for Fire Protection NFPA 16, Standard for the Installation. of Foam-Water Sprinkler and Foam-Water Spray Systems NFPA 20, Standard for the Installation of Stationary Pumps for Fire Protection NFPA 25, Standard for the Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Water-Bajed Fire Protection Systems The codes and standards produced by the NFPA are "consensus based", meaning that many affected stakeholders with different opinions, ideas and interests work together to create the best set of standards that will apply to everyone. A code or standard must be consensus based if it is to receive approval from the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). All of the NFPA codes and standards meet the criteria to be ANSI standards. The NFPA has a long history of bringing various interests together to establish the best possible installation rules. The Standards Making Process Currently, hundreds of committees made up of roughly 6,000 NFPA members have been established to write documents on specific areas of fire protection. It all begins with the NFPA Board of Directors that appoints the thirteen members of the NFPA Standards Council. The Standards Council oversees the process and appoints the individual members of the Technical Committees (TC's). The TC's are the basic groups that get the major work done in writing the codes, standards, recommended practices and guides, Where multiple committees work on the same document, or where multiple documents need to be coordinated so that there are minimal conflicts, the TC' s report to a Technical Correlating 25

## Page 32

Committees (TCC) that works to keep the document(s) consistent. TC's and TCC's often fonn ta•sk groups to investigate and address specific issues relevant to their scope of work. The maximum number of people that are appointed to an NFPA committee is 30. There are a few situations where the NFPA has permitted a committee to exceed 30 members, but these are rare situations where all of the people on a committee are interested (and affected) parties to a document, but a group can make a case that their interests are not being served by a current committee member. In such rare cases, the NFPA might appoint additional member(s) to a committee to make sure that all interested parties have some form of representation. Each member is also allowed to have an alternat% making the total possible committee roster 60 people plus a staff liaison. In order to make sure that no single interest group can take over a committee, the NFPA places each potential committee member into one of nine different interest categories, According to the NFPA regulations, each committee is not allowed to have any more than one-third of its members from any single interest category. Since it takes two- thirds of the committee to make a change to any document, this rule makes sure that no single group can force rules into the document. The interest categories are: e Consumer — the ultimate purchaser of a product that is also not considered a "User" as defined below. o Enforcer — for people that enforce the requirements of the document such as fire and building officials. o Installer/Maintainer — for people that work to put together or care for systems in the scope of the document. Insurance — for representatives of companies that provide insurance coverage for people or property.. o Labor a representative of the people performing work related to the scope of the document who, among other related factors, is concerned with safety in the workplace. o Manufacturer for producers of the products in the scope of the document. o Research and Testing — a representative of an independent laboratory or applied research organization that promulgates or enforces standards. o Special Expen — a person that does not meet any of the other categories in this list, but has »ecial expertise in the scope of the committee. • User — an entity subject to the provisions of the document, or who voluntarily decides to comply with the document. 26

The NFPA makes an attempt to get members from each interest group onto each committee responsible for writing documents. However, since the partieipatiön in the process is voluntary, and since it is difficult to find interested parties in each category, there are many committees that do not have every one of these interest groups covered. Still, each committee has a broad group of interests represented and no interest group has any more than a third of the membership of any given committee, In the rare occasion where a committee is out of balance due to a resignation by a member, the NFPA actively solicits membership applications from other interest groups to get the committee back in balance. In many cases, there are waiting lists or people wanting to get on committees that are full, so it is not difficult to take people off of the waiting list and get them on the committee. The NFPA has a formal process for revising existing documents on a regular time- table. For the creation of new documents, the process is the same, but there are extra steps in the beginning for the committee to create a draft version of the document and then start the process of revising the draft just like they would if they were revising an existing document. Each NFPA document is currently in a revision schedule every 3 years, 4 years or 5 years. NFPA 13, NFPA 13R, NFPA 13D and NFPA 24 are all in 3 year revision cycles, meaning that there will be a new standard every 3 years. The next edition of these standards will be the 2007 edition, and the next edition after that will be the 2010 edition, barring some unforeseen circumstance. The following is a summary of the revision process that each NFPA document goes through: 1, The committee makes a call for proposals to change the document. Anyone can submit a proposal. Every NFPA standard has a form that you can use to submit a proposal. You do not need to be a member of the NFPA to submit 27

## Page 34

a proposal, you only need to be able to explain what you would like to change and why you want to change it, 2. The Committee then acts Oli the proposals, While meeting to act on the proposals received from the public, the committee is allowed to create their own proposals as well. The committee must deal with every proposal that they receive before the proposal closing deadline. The committee has the following choices in dealing with each proposal: a. Accept the proposal — do exactly what the submitter asked with exactly the language proposed by the submitter, b. Accept the proposal in principle — do what the submitter asked, but rephrase the language or place the language in a different location than was proposed by the submitter. The committee must justify in an official statement why they made changes or moved the text to a different location. c. Accept the proposal in part — do some of what the submitter proposed, but not all of it. The portion that gets accepted goes into the standard in exactly the location proposed by the submitter and with exactly the same words proposed by the submitter. The committee is required to explain in an official statement why they did not accept the whole proposal, d. Accept the proposal in palt and in principle — do some of what the submitter proposed with revised language or revised location, but do not do the rest of the proposal. Once again, the committee must explain in an official statement why they revised or moved the text as well as why they did not make some of the changes requested by the submitter. e. Reject the proposal — Do not do make any changes to the standard on this subject. The con•mittee is required to explain in an official statement why they did not make any of the changes proposed by the submitter. 3. The committee generally meets (face-to-face) to establish the actions as described above for each proposal, but these meetings are not the official position of the committee, After the meeting, the actions of the committee are submitted to an official letter ballot of each member. In order for an action be approved, it must have at least two-thirds of the voting members agree with the action, Once the committee has voted, the NFPA compiles all of the actions on the proposals into a single book called the ' 'Report on Proposals", also known as the ROP. 4. The ROP is published and distributed by the NFPA. In the written form, it is available from the NFPA for free. In an electronic form, it can be 28

downloaded by any member of the public from the NFPA website (www.nfpa.org) for free. The public usually has several months to review the ROP. 5. Ifthe comment deals with a subject that was not included in the ROP, it will be considered out of order and would only be appropriate to be considered in the next cycle of the document. 6. The Conunittee must take action on each public comment. The committee is also permitted to develop its own comments. The Hold for Further Study action is treated the same as a "Reject", but is automatically slated for discussion as a new proposal in the next cycle of the document without the submitter needing to resubmit. 7. The committee actions are then submitted to a formal letter ballot. At least two-thirds of the voting members are required to agree with an action in order for it to pass. 8. document as voted on by the membership, or send the document back to the responsible committee for further processing. Once the Standards Council issues a document, it becomes part of the NFPA set of Codes, Standards, Recommended Practices and Guides that are collectively known as the NFPA Fire Codes. 13. Decisions of the NFPA Standards Council can be appealed to the NFPA Board of Directors, This is very rare, but occasionally there are some parties that feel that they want this extra level of review and oversight over the Standards Council. Using the International Building Code The Codes and Standards are the most often used "Rules Governing Installation". It is important that the technician be familiar with the location and contents of the vast amount of combined knowledge found within these documents. When the A&E Team (Architect and Engineer) designs a building, they are governed first by the building code. As dis•cussed previously, the most frequently used building code in the United States is the International Building Code (IBC). It is within the building code that we find out if sprinklers will be required. The process usually stans with the architect or engineer establishing the use of the building. Chapter 3 of the IBC, "Use and Occupancy Classification", tells us how to classify buildings. Chapter 4, "Special Detailed Requirements Based on Use and Occupancy", covers special situations for certain occupancies or building features and does include some requirements for sprinkler protection. Chapter 5, "General Building Heights and Areas", contains the requirements for the maximum size of buildings and their maximum height. This chapter allows buildings to be larger or taller when sprinklers are installed. Chapters 6 "Types of Construction", 7 "Fire Resistance Rated Construction" and 8 "Interior Finishes", contain requirements for fire resistance ratings for portions of the building and sometimes permit reduction of the rating required when sprinklers are installed. All of these Chapters require a system in accordance with Section 903.3.1.1" be installed in the built environment. This is where we would find which NFPA standard will apply to the layout and installation of the sprinkler system. Chapter 9 of the IBC is titled "Fire Protection Systems" and the third section of that chapter (903) is titled, "Automatic Sprinkler Systems". While this is where the bulk of the sprinkler requirements are located, there are other sections of Chapter 9 that effect our work. For example, Section 907 is titled, "Standpipe Systems". Browsing through these chapters of the building code is a great "first step". However, if you are going to be a productive layout technician, you will have to read through these chapters in-depth to understand the requirements and allowances. 30

## Page 37

Using NFPA 13 Knowing the layout of NFPA 13 can be extremely useful in finding a particular rule or requirement, While some people are frustrated by the size and complexity of the document, it is not too difficult to find a specific requirement if you just take a moment and consider the layout of the standard. The committees responsible for writing NFPA 13 have tried to take the approach that you generally move du•ough the document from beginning to end, starting with the basic information and moving to the more specific requirements. The first four chapters of NFPA 13 are the same as every NFPA document, with Administration, Referenced Publications, Definitions and General Requirements. From there, the standard moves on to identifying the hazard (Chapter 5), understanding the limitations of components and knowing the rules for installing the system (Chapters 6-10), After that, the rules continue for determining the Discharge Requirements (Chapters 11, 12 and 13), pelfonning the Hydraulic Calculations to compare to the Water Supply (Chapters 14 and 15), Finally, the document is concerned with conducting the Acceptance Test (Chapter 16). A chapter that was tacked on to the end of NFPA 13 a few years ago was Chapter 17 for Marine Systems. This chapter was originally part of the U.S. Coast Guard rules and was published under the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The public that needed these rules had a hard time finding the correct CFR regulations and had a difficult time convincing the Coast Guard (and the U.S. Congress) each time they wanted to make minor changes. Under an agreement between the NFPA and the Coast Guard, the NFPA added this extra chapter to NFPA 13 and the Coast Guard agreed to enforce NFPA 13 instead of their own CFR. The absolute last Chapter in NFPA 13 is a simple statement to inspect, test and maintain the sprinkler system after it is installed in accordance with NFPA 25. The chapters of NFPA 13 are as follows: Chapter I -- Administration Chapter 2 - Referenced Publications Chapter 3 -- Definitions Chapter 4 - General Requirements Chapter 5 - Classification of Occupancies and Commodities Chapter 6 System Components and Hardware Chapter 7 System Requirements Chapter 8 Installation Requirements Chapter 9 - Hanging, Bracing, and Restraint of System Piping Chapter IO - Underground Piping Chapter 11 - Design Approaches Chapter 12 - Storage Chapter 13 - Special Occupancy Requirements Chapter 14 Plans and Calculations Chapter 15 Water Supplies Chapter 16 - System Acceptance Chapter 17 - Marine Systems Chapter 18 System Inspection, Testing, and Maintenance Annexes - Explanatory Material, Miscellaneous Topics, Test Data, Info from NFPA 101 31

If you know the Chapter titles, it is easier to find information. This is an important point that many experienced designers have overlooked. You will notice that many of the people in the office where you work tum immediately to the index to find references for the information they need. However, if you take the time to learn how the chapters are organized, you will find everything you need quickly and easily. As an example, some of the rules governing installation concern the types of pipe that may be used. Where might we find his information in NFPA 13? If you look at the table of contents in NFPA 13, or the chapters listed above, you can see that Chapter 6 is titled, "System Components and Hardware". This is the quickest indication of where you may find the requirements for the materials used in fire sprinkler systems. There are also specific mles for spacing and positioning sprinklers in NFPA 13. Most of the rules for sprinkler locations are found in Chapter 8. But, there is a bit more to know than that. Beginning with section 8,5, the chapter is organized with sections based on the type of sprinkler being used. Chapter 8.5 is titled, "Position, Location, Spacing, and Use of Sprinklers". This section applies to all types of sprinklers except as modified in the sections that immediately follow. Sections 8.6 du•ough 8,12 address specific types of sprinklers as listed below: 8.6 Standard Pendent and Upright Spray Sprinklers. 8.7 Sidewall Standard Spray Sprinklers. 8.8 Extended Coverage Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinklers. 8.9 Extended Coverage Sidewall Spray Sprinklers. 0 8.10 Residential Sprinklers. 0 8.11 Large Drop Sprinklers in All Applications and Other Specific Application Sprinklers Used for Storage Protection. 8.12 Early Suppression Fast-Response Sprinklers. These sections are all written in a similar format. The first subsection is titled ' 'General". The second subsection is titled "Protection Areas per Sprinkler", For all of sections 8.5 through 8.12, the pattern is the same. The following example illustrates this pattern. If we needed to find the maximum allowable distance between Standard Pendent and Upright Spray Sprinklers we would start by looking in the section for these type sprinklers (8.6), where we would find that the title for 8.6.3.1 is "Maximum distance between sprinklers". Therefore, it would be reasonable to expect that the subsection for each type of sprinkler would always be the portion of the chapter that deals with maximum allowable distance between sprinklers, And so it follows that we know the "Maximum distance between sprinklers" for Extended Coverage Sidewall Spray Sprinklers will be found in chapter 8,9.3.1. 32

Local Authorities There are many different kinds of local authorities that may be an AHJ on a project that you are involved with. One of the first steps on any project is to find out which governmental authority has jurisdiction over the project. You will need to know if the project is required to comply with the lilles of a local jurisdiction, state or federal entity. The local jurisdiction rules could come from one or more of the following: village, township, city, or county govemment. Some projects are subject to more than one of these authorities at a time. In that case, the more stringent requirements will always apply. At the local level, you may have to submit your plans to a building code department, fire department, fire prevention bureau or fire marshal's office. At the state level you may have to submit plans to a state building department, fire marshal's office, public health department, or a public school department. At the federal level, you may be required to submit plans to the Army Corps of Engineers, the Naval Facilities Division (NAVFAC), the General Services Administration (GSA), or the Department of Health and Human Services. Nearly every level of authority we have discussed will require that you use the NFPA Standards when laying out a fire sprinkler system. However, many of these authorities have modified some of the NFPA requirements. At the end of this Chapter, we have included some samples of tules from these authorities that modify the NFPA Standards, Why would they amend the requirements of the NFPA documents? Each local authority has special considerations when it comes to protecting life and property in their jurisdiction. It will take some time to learn the various requirements of the local authorities where you will be submitting plans. This is one of the things your mentor or other designers in the office will be able to help you understand. When your office does work in a new location for the first time, you should contact the local authorities to ensure•that you will meet any criteria they have for projects under their jurisdiction. The same can be said for any complex systems you may find yourself involved in. Always contact the local authority to ensure you meet any special requirements they might have. Insuring Authorities There are a few insuring Authorities that will require you to submit your plans to them as• well. Some of the insuring companies that will review your plans include: Swiss Re (the old Industrial Risk Insurers), Factory Mutual, Kemper Insurance, and Liberty Mutual Insurance. All of these authorities will have some requirements that will vary from the NFPA Standards, Some have even published their changes to NFPA Standards as "interpretive guides". As an example, Factory Mutual publishes Data Sheet 2-8N that is a complete version of NFPA 13 with their modified requirements highlighted throughout the document. This helps to know which modified rules will apply to your projects. Insurers also employ engineers to evaluate the specific risks involved on a project and make 33

## Page 40

recommendations on how best to protect the project, You should receive documentation from the building owner that has the insuring company's requirements for your project. You should always contact the engineer responsible for the account to discuss any additional requirements for your project. For most insurance companies, you will need to provide the project account number to discuss the project with them, Product Standards and Approvals For any given type of material used in a fire sprinkler system, there are many documents indicating how they are to be tested for listing, used, and manufactured. There are several laboratories that provide a "listing" for a product. The two most widely used in the fire protection industry are Underwriter's Laboratories (UL) and Factory Mutual (FM). Standards and manufacturing specifications are also produced by ASTM, ANSI, and ASME Architects and Engineers often refer to these standards when specifying which materials may be used on a project. NFPA 13 also references these standards to determine what •materials are appropriate for 'use on sprinkler systems, In order for a device to be considered as "listed" it needs to be tested by a laboratory approved by the Authority Having Jurisdiction, The laboratory not only needs to test one of the devices, but it needs to follow up with tests of the quality control in the factory where the objects are produced in order to make sure that each device is made to the same specifications as •the device that was tested originally. Factory Mutual tends to use the term "approved" to refer to the devices that they will pennit to be installed on systems for customers that they insure. Because of the procedure that Factory Mutual uses to conduct their decision for approval, most AHJ's agree that the Factory Mutual "approval" meets the NFPA definition of "listed". Project Specifications Nearly every project you work on will have a set of criteria specifying the rules for you to follow when detailing the fire sprinkler system. The A&E Team (Architect and Engineer) try very hard to develop a precise document that will specify the way a built environment is to be created. These criteria are compiled in the documents known as the "Project Specifications". They have requirements that are specific to a given project and are often more stringent than the requirements of the Codes and Standards, You will be able to recall the requirements of a project specification by memory as you grow in your career. This is likely the first document you will read as you begin a new project, We will continue this discussion about project specifications in more detail in the next chapter. 34

CHAPTER 5 CONSTRUCTION SPECIFICATIONS When we think of construction specifications (specs) we generally move right to the technical requirements that govern the materials we use and the methods of installation that are mandated by architects and engineers. In reality, the specifications cover much more than that. This section will provide a general overview of what construction specifications include, who prepares them, and what are the various types we might see in the normal course of business. What is Included Let's look at what we might find in the "spec" book for a typical project, First we might find the actual contract in the book, but most often the contract document itself will be separate. See Chapter 6 of this textbook for more information on Contracts. The specifications do include sections called General Conditions and Special Conditions that are the administrative guidelines on how the contract will be performed and interpreted. These sections spell out details such as how many copies of submittals and drawings need to be made and the format such as hard copies or reproducible transparencies or disks. They will describe procedures for settling disputes and who has the final authority on the job. They may also describe priority of the documents. An example would be a statement that says details take precedence over small-scale drawings and specification descriptions take precedence over drawings if there is a conflict between the two. In essence these sections govern the conduct of the job, set reporting responsibilities and the procedures that tell how the various parties to the contract relate to each other. The General Conditions also describe requisition and pay procedures and insurance requirements. In essence these sections cover your rights, responsibilities, and, in the Special Conditions, any modifications to the General Conditions that are specific to the project. The Technical Specifications are what the FP Engineering Technician will use the most. This section contains the formal, detailed description of the work. It includes a definition of all materials to be used, as well as, any particular methods of installation. This is where the quality of the finished product is established. When it gets down to specifying any particular item, there are two types of specifications: Open and Closed. 37

## Page 44

Types of Specifications Open specifications are general in nature, and act as guidelines that give the contractor flexibility and choices. Items might be specified as to size, finish, function, and several brand names might be given as well as an ending statement, "or approved equal". For instance the specifications might be as general as saying sprinklers shall be spray pendent, chrome plated, temperature rating of 165 OF, and then give several manufacturers. Another example would be that, "a wet pipe sprinkler system is to be installed throughout in accordance with NFPA 13 — 2002". The requirement for the contractor is to provide an approved system using the kinds of materials listed and referred to. Closed specifications also establish the quality of the finished product. However, when it gets down to specifying any particular item there will be only one choice, the exact product that is in the specs. There are no substitutions allowed. The Architect and Engineer, by law, in every state, have the absolute right to determine what they want installed, and the qontractor must install them, as long as their use is in accordance with applicable codes and the materials are available. There are ways to negotiate for the use of non-specified material, but that is not for this course. Let's look at the examples cited in the previous paragraph and see how they would differ: the spec for the sprinkler might read, "Sprinkler heads shall be spray pendent, chrome plated, temperature rating of 165 OF, recessed model XXX, manufactured by ABC Sprinkler Company." The system example would be that, "a wet pipe sprinkler system is to be installed throughout in accordance with NFPA 13 — 2002" and Factory Mutual standard 8-2N. All piping shall be schedule 40 with threaded ends for 2" and smaller, and schedule 40 with cut groove ends for 2 h" and larger". The requirement for the contractor is to bid and provide exactly what is written in the specification, Who Prepares Specifications In most instances, specifications will be prepared by a Design Professional. By definition a Design Professional is a person or organization qualified by education, experience, and licensure to make design and engineering judgments. They determine level of protection and administer the design, are responsible for construction oversight of the entire project, and render decisions on conflicts that arise during the course of the work. These people may be from a small, one-man firm or part of a large organization. The specifications may be developed for the specific project or come from the organizations "library of standard specs". In some instances the professional may have limited knowledge of the trade and will rely on the contractor's expertise to get the job done, It must be remembered that setting the level of hazard and protection requirement is a registered engineer's job. Most codes require the design professional to be the responsible party, The contractor's job is to make sure that all specified work is in compliance with NFPA and other AHJ requirements and confonn to the local code. In that respect the contractor ftnctions as a check of the professional. 38
