CSI Master specs Specifications for construction of an entire building can be huge documents with hundreds of thousands of pieces of infonnation. Without some organization, the specifications would be impossible to read because individual contractors responsible for different parts of the work would not be able to find the specifications that apply to the work that they need to do. The Construction Specification Institute (CSI) writes a Master Specification document to standardize how the specifications are organized. Different subjects are placed in "Divisions" that are like chapters in a book. As long as the architects and engineers that write specifications follow the Master Format} the subjects .that a sprinkler contractor needs to know will always be found in the same Division. Within each division, there are subdivisions that cover specific topics within the subject, The CSI Master Format that many architects and engineers are using was written in 1997. The different divisions are as follows: Division 1 General Division 2 - Site Work Division 3 Concrete Division 4 - Masonry Division 5 - Metals Division 6 - Wood and Plastic Division 7 - Themal & Moisture Protect. Division 8 - Doors & Windows Division 9 - Finishes Division 10 - Specialties Division 11 - Equipment Division 12 - Furnishings Division 13 Special Construction Division 14 - Conveying Systems Division 15 Mechanical Division 16 - Electrical 39

## Page 46

In the list of Divisions on the previous page, Division 13 — Special Construction is in bold type because this is where fire sprinkler system specifications are supposed to be found. Many architects and engineers end up putting fire sprinkler system information in Diviéion 15 — Mechanical Systems because they feel that the sprinkler system is just another mechanical system in the building. But fire sprinkler systems are not just another mechanical system. They need to be integrated with other fire protection equipment. Fire sprinkler system specifications were specifically moved out of Division 15 and into Division 13 in the 1997 Master Format. But Division 13 is not the only place that sprinkler system contractors need to look for specification information, Other features in the building need to be coordinated with the sprinkler system. The contractor will also need to understand the general construction schedule, which can be better understood by reading all of the specifications. The following is a list of the other specifications that will contain important information for the sprinkler contractor: Division 2 - Trench Work Division 3 - Valves & Pits Division 4 - Dry Valve Enclosures Division 9 - Painting Division 15 - Mechanical Division 16 - Air Compressors, Pump Controllers The CSI re-wrote the Master Format in 2004 and spread out the subjects into 49 different divisions, with some of them being reserved for different types of systems that are not yet common enough to warrant their own division yet. A list of the new divisions is included in Figure 5-1 on the next page, Fire sprinkler systems are now in their own division, Division 21 along with other fire suppression systems. Even though this new Master Format was released by the CSI in 2004, it has not yet met with widespread acceptance from the architect and engineering community. With fire suppression systems having their own Division, the fire sprinkler industry is better positioned to have more complete and easier to find specifications. We continue to encourage architects and engineers to upgrade their specification wfiting to use the new Master Format, 40

CHAPTER 6 CONTRACTS Before discussing the concepts •of a contract, we first must discuss the people involved in entering into contracts and the methods they use for managing the project of constructing a building and/or putting a sprinkler system into a building Most building owners will begin a construction project by hiring a design professional, We will define a design professional as, "A person qualified by education, experiences and licensure to make design and engineering judgments." The function of the design professional is to: Determine level of protection and administer the design Act as the ownerls representative Conduct invitation to bid Receive bids Award contracts Responsible for construction oversight of entire project Render decisions on conflicts that arise during the course of the work There are a number of different types of organizations that can provide these design professional capabilities. These include architectural firms, engineering firms, combination architecture/engineering firms, and general contractors. Architectural firms provide fom and substance to the construction project. Often, the smaller firms limit their practice to specific occupancies such as churches or schools. As the need arises, they may hire additional engineers or architects to complete the project design work. There are generally two different types of engineering firms. The large firms are sometimes known as General Consultants and usually have total in-house capabilities to provide structural, electrical, sanitary, mechanical and fire protection design services all using employees of the firm. Smaller firms are generally specialists, limiting their practice to one of the major disciplines. These firmy act as consultants to architects and other design professionals. 43

## Page 50

Combined architectural/engineering (A&E) firms tend to be the larger organizations with full in-house capabilities. With a full staff of professionals that are skilled in almost every aspect of the design process, these firms can generally handle all of the responsibilities of the design professional. However, these firms will occasionally hire specialists to handle specific poltions of the design process for an unusual situation where the specific expertise necessary is not contained in-house. Contractors can also perfonn the responsibilities of the design professional. These contractors have licensed engineers or architects on their staff that are needed when the permit process requires a Professional Engineer's seal. The engineers on staff will review and supervise all of the in-house work. In the larger firms, there are sufficient engineers with enough experience in varied subjects to provide in-house design capabilities. Obtaining and Managing the Project The design professional can help the building owner make decisions regarding which installer that they will use for different portions of the construction. In general, a building owner, with the design professional, will let potential installers know about the project by extending an offer for the installer to present a bid on how they would complete the services requested and how much they would ask for in compensation. These bid offers can be either "open" or "closed". Most bid situations are competitive, meaning that more than one installing contractor will be trying to secure the work. "Open bids" are general announcements made in public publications allowing any contractor to submit a bid. Open bids can be placed in advertising sections of local newspapers or in special publications specific to the construction industry. Open bids are common for government contracts where the public's money is being spent in order to make sure that there is no impropriety in dealing with public funds. Often, open bids will include minimum requirements that the bidding firm will have to meet in order to be awarded the bid. It is the responsibility of the bidding contractor to respond to the bid with sufficient detail to make sure the owner understands that they meet the requirements of the bid. "Closed bids" are those that only go to specific installing contractors that are hand picked by the owner or the owner's desigtl professional. Closed bids usually go to small number of contractors that the owner (or their design professional) is interested in having perform the work, Each of these contractors is usually known to the owner or their design professional, so there are usually less conditions that the contractor has to prove in a response to a bid. It is possible for an owner to request that a single contractor perform the work, rather than send out a closed bid to multiple contractors. These situations are generally not considered "closed bid" because there is no competition for the job. Instead, these solicitations are generally considered "single-source contracts" or "negotiated work." Most building owners will only consider asking a contractor to perform negotiated work if they have some son of relationship with the contractor. The relationship might be personal 44

## Page 51

knowledge of the individuals running the company, or it might be prior work experience with the contractor. In general, an owner only asks a contractor to perform negotiated work if they believe that they will get superior work performed rather than put the job out to bid. This kind of work is generally more expensive than putting a job out to bid, but the higher quality work is considered a reasonable trade-off. In the past, the typical process for constructing a building was for the design for most of the building structure and systems to be completed before construction begins. But increasingly, owners are ina huge hurry to get their building finished. To keep up with this trend of finishing buildings sooner, the concept of "fast tracking" has been established. In a fast track situation, consffuction proceeds along with the development of the drawings. As each trade's work is designed, bidding is accomplished and contracts are awarded. A variation of the fast track concept is the "design build" trend, Here, a firm will bid on the total building design and construction. These firms will usually be •the larger E&E firms that include construction capabilities or contractors that have A&E capabilities, If the firms are missing specific areas of expertise, they can engage others to work with them on the constluction. The owner of a building will usually need some help in managing the constmction project. There are a number of different methods that can be used for sending out the bids, receiving the bids and evaluating the bids in order to make a determination as to which contractor will be awarded the contract. While the owner will provide the funding for construction and be the ultimate decision maker, the owner will usually delegate many of the decisions regarding managing the bids in one of the following manners: Hire a General Contractor — This will be a person or firm involved in the construction for this panicular building that will subcontract work on the other portions of the project. The General Contractor will be responsible to the owner and will, for the subcontracted work, obtain the bids, award the contracts, coordinate the trades and settle any job disputes. Hire a Construction Manager This will usually be a person that is familiar with the consåuction process, but will not be involved in actually constructing this particular building. Instead, the Consttuction Manager assigns the trades their specific jobs, administer the documentation, enforce the coordination and make sure that the contracted trades understand their respective responsibilities. Elfre and Architect/Engineering Firm In this case, the A&E firm will act as the owner's agent, being the final interpreter of the intent of the documents, handling all bids and approving all work, 45

The Contract The contract is not actually a single document, but a series of documents that include the following parts: Agreement or Contract Plans and Addenda (dated and enumerated) Specifications: General Conditions Special Conditions Technical Specifications Shop Drawings Documents developed during the execution of the work A contract covering construction activities has a number of purposes including procedures for administering the relationship between the parties to the document. The document itself is commonly referred to as either the contract or the agreement. The first thing we need to do is to define what it is intended to do: The intent of a contract is to define the work to be performed and to assign responsibility for the execution of the work covered. The document also defines risk assumption. If you remember your high school English class, a good way to remember what a contract does is to think of it as a document that defines, "who, what, when, where and how work is to be performed. In essence, a Contract is an agreement between parties to perform services or provide products for a stipulated sum in accordance with agreed-to terms and conditions. Types of Contracts There are contracts commonly called Standard Form. These are preprinted documents that have been prepared by trade assöciations to cover a wide range of relationships. The most common standard fonns are those published by the American Institute of Architects (AIA). There are those that relate to the Owner and the General or Prime Contractor (AIA 101), and those that relate to the relationship between the General Contractor and the Subcontractor (AIA 401). The General and Special Conditions are covered in another standard form, AIA 201. Another organization, Associated General Contractors (AGC), also publishes a set of standard forms including AGC 640 and AGC 650/655, These were developed by AGC to provide better protection to the general contractor by causing liability to be shifted away from the GC. 46

## Page 53

In addition there are Proprietary Contracts, which are developed by individual companies. These tend to be one-sided in nature and again shift liability away from the company that developed the agreement, Care needs to be taken to examine how much risk is shifted to your company when executing AGC and proprietary agreements, Contents All items that are necessary to desclibe a party's responsibility are included in the contract, A number of them are included by reference. For instance, if the specifications are separately published, they would be referenced by title, date and reference number if appropriate. The contract drawings, •likewise, would be referenced by a drawing list and date of issue. The form of the contract amount would be included. Contract drawings are depictions of the construction sufficient for the bidding and decision making regarding the award of the bid. The drawings need to include: e Graphic representation of the work to be done o Graphically depict locations of HVAC, lighting, walls, structural, conveyors, piping systems, etc. May not be detailed enough for fabrication, assembly or erection o More detailed drawings will be needed for construction, these will be the shop drawings prepared by the contractor responsible for installing the particular system There are a number of ways that set the price of the work. The following outline some of the methods that are used to establish payment, but there are other variations. The common methods include: o Lump Sum — The contractor agrees to do all the specified work for a fixed price regardless of any errors of omission during the bid phase. e Time and Materials or Cost Plus — In this form the contractor submits invoices based on cost of materials and labor and an agreed percentage mark-up above all recognized costs. o Guaranteed Maximum — This is a variation of either Lump Sum or Cost Plus used when not all owners requirements are known when the contract begins. The contractor would analyze the projected completion and estimate how much more than the original sum would need to be added. o Fixed Fee— In another variation of Cost Plus; the contractor agrees to do the work for a fee that does not change regardless of the accumulation.of costs. 47

## Page 54

Some additional terms of interest are: Addendum - This is a supplemental document from the Architect or Engineer prior to the bid date, which can be corrections or modifications to drawings and specifications. Addendums may also be issued to extend bid dates or to modify Terms and Conditions Alternate These are used to create a Base Price with separate process for Substitutionsi Additions or Deletions to the base bid. An example would be to include a separate price for painting the sprinkler pipe or doing all wiring for i10 V service for the air compressor. Allowances These are basically Unit Prices for variations in design and/or specified quantities. An example would be The design professional's preliminary design specifies 400 sprinklers and the sprinkler contractor is required to give a price for sprinklers both under and over the 400 sprinklers specified, General Conditions and Special Conditions These are the administrative guidelines on how the contract will be performed and interpreted. These sections spell out details such as how many copies of submittals and drawings need to be made and the format such as hard copies or reproducible transparencies or disks. They will describe procedures for settling disputes and who has the final authority on the job. They may also describe priority of the documents. An example would be a statement that says details take precedence over small-scale drawings and specification descriptions take precedence over drawings if there is a conflict between the two. In essence these sections govem the conduct of the job, set reporting responsibilities and the procedures that tell how the various parties to the contract relate to each other. The General Conditions also describe requisition and pay procedures and insurance requirements. As stated in the beginning of this chapter a contract also defines the assumption of risk, This is most apparent in the sections of the contract dealing with Indemnification and Hold Harmless, These terms are usually found in the Insurance paragraph. As an example let's look at Indenmification. There are tlu•ee forms of this action which deal with the assignment of responsibility for property damage and personal injury should an accident or negligent action occur on a job. rlhe three forms are Limited, Intermediate and Broad. In as simple language as can be stated, in the Limited form, if an accident occurs the party responsible for the act that caused the damage will pay. In the intermediate form, even if there is shared responsibility, the subcontractor will pay. And in the Broad form it doesn't matter who caused the damage, even if wholly by the Prime Contractor, the subcontractor will pay just because he is on the job, As you can see, this clause can have a considerable effect on the conduct of a relationship. These risks are insurable, and most contractors have the insurance coverage, However, eventually, the cost of business is affected as insurance premiums are related to loss experience, In essence the General and Special Conditions sections cover your rights, responsibilities and establish a risk bearing relationship. The Special Conditions contain any modifications to the General Conditions that are specific to the project. 48

CHAPTER 7 BASIC MATHEMATICS FOR SPRINKLER SYSTEMS Mathematics is an essential foundation to the layout and detailing of a fire sprinkler system. This chapter will review the basic concepts of algebra, geometry, trigonometry and exponents. There is no way that every mathematical concept necessary for the fire sprinkler industry can be covered in this one chapter. Instead, this chapter will be a summary of the basic concepts. Additional information can be found in any high school algebra and geometry textbook. Notation Expression of numbers assists in the communication of concepts. Fractions versus decimals or percentages can vary the ease of comprehension on the end user. The desired notation may also vary with the use of the number, For example, details on plans may indicate a 3/8-inch rod being used for a hanger. If this information was presented as 0.375 inches it may slow the understanding even though % is equal to 0.375 the notation customarily used is the fraction, and consistency promotes ease of comprehension. With the increased use of computers for the layout of sprinkler systems, decimals are most commonly used as input although fractions may be used in dimensions or material notations. Therefore, it becomes important to know how to conven from one to the other. In order to convert a fraction to a decimal, the denominator or value below the fraction bar gets divided into the numerator or number above the fraction bar. For example: Example #1: 5 — is 16)3 which is 0.3125 16 To reverse the process, the number following the decimal would be used as the numerator and the place of the last decimal would determine the denominator. Once a fraction is created, it can then be reduced by common factors. In other words, if the top and bottom are divisible by the same number, it can be factored out. Here is an example: 51

For example, if a dry system requires a 30% design area increase on a base value of 1500 fc2, then 1500 needs to be multiplied by 1.30 (representing 130%) to alTive at 1950 fc2. For scenarios where there are very large or very small numbers, scientific notation can be used. This is where one number is prior to the decimal and 2 to 4 digits follow it on average. The number of decimal places that the decimal point is moved are counted and used as an' exponent for the factor of 10. Negative exponents are used when the decimal is moved to the right and positive exponents are used when the decimal is moved to the left. This concept is more clearly understood using an example: Example : 0.000325 is 3.25 x 104 3,025,000 is 3.025K106 In general, it is good to be flexible with the notations used and learn how to convert from one to another. It is also important to recognize and become familiar with which notations will help move the job along the quickest. Metrication The metric system is used globally. Even the United States declared it the preferred system of measurement in 1988. The construction industry, however, tends to remain using the traditional English units (also known as the ft-pound units). Interestingly, the federal government has declared that plans for all federal jobs are expected to be in metric. Metric is also referred to as SI units or the International System of Units. It is a decimal based system of measurement, which makes it simpler than the English units to use measurements. Lengths, for example, are based on meters (m), When items require smaller measurements, millimeters (mm) or centimeters (cm) are used. When items require larger measurements, decameters (dm) or kilometers (km) are used. In order to convert from one length to another factors of 10 are used, which allows the units to be changed by moving the decimal point. For example, 10 meters is equal to 0.010 kilometers or 10,000 millimeters. The sprinlder industry more commonly uses the English system of measurement, so it becomes necessary to convert from metric to English or vice-versa. There are two forms to do this, one is "hard metrication" and the other is "soft metrication". Hard metrication is where the metric values used are rounded to the nearest metric unit. Examples would be making rooms 5m x 5m x 3m high instead of 16 ft x 16 ft x 10 ft or spacing sprinklers 3m x 3m instead of 10 ft x 10 ft. Soft metrication is found by taking the English units and multiplying by appropriate conversions. 52

As more buildings and systems are done in metric, it will become more common to use hard metrication where the values are rounded. CHAPTER 9 PRINCIPLES OF COMBUSTION AND FUNDAMENTALS OF EXTINGUISHMENT Principles of Combustion Combustion is the process that a product goes üu•ough when it burns, By exact definition it is either "the process of burning" or ' 'a chemical change, especially oxidation, accompanied by the production of heat and light." [1] The concept is tillly the study of fire and how it burns and grows. This information is of great value as it is necessary to understand the animal before you can control it, To begin, it is important to review its basic characteristics. Then many agents will be reviewed that can be used to either control or suppress the fire. Fire, itself, is a rapid exothermic oxidation reaction. This means that it is fast growing, gives off heat and uses oxygen to chemically decompose fuel. The speed of a fire is often overlooked thanks to the many myths created by movies and television where the amount of smoke, visibility and fire growth are rarely shown in an accurate fashion. Also, the heat that is produced by the fire will vary depending on the fuel that is burning. The definition above leads to the conclusion that fuel, heat, and oxygen are necessary in order to have a fire. In addition, there is a chain reaction that occurs chemically with the combination of an ion comprised of oxygen and hydrogen (OH). This is chemical combination, which can occur from the negatively charged ion, such as 01-1-, bonding with the fuel as it breaks down during combustion. Examining the combustion process should include a review of the states of matter. There are three states of matter as follows: o Solids Liquids o Gasses Objects can move from one state to another under different heat and pressure situations. (For a more in-depth review, see Chapter 8 of this text, Physical Science,) Even though there are three states of matter, it is important to know that solids and liquids do not burn. Only gasses 73

## Page 80

burn! This might sound like an outrageous statement. You may even think of flammable liquids and solids that you think will burn. For example, wood is a solid and fuel oil is a liquid, and these products are generally considered "combustible". So how can we make the statement that only gasses can burn? The answer is that the solids and liquids need to go through a physical change to a gas before they can bum. Wood, oil and other combustible materials are those materials that easily make the transition from a solid or liquid to a gas when heat is nearby. During the fire process, chemical decomposition of solids and liquids occurs through the application of heat. This is called "pyrolysis", although it is sometimes also known as "gasification". These gasses then combine witli oxygen and give off heat as a by-product of the fire. A case where pyrolysis can be visualized is with a candle flame as shown in Figure 9-1. When a candle is first lit, the wax has to melt and pyrolyze. Once there are sufficient gasses to hold the flame, the heat produced by that flame continues the process. The wick of the candle gives the flame a location to attach to. Heat from the flame travels back to the wax via electromagnetic waves pyrolyzing the wax, allowing the wax fumes to mix the oxygen in the air, and permitting combustion. The flame from this combustion travels back to the wax and continues the cycle of combustion. Figure 9-1: Candleflame demonstrating pyrolysis Heat is created by many sources. Since heat is one of the key elements needed to have a fire, it will be valuable to know where heat originates in order to control a fire, or prevent a fire from occurring. The sources of heat include chemical, mechanical, electrical and nuclear. Chemical heat energy can come from common fuel sources such as oil, wood and even food. The heat energy is released when a reaction occurs between chemicals that get mixed, or when a chemical spontaneously breaks down due to some instability. Mechanical heat energy can be created by the friction of objects rubbing against one another. For example, if you rub your hands together for a minute, the warmth can be readily felt. This is heat produced from the friction between the skin on your hands as you rub them together. The old story of Boy Scouts starting a fire by rubbing two sticks together is a true story. Although it takes some time, and the sticks have to be moving very quickly, it is possible 74

## Page 81

to generate sufficient heat to start a fire by rubbing two sticks together and creating mechanical energy. Electrical heat energy sources include electricity and lighting. Heat is created by the movement of electrons around an electrical circuit. When the circuit gets broken, the electron flow stops. But if a person or an object touches the open electrical circuit, they allow the flow of electrons to continue and potentially allow sufficient heat to start a fire. Finally, nuclear energy heat sources include both fission and fusion, thc splitting or combining of atoms on a molecular level. Nuclear power plants take advantage of the energy released by radioactive substances in order to generate electricity. The ultimate example of fire created by nuclear heat is the nuclear bomb. Once sources of heat energy are established, the next step is to examine how the heat moves beyond its area of origin. There are three methods of heat transfer, all of which are important to understand because fire does not grow and cause problems without some form of heat transfer. The three methods of heat transfer are: Conduction Convection Radiation Conduction is the transfer of heat through bodies that are in contact with each other. An example of this is hot coffee in a mug. The exterior of the mug is not the same temperature as the coffee but warmth, or some of the heat from the coffee is transferred dlrough the ceramic. The heat is carried from one molecule to the next of any material in contact with the hot substance, continually warming cooler areas. In a fire, heat is often conducted through a wall or ceiling. The fire heats up the wall and ceiling in the room of the fire's origin. This heat moves (conducts) through the wall and warn-is up the surface of the wall in the next room over and the floor of the next room above the fire. If this heat increases sufficiently in•the rooms adjacent to the fire, objects in the room begin to undergo pyrolysis and the fire can spread to these rooms without physically burning through the wall or ceiling. Convection is the transfer of heat through the air. Air movement is a continuous part of a growing fire. As hot gases rise they come in contact with cooler neighboring air and the contact warms the cooler air. Heat is always transferred from the hotter to the colder air, fluid or object. Similar to conduction the transfer is from one molecule to the next, but instead of a solid material, the heat transfer is through the fluid air. A fire gives off many hot gasses as it bums. This makes convection the chief method of heat transfer for a fire. It is a physical fact that hot gasses rise above cooler gasses (called the buoyancy principle). During a fire, the convection heat transfer occurs mostly above the fire. The fire plume (hot gasses from the fire) only moves approximately 20% horizontally for every 100% that it moves up. This means that a fire occurring on the floor of a room that is 10 ft high to the ceiling will have hot gasses extended out about 2 ft from the side of the fire when the hot gasses hit the ceiling, 75

## Page 82

Radiation is the third component of heat transfer. This method is the same as the sun warming the earth. By definition, radiation is "emission and propagation of energy in the form of rays or waves" [1]. The flames of the fire provide the radiation to heat other parts of the room/space. The waves can transmit heat to any object within direct view of the flames. When you stmt a fire in your fireplace, the wannth that you feel standing in front of the fireplace is from radiation. As explained in the previous paragraph, most of the heat from the fire is going up the chimney as convection. Recognizing that much of the heat is being lost, some chimney builders have started to include heat exchanger fans that capture some of the wannth going up the chimney as convective heat transfer and blow that heat back into the room. Assuming that you do not have one of these heat exchangers, the only heat you get in the room from a fireplace is dirough radiation. Radiation is not a very efficient mechanism for heat transfer. The effect of radiation diminishes exponentially as the object gets farther away from the heat source. Fire growth can occur in a space due to any or all of the three methods of heat transfer. Consider a fire in a compartment. As the fire grows, the temperature in the compartment rises. When the temperature in the compartment has risen to the point where all the possible fuels are at or above their ignition temperatures (undergoing pyrolysis and giving off enough vapors to support combustion) the fire spreads to every surface in the compartment. Once the fire reaches this stage, the amount of burning is completely controlled by the amount of oxygen that can get into Lhe room. The instant that everything in the room is pyrolyzing and giving off enough gasses to support combustion, and everything starts to burn, is called "flashover". Once flashover has occurred, the fire will only burn as it gets oxygen into the room, so we call this kind of fire a "ventilation controlled fire". Flashover is a very serious event that kills people every year. The goal of fire sprinklers is to make sure that flashover does not occur in sprinklered rooms. In order to understand flashover better fire tests are conducted in rooms without fire sprinklers, and in rooms with fire sprinklers. When conducting these fire tests, a ball of newspaper is usually set on the floor. As the fire grows in the room, it pyrolyzes the fuel in the room from the top down. The definition of the moment of flashover is usually the moment when the newspaper on the floor ignites. At this point in time, everything in the room from the top down is usually burning. Successful sprinkler tests do not allow the fire to get anywhere near the stage where pyrolysis of the majority of fuels in the room is occurring. Consider a cigarette fire started in a chair in a comfortable living room like the one shown in Figure 9-2. As the fire starts to burn, the hot gasses rise and are confined by the ceiling and walls of the compartment, With the passing of time, the fire continues to grow as convection heats up portions of the chair higher than the start of the fire, as conduction heats up portions of the chair in contact with the fire and as radiation heats up objects near the fire. The growing fire produces more hot gasses and a layer of smoke and hot gasses will begin to descend from the ceiling. As the layer of hot gasses comes down from the ceiling, radiation will begin to cause pyrolysis of all the objects in the room from the top down such as the lamp shade, the paintings on the wall and the entertainment center. Once these are giving off sufficient gasses to sustain combustion, the heat in the room will increase and the hot gasses will drop to the point where they are causing pyrolysis of the couch and carpet. Once these start to burn, flashover will occur. 76

They put these three elements together in a pictorial representation called the "Fire Triangle" as shown in Figure 9-3. Each leg of the Fire Triangle represented one of the elements necessary to sustain combustion. The theory went that if you removed any single leg of the Fire Triangle, the fire would go out. Heat Oxygen Fuel Figure 9-3 The Fire Triangle 77

## Page 84

The problem with the Fire Triangle is that when Halon (a family of gasses that extinguish fires) was invented, no one could completely explain how it extinguished the fire. It did not remove the fuel. It did not displace the oxygen (it extinguished fires in rooms where the concentration of oxygen should have been sufficient to allow combustion) and it did not cool the fuel. A new understanding of fire was necessary to completely explain the process of combustion. As previously mentioned in this paragraph, in addition to the fuel, heat, and oxygen necessary to sustain combustion, there is also the sustained chain reaction that is necessary for fire to exist. In order to represent these four elements in a single object where all of the elements touch each other, the Fire Tetrahedron was born. A tetrahedron is a three-dimensional object consisting of four faces with each face as a triangle (kind of a three sided pyramid). See Figure 9-4 for a picture of the Fire Tetrahedron in which the Chain Reaction and Fuel faces are visible in the picture, The Oxygen face is opposite of the camera and the Heat face is down on the floor. In order to put out any fire, remove any one of the four elements represented by a face of the tetrahedron: Fuel, Oxygen, Heat or the Chain Reaction. Figure 9-4 Fire tetrahedron depicting the four necessary elements to sustain afire Remove the Heat There are a few options in order to remove the heat from a fire. The first is to cool the flame. The next is to cool the fuel. Either option is generally accomplished by using a gaseous or liquid agent that is capable of absorbing heat. An excellent method of cooling either the flame or the fuel is to apply water, which is capable of absorbing huge amounts of heat as it goes from being a liquid to a gas, The most efficient mechanism for delivering water is to break the water up into droplets to increase the surface area of the water that is touching the hot material. This is the job of the sprinkler deflector on a sprinkler, to break up the stream of water into efficient water droplets to absorb the heat of the fire, cool the surface of the burning fuel, and to cool the surface of objects around the fire so that they do not start to pyrolyze. 78

## Page 85

Another way to remove the heat is to diffuse the heat source. Diffusing the heat source uses a material to conduct heat away from the fire. For example, placing a wire mesh over a fire source will dissipate the heat and put out the fire. These methods will reduce temperatures and eventually get the fuel below its ignition point stopping the fire. Remove the Oxygen The next method to look at for extinguishing a fire is depleting the oxygen source. One way to remove oxygen is to cover or smother the fuel. The fastest way to put out a fire in a pan on the stove is to cover Che pan with a tightly fitting lid. The fire will consume the oxygen under the lid and then go out because there will not be any more oxygen. Unfortunately, when the fire consumes the oxygen in this situation, it creates a vacuum, sealing the lid to the pan. You may never be able to separate the lid from the pan, but you put the fire out. Another method of smothering a fire is covering it with a noncombustible product like sand or baking soda. Figure 9-5 shows baking soda being poured on a grease fire to smother the flames. Figure 9-5 Baking soda being poured on a grease pan fire on a stove Another way to remove the oxygen is to add another gas to the air, which will displace the oxygen in the same room as the fire and reduce the oxygen concentration. It is important that the added gas be inelt so that it will not add to the fire hazard. Nitrogen and carbon dioxide are both éxamples of gases used in fire protection to displace the oxygen. Another gas commonly used in fire protection is called Inergen, which is a combination of nitrogen, argon and carbon dioxide, all inert gasses that will not burn and will displace the oxygen in a room. It should be noted that the use of carbon dioxide as an oxygen displacement mechanism is very hazardous to people. In order for the oxygen to be displaced by the carbon dioxide sufficiently to extinguish a fire, the oxygen content left in the room is so low that it cannot support human life. In other words, if you were in a room where a carbon dioxide fire extinguishing system went off, and you did not get out of the room immediately, you would literally drown in carbon dioxide. Over the years, several deaths have occurred during the accidental tripping of carbon dioxide fire protection systems, or during the testing of carbon dioxide systems. Carbon dioxide fire protection systems should only be used in spaces where there are not going to be any people, such as the underfloor portions of computer rooms where

## Page 86

fire might occur in the space reserved for cables, Even in such spaces, the computer room above should have a specific alann that wams people that the carbon dioxide system below has activated and that they should leave the room. NFPA 12, the standard for the design of carbon dioxide fire extinguishing systems allows these systems to be installed in rooms with people, however, in such cases, it requires a delay in activation of the carbon dioxide system and an alarm must sound during the delay. People in the room with the carbon dioxide system need to be lrained to know that when this alann sounds, they .must leave the room immediately. Typically, the alarm gives people about 60 seconds to exit before dumping the carbon dioxide into the room. Some building owners put oxygen masks in these rooms so that people have a better chance to escape. But given all of the other options available in this day and age, it does not seem to make sense to design a carbon dioxide system for a room that will have people in it. The extra cost for the equipment described above, plus the extra concerns about life safety, make this choice of systems undesirable when people are going to be in the space, Remove the Fuel The third way to stop a fire is to remove the fuel. An example of removing the fuel source would be to use a high pressure spray that would push the flame and fire off of the fuel. Another simple method is to shut off the fuel supply, such as closing a valve on a gas line. When you blow on a candle flame to put out the candle, you are really removing the fuel. Technically, you are blowing hard enough to move the flame away from the fuel. Without the flame being in close proximity to the fuel, heat does not travel back to pyrolyze the surface and sustain the combustion. In a large scale manner, this is how dynamite is used to put out oil well fires. During the first Gulf War, when the Iraqi army pulled out of Kuwait, they set fire to thousands of oil wells, Most of these fires were extinguished with the use of dynamite. The charge of dynamite was set at the head of the well and used to blow the flame away from the opening of the well. Interrupting the Chain Reaction The final piece of the fire tetrahedron, the chain reaction, can also be used to extinguish a fire. This can be done by either mechanically or chemically preventing the chain reaction from occurring. Mechanically inhibiting the chain reaction can be done with either sound or electromagnetic waves that prevent the heat from a fire from getting back to pyrolyze the fuel surface, This method of fire extinguishment is mostly theoretical, with limited sizes and types of fires that have been actually extinguished in this manner. The chemical means of interrupting the chain reaction is done by an agent combining with the OH- ion produced during combustion. The chemical decomposition that occurs in a fire is producing these OH- ions. An agent that works in this fashion is Halon. As explained earlier 80

## Page 87

in this chapter, it was the study of Halon, trying to understand exactly how that agent controls the fire, that helped to discover the sustained chain reaction and its effect on the fire. Halon prevents the founation of the OH - ion necessary for the pyrolyzed gasses to mix with oxygen to form combustion. Unfortunately, Halon has a ten•ible side effect of being oneof a family of chemicals that is depleting the Earth's ozone layer. Since we need ozone in the upper atmosphere of the Ealth to suwive, and since there are other alternatives, there are very few people around the world using Halon gas for fire protection anymore. You may run across it in your career if you find an old system that has not been converted to another gas yet, or you may find one of the few applications where the government allows the use of Halon because there is no other substitute that will do as well. Classes of Fuels and Agents to Extinguish Them In order to understand the science of combustion and controlling or extinguishing fires, one also needs to understand the different classifications of fuels. There are four (4) main classes of fuel, designated A through D. Class A is ordinary combustibles, which includes wood, cloth, plastics, and most common products. Class B fuels are more hazardous than Class A and are basically flammable and combustible liquids. Class B fuels have been given their own classification because there are different agents used to protect the fuel. Many flammable liquids float on water, making it difficult to extinguish fires of Class B with a stream of water. However, when water is broken up into droplets, as from a sprinkler, it is still possible to extinguish a Class B fire. Class C consists of energized electrical equipment. Once again, this class was considered separate from Class A because of the concern over the use of extinguishing agents that would conduct electricity. One way to deal with this problem is to cut off the power. Once the equipment is no longer energized, a Class C fire becomes a Class A fire. Class D includes combustible metals. There are a number of special metals that will undergo combustion when exposed to other chemicals. Some metals burn when exposed to air. Other metals burn when exposed to water. Knowledge of the specific metal and what it will react with is necessary in order to extinguish a Class D fire. Some classification lists for fuels also include a fifth class, Class K for kitchen hazards such as grease fires. This is more of a marketing scheme for specific hand-held extinguishers than it is a different class of fuel. Since kitchen grease fires are really flammable liquids, we will consider Class K the same as Class B for the discussion in this textbook. With many fire protection agents on the market, it can be difficult to choose one agent for the job. Each agent has suitability for different types of hazards and applications. The following table shows a number of different agents, their method of extinguishment, suitability for different hazards and some typical applications. 81

Agents can be broken down into three categories: clean agents, dilty agents, and aqueous agents. Clean agents are typically gases and include halon, nitrogen and specially listed inert gases. Dirty agents imply that clean up will be necessary after the fire has been extinguished in the space. Dilly agents include dry powder or wet chemical. Aqueous agents are water-based agents for fire protection. These include water, foam and potassium chloride. The maintenance required by a system should also be reviewed when selecting an agent for any application. For example, most foam concentrates have shelf lives. This means that even without activity the foam may have to be drained, remixed and refilled in a system every so many years. The length of time that can elapse will vary with the specific foam and brand chosen for the project. Although all fire protection systems require some maintenance, there are different levels of attention that are necessary depending on the agent used. The amount of maintenance can affect the cost of the system and efficiency of operations. Therefore, the owner of the building or their representative should be made aware of the required maintenance for their selected fire protection system. Another point to think about in selecting fire protection agents is the clean up that will be involved post fire. All fires will involve some clean up but owners and occupants are not always aware of what is truly involved with the agent they have selected for fire protection. As an example Metal X (an agent commonly used for Class D fires) requires a large amount of agent to control even small fires. This means that on a commercial application large quantities are needed. When those amounts are discharged to extinguish a fire, it will have to be cleaned up after the fire in order to restore normal business operations. Any of the dirty agents typically have to be concerned with cleaning up after the fire, as that is where the term "dirty agent" originated. Also, agents such as carbon dioxide, an invisible gas, can create additional clean up by staining items in the area of discharge brown. This too would require cleaning, which may not be initially anticipated. In addition, many foam solutions can require additional clean up procedures depending on the jurisdiction where the system is installed. The concern is the environmental impact of the foam, and it may be necessary to have a means of collecting and disposing of it. Halon is one of the agents listed in Table 9-1. It should be noted that the production of Halon was ceased by the Montreal Protocol in the late 1970's due to its chemical ability to break down the ozone layer of Earth's atmosphere. However, it is possible to still find these types of systems installed in areas such as computer rooms. There are some third world countries that still produce Halon because they have never signed on to the Montreal Protocal. If a Halon system activates it is possible to recharge that system by acquiring more Halon from a "Halon bank," which stores Halon for just such purposes. In addition, if a Halon system is being removed from a building the Halon can be given to a Halon bank for storage rather than releasing it into the atmosphere where it will do damage. Water spray is listed at the end of Table 9-1. This can include fire sprinkler systems, water spray systems or even water mist systems. Water is an excellent fire protection agent because it can absorb approximately 8000 BTU per pound of water. It also has the added benefit of expanding at a ratio of 1700 to 1 when converted from liquid to steam. This means that water 83

## Page 90

uses the reduction of oxygen in a compaltment as a secondary method of helping to extinguish a fire. Summary In closing, it is extremely important to make sure that whatever agent has been selected for the job that it is appropriate for the fuel and the environment. All of the different agents have their place where they are effective and useful. The decision should be made based on the fuel, the expected fire, system maintenance, and the owner's operational needs. CHAPTER 10 THE LAYOUT PROCESS At the beginning of this book we presented a concept on what the role of a Fire Protection Engineering Technician is as a member of his company's team. "To produce clear and complete plans that result in the lowest installed cost of a fire sprinkler system consistent with project specifications, applicable requirements of codes and standards, and quality for the customer". The technician is responsible for producing clear and accurate plans that are used by other departments and outside agencies. One way to accomplish this goal would be to follow a logical step-by-step procedure to guide the preparer through the process. One such procedure is an eleven-step checklist: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9, Define the hazard Analyze the structure Analyze and determine the water supply Select or determine the system type Consider different types of sprinklers approved for the application Determine the most appropriate piping materials and layout for the hazard Determine hanging and bracing methods Determine what system attachments are appropriate. Type and location Hydraulic Calculations 10. Notes and Details 11. As-built drawings 85

## Page 92

Remember that the lowest possible installed cost is dependent on doing the job right thc first time. Pipe size is not as important as pipe arrangement and routing, hanging and avoiding conflicts. We all rely on hydraulic calculations, and this is the sophisticated part business. However, no hydraulic calculation can ever take the place of proper layout. Do an analysis to make the system best for the structure and project under consideration. There is no panacea that makes one system fit all conditions. Let's look at the layout process and the checklist in a little more detail. Define the Hazard In most instances this will be done by a Design Professional, the person who wrote the specifications. It is incumbent on the Technician to confirm the hazard classification, and this is best done by a call to the AHJ. This will confirm that what was given in the specifications is what the Building Department and Fire AHJ will accept. Before making this call, find out what Building Code is being used and what it's year of publication is in force. The building code determines the installation standards and their year (edition) will be enforced for the project. Care must be exercised, as the Design Professional may have published a "library" specification, and the project may be in a different state. Any discrepancies must be immediately reported to your supervisor and the party with whom you have a contract. This is always the first step, and if there is no design professional, or if there isn't one on staff, you are best advised to get one to establish this parameter. Analyze the Structure This is the first time we fomally look at the places into which we are going to fit pipe and devices. We are going to come back to this step often in our goal to make the system fit correctly for the first time. We need to determine materials of construction of the structure. We find this information on the structural and architectural drawings by looking at plan views, sections, elevations, legends, and finish schedules. We are looking at the geometry of the structure and whether the members and finishes are combustible or non- combustible. Next we are going to determine obstructed or unobstructed construction, which guides us to placement of sprinklers and area of coverage. Remember the type of sprinkler to be used is also a determinant of placement with regard to structure and obstructions. The next item would be to look into how to we are going to hang the system and brace it if the project is in an area that requires earthquake bracing. The choice of how we attach the hanger to the structure depends on, to list a few, the technical specifications, composition of the structure, and geometry of the structural member. 86

## Page 93

This might be called the visualization step. We are looking to get a "feel" for how the system is going to be placed in the building. If we are going to start drafting or input anything to the CAD program it would be the background items that affect our system. As stated above, we shall return to this step time and again. Water Supply The driving force for delivery of water to a fire area in the building is the strength of the water supply. By strength it is meant that the water supply has sufficient capacity or flow rate for a specified time as determined by the hazard classification, and enough pressure so that the sprinklers deliver enough water to control or suppress the fire. There are a number of ways to get the information you need.' The information could be given in the technical specifications. This is the best way from a contractor's perspective since it is part of the "design" and comes from the design professional. This information should be verified as to acceptability to the AHJ based on the currency of the information. With permission from a municipal water or private water company a fire flow test can be conducted. Again, the acceptability to the AHJ and, in this case, the design professional should be verified. A theoretical flow rate and pressure could be supplied by the water purveyor. In this scenario, even though the flow and pressure at the street connection might be different than the theoretical supply, it is the theoretical that must be used in hydraulic calculations. If this is the procedure it is imperative that a true fire flow test be conducted to make sure system pressures are below the rating of all devices on the system. If there is no municipal or private supply, then a water storage tank of some type will most likely be the system supply. The size and location of the tank and its operating pressure (if a Pressure Tank) needs to be determined. If a ground level gravity storage tank is chosen, then its capacity, location and the size and location of a fire pump would need to be determined. If these items were specified by a design professional, you would need to verify the details. If not specified, then they need to be worked out and verified by a design professional. Remember, without enough water, even the best laid-out sprinkler system, the best fire fighters with the best equipment will not be able to control and extinguish a fire. 87

## Page 94

Select System Type This may be the simplest of the steps. We usually know what type of system will be used for the project. In most cases it will be one of the four basic systems: WET e DRY 0 PREACTION o DELUGE A wet pipe system is where water is present in all parts of the system under the pressure required to control or suppress the fire. The building must be at 40 OF or above in order to prevent freezing. This type of system is the most reliable and it immediately delivers water over the fire area when sprinklers fuse. A dry pipe system is where a special Dry-Pipe valve separates water in the valve room from the rest of system piping that contains air in unheated areas subject to freezing. This type of system operates when a sprinkler fuses and air is released from the piping network, and when it drops to a certain level;the dry-pipe valve "trips" and lets water into the piping where it discharges over the fire area. As described, water is delayed getting to the fire area, and, in general, the fire will be larger than in a wet pipe system and this affects the hydraulic design area, A preaction system always uses a secondary detection network. These types of systems are used in locations where owners do not want water in the piping over areas where high dollar value material or equipment is in use. They can be used in areas with or without heat. Water is held in a valve room until some type of action is initiated by the detection network. Detection can be electronic, hydraulic or pneumatic. There are three basic types of preaction systems; non- interlock, single interlock and double interlock. They differ in method of allowing water to enter the piping network:\ o Non-interlock — Water is released from a special valve when either the detection network sends a signal to a release control panel or a sprinkler(s) open. There is a requirement for at least 7 psi of supervisory air pressure in the system. o Single interlock - Water is released from a special valve only when the detection network sends a signal to a release control panel. A fused sprinkler will not cause a valve trip. There is no requirement for supervisory air, but a system could be set up to monitor and annunciate loss of supervisory air. Double interlock - Water is released from a special valve when both the detection network senses fire and a sprinkler opens, In other words two signals are necessary for water to be released into the piping by a release control panel. There is a requirement for at least 7 psi of supervisory air pressure in the system. This type of system is used in freezers. 88

## Page 95

Preaction systems can delay water getting to the fire area, and, depending on the type of system, the fire will be larger than in a wet pipe system and this affects the hydraulic design area. A deluge system is one where all the sprinklers on the piping network are open. Water is held in a valve room until a separate, supervised detection network sends a signal through a release control panel to open the valve and admit water. Detection can be electronic, hydraulic or pneumatic. Water flows from all sprinklers on the system at the same time. There are other systems that should be mentioned. A multipurpose piping system supplies sprinklers and another building service such as heating water. There are special rules regarding device ratings and system configuration. An Anti-freeze system can be an auxiliary section of piping system attached to a wet pipe system or a stand-alone system. Again, there are special rules for installation and piping configuration. The type of system installed affects economics through both primary installation costs and maintenance costs. The type of system requires technical analysis with an eye toward the requirements for hydraulic calculation. Finally, the type of system affects installation methods and consideration of features such as system size, piping material, drainage of piping, and selection of sprinklers. Selection of Sprinklers At this step we shall start to integrate our knowledge of the structure and obstruction rules with the requirements of the specification. If the design professional has specified a particular kind of sprinkler then our choices would be nm•rowed to selecting from various manufacturers based on flow and pressure considerations, appearance and economics. If you were in a position to choose the type of sprinkler for as particular occupancy within a building there would be the opportunity to make a selection from a wider range of options. Obviously, there is a need to choose the correct basic type of sprinkler form upright, pendent or sidewall. Within the pendent and sidewall classes there are additional choices. Pendent sprinklers could be standard, recessed, or concealed. Sidewalls could be standard or horizontal, recessed or surface mounted. Then we would consider coverage as standard or extended and response time as to standard or fast. NFPA standards also guide us. For instance, response time for all light hazard occupancies shall be quick response. NFPA 13 also provides guidance as to temperature ratings in various locations depending on ambient room temperature, proximity to heat sources and location within the structure or finished area. An example would be to use intermediate temperature rating when installed .in a skylight. For storage occupancies other considerations enter. We have the choice of upright and pendent standard spray sprinklers, extended coverage spray sprinklers large drop sprinklers and ESFR sprinklers. Once we have worked our way through this maze of choices, then there is the subject of finish. Brass, chrome, painted, and special coatings for corrosion are available. We also have another area to search special application sprinklers. These would include residential sprinklers, attic sprinklers, combustible concealed blind sprinklers. There will be 89

more of these special application sprinklers as time goes by. A look at the following decision Cree gives some idea of the variety of options available. Sprinklers Conventional Standard Response Residential Quick Response Spray Sprinklers Large Drop everal Orifice Sizes Several Orifice Sizes Extended Coverage (See Listing) ESFR Quick Response Extended Coverage (See Listing) Extended Coverage Extended Coverage Ordinary Hazard Light Hazard With all that was discussed in the preceding paragraphs it is likely to be confusing. The keys are: 1. First and foremost each sprinkler must deliver the specified quantity of water over the area it is protecting. 2. Check and follow the specifications 3. Select the sprinkler based on ease of installation considering the number of sprinklers to be installed, the obstruction criteria per the listing and NFPA standards and hydraulic calculation performance. Determine the Most Appropriate Piping Material and Layout There are three basic classes of materials to consider for interior piping: steel, plastic, and copper. If only it was that simple our decisions would be straightforward and relatively easy. Jn Chapter 25A, we shall explore choosing the most appropriate material in detail. At this time let's look at the basic materials and choices within each class. Steel pipe is still the most predominate material used for fire sprinkler systems. In the early days of the industry, there was really no option but to use schedule 40 black or galvanized steel pipe. The specification was A-120 and the fittings were black or galvanized cast iron screwed. Some plain end fittings were available as were flanged fittings, and, of course, some welded fittings. Fast forward to the 21st century and our options are wide and varied. We now 90

## Page 97

have schedule 40, 30, 10, 7, and 5 steel pipe. The difference is the wall thickness and inside diameter; the lower the schedule, the larger the inside diameter. Joining the pipe depends on the schedule and listing. Only schedule 40 and 30 and specially listed schedule 10 can be threaded and joined with threaded cast iron or ductile iron fittings. The small schedule pipe can only be joined with listed plain-end or roll grooved fittings. The reason to choose the lower schedules is for economics and hydraulic calculation reasons. THINWALL STEEL PIPE w1TH WELED OUTLETS We shall discuss this in detail in Chapter 25A. Steel pipe and fittings can be used for all types of systems. Plastic pipe has been a great innovation for the industry. It is lighter and more corrosion resistant than any kind of steel pipe. The majority of plastic pipe used in the industry is listed CPVC. It is identifiable by its bright orange color (see Figure 10-1). It is joined by using listed CPVC fittings and a solvent/cement. It is especially useful and appropriate for retrofit in new light hazard construction and existing occupied light hazard buildings and most residential construction. CPVC is approved for all light hazard and residential occupancies. The installation and protection of piping must follow specific manufacturer installation instluction. Figure 10-2 Cross Linked Polyethylene (PEX) Figure 10-1 CPVC Pipe Another type of plastic is h" listed PEX pipe, which only be used for network systems in NFPA 13D systems in One and Two-Family Dwellings and Manufactured Homes. Network piping systems require special layout with at least three paths to each sprinkler (as shown in Figure 10-2) and hydraulic calculations for every sprinkler on the system in order to be sure that sufficient water arrives at the sprinkler in order to control or suppress the fire. A fourth line is permitted to run from the sprinkler to feed a plumbing fixture. All plastic piping is limited to use in wet systems and offers higher "C" factors than steel making it hydraulically more efficient. Copper pipe comes in three types: K. L, and M, with type K having the thickest wall (smallest inside diameter), and type M having the thinnest wall. The primary method of joining copper is brazing. Copper may also be joined by soldering under certain conditions and occupancy classifications. A special listed copper bond adhesive may also be used as listed for specific size tubing and occupancy conditions. The soldering and brazing methods of joining are limited by the fittings used, and follow NFPA 13 and the manufacturer's instructions when joining. Copper fittings are standard pattern tees and elbows, and there is a method of making 91

## Page 98

fittings right on the pipe using a tool called a "T" Drill. Copper offers higher "C" factors than steel, the same as plastic, making it hydraulically efficient. It is approved for a wider range of occupancies then plastic, up to and including ordinary hazard. o The choice of material will be controlled primarily by the Specifications, There may be restrictions on pipe schedule, joining techniques, and basic material - steel, plastic or copper. o After reviewing the specification, then we go back to the stmcture and determine what system could be installed most efficiently. The distance between structural members influences placement of hangers and hanging and bracing attachments. NFPA 13 and the manufacturers of plastic pipe specify the maximum distance between hangers for the different types of materials. Again, we shall discuss this in later chapters of this text, along with the economic factors that influence our choice. The layout of the system will be dictated by another series of factors. These include: Geometry of each area of the building to be protected. Installation factors based on crew expertise, type of material being used, Space available for the piping and coordination with other building services. Type of project — new construction, remodeling, retrofit into occupied building, service and daywork, or residential. Fabrication capabilities, either in-house or purchased. Job conditions. Available water supply. Type of sprinklers chosen. System configuration is limited to three choices: Tree, Loop or Grid. If a building is served by a single system, then most likely that system will be one of the three configurations. If the building has many areas and multiple systems and/or floors, each area should be analyzed as to which will be best for that section. The tree type system is the simplest and uses the least amount of pipe. The loop (cross mains) should be used to help distribute water to the system, and if there is an obstacle to go through that would involve large amounts of cutting and drilling. In essence go around the obstacle instead of through it. Gridded system configurations are used when large quantities of water must be distributed to the sprinklers and it is desired to reduce both main and branch line size, 92

There is an adage in our industry that still rings true most of the time: The least amount of pipe on the job usually leads to the lowest labor cost, Think about that as you go through this step in the procedure. The main parts of braces arc the brace, the brace fittings and the brace attachment. Bracing in an earthquake zone is required for all piping 2 h" and larger. Restraint is a lesser procedure for stabilizing branch lines. In addition, the technician must check the building code to determine if the procedures in NFPA 13 are acceptable. The cun•ent editions of IBC and NFPA 5000, the two most widely used Building Codes require a seismic analysis of where a new building is being constmcted before a permit can be issued. System Attachments This topic deals with a multitude of concerns and specific devices and techniques for assuring that a fire sprinkler system operates as intended when called upon to control or extinguish a fire. Within this particular step we deal with secondary water supplies, testing, draining, and some special devices that are either attached to or are part of the system. First, let's deal with the Fire Department Connection (FDC). This device and is required on almost all NFPA 13 and NFPA 13R systems. Its purpose is to provide the responding fire department with a method of providing water to a sprinkler system to assure an unintermpted flow of water to a fire area, In essence the fire department takes water from a municipal or private source, boosts pressure by passing it through a pump on the fire engine and sending it into the system through the FDC. Usually, the fire department "drafts" the water from the same source as the direct supply to the system. The location on a building is dictated by the fire department, not the installing contractor or design professional. It is always considered an emergency service device, and must be where the first responders can easily get to when they arrive on-scene. The specific piping configuration and added devices like check valves are based on the type of system protection the property. See the diagram for a typical configuration for a single dry pipe system, The objective is to make sure water flows into the system, and not back into the underground piping. That's why a check valve is installed under the control valve in this case. NFPA 13 and NFPA 13R should be consulted for specific piping configuration for each type of system. NFPA 13D systems do not require a FDC a local ordinance specifies one. The next item we should discuss is backflow. Unfortunately, most health and water departments now require some form of backflow prevention. In most cases this takes the form of either double check valve assemblies (DC VA) or reduced pressure zone backflow preventers (RPZ). These devices must be listed for fire service as they are in the direct path of the water 94

## Page 101

supply to sprinklers. It is a requirement that these devices be tested at full fire flow demand including hose streams and hose connections when installed downstream of the DC VA or RPZ. Additionally, they shall be tested annually for backflow as directed by the AHJ. Some of the concems for this annual testing is how to conduct the test and how and where to dispose of the water. Technicians should provide for safely conducting these tests during the layout process. Other type of devices must be listed for fire services since they are in the direct path of the water supply to sprinklers are pressure regulating and reducing valves. These valves are used to. lower system pressure to all or portions of systems where the incoming pressure to the device exceeds the rated pressure of the sprinklers and other devices downstream of the valve. Again, the concern is to provide for testing and disposal of water from such devices. Most of the rest of the connections deal with providing a means for testing the system to send alarm and supervisory signals or measure some aspect of required system performance. These would be called drains and test connections. The picture shows a typical situation that one might find in a hi-rise building at one of the floors. We must be able to drain the sprinklers, test the flow alarm switch and provide a safe method for water disposal. There are a number of new devices available to accomplish these tasks. There are "drain and test" devices as one unit or it can be done with standard piping. There is a device that can test•the flow alarm without having to flow water down the drain riser. Alarm attachments must be listed while drain valves, since they do not control water flowing to a sprinkler do not have to be listed, Test connections for dry pipe systems shall be located at the most remote palt of the system. This is a valved connection terminating in an orifice that is the size of the smallest sprinkler on the system. It is used to conduct a trip test that shows the amount of time it takes the dry valve to trip and to show how long it takes water to travel tlu•ough the system. The next topic deals with drains. NFPA 13 gives clear instruction on how to set up drain connections for all types of systems. Section 8.15.2 (2002 edition) covers this in detail, The table indicates some of the requirements for auxiliary drains for Dry and Preaction systems. Obviously we do not want water to be retained in areas subject to freezing. This would eventually lead to damaged piping and property. The primary goal is to have all the water be able to drain back to a location not subject to freezing but this is not possible at all times. Therefore, the configuration and size of drains is such that sections of trapped piping must drain to safe locations where all the trapped water can safely be removed f01T11 the system. The technician should consider this during the layout process and locations should be chosen for ease of accessibility and safety to the fitter and property owner, They should be clearly identified on the plans and marked and visible in the building. These drains will be needed should future modifications to the system be undertaken. One other factor in the location of drains is disposal of the water. There are plumbing codes, health codes, EPA agencies and local water and sewer departments that control how and where water can be drained. Be sure you know what the requirements are in the location of the project. We did not yet speak of the system main drain. This is usually a 2" connection at the system riser. This is the primary drain for the system and again, water disposal and safety are 95

## Page 102

paramount. This drain is also used for verification of the condition of the incoming water supply. NFPA 25 mandates an al least an annual test. However, should there be a backflow preventer on the system, the main drain test shall be conducted quarterly. This is not a fire flow test, but it is essential in that it shows how the water supply compares to system acceptance tests. There are other items generally classified as system connections. For instance, pressure gages must also be listed and their installation requirements are given in NFPA 13. There are other types of systems such as anti-freeze systems. These are basically wet pipe systems with an additive to prevent freezing. NFPA 13 details special requirements for these types of systems including how they are to be isolated from the primary system or water supply. Again, NFPA 13 is not the only standard that enters into the picture. We have water departments and health departments interjecting regulations that must be followed. Another type of system is a combined system where there are non-fire devices attached and the system serves more than one function, In the area of residential systems we have combined systems and network systems. NFPA 13D covers these situations. Provisions for flushing piping must be made. One provision of NFPA 13 is that there shall be a flushing connection at the end of each main. These connections do not have to be piped to a safe location. Contractors use different methods ranging from a nipple and cap to a grooved end pipe with a blind flange and coupling on the end. The only requirement is that the provision for flushing be present. The technician should give some forethought as to the type of connection and how flushing might be safely conducted in the future. Fire pumps might also be considered an attachment, but they are more of an overall system component. Chapter 33 of this textbook covers this topic in detail. The process also accomplishes the following: Analyze configurations for minimum pressure loss, cost of materials and minimum installed cost. If the computer printout shows a water requirement for sprinklers of 285 gpm, something is wrong. Likewise if any sprinkler discharges less than its floor coverage times the density, it's wrong. The last point to make here is that your hydraulic notes and data sheets must coordinate with each other. Other people, the AI-IJ and the design professional will be looking at your work.
