CHAPTER 11 DRAFTING AND FIRE PROTECTION SYMBOLS Communicating through Shop Drawings We have many ways to describe a sprinkler system: verbally, sketching freehand or using tools on a drafting table to "draw" on graph paper, or by using a computer to create a "viltual" image of our system. The concept of communicating through sketches and diagrams is as old as time itself. The first known "engineered drawing" is a temple plan dated around 2130 B.C. The plan is etched in a clay tablet that is part of a statue (see Figure 11-1) that also holds a stylus and a notched bar (perhaps a scale). In about 1500 B.C., the Egyptians are known to have used papyrus with grids as the first "graph paper". They dipped string in ink and touched the papyrus to create the lines of the grid on the papyrus as a visual scale for "drafting". 1 Figure 11-1 Roman builders had a different approach, they would draw the building out to full scale on the ground to make sure the blocks they cut would fit. They would even draw full size views of the side of a building on the ground. One Roman builder named Vitruvius said that a technician must have a knowledge of drawing so he can make sketches of his ideas."2 101

## Page 108

It wasn't until around 1500 A.D. that scaled drawings with multiple views and projections started to appear in Italy during the Renaissance, Leonardo Da Vinci's sketches are grand examples of the sketching techniques that are still employed to communicate ideas today. But, even his skill as a designer was a mostly freehanded eff01t. In 1795, a French mathematician wrote a manuscript on "Descriptive Geometry" which has been the basis for mechanical drafting for over 200 hundred years. This methodology provided a scientific process to communicate spatial relationships in drafting. With the advent of the personal computer (PC's), drafting has shifted from merely creating lines and circles, to creating 3-D models of our ideas. Most of today's Computer Aided Design (CAD) programs will create a 3-D representation of a sprinkler system. As we have shifted away from the drawing board and manual drafting tools, we have also shifted our expectations for engineering technicians. The engineering community delivered the results of a survey to educators and found which, of a given 14 goals for the technician, were most important to those educating technicians. On a scale of 1 to 5, with 5 representing "very important", the educators found the following skills to be the most important: TECENICIAN GOALS 1. Ability to Create 3-D Solid Computer Models 2. Ability to Sketch Engineering Objects in the Freehand Mode 3. Ability to Visualize 3-D Solid Computer Models 4. Ability to Create Dimensions SCORE 4.75 4.67 4.38 4.33 5. Ability to Generate Engineering Drawings from Computer Models 6. Ability to Create 3-D Assemblies of Computer Models 7. Ability to Create 2-D Computer Geometry 8. Ability to Create Section Views 4.29 4.21 4.13 One can certainly see where computer models have made their way into the important tasks that challenge technicians. More importantly, we can see that professionals suggest that freehand sketches, dimensions, 2-D drawings, and section views are as critical as any 3-D detailing done on a computer. The difference is that 2-D design takes a level of critical thinking on the part of the technician. In order to be a successful fire sprinkler technician, you must be able to conceptualize the 3-D system in your mind from the 2-D drawings that you will be required to create. You can also see what the educators found to be less important. The following were the tasks that settled at the bottom of their list: 12. Ability to Create Presentation Graphics 13. Ability to Solve Traditional Descriptive Geometry Problems 14. Ability to Create Geometric Construction with Hand Tools 3.42 2.29 2.13 This list shows us that the computer has replaced the need for the technician to be able to create multiple views through geometric calculation. The computer also enables us to see the three dimensional product of our ideas without having to assemble the final product ourselves. With that said, nothing will take the place of some practical field experience on the pan of the 102

fire sprinkler technician. There is no substitute for the experience gained from using wrenches to assemble a sprinkler system from shop drawings. The word 'communicate' keeps coming up. What are we trying to communicate and with whom? In the fire sprinkler industry, we are trying to explain the level and quality of fire protection that is being provided by a fire sprinkler system within a built environment to: the owner and the AI-IJ (submittal drawings and hydraulic calculations), the installer (field installation drawings), and the fabrication shop (fabrication lists). We are also trying to show interaction with other systems within the built environment to the people responsible for those systems. This is a lot of communicating! So how do we express ourselves so that everyone can understand what we are trying to say? Many people have tried to answer tllis question. As we create drawings, it is important that we use a typical and consistent system to communicate the things we propose for acceptance and installation. Drawing to Scale One of the most important pieces of information on your shop drawings will be the drawing scale. You will need to include a graphical representation of the scale on each plan or detail in your shop drawings. The scale should always be indicated in the title block of the drawing. The title block should always be in the lower right hand comer of the drawing. Using scale helps to show the relative size of objects on your drawings. There are basically two types of scales: Architectural and Engineering. Architectural Scales are expressed as "fractions of an inch" equals "one foot". Examples include 1/4" = 1'-0", 1/8" = 1'-0", and 1- 1/2" = 1'-0". Nearly every category of drawings will generally use "Architectural Units" as the representative scale. Engineering Scales are usually used on site plans and civil drawings. They are used to represent larger areas in the project blueprints. In the United States, Engineering Scales are expressed in "one inch" equals "so many feet". Examples include: 1" = 20', 1" = 30 and Drawing Views There are three basic types of views we will discuss in this Chapter: Orthographic, Isometric, and Perspective. The two other types of views we will look at are Sections and Elevations. The Orthographic Projections on a plan are always drawn to scale and are usually the Front, Side and Top views of the drawing subject. These views are taken at 90 degree angles aligning with the axis of the X, Y, and Z planes. (See Figure 11-2 ) 103

## Page 110

top view front view top side view side front Figure 11-2 In an Isometric View, the object's vertical lines are drawn vertically, and the horizontal lines in the width and depth planes are shown at 30 degrees to the horizontal. When drawn under these guidelines, the lines parallel to these three axes are at their true (scale) lengths. Lines that are not parallel to these axes will not be of their true length (See Figure 11-3). This the view that the Fire Sprinkler Technician will use most often for piping diagrams, like the Riser Detail. •a b" 300 a 22 b = c Figure 11-3 Isometric Views of Different Shapes The advantage to the Isometric View is that the distances between points in the three axis can be determined from the diagram. The problem with the Isometric View •is that it looks dist01ted to the human eye. The next type of diagram will look less distorted when people look at it. 104

Reflected Ceiling Plans (RCP) This is the plan that most technicians use when spacing sprinklers, because they usually show the locations of lights, diffusers, and other components that are placed at the ceiling level Building Elevations o These are views from the building's exterior. Building Sections These sections give you a good understanding of how the building will go together. Building Details e This can include wall details, enlarged room and stairwell plans, and interior room elevations. This is critical as you start to think in three dimensions while detailing the system piping. Next in the project blueprints are usually the "Structural Drawings" (labeled S). These drawings will describe the backbone of a building, the building's supportive structure. First in this category are usually the Foundation Plans. They describe the footings and foundations that are usually found below grade. These drawings can be helpful when determining the location and routing of any underground piping that enters the building envelope. Second in this category are usually the framing plans. They describe the layout of the stmctural frame. This includes beams, joists, trusses, purlins, wind bracing and blocking. You will use this inforrnation to determine piping routes and hanger locations for the aboveground piping. There will also usually be detail drawings for the stmctural connections in this category. usually followed by a sheet with the column schedule. This schedule will describe each stmctural member being used on a project in more detail than the single linc blueprints. This is very important ilformation to the fire sprinkler technician when detennining how far above the floor the souctural members will be. The next plans in the project blueprints are usually the "Mechanical Drawings" (labeled M or H). These drawings will describe the Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems and their associated equipment. Usually, the first drawings in this category are floor plans of the ventilation ductwork. The best of these drawings give the widths and depths of the ductwork, so [hat you may coordinate your piping locations closely. You should also use these drawings to verify diffuser locations with the reflected ceiling plans (RCPs). The next drawings in this category may likely be the Mechanical Roof Plan. This plan shows the location of any roof penetrations by the mechanical systems. Many roofs have openings for Roof Top Units that force the air through the HVAC ductwork. The next drawings in this category are usually the Mechanical Piping Plans. These drawings will indicate the size and location of piping supplying the mechanical units. The last drawing found in this category is usually the Mechanical Equipment Schedule. This schedule can be helpful to the technician when determining the size of the ductwork that actually connects to the mechanical units, which often varies from the ventilation ductwork on the floor plans, The drawing set may also contain mechanical sections and enlarged floor plans that help in seeing complex rooms or multiple layers of ductwork in an area. The next plans in the project blueprints are usually the "Plumbing Drawings" (labeled P). The piping floor plans in this section will include domestic water piping, waste piping and drain piping from the roof. Remember that most drain piping has to pitch in a building. The "Electrical Drawings" (labeled E) are usually found after the "Plumbing Drawings" in the project blueprints, These drawings will show, among many other things: lighting layouts, power supplies, and locations for the connections to alarm bells, flow switches and tamper switches. There are other categories used for numerous other disciplines in the constiuction industry, but this gives you a good idea of the most common. 107

Symbols As you learned in previous chapters, the insurance industry has had a long lasting impact on the fire sprinkler industry. The insurance industry developed a series of symbols that they felt appropriate for use on fire sprinkler plans. Over the years, fire sprinkler companies started to develop their own symbols. The NFPA felt it important to attempt to develop and organize a set of symbols that would apply to the fire protection industry. They actually created four different documents to set the path: o NFPA 171, Public Firesafety Symbols, NFPA 172, Fire Protection Symbols for Architectural and Engineering Drawings, NFPA 174, Fire Protection Symbolsfor Risk Analysis Diagrams, and NFPA 178, Symbols for Fire Fighting Operations. These documents closely followed the International Standards Organization (ISO) standards that were already available. As technology brought all of these disciplines closer, it only made sense to combine all the standards that established symbols for drawings. So, ill 1994, the NFPA combined all four standards for symbols into NFPA 170, "The Standard for Fire Safety Symbols". This document has many symbols that are intended for use on drawings of fire sprinkler systems. The following tables are from NFPA 170 and should be used in the work we do as design technicians: Sunbol Description Public water main Private water snain Water main under building Suction pipe Thrust block Comments indicate pipe. size. and material Indicate pipe size. and material Indicate. pipe size and tnaterial Indicate ipe size and material Water Supply and Distribution Symbols (from Table 6.4) 111

CHAPTER 12 TYPES OF CONSTRUCTION In order for a fire sprinkler technician to completely understand the tasks that they need to pelform, it is essential that there be a basic understanding of the structural elements in a building. Remember the fundamental objective is to make the installation fit correctly the first time. Knowledge of structures, their components and elements will aid in meeting the objective. A side benefit is that you will see how we can use the positive aspect of placing sprinklers in a building to provide more flexibility in architectural design and let developers build bigger and taller buildings on the same lot, while lowering the overall project cost. During this chapter we are going to look at the various materials used to build structures and terminology we encounter while laying out a fire sprinkler system to correctly fit into the building to protect it and its occupants. Welcome to the world of codes and structures. Materials Buildings can be constructed from any of the following materials, or combinations of these materials: Steel Concrete Reinforced and non-reinforced Pre-cast Prestressed Post-tensioned Brick or Masonry Block Wood Glass Aluminum Plaster and Gypsum Board Plastics 115

As you can see, there are many materials and many methods available to contractors to build a building. Fire Resistance Rating and Building Codes Building codes organize types of construction by their combustibility and fire resistance rating. Based on the materials used, building codes tell us how large and tall a structure can be based on the occupancy (what the building will be used for) and the fire resistance of the materials. NFPA 220 is the "Standard on Types of Building Construction". The standard sets the time, in hours, that materials or assemblies can withstand a fire exposure without collapse or burn-through. The fire itself is built to deliver a certain temperature within a specified time period. Figure 12-10 is a reproduction of the "Standard Time/Temperature Curve" from NFPA 251. The fire resistance rating of materials and assemblies is evaluated against this laboratory fire. The materials are rated for their ability to withstand the fire for a given period of time without collapse or burn-through. 119 •reoil) 1000. 1300 ISSO ) 700 2001) Figure 12-10 'Cinn• 5 Oilin IO Illin Illin

Thus, a I-hour wall or separation would be abie to withstand burning at a final temperature of some 1,7000 F without being compromised. As stated earlier, building codes use this information to accomplish the following objectives: o To limit the flammability of structural members to avoid collapse during a fire. o To provide a barrier Io fire spread within buildings and from building to building. • To limit the risk to occupants by controlling the size and height of buildings allowed for each construction type. There are, in general, five types of construction based on fire resistance rating. They are designated by roman numerals I, II, III, IV, and V. The highest fire resistance is Type I and least fire resistant is Type V. What follows is a discussion of these types and how they are used by the building codes. For Type IA (refer to Figure 12-12), there is no limit to height, number of stories or area per floor. If we lower the fire resistance to Type 1B, then the building is capped at 160 feet tall and 11 stories, If we move further down the fire resistance ladder to Type ILA, then we are limited to 65 feet high, four stories and a maximum of 21,500 square feet per floor, The table uses the same method for all types of occupancies. Our interest in this information is that the building codes recognize the life safety and property protection benefits of sprinkler systems. From other places in the codes we are allowed to add a story and increase the area per floor by installing sprinklers. There are other benefits to sprinklers through lengthened egress paths and reduction of separation ratings, This, plus architectural flexibility given to sprinklered buildings provides incentives for fire sprinklers — we call these "trade-ups". Another benefit, maybe the biggest, is sprinklers allow the owner to use less fire resistive materials to build a similar size building. This reduces overall construction costs without sacrificing quality and it increases life safety. Classification for Building Design Other chapters in this book deal with placement of sprinklers in relation to configuration of the building's structural elements. Since it is also a method of classifying or stating a type of construction we shall provide a quick review here. There are two classifications for sprinkler design: Obstructed Constnlction and Unobstructed Construction. Further we consider whether the structural elements are combustible or non-combustible. Consideration of the types of construction based on Obstructed or Unobstructed we are more concerned with geometry of the element than we are with its strength. We want to know if heat getting to the sprinkler will be impeded so as to delay sprinkler activation and will water from the sprinkler be prevented from reaching the fire below. The combustibility of the structural element enters into sprinkler placement and coverage area. Some of the more cornmon nomenclature used in the industry to fit into the obstructed/unobstructed categories are smooth ceiling, open joist, bar joist, beam and girder, and panel construction. The two terms are defined in NFPA 13-2002 in paragraphs 3.7.1 and 3.7.2. There are further explanations and graphics in the Annex, paragraphs A.3.7.1 and A.3,7.2. Summary In this chapter we discussed types of constmction form the point of view of materials such as steel, concrete, masonry and wood. We looked at the structural elements including beams, trusses, girders, purlins and assemblies. We reviewed the fire resistance ratings and assigned classifications by the ability to endure fires for a specific length of time. The building codes showed how the fire resistance of a structure is used to limit the risk to occupants by controlling the size and height of buildings allowed for each construction type. And finally, we reviewed types of construction related to sprinkler placement and whether the type of construction is obstructed or unobstructed. 123

CHAPTER 13 TYPES OF SPRINKLER SYSTEMS There are basically four types of sprinkler systems; a wet pipe sprinkler system, a dry pipe sprinkler system, a preaction sprinkler system and a deluge sprinkler system. (i wet pipe sprinkler system utilizes sprinklers connected to a piping system which contains water supplied from a water source and when a sprinkler opens from a fire's heat water will immediately discharge from any open sprinkler(s). A dry pipe sprinkler systot! utilizes sprinklers connected to a piping system filled with pressurized air or nitrogen which IS released when a sprinkler opens from a fire's heat allowing the dry pipe valve to release water into the piping system and out of the open sprinkler(s). A preaction sprinkler system/ utilizes sprinklers connected to a piping system filled with air which can be pressurized or not, with a detection system installed in the same areas as the preaction sprinkler system. The detection system and/or the sprinkler system opens a valve releasing water into the piping system and out of any open sprinkler(s). A deluge sprinkler systenlutilizes open sprinklers connected to a piping system that is supplied from a water source. A valve, which is operated by a detection system installed in the area of the deluge sprinkler system, allows water to flow into the piping system and discharges from all of the sprinklers at once. All of these different types of sprinkler systems have many components in common, They all have control valves, pipe, water supplies, drains and test connections. Some of them may be fed from underground mains that also supply fire hydrants. Others may only be supplied by pumps and tanks that are dedicated to the sprinkler system only and serve no other systems. Some systems might have a single water supply while others may be connected to multiple supplies to make up for insufficient demand from a single supply, or to create redundancy in case one of the supplies fails. Figure 13-1 shows many of the pieces and parts of a fire sprinkler system connected to multiple water supplies and an underground main that also supplies fire hydrants, 125

## Page 132

Feed Many. ser tandpipe ater Flow Alarm Divisional Valves Yard Hydrant •SDrinkler Control Valvc Yard Maiil Fire Pump Suction Tonk Fire Department Connection Public Hydrant Supply Control Valve • Check Valvo Back Flow Preventor Public Water Main Figure 13-1 Typical sprinkler system and associated components in action Wet Pipe Sprinkler Systems A wet pipe sprinkler system is the simplest, most common, most reliable, most economical and requires the least maintenance as compared to other types of sprinkler systems. Because the system is filled with water it immediately discharges water when the sprinkler opens due to the heat from a fire. Fewer system components increase the reliability of the system, decrease the cost and simplify maintenance. Because of this it is the best choice for most installations where the temperature can be maintained above 400F (40C). If the temperature can not be maintained above 400F (40C)9then antifreeze can be used in a wet pipe sprinkler system. An antifreeze sprinkler system is a type of wet pipe which contains an antifreeze solution. When the system activates the antifreeze solution is discharged out of any open sprinkler(s) and is then followed by water. The antifreeze solution must have a freezing point below the expected minimum temperature. The specific gravity of the solution has to be checked using a hydrometer or refractometer. Check with state and local health organizations to ensure that the antifreeze solutions conform to their regulations. Configurations of wet pipe sprinkler systems could include a shotgun riser (Figure 13-2) or an alarm check riser (Figure 13-3 and Figure 13-4). The shot gun riser uses a swing, internally loaded, or butterfly type check valve and a flow switch. An alarm check riser utilizes an alarm check valve on the riser connected to a retard chamber which will fill when the alarm check valve clapper swings open. The purpose of the retard chamber is to prevent false alarms due to pressure surges from the water supply. 126

Dry Pipe Sprinkler Systems A dry pipe sprinkler system is an option when a wet pipe sprinkler systems cannot be used because of the chance of freezing temperatures or when temperatures can not be maintained above 400 F (40C). The piping system is typically under pressurized air or nitrogen. A dry pipe valve is installed to keep the water in a heated area from entering the piping until the dry pipe sprinkler system is activated, They are usually used to protect unheated areas such as parking garagcs, attics or frcczcrg. See Figure 13-5 for an example of the inside of a dry-pipe valve. There is a 30% increase in the area of sprinkler operation to account for the delay in water delivery. Gridded systems are not allowed to be used due to the long delay in the time it takes to allow all of the air to escape from the piping before water will discharge from the open sprinklers. Large area in contact with air Small diameter in contact with water Figure 13-5 Inside ofa differential dry-pipe valve. All dry pipe systems with a volume over 500 gallons must have a quick opening device unless water can be delivered to the inspector's test connection in 60 seconds. A quick opening device is either an exhauster or an accelerator that helps to trip the dry- pipe valve faster in order to speed up the arrival of water to the sprinklers. It can also be omitted if water can get to the Inspector's Test Connection within 60 seconds or if the system is under 129

Dry pipe sprinkler system operation sequence 1. 2. 3, 4. 5. 6. The dry pipe valve is in the closed position with air pressure holding it closed (see Figure 13-7) The heat form a fire activates sprinklers near the fire. The air pressure in the piping system is reduced The dry pipe valve trips open (see Figure 13-8) Water enters piping system Water discharges from any sprinkler that is opened by Lhe heal of the fire The colTect air pressure to water pressure ratio allows the dry pipe valve to remain in the closed position while the pressure from the water supply is pushing against it. The ratio is determined by the manufacturer and provided in the cut sheets for the product. When information on the maximum pressure from the water supply is available the necessary pressures can then be calculated. By dividing the maximum water pressure by the ratio number the trip point of the dry-pipe valve is found. In order to add a safety factor and prevent the dry-pipe valve from tripping due to a random pressure surge in the water supply, the air pressure needs to be 20 psi in excess of the trip point. A differential dry pipe valve (see Figure 13-5) is one with a ratio that is greater than 1 to 1 (1:1), meaning that the surface are of the valve in contact with the air is much larger than the surface area in contact with the water. Consider a valve with an air to water ratio of 5:1 on a water supply with a maximum static pressure of 105 psi. According to the valve ratio, one psi of air will hold back a pressure of 5 psi of water. The ratio also means that 20 psi of air will hold back 100 psi of water. In order to determine the correct air pressure to hold in the system, divide the maximum water pressure by the valve ratio to achieve the trip point: 105 +5 = 21 psi Adding the 20 psi safety factor, we find the maximum air pressure that should be kept in the dry-pipe system piping: 21 +20 = 41 psi This dry-pipe system should never have more than 41 psi air pressure even though the water pressure gets as high as 105 psi. Too much air in the system will delay the delivery of water to a fire because it will take longer for the valve to trip and for the water to push the air out of the system. Dry pipe sprinkler systems generally use upright sprinklers in order to keep sediment from settling on the sprinklers every time the system is filled and drained down. Regular pendent sprinklers are not permitted to be installed directly on the pipe, but regular pendent 132

## Page 139

sprinklers are penniLted on return bends if the sprinkler and retucn bend are all in heated spaces. Special dry-type sprinklers are permitted to be installed directly on the piping, even in freezing area, because these specially listed sprinklers have been designed to prevent sediment from building up on the sprinkler's orifice. Preaction Sprinkler Systems A preaction piping system contains air or nitrogen which can be pressurized or non- pressurized. Water is held back by an automatic control valve (called a preaction valve) that is also connected to a fire detection system. If a fire occurs, the detection system sends a signal to the preaction valve, which opens, and sends water into the piping system. A small amount of air pressure is beneficial in a preaction system under normal conditions so that any leak or break in the system is detected by the loss of pressure. Supervision for system piping and detection devices is required when more than 20 sprinklers are used. The basic design concept is to make detectors more sensitive than the sprinklers so that when a sprinkler opens there will already be water at the sprinkler. In order for the preaction system to work, there need to be detectors in every compartment where there are sprinklers. Once the preaction valve opens and lets water flow into the system, it basically becomes a wet system. Sprinklers will only open due to the heat of the fire and water will only flow from the sprinklers that open. One of the advantages of the preaction system is that if a leak occurs, then the air pressure will drop and sound an alarm, but the preaction valve will continue to hold the water back until a smoke or heat detector activates. Figure 13-9 shows a preaction system with many possible types of detection systems that can be connected to the preaction valve. Typically, the detectors are not attached directly to the preaction valve, but to an alarm panel, which will trip the preaction valve when it receives a signal from the detection system, The detection system can consist of heat detectors, smoke detectors, rate-of-rise detectors, beam detectors, or even manual pull stations. Any device that sends an electrical signal upon detection of a fire can be used for a preaction sprinkler system. 133

CHAPTER 14 COMMON COMPONENTS AND CONNECTIONS In this Chapter, we will discuss the parts and pieces that make up most fire sprinkler systems. The common components of these systems all carry specific requirements for their manufacture, use and installation, The initial requirements for the types of products we can use are found in NFPA 13, Chapter 6, "System Components and Hardware Other requirements regarding use and installation can be found in Chapters 7, 8, 9, 10 and in various locations in other chapters of NFPA 13. The first thing that Chapter 6 tries to explain to the NFPA 13 user, is that any material that is listed for use in fire sprinkler systems will be acceptable. This acceptance requires the material to be installed in accordance with its listing. What does "listed" really mean? NFPA 13 defines the term 'listed" as, 'Equipment, materials, or services included in a list published by an organization that is acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction and concerned with evaluation of products or services, that maintains periodic inspection of production of listed tequipment or materials or periodic evaluation of services, and whose listing states that either th tequipment, material, or service meets appropriate designated standards or has been tested and (found suitable for a specified purpose. " That's a lot of words to describe the basic requirements. A product can only be considered listed if: The product appears in a list published by a testing agency. This includes agencies such as Underwriter's Laboratory (UL) or Factory Mutual (FM). The testing laboratory periodically inspects the manufacturer's facility to ensure consistency in manufacturing. The product has been made to a specific standard or has undergone tests to prove its suitability for use in fire protection systems. It is very important to remember that every single part or piece of a sprinkler system is not required to be listed. Chapter 6.1.1.5 of NFPA 13 puts it like this,' Components that do not affect system performance such as drain piping, drain valves, and signs shall not be required to be listed. 't The previous section of NFPA 13 also points to certain hanger components that are not required to be listed. (See sections 9.1.1.2, 9.1.1.4.2, and 9.1.1.4.3 of NFPA 13) 139

## Page 146

Water Supplies If we were to "be the water" and travel through a sprinkler system, we would start at the source. That is a good place to start when it comes to understanding the requirements for products in a fire sprinkler system. A water source must be an "automatic" supply. That is to say, that water must flow when a sprinkler is activated. Here is a sh01t list of possible water supplies and the chapters of this book that you will find a discussion related to their requirements: o Municipal or private water supply Chapter 16 o Water storage reservoir (usually a tank) and a fire pump Chapters 33 and 34 Pressure tank o Gravity tank Underground Piping Chapter 34 Chapter 34 Most of the time, we connect these supplies to the fire protection system inside of a building with "Underground Piping". NFPA 13, Chapter 10 actually tells us all of the requirements for underground piping, This includes the types of pipe that are acceptable for use (table 10.1.1). These include: Ductile iron Copper Fiberglass filament wound epoxy Polyethylene Polyvinyl chloride Chlorinated polyvinyl chloride Reinforced concrete Other listed materials Underground piping is not required to be listed. However, all of these types of pipe must be manufactured to AWWA or ASTM standards. There is one major difference between underground and aboveground piping, besides the fact that underground piping must be able to withstand its environment. Underground piping must have a working pressure of 150 psi, as allowed by the AWWA for waterworks piping. However, aboveground piping must have a working pressure of 175psi, just like all other aboveground components of a fire sprinkler

## Page 147

system. Underground piping must also undergo a pressure test prior to acceptance, this assures system integrity. This requirement is similar to aboveground piping. The underground piping must also be flushed prior to connection of the aboveground piping, We will cover these testing requirements in Chapter 15, "Underground Piping". geml Above Ground Piping We go back to NFPA 13, Chapter 6 for types of piping that are acceptable for use as aboveground piping. Chapter 6.3 is titled, "Aboveground Pipe and Tube". Table 6.3.1.1 lists the types of pipe or tube that are acceptable for use in a fire sprinkler system. Just like underground piping, these pipes should be manufactured to acceptable standards. The acceptable piping and their standards include: Steel piping: Schedule 40, Schedule 30, Schedule 10, and Schedule 5 o Specification for black and hot-dipped zinc-coated (galvanized) welded and seamless steel pipe for fire protection use o Specification for welded and seamless steel pipe o Wrought steel pipe o Specification for electric-resistance-welded steel pipe Copper Tube (Drawn, Seamless) o Specification for seamless copper tube o Specification for seamless copper water tube o Specification for general requirements for wrought seamless copper and copper-alloy tube Other Types of Pipe Nonmetallic piping specification for special listed chlorinated polyvinyl chloride (CPVC) pipe ASTM A 795 ASTM A 53 B36.10M ASTM A 135 ASTM B 75 ASTM B 88 ASTM B 251 ASTM F 442 In the 2002 edition of NFPA 13, Table 6.3.6.1 also shows a listedpolybutylene piping as acceptable alternative. You should be aware that this product is no longer offered on the open market. The manufacturer of this product no longer produces or sells this type of pipe. The standard always allows products to come to the market through the listing process. New pipes can be listed and then used in fire sprinkler systems. NFPA 13, Chapter 6.3.6.1 says it like this, "Other types of pipe or tube investigated for suitability in automatic sprinkler installations and listed for this service, including but not limited to polybutylene, CPVC, and steel, differing from that provided in Table 6.3.6.1 shall be permitted where installed in accordance with their listing limitations, including installation instructions."

On a very basic level valves can be placed into one of three categories in NFPA 13: Control Valves, Check Valves, and Valves for Testing and Draining. Control valves are defined as a valve that controls watcr to fire sprinklers. In other words, closing a control valve will prevent water from reaching fire sprinklers. Don't confuse a control —valve with a drain valve or testing valve. These other types of valves perform different functions and have different requirements as you will see later, NFPA 13, Chapter 8.15.1.1.1.1 "Each sprinkler system shall be provided with a listed indicating valve in an' •accessible location, so located as to control all automatic sources of water supply. " Control valves must be a listed indicating valve or a valve with a listed indicating assembly. There are a few types of listed indicating valves and they are shown in Figure 14-1. Every system is required to have a check valve that separates the system from the supply. The check valve is usually found in the system riser. This valve is required to be listed and must be installed in the vertical or horizontal position in accordance with their listing. Most check valves are listed for upward flow or horizontal flow. However, most are not listed for downward flow or top-down installation. Since check valves separate the system from the water supply there has to be one check valve at every water supply to a system (8.15.1.1.3 in NFPA 13). When there is more than one water supply to a system, there have to be indicating control valves installed on either side of each check (8.15.1.1.4.1 in NFPA 13). This will allow repair or testing of each individual check valve while leaving the other water supplies in operating condition. Figure 14-7 A Swing Check Valve A swing check is the type of check valve shown in Figure 14-7. It has the least number of working parts and uses gravity and the flow of water to help ensure proper operation. Unfortunately, it does allow some small amounts of water to flow backward in a system, making its use less common in recent years. 145

## Page 152

Figure 14-8 is an internally loaded check valve. This type of check valve has become very popular because it is the least likely to allow water to flow backwards in the system. The spring inside the device helps to keep the device closed under low flow or no-flow conditions. The disadvantages to this kind of check valve include: o Springs lose their memory under tension o The valve has more operating pmts, meaning more potential failures o The extra tension on the valve requires more water pressure to move the seat of the valve o Higher friction loss across the device, which effects the hydraulics of the sprinkler system Figure 14-8 Internally Loaded Check Valve o Device costs more than swing checks There are two other types of valves that are considered check valves for the purposes of NFPA 13. An alarm check valve is intended to send an alarm when the clapper is lifted from its seat. We will look at the operation of this valve later in this chapter. NFPA 13 allows the use of these valves as the system check valve. NFPA 13 also allows the use of a backflow preventer as the system check valve. We will discuss backflow preventers and their use in Chapter 18 of this textbook. Fire Department Connections The next item on a sprinkler system we will discuss is designed to serve two purposes. This connection allows the responding fire department to verify that water is flowing in a sprinkler system during an emergency. This connection also allows the responding fire department to support the fire fighters in the building by supplementing the water supply available to the sprinklers and any hose stations. This "Fire Department Connection" (FDC) that you may have seen on or near a building is designed as an inlet. It allows the fire department pumper truck to connect and pump additional water into a building's system. It is not an outlet that provides water to hoses or a truck. Because the fire department will rely on this piece of equipment, the fire department must approve the location of the FDC, The FDC must also have National Standard Hose Threads or be of the proper type of connection for the apparatus used by the fire department (6.8 of NFPA 13). Some fire departments have their very own type of hose threads. Some fire departments have begun to use a hose that has no threads in the coupling. In any case, when you are detailing the sprinkler system, you must use an FDC that has the appropriate type of connection for the equipment that 146

Water Flow Alarms As we continue along the sprinkler system, we would next come to the alarm apparatus that is required on every system installed in accordance with NFPA 13, Chapter 6.9.1 of NFPA 13 tells us the basic requirements for water flow alarms: Alarm apparatus must be listed o Alarm must sound upon water flow equal to the smallest orifice sprinkler on the system o Audible alarm must sound on the premises within 5 minutes of water flow Then section 6.9 of NFPA 13 goes on to describe the two basic types of alarm apparatus that are available for use on sprinkler systems. The first type of acceptable water flow detection is an Alarm Check Valve, When water flows in an alarm valve, the clapper comes up off of its seat and allows water to enter a port under the seat. That circuit is wired to an alarm unit, usually an electric bell. The electric bell must also be listed (see Figure 14-16). This sprinkler is intended to spray water up to the ceiling above where it is installed as well as down towards the floor below. This type of sprinkler is called a "conventional" or "old style" sprinkler, see Figure 14-21. With a conventional sprinkler, approximately 40% of the water is discharged up toward the ceiling, while roughly 60% of the water is discharged to the floor. Because so much of the water goes up, the spray pattem for these types of sprinklers are narrower than most other sprinklers, so they need to be installed closer together. When it comes to orientation, the type of sprinkler to use in any given area of a project is usually a practical and simple decision. Some factors for determining which sprinkler orientation to use are: architectural specification, the type of ceiling, the type of pipe and fittings being used, and the proximity to building features. If every sprinkler system is required to have a way to detect water flow, how would one go about proving that water flow would indeed activate an alarm? The answer is found in NFPA 13, Chapter 8.16.4 System Connections. This is the chapter that calls for what is commonly known as the 'inspector's test connection'. Wet systems are required to have an "alarm test connection" (8.16.4.2 in NFPA 13) for each water flow device for each system. This test connection must be at least 1" pipe leading to a smooth bore orifice that will provide the flow equivalent to that of the smallest sprinkler on the system. This alarm connection may be found anywhere downstream of the water flow device. Dry systems are required to have a "trip test connection" (8.16.4.3 in NFPA 13) installed "on the end of the most distant sprinkler pipe in the upper story". This test connection must also be at least 1" pipe leading to a smooth bore orifice that will provide the flow equivalent to that of the smallest sprinkler on the system. The inspector?s test connection on a dry system is intended for trip testing the valve. Water flow devices are tested with the trim valves on the dry-pipe valve. Preaction systems are only required to have inspector's test connections when the system uses supervisory air (13: 8.16.4.4). The air pressure and water flow devices are tested with the trim valves on the preaction valve. Deluge systems do not require inspector's test connections. 155

All test connections must be readily accessible and they must terminate [o the exterior of a building or to a drain Chat is sized to accept full flow under system pressure. Hangers Wc havc gone tlu•ough the majority of the parts and pieces that make up the sprinlder system. However, there is one other component of the sprinkler system to briefly discuss. The pmts and pieces we use to attach the sprinkler system to the building's structure. These components are known as the system's hangers. The parts making up the hangers must be made of ferrous materials. The NFPA Committee wanted to ensure that hangers can withstand a fire scenario, so they require hanger components to be contain iron unless they have been listed otherwise. The portion of the hangers that attach to the building and to the pipe must be listed. The threaded rod we use to connect these attachments are not required to be listed. Hangers components that attach to wood structures are not required to be listed but must be made to certain ASTM or ANSI standards. All hangers on a sprinkler system must be capable of supporting five times the weight of the water filled pipe plus an extra 250 pounds. The extra 250 pounds is a safety factor that provides for a sprinkler fitter catching themselves on the sprinkler piping if they should lose their balance. However, you may not support any non-system component with sprinkler piping or hangers (clumsy sprinkler fitter's excluded). As a very general rule of thumb, each piece of sprinkler system piping is provided with a hanger. There are many more rules for hangers and many more exceptions to the rules, we will discuss more about hangers later. Summary One of the more important points of this chapter is that every component of a sprinkler system is D required to be Jjited. Nearly every component must be made to a national standard. And the requirements are as varied as the importance of each component. Keep in mind that every component = be approved. If you can't remember the NFPA's definition of "approved", it is worth one final look. NFPA 13, Chapter 3.2. I defines "approved" as, "Acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. " 156

CHAPTER 15 HAZARD AND COMMODITY CLASSIFICATIONS It is our privilege to protect lives and property from the devastation that fire can bring, Yet how are we to accomplish that without an understanding of those things that we are trying to protect? In this chapter, we will explore the way buildings and their contents are classified so that we may provide an appropriate level of protection as prescribed by the codes and standards. As you can imagine, protecting people and property from fire in a meeting room is less demanding than protecting a facility that upholsters furniture. As with most situations in our industry, it was the insurance companies that started classifying buildings with regards to their vulnerability to damage from fire. In the late 1800's there were some 584 classifications for use by the insurance industry (J.H Finnegan, Statistics of the National Board of Fire Undenvriters 1956). This was eventually reduced to 26 classes in 1932. By 1946, the NBFU had gone back to 100 classes but had divided them into six categories based on the type of construction of the building. As you learned in Chapter 12 of this text, the NFPA subscribes to this line of thinking and still classifies buildings according to type of construction. It is important to remember that the Building Codes pay special attention to the types of construction when determining whether fire sprinkler protection will be required. These days, NFPA 13 contains three basic classes of general occupancies and seven basic classes for storage occupancies. This chapter will help you to understand the differences between the types of general occupancies. The storage chapters later in this text will address the classification of storage commodities. NFPA 13 addresses the three different occupancies in a different manner from the building codes and even other NFPA documents, The building codes generally address the use, size and construction of a building. In fact, NFPA 13 is very clear to indicate that the classifications we are discussing are only intended to help know which rules to use for designing, installing and supplying a fire sprinkler system. NFPA 13 states the following in Chapter 5: 5.1* Classification of Occupanéies. 5.1.1 Occupancy classifications for this standard shall relate to sprinkler design, installation, and water supply requirements only. 5.1.2 Occupancy classifications shall not be intended to be a general classification of occupancy hazards. 157

## Page 164

NFPA 13 considers the four following factors for classifying an occupancy: Combustibility of Products o Amount of Combustible Products Height of Storage Rate of Heat Release Using these factors, the NFPA 13 Committee has established three basic classes of general occupancy. They are Light Hazard, Ordinary Hazard and Extra Hazard. As you can see from their names, they each represent a different level of challenge. Ordinary and Extra Hazard occupancies are further divided to cover the broad range of conditions found in the built environment. Can you see where buildings might present different challenges to us, depending on what is found within the building? What should you do if a building has wood working in it instead of just an office environment? Would we need more water delivered from a sprinkler system for the wood working areas if there were a fire? Let's explore the definitions of each of these occupancies as spelled out in NFPA 13: 5.2 * Light Hazard Occupancies/ Light hazard occupancies shall be defined as occupancies or portions of other occupancies where the quantity and/or combustibility of contents is low and fires with relatively low rates of heat release are expected. 5.3 Ordinary Hazard Occupancies. 5.3.1 * Ordinary Hazard (Group 1). Ordinary hazard (Group 1) occupancies shall be defined as occupancies or portions of other occupancies where combustibility is low, quantity of combustibles is moderate, stockpiles of combustibles do not exceed 8 ft (2.4 m), and fires with moderate rates of heat release are expected. 5.3.2 * Ordinary Hazard (Group 2). Ordinary hazard (Group 2) occupancies shali be defined as occupancies or portions of other occupancies where the quantity and combustibility of contents are moderate to high, stockpiles do not exceed 12 ft (3.7 m), and fires with moderate to high rates of heat release are expected 5.4 Extra Hazard Occupancies: 5.4.1 * Extra Hazard (Group 1). Extra hazard (Group 1) occupancies shall be defined as occupancies or portions of other occupancies where the quantity and combustibility of contents are very high and dust, lint, or other materials are present, introducing the probability of rapidly developing fires with high rates of heat release but with little or no combustible or flammable liquids. 5.4.2* Extra Hazard (G/oup 2). Extra hazard (Group 2) occupancies shall be e defined as occupancies or portions of other occupancies with moderate to substantial amounts of flammable or combustible liquids or occupancies where shielding of combustibles is extensive. 158

## Page 165

The definitions from NFPA 13 can be summarized as shown in this chart: Hazard Definition Product Combustibili Quantity of Combustibles Heat Release Rates Flammable Liquids Shielding of Combustibles Light Hazard Low Low Low None None Ordinary Hazard Group One Low Moderate (8' high max) Moderate to High None None Ordinary Hazard Group Two Moderate to High Moderate to High (12' high max) Moderate to High None (Limited) None Extra Hazard Group One Very High Very High High & Rapidly Develo ing None (Limited) None Extra Hazard Group Two Very High very High High & Rapidly Develo ing Moderate to Substantial Anticipated NFPA 13 contains some examples of hazard classifications that you can use as a guideline when determining which hazard to use in detailing a sprinkler system. These examples are located in the Annex of NFPA 13 in sections A.5.2 tln•ough A.5.4. The annex is a good list that helps you determine the hazard classification for any given project. It is imponant to note that the lists shown in the Annex represent an average expectation of the factors in the chart above. If there is more of a fuel load and higher characteristics of combustibility, then these factors need to be accounted for when considering which hazard to use in design. A Light Hazard occupancy is the least challenging of the five levels of hazard classifications. Offices, churches and residential occupancies are typical examples of the light hazard classification. Fuel loads in these buildings are relatively small (as compared to the factories and warehouses that used to be sprinklered before it was common to sprinkler offices, churches and residential occupancies). There should be no manufacturing or storage in light hazard spaces, although buildings are allowed to have individual spaces protected in accordance with different classification rules. The same building might have offices and storage. The office area is permitted to be protected using the light hazard rules and the storage is permitted to be protected in accordance with the storage rules appropriate for the commodity being stored. The separation requirements for these areas will be covered later in this text. Light hazard occupancies offer the most options for design of the sprinkler system, while requiring the least amount of water for control of a fire event. Examples of light hazard occupancies include (see A.5.2 0fNFPA 13): Churches Clubs Hospitals Residential Unused Attics Libraries, except large stack rooms 159

## Page 166

A fire in an Ordinary Hazard occupancy is more challenging to control than a fire in a light hazard occupancy. Because there is such a wide range of facilities that fall under the ordinary hazard classification, there are two separate categories under ordinary hazard. The least challenging of the two categories are Ordinary Hazard Group 1 (OHI) occupancies. These occupancies are generally made up of light manufacturing and service industries with mostly noncombustible products. There should be no storage higher than 8 feet within (OHI) occupancies, Even if the storage is lower than 8 ft, the classification might not be OHI, Tn order to qualify as OHI, the use of the space must be predominantly non-combustible. If storage is present, the rules for miscellaneous storage or low piled storage must be followed. The lilles for miscellaneous storage will be discussed in the storage chapters of this text. Examples of OHI are as follows (see A.5.3.1 in NFPA 13): o Automobile parking and showrooms Bakeries o Electronic plants o Laundries Restaurant service areas The most challenging category under ordinary hazard is the Ordinary Hazard Group 2 (01-12) occupancy. OH2 occupancies are generally made up of manufacturing and processing facilities that have a higher amount and combustibility of products than is found in OHI occupancies. The miscellaneous storage in OH2 occupancies is allowed to be stored as high as 12 feet. An extremely limited amount of flammable or combustible liquids are allowed in OH2 occupancies. Generally speaking, the following types of occupancies are OH2 (see A.5.3.2 of NFPA 13): Machine Shops Repair Garages Post Offices Paper Mills Printing/Publishing Tire Manufacturing A fire in an extra hazard occupancy is the highest challenge fire that can be protected using the occupancy hazard method. Extra Hazard Group 1 (EHI) occupancies may have hydraulic machinery and some closed equipment with flammable fluids. They may also have lint or dust suspended in the air, as in some textile manufacturing facilities. Some examples of EHI include (see A.5.4.1 of NFPA 13): Assembly lines with hydraulic equipment Particle Board Manufacturing Textile Picking Textile Carding Saw Mills Upholstering with Plastic Foam 160

## Page 167

Extra Hazard Group 2 (EH2) is the highest hazard we contemplate protecting wilh the occupancy hazard method. EH2 occupancies have more than just small amounts of flammable and combustible fluids (although they must be under the quantities allowed by NFPA 30). For storage and use of larger quantities of flammable or combustible liquids, the sprinkler requirements of NFPA 30 must be used. Typically, the flammable or combustible liquids protected in accordance with NFPA 13 are usually found in open systems that allow these fluids to pyrolyzc vcry rapidly when exposed to higher arnbien[ temperatures, Extra Hazard Group 2 also includes facilities where extensive shielding of a fire will occur because of what actually occurs in the building, not because of the building structure. The water from sprinklers may not be able to reach the fire because of this extensive shielding. Extra Hazard Group 2 occupancies include (see A.5.4.2 in NFPA 13): o Flammable Liquids Spraying Manufactured Home Assembly Facilities o Varnishing Processes. What should you do when a building has more than one type of occupancy? Well, the answer is it depends. Most often, you may protect the different areas using the different rules for the hazard category that describes that area. If some part of a building has an area that meets the description of Ordinary Hazard, you protect that area using the rules for Ordinary Hazard occupancies. If there are areas in the same building that meet the rules for Light Hazard, then you would use the rules for Light Hazard occupancies in those areas. If there is a wall with openings, or even curtain walls at the ceiling level, this would be enough to separate areas by occupancy. Ifthe areas are open to each other with no separation, then you could use the rules for the more challenging hazard (Ordinary Hazard in our example) for the entire area. Alternatively, you may want to use the rules for the higher hazard 15 feet or more into the lower hazard space. The idea of using the rules for the higher hazard to protect 15 feet beyond its own area originated in some of the older rules for Storage Occupancies. Chapter 11 of NFPA 13 says it like this: 11.1.2 For buildings with two or more adjacent occupancies that are not physically separated by a barrier or partition capable of delaying heat from afirå in one area from fusing sprinklers in the adjacent arearthe required sprinkler protection for the more demanding occupancy shall extend 15 ft (4.6 m) beyond its perimeter. " Protecting occupancies that have Storage is very different from using the Occupancy Hazard Method. The first thing you need to know is that the things we store in a building are called "commodities" in the NFPA documents. Classifying storage commodities is covered in Chapter 35 of this book. 161

Chapter 16 Water Supply Requirements and Testing In order for any fire sprinkler system to work, it needs to be connected to a supply of water that has sufficient volume (flow), pressure (energy) and capacity (duration) to suppress the fire or control it for a long enough period of time that the fire runs out of fuel, or fire fighters can finish the job of putting the fire out. This chapter will focus on the use of public water utility mains as the source of the water supply for the fire sprinlder system. Other chapters of this text will deal with the use of other water supplies such as pressure tanks or atmospheric tanks and pumps. (This chapter is an excellent reference text for NICET Work Element 13007, Water Supply Requirements, which covers the methods used to analyze the strength of the water supply and its ability to provide water to a fire protection system. The importance of an adequate water supply is summed up from this quote from the Alliance insurance company publication Simplified Water Supply Testing, "Without enough water even the best equipped fire department and the best trained fire fighters can do very little to bring a fire under control and preserve life and property." Similarly, the best designed fire protection system in the world will be useless without a sufficient water supply. Flow Flow is the expression of the quantity of water that passes by a given point in a piping system in a given period of time. Because the flow is associated with the concept of quantity, it is given the mathematical symbol of "Q" in most formulas and equations dealing with flow. Flow is generally expressed in terms of a quantity over a unit of time. In the English system of units, flow is most frequently represented in terms of gallons per minute, although it also can be expressed in terms of cubic feet per minute, gallons per second or cubic feet per second, Ln the metric system, flow can be expressed in terms of Liters per minute, Liters per second or cubic meters per minute. Any quantity divided by a unit of time is acceptable, In this text, we will most frequently use gallons per minute. If other units are used, we will make sure we point them out. Make sure when working on any project that you understand what units of flow are being used by the people that you are communicating with. More than one project has been messed up by someone reading a number off of a report and then getting the units inconect. 163

## Page 170

Pressure The pressure is the expression of the energy held in the water that is responsible for pushing the water through the pipes in the system. Pressure and flow are related, but different variables. The higher the pressure, the more flow that will result in the system, because the water has more energy. However, as the water flows through the pipe, it rubs against the walls of thc pipc and loses energy. It also takes energy to get the water to move uphill against gravity, so the pressure in a fire protection system high up is always going to be smaller than the pressure at a lower elevation in the same system. Likewise, water gains energy when it goes downhill, so the pressure at the bottom of a system will always be the greatest pressure. See the Basic Hydraulics Chapter of this text for more information on pressure. Pressure is generally measured in units of force over area. In the English system of units, the pressure is measured in pounds per square foot (psf) or pounds per square inch (psi). In the metric system of measurement, pressure is measured in units of force over area, and then given the special names of a Pascal or a bar. The bar has the distinction of being the unit of measure approximately equal to atmospheric pressure. In this text, we will usually use pounds per square inch (psi) as the units for expressing pressure. Duration The fire protection system will need to discharge water at the correct flow and pressure for as long as the fire still needs to be controlled. This might only be a few minutes (for a sprinkler system that has extinguished a fire) or it might be a few hours (for a sprinkler system in a complex industrial facility where the fire department needs time to set up their equipment and complete putting out the fire that has been controlled by the sprinkler system). The NFPA standards contain the rules for the minimum required supply for different types of sprinkler systems. Typical durations range from 10 minutes (for single-family dwellings under NFPA 13D) to 120 minutes (for some storage occupancies per NFPA 13). The general assumption is made in fire protection that the public water main that belongs to the local utility is sufficiently reliable that it meets all of the duration requirements of the NFPA standards. No specific test of the water supply is necessary in order to determine the duration; however, this variable still should not be taken for granted. Whenever connecting a sprinkler system to a public utility, the sprinkler contractor should ask the question, "how reliable is this utility?" In order to answer this question, you may need to have knowledge of the other systems that are connected to the utility and how well the utility supplies them with water. In general, water utility customers do not find it acceptable to be without water for even short periods of time. Water utilities spend a great deal of money making sure that they have redundant systems and the ability to overcome serious problems. For the most part, public utilities are very reliable and are the best choice for the supply of a fire protection system. 164

## Page 171

Evaluating Water Supplies The most frequent method used for evaluating a water supply is to actually flow water from the supply and take some measurements while the water is flowing. While this is the most popular method of evaluating the water supply, it is not the only method. Methods of evaluating water supplies include: Water authority (utility) projections Predictions from an engineer — prepared by looking at potential supplies and anticipated demand o Flow testing The projections prepared by a water utility generally take into account future use in the system and potential expansion of the system, depending on the master plan established by the utility. Such projections may be reinforced from time-to-time by the utility conducting a flow test of the supply to compare to their predictions. Predictions from an engineer may be necessary when the water supply is not in place. This frequently occurs when the building with the fire protection system and the water supply are both in the planning stages. The engineer will need to predict the abilities of the water supply by considering future .growth in the demands connected to the water supply in addition to the use of the supply when it is new. Of all the methods used for evaluating water supplies, the flow test is the only one that does not directly account for future use. This means that the results of the test need to be adjusted to account for the fact that the water supply may not be tested at the time when it is under the most stress (demand), Reasonable adjustments will be discussed at the end of this chapter in this text. Flow tests are not only performed for the obvious reason of determining the strength of the water supply, but they are also performed for a variety of other reasons: To determine the flow available at a given pressure from the water supply To determine the pressure available at a given flow from the water supply To determine the effect of dead-end mains or small mains on the system To determine the effect of old cast iron, concrete or even wood mains on a system To spot check developments (expansion) of the water supply and their effects To make periodic checks of the availability of the supply to compare to predictions To make sure that private water systems with private water sources are continuing to meet the demand requirements of the fire protection systems To account for unusual geographic features that are difficult to predict 165

## Page 172

Water Supply Requirements and Testing The water supply test will be performed to determine how strong the water supply is. Then the fire protection system will be calculated to determine how much flow and pressure will be required from the water supply. The available supply will be compared to the fire protection system demand. If the water supply exceeds the demand of the fire protection system, everything will work fine. If the water supply is not capable of meeting the demand of the fire protection system, then either the fire protection system will need to be redesigned to meet the available supply, or the water supply will need to be augmented with a pump and/or additional water source. When calculating the flow demand of a fire sprinkler system, NFPA 13 requires not only enough water to satisfy the open sprinklers, but also sufficient water to allow fire fighters to put hose streams into operation. The fire fighters might put hose streams into service from inside or outside the building. The amount of water that is required to be added to the sprinkler demand in order to determine the total flow demand is included in Table 11.2.3.1.1 in NFPA 13 for light, ordinary and extra hazard occupaßcies and du•oughout Chapter 12 for storage occupancies. Safety Considerations Before conducting any water supply flow test, it is important to consider safety concerns. The following issues need to be considered: o Site grading where is the water going to go after it comes out of the fire hydrant? Is it going to flood low lying areas? Is it going to wash out loose dirt or gravel near the hydrant? During the test, it is possible for several hundred gallons of water to discharge from the hydrant, so plan for where the water is going to go. o Water flow direction — see the discussion above for loose dirt and gravel as well as nearby low-lying areas, • Objects near hydrants — water can flow from hydrants with enough force to strip the paint off of nearby cars and cause damage to any object nearby. Survey the sight to make sure all objects are clear of where the water is going to discharge from the hydrant. o Safety equipment — make sure that you have correct equipment to keep everyone at the test location safe. For the person taking the flow readings, safety glasses should be used to protect their eyes from water discharging at high velocity. If hoses are going to be used to redirect flow to safe locations, the hoses need to be sufficiently restrained so that they won't whip around and strike people or objects. 166
