Selecting Hydrants for Flow Test In order to perform a flow test, the pressure and flow in the water main need to be found at a known location. Since most water mains do not have pressure gauges built in at regular intervals, nor do they have flow meters in the pipes, other means of determining the pressure and flow at a given point need to be found. Fire.hydrants provide a convenient method for determining flow and pressure. Even though fire hydrants do not have built-in pressure gauges or flow mctcrs, thcrc arc rclativcly easy methods of determining these variables at a fire hydrant, Two fire hydrants will be needed for each flow test. The first hydrant is known as the "gauge hydrant" and the second hydrant is known as the "flowing hydrant". The "gauge hydrant" is given its name because this is the hydrant to which the pressure gauge will be attached in order to read the pressure in the water main during the test. The "flow hydrant" is given its name because this is the hydrant that will be used to create flow from the water main. The purpose of the flow test is to determine the water supply that needs to be available at a specific piece of property, Fire hydrants need to be selected so that they are as close as possible to the property being protected. If the water main passing near the property is a dead- end main (water can only come from the utility in a single direction) as shown in Figure 16-3, then the gauge hydrant should be the one upstream of the flow hydrant, as shown in Figure 16-3. Building Gauge Hydrant Flow Hydrant Figure 16-3 Gauge and Flow Hydrants Near a Dead-End Main If the water main passing near the property is a part of a gridded or looped water delivery system, then the decision as to which hydrant to pick as the gauge hydrant and the flow hydrant is more difficult. The results of the flow test are going to be valid at the location of the gauge hydrant, so this hydrant should be as close to the property as possible, as shown in Figure 16-4. The flow hydrant should then be the next closest hydrant. 169

## Page 176

Building Gauge Hydrant Flow Hydrant Figure 16-4 Gauge and Flow Hydrants Near a Gridded Main However, if the flow hydrant is very far from the property, or if there is a valve closed between the flow hydrant and the gauge hydrant, then the flow created by opening the flow hydrant may not be a reasonable representation of the flow truly available at the building, so the hydrants should be reversed. In rare cases, it may be necessary to open more than one hydrant to create a great deal of flow. In this case, any additional flow hydrants should be as close as possible to the property in question. Test Data During the test, there will be three pieces of data that will be very important to collect: the static pressure, the residual pressure, and the flow from the hydrant. The following is•a description regarding the importance of each of these variables. The static pressure is the pressure in the water main (at the gauge hydrant) without any water flowing from the flowing hydrant. In a petfect world, this would be the pressure in the water main with no water flowing anywhere in the water utility system. But it is not reasonable to expect to run a test when no one else is using water in the entire water utility. Instead, we consider the condition as "static" (meaning that no water is flowing) to be relative to the fact that we have not yet opened the flow hydrant. This is actually good fire protection in that when a fire occurs, it is likely that water will also be in use elsewhere in the water utility's distribution. The residual pressure is the pressure that is left over in the water utility main (at the gauge hydrant) when water is flowing from the flow hydrant. This pressure only has meaning when expressed in conjunction with the flow from the hydrant. In other words, knowing that the residual pressure in a given water main is 25 psi is meaningless unless you know the flow that was necessary to create that residual pressure. A residual pressure of 25 psi has one meaning 170

## Page 177

when the flow associated with it is 2000 gpm, and another meaning when the flow associated with it is 200 gpm. You should get used to expressing residual pressures and flows together. The residual pressure will always be lower than the static pressure. This is because the water supply uses up some of its stored energy in getting the water to move. In some cases, it is possible that the residual pressure will rise during a flow test above the value of the original static pressure. In this case, what has most likely happened is that a pump in the water utility system has sensed the flow from the hydrant and turned on to stabilize pressure in the main. If this happens during a test, the flow should be stopped and a new static pressure reading taken with the new pump running. Then flow can be resumed to get a new residual pressure reading. The flow is the quantity of watcr cxiting the fire hydrant over a period of time. As discussed earlier in this chapter, the flow is usually expressed in terms of gallons per minute (gpm). In most cases, flow meters that read flow directly in tems of gallons per minute are not considered sufficiently accurate enough to perform hydrant flow tests, so a device called a Pitot Gauge (described earlier in this chapter) is used to determine the flow from the hydrant. The Pitot Gauge was invented in 1730 by a man named Henri Pitot and has changed little in the almost 300 years since his original design. When placed in the flow stream, a Pitot Gauge provides a reading of the velocity pressure of the water exiting the hydrant in terms of psi. This value can be converted to a flow in gpm using the following formula: Q = 29.83cd2(Fp Where: Q = flow from the hydrant in gallons per minute c = hydrant coefficient (0.9, 0.8 or 0.7 depending on hydrant configuration) d = inside diameter of hydrant butt (outlet) from which water is flowing Pp = velocity pressure from Pitot Gauge When taking a Pitot Gauge reading, the device needs to be held properly in the flow stream of the water exiting the hydrant. While holding the Pitot Gauge firmly in both hands, the blade needs to be placed so that the tip is in the center of the flow stream, approximately one-half of the diameter of the outlet away from the edge of the outlet, as shown in Figure 16-5. 171

## Page 178

Taking pitot roading at hydgønt but! Figure 16-5 Taking Pitot Gauge Reading Note that the tip of the Pitot Gauge is not actually inside the hydrant, but a short distance away from the hydrant (about li/4 inches from a 2h inch outlet). This is where the Pitot Gauge is calibrated to work properly. If the tip of the gauge slips inside the hydrant, the assumption that the velocity pressure is the only pressure acting on the water (a key assumption in developing the Pitot Gauge formula discussed above) is no longer valid, and the formula developed to convert the Pitot Gauge reading to a flow in gpm is no longer valid. Many people, when performing a flow test on a hydrant brace the Pitot Gauge against the hydrant butt to steady themselves while getting a reading on the gauge. While this does help steady their hand, it creates a false reading because it allows the tip to curve inside of the hydrant, You either need to use a strong hand to hold the Pitot Gauge in the proper position, or you need to purchase a Pitot Gauge that has a brace built into the blade so that you can hold it against the hydrant butt and still keep the tip in the correct location, There are also device manufacturers that build Pitot Gauges into devices that screw on to the hydrant outlet and automatically hold the gauge in the correct location. Such gauges are nice because they eliminate some variability in the test, Most Pitot Gauges are accurate over the entire range of the readings on the gauge. However, the formula described above makes certain assumptions about the water discharging from the hydrant butt. The first assumption is that the velocity pressure will be at least 10 psi. If the velocity pressure is less than 10 psi, then there is a chance that the water is not discharging from the entire circumference of the outlet, and the formula for converting the velocity pressure reading to a flow will not be valid. If the velocity pressure reading is less than 10 psi on a Pitot Gauge during a test, shut off the flow from the hydrant and place a reducer on the outlet to make the flow from the hydrant discharge from a smaller outlet, this will raise the velocity pressure and the accuracy of the test. 172

## Page 179

The second assumption regarding Lhe velocity pressure during the test is that the velocity pressure will not exceed 30 psi during the test. When the velocity pressure exceeds 30 psi, it is possible that the hydrant is experiencing feedback while trying to discharge so much water and the test conditions will also be invalid. If the Pitot Gauge reading is greater than 30 psi, it is a good idea to open additional outlets on the hydrant simultaneously to allow the greater flow to discharge from multiple outlets. This reduces the individual flow at any single outlet. Hydrant Coefficients In the formula discussed earlier in the chapter for converting the Pitot Gauge reading in psi to a flow in gpm, there was a variable "c" that we called the "hydrant coefficient". The hydrant coefficient is a measure of how easy it is for the water to come up through the barrel of the hydrant and discharge from the outlet. Hydrants that make a smooth transition from the barrel to the outlet have high coefficients (as high as 0.9) and hydrants where the water has Io travel a complex path before it discharges from the outlet have lower coefficients (as low as 0.7). Figure 16-6 shows three different fire hydrants where the barrel is making the transition to the outlet. In each case, the thick arrow shows the water traveling up the barrel and out of the outlet. These three fire hydrants make up the vast majority of configurations on the market. If you encounter a fire hydrant that does not meet one of these three configurations, then you need to contact the manufacturer and ask them about the flow test coefficient for that particular model hydrant. They should be able to help you out. Smooth transition from hydrant wall to outlet (c = 0.9) Squared off transition from hydrant wall to outlet (c = 0.8) Squared off transition that penetrates behind hydrant wall (c = 0.7) Figure 16-6 IYpical Hydrant Coefficients In order to determine which kind of outlet you have for running the flow test, you will need to stick your hand inside the hydrant. You will only need to do this for the flow hydrant. The hydrant coefficient is not necessary to know for the gauge hydrant. This is why we recommended a flashlight in the list of equipment to bring to a flow test. Prior to opening the hydrant and flowing water from it, take off the outlet cap and shine the flashlight inside the 173

## Page 180

ban•el of the hydrant. Make sure that there are no objects inside the hydrant that will cause problems during the test. Once you are convinced that the hydrant barrel is clear, slide your finger along the transition from the outlet to the barrel and determine the hydrant coefficient as follows: o If the transition is smooth and curved, as shown in the left hand portion of Figure 16-6, then the hydrant has a coefficient of 0.9. If the transition is squared off and goes straight down to the barrel as shown in the middle of Figure 16-6, then the coefficient is 0.8. o Ifthe transition is squared off and protrudes back into the barrel so that the water encounters a horizontal obstruction coming up the barrel, as shown in the right hand portion of Figure 16-6, then the hydrant will have a coefficient of 0.7. Procedure for Conducting the Flow Test The following general procedure should be used when conducting a flow test. There are other methods that can be used with different situations and different pieces of equipment. This procedure assumes that only a single outlet on a single hydrant will be sufficient for creating the necessary flow. If additional outlets are required or additional hydrants are required to be opened to create additional flow, the basic procedure can still be used, but the opening of hydrants will need to be coordinated. After the procedure, the steps that need additional commentary will be discussed in greater detail: 1) Assemble the necessary tools as discussed at the beginning of this chapter. 2) Select which hydrant will be the gauge hydrant and which hydrant will be the flow hydrant. 3) Remove the 2h inch cap from one of the outlets on the gauge hydrant and attach the outlet cap that has the pressure gauge. 4) Using the hydrant wrench, open the gauge hydrant. 5) Record the static pressure. 6) Follow the safety procedures discussed at the beginning of this chapter for determining where the flow is going to go. 7) Remove one of the 2h inch outlet caps from the flow hydrant that will permit safe flow of water from the hydrant. 8) Using the flashlight as described above, make sure that they hydrant is clear and determine the hydrant coefficient. 9) Using a ruler, determine the actual inside diameter of the outlet in inches. 174

## Page 181

10) Using a hydrant wrench, open the flow hydrant. 1 1) Place the Pitot Gauge in the flow stream to obtain a velocity pressure of the water discharging from the hydrant. 12) Signal back to the gauge hydrant to take the residual pressure at the same time that you are obtaining the velocity pressure reading. 13) Record all data. 14) Shut down the flowing hydrant. As the water drains from the barrel of the hydrant, put your hand over the outlet. You should be able to feel the vacuum created by the drainage. If you do not feel the vacuum, the barrel is not draining conectly. 15) At the gauge hydrant, shut off the hydrant and remove the hydrant cap/pressure gauge. As the water drains from the balTel of the hydrant, put your hand over the outlet, you should be able to feel the vacuum created by the drainage. If you do not feel the vacuum, the barrel is not draining correctly. 16) Evaluate the data from the test. 17) Make appropriate adjustments to the water supply to account for elevation differences between the hydrant outlet and the base of the riser where the fire protection system will 18) Make appropriate adjustments to the water supply to account for reasonable daily and seasonal fluctuations in the water supply. Opening and Closing Hydrants Most water utilities do not want sprinkler contractors touching their hydrants. In these cases, you will need tö coordinate the flow test so that the employees of the water utility are the ones that are actually opening or closing the hydrants. If you are the one to actually open or close the hydrants, remember that you are making a significant change to the water delivery system when you do so. Water delivery systems do not handle the shock of suddenly staffing or suddenly stopping the flow of water. Fire hydrants should always be opened and closed very slowly, to give the water delivery system time to deal with the changing flow conditions. If a fire hydrant is opened or closed too quickly, a hydraulic shock might occur that allows a condition called "water hammer" to start. "Water hammer" is a series of pressure waves that bounce back and foflh (oscillate) inside of the pipe. When the pressure waves collide, they add their energy to each other and cause severe damage inside of the pipe, Whenever opening or closing a fire hydrant, always do so very slowly in order to prevent the occurrence of water hammer! 175

## Page 182

Evaluating the Data from the Test Once the test has been performed, thc data needs to be evaluated so that it can be understood and used to determine whether or not the water supply is sufficient for the fire protection system that will go into the building. The easiest way to evaluate the data is to draw a graph of the water supply on graph paper. Unfortunately, regular graph paper is not sufficient for this task because the relationship between flow and pressure is not a linear relationship, Luckily, special graph paper has been developed to address this concern, which allows us to plot the results of the test as a line. Plotting the test as a line has a distinct advantage in that wc only need two points to determine a line, and we only have two points to work with (static and residual). If we were to work with regular graph paper, we would need three points to draw a curve, and we only have two points to work with, So we would be in trouble. The special graph paper that we use is called "Log 1.85" graph paper and is made by plotting the flow on the "x" axis (horizontal) with the pressure on the "y" axis (vertical). The flow axis is not linear. The flow axis is laid out to the 1.85 power. For example, if flow of 100 gpm was going to be represented by 1 inch (from the zero flow line), then 200 gpm would be represented by a line 3.6 inches from the zero flow line (2 raised to the 1.85 power is 3.6). Using this same scale, 300 gpm would be represented by a line 7.6 inches from the zero flow line (3 raised to the 1.85 power is 7.6). See Figure 16-7 for an example of Log 1.85 graph paper. The good news is that you do not need to make your own Log 1.85 graph paper, ithe NFSA sells pads of graph paper for you to use through its Resource Center. Typical Log 1.85 graph paper will have several scales on the flow axis. This allows for maximum flexibility for the user. You are not required to stick with these scales. You can create your own scale by multiplying the numbers given by a constant. In effect, this redefines the base measurement, but maintains the 1.85 relationship between lines. For example, consider the measurement system above with the lines representing 0 flow, 100 gpm flow (1 inch away from the 0 flow line), 200 gpm flow (3.6 inches away from the 0 flow line) and 300 gpm flow (7.6 inches away from the 0 flow line). If we didn't want to use this scale, we could multiply all of the flow values by 2 so that the line 1 inch away represents 200 gpm (100 x 2), the line 3.6 inches away represents 400 gpm (200 x 2) and the line 7.6 inches away represents 600 gpm (300 x 2). If you are going to alter the scale on a piece of Log 1.85 graph paper, make sure that you do it clearly so that everyone knows what you did. If you are using a prepared piece of log 1.85 graph paper with multiple scales, make sure that you circle the scale that you used, or cross out the other scales so that everyone reading the graph is clear about which scale applies. 176

This is an important point to know for most water supplies. Most water utilities don't want the water supply drawn below 20 psi, so you need to know what the maximum flow is that the water supply can provide without getting to this point. For this example, the water supply can deliver a maximum of about 875 gpm at 20 psi. Even if a pump is added to the fire protection system, it can't increase the flow any more than 875 gpm without drawing the water supply down below 20 psit 178

Any information that can be represented by graph paper can also be represented by a formula. Rather than rely on reading a graph to plot the results of a flow test, you can also express the results of a flow test with a formula as follows: 1.85 Where:P = pressure at any given flow PR = residual pressure from flow test PS = static pressure from flow test Q = flow at which you want to know the pressure QR = flow at residual pressure in gpm converted from Pitot Gauge velocity pressure The results from any flow test can be plugged into the equation to yield a unique equation for the specific water supply being tested. For example, for the water supply example above (with the static pressure of 80 psi, and the residual pressure of 47 psi at 630 gpm), the equation can be filled in as follows: 1.85 1.85 1.85 +80 = (47-80 627.5 627.5 The last version of the equation above can be used to determine the pressure at any given flow available from this water supply. For example, the equation predicts that at a flow of 400 gpm, the water supply will provide a pressure of 65.6 psi as follows: 1.85 1.85 400 +80 = 65.6 P = (-33) 627.5 627.5 Note that the pressure predicted by the formula (65.6) is very close to the pressure read from the graph (66). The advantage of the formula is that it removes some of the variability found in interpolating results from a graph. The disadvantage to the formula is that it is more cumbersome to use than the simplicity of the graph. Either method is acceptable for fire protection. Alternative for Finding Velocity Pressure If you don't have a calibrated Pitot Gauge when you need to run a flow test, there is an alternative method for running the test that can be used. The alternative is less accurate than the use of a Pitot Gauge, but it can be used in a pinch. In order to use the alternative, you will need an extra 2V2 inch hydrant cap. with a pressure gauge attached. This is over and above the cap with pressure gauge used on the gauge hydrant. 180

## Page 187

In order to run the test, use the same procedure as described above for thc test, cxccpt prior to opening the flowing hydrant, attach the extra hydrant cap and pressure gauge to the 21/2 inch outlet that will not be used for flowing water. Then open the hydrant to allow the flow to discharge from the other 2h inch outlet. The velocity pressure of the water discharging from the 2V2 inch outlet will create an equal and opposite reaction at the other 2h inch outlet, with the pressure gauge on it (see Figure 16-9). The normal pressure at this gauge will match the velocity pressure. This value can be used in all of the formulas above where the Pitot Gauge pressure is used, Figure 16-9 Equal and Opposite Reaction at Hydrant Cap with Gauge Use of Other Outlets for Flow Up until now, we have been talking about using the 2h inch outlet to discharge water from the fire hydrant. This is the most accurate way to use the formula for converting the Pitot Gauge reading into a flow. The formula needs the input of the diameter of the opening where water is flowing and assumes that the flow is across the entire opening. Most fire hydrants have another size opening that is 4, 4h or 5 inches in diameter and is used by the fire department when they need really significant volumes of water. The large outlet on the fire hydrant is often called the "steamer connection" recalling the days when fire departments first started using horse-drawn steam engines. These larger pieces of fire apparatus could move more water than any of the hand pumped pieces of the past and could utilize larger openings in fire hydrants. When fire hydrants were redesigned in the late 1800's to add the larger outlet to accommodate the steam engines, the new connection was called the "steamer connection" and the name has stuck for more than 130 years. When the steamer connection is used, it introduces a small amount of variability in the flow test. The steamer connection should not be used unless there is no other way to increase the 181

flow. If the steamer connection is used, an additional correction factor needs to be added to the formula that converts the Pitot Gauge reading to the flow in gallons per minute as shown in Table 16-2 below, The concept of the additional conversion factor was in NFPA 291, the Recommended Practice for Flow Testing Fire Hydrants on Private Water Supplies, The NFPA discontinued publishing this recommended practice because it did not need to be maintained like other standards, and the language has not completely been picked up by other NFPA documents, but the concept is still valid, The new formula to follow for converting the Pitot Gauge reading into a flow in gpm when the steamer connection is used to discharge water is as follows: Q=29.83Cncd2 Pp Velocity Pressure from Pitot Gauge Taken From Discharge Out of Steamer Connection 2 si 3 si 4 si 5 si 6 si Correction Factor (CH) 0.97 0.92 0.89 0.86 0.84 0.83 Table 16-2 Correction Factors men Using Steamer Connection For example, consider the situation where the steamer connection is used on a fire hydrant (smoothness coefficient of 0.9) with a diameter of 4 inches and the Pitot pressure turns out to be 4 psi during the test. Without making the correction, you might believe that the flow from the hydrant is: Q = 29.83cd2JÄp = = 859 However, after using the correction factor, the true flow is closer to: Q = 29.83%cd2JÄp = = 765 By using the correct formula, the flow is more closely approximated to 765 gpm. Without using the extra correction coefficient, the flow would be over-predicted by 94 gpm or about 11%. 182

## Page 189

Adjustments for Elevation Differences The results of the flow test are accurate at the elevation of the gauge on the gauge hydrant. If the sprinkler system is going to be installed at a different elevation, a correction to the static pressure and residual pressure need to be made. Without an adjustment to the flow test data, the fire sprinkler system might not get the pressure it needs to work sufficiently. There arc two acceptable methods of making the adjustment. The first method is to determine the difference in elevation between the base of the riser on the fire protection system and subtract or add it to the values of the static and residual pressure data obtained at the gauge hydrant using an adjustment of 0.433 times the elevation (in feet). Elevations lower than the fire protection system are subtracted and elevations above the fire protection system are added. For example, if the sprinkler system is going to be installed at the top of a hill, 50 ft pressure measured during the test were 75 psi and 59 psi respectively, the results of the test need to be adjusted by subtracting 22 psi (0.433 x 50 ft elevation difference). That means that the effective results of the flow test are a static pressure of 53 psi (75 — 22) and a residual pressure of 37 psi (59 — 22). Note that the Pitot Gauge pressure does not need to be adjusted because it is only used Io convert Lo a flow at the hydrant. The second method of adjusting for the difference in elevation is to actually perform the hydraulic calculations all the way to the hydrant, taking into account true elevation changes in each step. In the example above, the water supply data would not be adjusted, but the demand calculations for the fire protection system would include another 22 psi in pressure loss, increasing the demand by this amount and forcing the water supply to be strong enough to get the water up the hill. Adjustments for Daily and Seasonal Use The results of the flow test are accurate at the time and place of the flow test. They are not necessarily true and accurate for every moment in time. The pressure and flow available at any given time might be greater than or less than the values found during the test. In order to make appropriate adjustments, regular knowledge of the water supply is needed. Most residential neighborhoods have peak usage between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m. and between 6:00 and 8:00 p.m. At these times, people are showering, fixing meals, and generally using the most water. In commercial/industrial neighborhoods, peak water usage time will depend on the industrial processes going on and the shift time of workers. Processes that run around the clock might make for fairly constant pressures in the water mains as water usage is even whereas a factory that only has workers in it from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. might reach peak usage at a specific time during the work day. Without knowing the exact situation in a water supply, it is impossible to make a reasonable adjustment. If you don't have knowledge of the water supply and peak usage times, speak with representatives of the water utility. They will know when their peak usage times are. 183

## Page 190

One method of being sure to get the results of the flow test accurate for daily usage is to run the flow test at the time of peak usage. While this might be at an unusual time of day, it does help verify the results of the test. However, this does not account for seasonal fluctuations. In many residential areas, peak water usage time occurs during the summer (when people are filling pools and using water to keep cool). In other areas, peak water usage occurs during the winter when they•are using water to make snow. Again, it is possible to run the test at the time of peak water usage, but you may not be able to wait that long and you may not be able to run the test in cold weather, Another method of making adjustments for daily and seasonal fluctuations is to run the test at a time that is convenient and subtract a reasonable amount based on knowledge of the water supply, Arriving at a reasonable amount is a judgment that is best made by a professional familiar with the water supply. One way to at least arrive at a reasonable daily adjustment is to attach a 24 hour pressure gauge to the gauge hydrant used during the test. This type of gauge records the pressure over a 24 hour period, letting you know what the fluctuation was in the water supply over that period, This at least helps the user make an informed decision about daily fluctuations, although seasonal fluctuations also need to be taken into account, See the article in the NFSA Splinlder Quarterly magazine, "Water Supplies, How Low Should You Go?" NFPA 13 (section 15.2.1.2) requires that the adjustment be made to the flow test results because we cannot predict when a fire will occur and it might occur during a time of peak usage. There are some Authorities Having Jurisdiction that have made blanket statements regarding the need for a 10 psi or a 10% "safety margin" between the water supply and the calculated demand of the fire protection system. This blanket statement is generally insufficient to necessarily be true for every daily and seasonal fluctuation in every water supply, However, such statements are sometimes the only information available regarding the adjustment of the results from the water flow test. While such a request for a safety margin is technically not an adjustment of the water flow test data, it serves the same purpose and should not be combined with water supply tests that have been sufficiently adjusted as that doubly penalizes the legitimate sprinkler contractor that follows NFPA 13. Note that NFPA 13 does not require an adjustment to take into account instantaneous peak demands. In most water supplies, an instantaneous peak demand occurs during half-time of the Super Bowl, This drop in water pressure comes right back in a few moments. It is not realistic to design systems based on a single short event that only occurs once each year. The following is an example of making an adjustment to a water supply flow test, Start with the same basic data as we had for an earlier example. A flow test is run in March with a static pressure of 80 psi and a residual pressure of 47 psi at 630 gpm. The data is plotted as the higher water supply curve shown on Figure 14-10. After discussion with the local water utility, it is determined that during each day in the spring, the static pressure fluctuates between 70 psi and 90 psi. During the summer, the static pressure typically fluctuates between 65 psi and 90 psi. The water utility also verifies that the water supply is mature and no additional growth is expected. It would be reasonable to use 65 psi as the new static pressure for the design of fire protection systems (15 psi lower than the value during the test) and 32 psi as the value for the 184

## Page 191

residual pressure at 630 gpm (also 15 psi lower than during the test). This adjusted water supply curve is shown as thc lower curve on Figure 16-10. The fire protection systems should be permitted to be designed to this water supply curve without any additional safety margin because it has already been adjusted for daily and seasonal fluctuations. CHAPTER 17 UNDERGROUND PIPING As we detail fire splinkler systems, we often focus on the system piping within the building. When it comes time to determine pipe sizes and types of sprinklers, we start to consider the arrangement of the water supply. It's the piping system that connects the sprinklers inside a building to the water supply that is sometimes overlooked by the design technician. This is especially true if their company does not routinely install this portion of a sprinkler system. This piping is usually referred to as 'the undergound' system. This underground portion of the system is governed by Chapter 10 of NFA 13. The wording for chapter 10 comes directly from NFPA 24, Standard for the Installation of Private Fire Service Mains and Their Appurtenances. Ironically, the requirements for underground pipe were originally found in NFPA 13 in the early 1900's. Then, in 1925, the NFPA 24 standard was issued to cover more than just the piping feeding sprinkler systems. This included fire hydrants, monitor nozzles and house houses. In 1999, the NFPA 13 Committee decided to extract, word-for-word, all applicable language directly from NFPA 24 and place it back in NFPA 13. This helps to ensure that the requirements in both standards are the same. We have already discussed Table 10.1.1 of NFPA 13 in this text. This table discusses the acceptable types of underground piping. Remember that the type piping used must be in that table, must be made to the standards shown in that table, or must be specially listed for this application. The piping must have a minimum rating for working pressures of 150psi. Ferrous metal piping, like ductile iron pipe, must be lined to help prevent extensive corrosion. Steel piping is only allowed to be installed below grade to reach Fire Department Comlections. This special allowance for steel piping below grade requires galvanized pipe with external wrapping and coating. You may wonder how underground piping is put together during installation. rlhe type of joints and fittings must only be approved (13: 10.2.5). Joints and fittings may also be part of the listing for specially listed underground piping. NFPA 13 requires joints and fittings to be installed by persons experienced with the type of materials being used. Pieces of Ductile Iron 191

So how do we prevent the piping from moving and becoming dislodged at the joints if the soil won't hold it together? One method is to install concrete blocks (also known as thrust blocks) at the bend or fitting to hold it in place. Another method is to use threaded rod and bolts to hold it al together. Thrust Blocks NFPA 13 requires thrust blocks to be placed against suitable, undisturbed soil. The concrete that is used must not be leaner than 1 part cement, 21/2 parts sand, and 5 parts stone. The area of the block at the fitting must spread out to a larger area where it meets the undisturbed soil. This allows the energy from the pipe to be spread out into the surrounding soil. The first assumption will be the height (h) of the thrust block. This should be no more than half the total depth to the bottom of the block, and not less than the diameter of the pipe being installed. The width (b) of the block will determine the total area of the thrust block bearing on the soil (see Figure 17-4). This width (b) should be between one and two times the height. Formulas to determine the width take into account how firm the soil is, what the system pressures are, and the angle of a turn where the force of the thrust will be encountered. 194

Acceptance Testing The installer for the underground piping must complete the Contractor's test Certificate for Underground Piping found in NFPA 13. This serves to document acceptance testing (flushing, hydrostatic and leakage tests) as well as provide basic data for the system. The test certificate must be witnessed and signed by the owner's representative as well as contractor's representative, The piping must undergo a flushing test and a hydrostatic test. The flushing lest is designed to clear any debris from the piping and ensure an adequate connection to the supply has been made. The minimum flow required for flushing is a velocity of I()ft per second, The amount of water in gpm is given in Table 10.10.2.1.3. If the water supply is incapable of producing this flow, maximum available flow should be used. The flushing should continue until the water is clear. The test is required to be 2- hours long at not less than 200 psi, but at least 50 psi above the maximum expected static pressure. The installer is allowed to backfill between joints to prevent movement of piping during the test but must take responsibility for and fix any problems during testing. Leakage of new installations with rubber-gasketed joints expected to be nonexistent, but is limited in any case to 2 quarts per hour for every 100 joints. Leakage amounts during testing must be determined by pumping from a calibrated container. See NFPA 13 for additional leakage allowed for metal seated valves and dry barrel hydrants. 197

CHAPTER 18 BACKFLOW PREVENTION History The fire sprinkler industry began in the late 1800's and has provided an exemplary record of life safety for more than 100 years. The fire sprinkler industry is concerned with life safety, not only from a fire protection standpoint, but also a public health standpoint. We do need to make sure that we do not create a problem for the potable water supplies that we are connected to. The University of Southern California Foundation for Cross-Connection Control and Hydraulic Research publishes a manual of Backflow Prevention and Cross- Connection Control. In the Seventh Edition of the Manual, they list 248 known cases of backflow causing 60,000 injuries and 374 deaths between 1900 and 1985. Of those known backflow incidents, only two cases involved fire sprinkler systems, which did not cause any injuries or deaths. Another 4 cases are attributed to "fire protection systems" and are responsible for 308 injuries and 1 death. These tend to be situations where something was pumped into a fire hydrant or where chemicals used for fire fighting got mixed with potable water. While the incidents listed above are not all-inclusive, they do represent some important concepts. All-in-all, fire sprinkler systems are not serious threats to public health. Still, it is our job to make sure that we do not create a problem when we connect the water supply to our fire sprinkler system. What is a Cross-Connection? A cross-connection is defined as "Any unprotected connection between a public or consumer's potable water system and any other source of water or system through which it is possible to introduce used water, industrial fluid, gas or substance other than the intended potable water with which the system is supplied" Backflow is then the process by which a cross-connection allows nonpotable water (or some chemical) to flow back to the potable water supply. In order for the water (or other substance to flow backwards) the pressure in the non-potable portion needs to exceed the pressure of the potable supply. 199

## Page 206

How Much of a Problem are Sprinkler Systems? There are four concerns when it comes to the quality of water in sprinkler systems: Quality of water going into the sprinkler system from the waler supply to start with Actual direct connections with non-potable sources Use of pipes that are not rated for canying potable water Potential for stagnant water sitting in the pipes to permit bacterial growth If the fire sprinkler industry uses water supplies that are potable to start with, and does not make any direct connections with any non-potable sources (so we don't pull out of a pond or reservoir on the same system) then we have solved most of the concerns regarding backflow. The issues regarding the type of pipe that we use and the stagnant water can be dealt with reasonably. From 1950 to 1998, there were eight major scientific studies in the United States and Canada specifically looking at the quality of water in fire sprinkler systems. All of the studies basically reached the same conclusions, that the water sitting in a sprinkler system is not pleasant, but it is not deadly. It is important to note that most of these studies looked at steel pipe systems. In the one study conducted by Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) that looked at CPVC and copper as the piping material for the sprinkler system, no problems were found, even with water that was stagnaht for long periods of time. One of the big studies was performed by the American Water Works Association Research Foundation. This study concluded that the water in sprinkler systems with steel pipe did not meet the Federal Safe Drinking Water Act in terms of metals in the water, but that under any significant backflow event, sufficient dilution of the water from the sprinkler system would occur and that the public was not in danger from existing fire sprinkler systems with alarm check valves instead of backflow preventers. The study went on to recommend backflow preventers for new fire sprinkler systems because the hydraulics could be accounted for in the original system design. But the study clearly indicates that mandatory retrofit of sprinkler systems with backflow preventers would be a bad idea. 200

## Page 207

Backflow Devices There are three different devices that are considered backflow prevention devices. In order to be used on fire sprinkler systems, these devices need to be listed for fire protection as well as approved by an authority on backflow like University of Southern California. The three devices are: Double check valve Reduced pressure zone (RPZ) valve Air gap Note that the backflow community does not consider a check valve as a backflow preventer, even an internally loaded one. Single check valves do not have the redundancy to insure that they will prevent water from flowing backwards. It is also difficult to test a single check valve to make sure that it is properly preventing flow in the wrong direction without taking the valve completely apart. Double Check Valves Double check valves are considered the lowest form of backflow prevention. They consist of two internally loaded check valves in line with two control valves as shown in Figure 18-1. In addition, there are four test ports on the valve that allow different chambers to be isolated and tested to make sure that the device is preventing water from flowing in the wrong direction. Double check valves have the lowest friction loss of all backflow preventers, so if you are going to have to install a backflow preventer on a fire sprinkler system, consider a double check valve assembly in order to minimize the friction loss. Before selecting a double check valve assembly, check with the water authority. In some circumstances a double check valve is not considered reliable enough to protect the public water supply and the local utility has passed regulations for a higher form of protection, One of the concerns with double check valves is that if the check valves get stuck open, backflow can occur across the device. COCK TEST COCK GHUT.OFF Figure 18-1 Double Check Valve 201

## Page 208

RPZ's Reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assemblies have two internally loaded check valves and two isolation valves just like double check valves. What makes these devices different is a chamber between the two check valves that can open to the atmosphere as shown in Figure 18-2. If the downstream check valve fails on the RPZ, and water starts to flow backwards, the chamber will open and dump the water on the ground rather than allow it to go back to the potable water supply. The RPZ is considered a higher form of backflow protection than the double check valve because of the drain feature. If you are going to install an RPZ on any fire protection systems you need to account for the greater friction loss that is going to occur across the device, and you are going•to have to make sure that there is a drain under the valve that can handle all of the flow that might come out of the valve. Given the size that we typically work with (6 inch or 8 inch) these drains can discharge hundreds and even thousands of gallons per minute. So, take this into account with the design of the fire protection system, o o o Figure 18-2 Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) Device In the RPZ shown in Figure 18-2, the top portion of the figure shows water at higher pressure up to the first check valve. As long as the water past the first check valve is at a lower pressure that the water to the right of the first check valve, the device will sit closed. But if water fills the chamber to the right of the first check valve at a higher pressure than the water to the left of the first check valve, the water will discharge to atmosphere as shown in the lower portion on the figure. 202

## Page 209

Air Gap An air gap is a physical separation in the piping that the water travels across, exposing the water to atmospheric pressure. Thc best example of an air gap is the faucet on your bathroom sink. The faucet discharges water above the bowl of your sink in order to make sure that if your sink filled up with water, the water would not be able to jump back up into your faucet. Air gaps are rare on fire sprinkler systems because once the water has traveled across the gap, it is exposed to atmospheric pressure and loses all of its energy. There are some rare situations where air gaps are used just prior to fire pumps by placing the water into a tank on the suction side of the pump. This is the only way that an air gap could be used on a fire protection system. AWWA M-14 The American Water Works Association publishes Manual M-14: Recommended Practice for Backflow and Cross-Connection Control. The first edition was published in 1966 and subsequent editions have been published in 1990 and 2004. This document provides guidance to water authorities on how to enforce backflow requirements on all sorts of water-based systems. There is specific information in the document on requirements for fire sprinkler systems. The first two editions of AWWA M-14 contained six different classes of fire protection systems. The kind of backflow device that was required was based on the class of the system. The newest edition of the document has not followed this style, but since the classes have become a part of the industry, they are still referenced by many local water authorities, so a review of the different classes is in order. The six classes of fire protection systems are: Class 1 - A direct connection from the public water main only; no pumps, tanks or reservoirs; no physical connection from other water supplies; no antifreeze or other additives; all sprinkler drains discharging to atmosphere, dry wells, or other safe outlets. Class 2 - The same as Class 1 except that a fire pump may be installed in the connections from the street mains. Class 3 - Direct connection from public water supply mains, plus one or more of the following: •Elevated storage tank (potable) •Fire pumps tanking suction from aboveground covered reservoirs or tanks 203

## Page 210

•Pressure tanks (potable) Class 4 - Similar to Class 1 & 2, with an auxiliary water supply dedicated to fire protection use and available to the premises, such as an auxiliary supply located within 1700 feet of the pumper connection. In other words, a pond or a river close to the FDC that the fire depattment has specifically said that they are going to use if [here is a fire in [he building. Class 5 - Interconnected with auxiliary supplies, such as pumps taking suction from reservoirs exposed to contamination, or rivers and ponds; driven wells, mills or other industrial water systems; or where antifreeze or other additives are used Class 6 - Combined industrial and fire protection systems supplied from the public water mains only, with or without gravity storage or pumps suction tanks. The older editions of AWWA M-14 go on to say that Class 1 and Class 2 systems "generally and ordinarily" do not need any form of backflow device. Class 3 systems generally need a double check device. And Class 4, 5 and 6 systems should have an RPZ. There are a few "special conditions" under which Class 1 and 2 systems do need backflow: o Underground mains parallel to and within 10 ft of sewer or toxic pipes o Occupancies that use, store or handle hazardous materials in a manner that could present a health hazard o Premises with complex piping Where fire departments use chemicals or nonpotable water The 1990 edition of AWWA M-14 also contained the statement "At any time where the fire sprinkler system piping is not an acceptable potable water system material, there shall be a backflow prevention assembly isolating the fire sprinkler system from the potable water system." This statement contradicted earlier statements regarding the fact that Class 1 and Class 2 systems did not "generally and ordinarily" need backflow and was one of the reasons that the standard was rewritten, to clarify when protection is needed. The latest edition of AWWA M-14 does away with the six different classes and discusses the different types of sprinkler systems in use today. For the most part, it requires at least a double check valve on most sprinkler systems, only making exceptions for small residential systems with all potable pipe materials. 204

## Page 211

Sprinkler Industry Concerns Since we are going to have to install backflow devices on many fire sprinkler systems, we are going to have to deal with a number of concerns as listed below: Friction Loss — This must be accounted for in the hydraulics. A backflow preventer should never be installed on an existing fire sprinkler system without a complete re-examination of the hydraulics to make sure that the pressure loss will not affect the ability of the sprinklers system to control or suppress thc fire. When accounting for the friction loss, make sure that you have the con•ect information from the manufacturer for the flow of the fire protection system. Also, make sure that you use the maximum friction loss between zero flow and the demand of the fire protection system, not just the friction loss at the demand for your fire protection system. Location We need to have enough space in the building to put the backflow preventer. If the water authority wants it to protect the underground pipe coming into the building, we will have to bury it in a pit outside or install it in a protected enclosure to protect it from freezing. o Orientation — Some devices are only allowed to be installed horizontally. Before using a backflow device in the vertical position, make sure that it has been listed and approved by all necessary authorities in the vertical position. • Listed Device (UL or FM) — In addition to being approved by USC or ASSE, backflow devices have to be listed for use on fire protection systems, o Interaction with Fire Pumps— Backflow devices cause a tremendous amount of turbulence, which is a problem for a fire pump. The best option is not to install the backflow device in the suction piping of a pump.. If you must install the device in the suction piping, make sure it is at least 10 times the diameter of the pipe away from the suction flange of the pump in order to allow the flow through the device to straighten out before it gets to the pump. o Antifreeze — RPZ devices are commonly used to separate antifreeze portions of sprinkler systems from the rest of the system. However, when the antifreeze gets warm, it expands and will increase the pressure in the system unless an expansion chamber is also installed. o Complexity and Reliability — We are always concerned that any device on a sprinkler system has the potential for rendering that system out of service if it breaks or if the system needs to be shut down in order to repair the device. Before a backflow device is placed on a sprinkler system, it should be proven that the good that it will perform outweighs the harm that it could do. o Retrofit of Existing Systems -- NEVER put a backflow device on an existing system without performing the hydraulic analysis discussed above. 205

OSHA Confined Space Entry Rules — For backflow devices in pits, OSHA Confinéd Space Entry Rules will have to be used to go down into the pil Io maintain the device, 206

CHAPTER 19 SPRINKLER SPACING Determining where to locate sprinklers is a complex and arduous task. The technician must balance a number of important factors while trying to make sure that each individual sprinkler does not cover too much area, or too little area. Often, the technician will feel like Goldilocks, looking for the coverage area that is "just right". This chapter will concentrate on the items that need to be considered when determining where the sprinklers need to be placed. It is an excellent study guide for the following NICET work elements: 0 13010 — Requirements of Spacing 0 13011 — Sprinkler Location and Position Even if a technician is not studying for the NICET exam, a fundamental understanding of the rules of where to put sprinklers is a vital portion of their job responsibilities. The technician is the initial expert that will determine the location of sprinklers from which all other information about the sprinkler system (length of pipes joining sprinklers, need for hangers to support pipe, etc.) will flow. Without an accurate placement of sprinklers, not only will the sprinkler system installation be in jeopardy, but the sprinkler system may not be capable of controlling or suppressing the fire with sprinklers in the wrong place, or sprinklers may be subjected to accidental discharge by being too close to heat sources. General Considerations There are a number of considerations that will determine exactly where sprinklers are going to be placed. In general, sprinklers are located at or near the ceiling for three reasons: 1) Heat rises — As hot gases come off of a fire, they rise up towards the ceiling. Placing a sprinkler close to the ceiling will get the sprinkler to react earlier to a fire. Sprinklers could be placed closer to the ground, but then they would not open until the fire was bigger and the fire would be harder to fight. 2) Gravity — Once the sprinkler has opened, the water needs to get to the fire. Gravity helps the water pick up speed as it travels down to the fire. Sprinklers could be placed closer to the floor, but the pressure at which the water discharges would have to be increased in order to obtain the same velocity of the water droplets. 207

## Page 214

3) Damage — If sprinklers are out of reach, they are less susceptible to physical damage. Sprinklers could be placed closer to the floor, but they would be much more likely to be snuck be objects moving about in the room. Just knowing that the sprinklers need to go near the ceiling is not enough. There are a number of other considerations that need to be taken into account before deciding where to put the sprinklers, The following is a list of the typical items Lhat need to be considered before determining where sprinklers can or can not be placed: Type of sprinkler being selected Upright, pendent or sidewall Spray, ESFR, large drop, extended coverage or residential Ceiling construction o Minimum allowable distance between sprinklers Placement of walls and room dividers Maximum allowable distances between sprinklers o Hazard classification of occupancy o Obstructions to heat flow and discharge o Heat zones near heat sources Ceiling Construction The first variable that will be discussed is the type of ceiling construction. In older editions of NFPA 13, the committee attempted to define all of the different types of ceiling construction (wood joist, composite wood joist, bar joist, wood truss, etc.). The problem with this approach is that every time an architect came up with a new form of construcfion, no one would know how to install sprinklers because the standard would not mention the construction technique by name. So, in the 1991 edition, the committee decided that it would be better to define what the concerns are and to state some simple tules that every type of construction could fit into. The concerns can be summarized into two basic areas: 1) How easy is it for the hot gases to move horizontally across the ceiling once they have risen from fire and struck the ceiling? Is the path of travel for the hot gases going to be obstructed by structural members? 2) How easy is it for the water from a sprinkler to get to the floor without hitting obstructions formed by structural members? 208

## Page 215

Types of construction (hat block heat flow and could obstruct the discharge from sprinklers are considered "Obstructed Construction". Types of construction that do not impede the flow of heat or the discharge of water from sprinklers are considered "Unobstructed Construction," A more measurable definition of Unobstructed Construction can be found in section 3.7.2 of NFPA 13. The important portions of this definition are: No matter what kind of structural members they are, even if they are solid, they are considered Unobstructed Constluction if they are more than 7V2 ft on center. The For structural members spaced less than 7h ft on center, the construction can only be considered Unobstructed if the openings in the cross section of the members are greater than 70%. The definition of Unobstructed Construction allows some forms of construction to be considered Unobstmcted, while less open versions of the same materials will be considered Obsttucted. Consider a wood truss with thick web members and a short distance between the top and bottom flange. This type of wood truss would be considered Obstmcted. A similar truss, but with a much longer distance between the top and bottom chords would be more open, and might be considered Unobstructed construction. All types of construction that do not meet the definition of Unobstructed, should be considered Obstructed. NFPA 13 contains a more specific definition of Obstructed construction, but this simple definition is much more useful. Basically, if construction cannot meet the definition of Unobstructed construction, it impedes the flow of heat and prevents water from the sprinkler from being distributed correctly. Generally, sprinklers need to be below Obstructed construction so that they sense the heat from the fire and can distribute the water. One of the special versions of Obstructed construction is Panel Construction, which is defined as construction, ' 'formed by members capable of trapping heat to aid the operation of sprinklers and limited to a maximum of 300 sq ft in area" (NFPA 13 section A.3.7.1(4)). See Figure 19-1 for an example of panel construction. The concept behind defining panel construction as "Obsttucted" is that the heat from a fire will build up quickly in the panel over the fire and spill under the panel. The placement of sprinklers following the rules for Obstructed Construction will allow the sprinklers to react to the fire as the heat spills under the structural members. 209

Other chapters in this text will provide rules for Early Suppression Fast Response (ESFR), large drop and residential sprinklers. Spray sprinklers include the following types of sprinklers in a variety of orifice sizes: Standard response sprinklers Quick response sprinklers Extended coverage sprinklers Quick response extended coverage sprinklers The rest of this chapter will concentrate on the rules for spacing standard response and quick response spray sprinklers. The rules for extended coverage sprinklers are similar, but will be covered in a different chapter of this text. 210

Upright. and Pendent Spray Sprinklers Distances Between Sprinklers The minimum allowable distance between sprinklers is 6 ft. Sprinklers are not allowed to be spaced closer than that because water spray from one sprinkler might prevent the sprinkler next to it from opening during a fire, and that next sprinkler over might be critical to controlling the fire. The concept of the sprinkler spraying water on the sprinkler next to it (and preventing it from opening) is refen•ed to as "cold soldering" in the industry. The maximum allowable distance between sprinklers is 15 ft in light and ordinary hazard occupancies and 12 ft in extra hazard and high-piled storage occupancies. Ln the circumstance where major structural members in extra hazard and high-piled storage occupancies are spaced 25 ft apart, the distance between sprinklers is allowed to extend to 12h ft to allow the bay to be protected with two branch lines. Also in extra hazard and high-piled storage occupancies, the distance between sprinklers is allowed to be increased to 15 ft where the fire is not expected to be extremely challenging. NFPA 13 indicates that a fire that is not expected to be challenging as one that can be controlled with a density of 0.25 gpm per sq ft or less. We have not discussed density yet in this text, but it should suffice to say that fires that need less water to control are not expected to be as difficult for sprinklers as fires that take more water to control. The distance between sprinklers on a branch line is always measured along the branch line or parallel to the branch line where sprinklers are offset from the branch line. The distance between sprinklers on different (adjacent) branch lines is always measured perpendicular to the branch line. Sprinklers are laid out on a rectangular pattern and the distance between sprinklers is always measured along the same rectangle, never on the diagonal across the rectangle. See Figure 19-3 for examples of measuring the distance between sprinklers. Branch Line 1 Branch Line 2 Sl, S2 and S3 are all correctly measuring the distance between sprinklers on the same branch line LI and 142 are all correctly measuring the distance between sprinklers on different branch lines Figure 19-3 Measuring Distance Between Sprinklers 212

## Page 219

In situations where the roof is not flat, the sprinklers need to be installed so that the deflectors are parallel with the roof. NFPA 13 defines a flat roof as one where the slope does not exceed a rise in 2 units in a run of 12 units. Roofs with a gentle slope less than 2 in 12 are allowed to be treated as flat and have the sprinklers installed with their deflectors parallel to the floor. Where sprinklers arc installed under a sloped roof or ceiling, the distance between sprinklers (to comply with the maximum and minimum spacing discussed above) is required to be measured along the slope. Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinklers — Distances Between Sprinklers and Walls The maximum allowable distance between a sprinkler and the wall is one-half of the allowable distance between sprinklers. It is important to note that the distance to a wall is allowed to be half of the allowable distance between sprinklers, not half of the actual distance between sprinklers. The distinction between these two measurements is important. Consider a light hazard sprinkler system with the sprinklers spaced 12 ft apart in each direction so that sprinklers always hit the center of the ceiling tiles. The maximum allowable distance to a wall is still 7h ft (half of 15), not 6 ft (half of 12). If the technician decides to place the sprinklers 7h ft from a wall, there will be important design considerations to take into account during the hydraulic calculations (the sprinkler near the wall will be covering more area and needs Lo discharge more water to cover the area) but this installation is allowed as long as these other issues are accounted for. See Figure 19-4 for an illustration of this example. 1 71/2 ft 1 12 ft 12 ft 12 ft 71/2 ft Figure 19-4 Example of Sprinkler Spacing to a Wall in a Light Hazard Occupancy with 15 ft x 15 ft Spacing Allowed 213

The minimum allowable distance between a sprinkler and the wall is 4 inches. Sprinklers are not allowed to be installed closer than 4 inches because there will not be enough room to get a sprinkler wrench in to install the sprinkler or remove it in case of activation. The distance between a sprinkler and the wall is normally measured in a line perpendicular to the wall. The exception to this rule is in rooms that do not have 90 degree comers. In this case, the distance to the wall is still measured perpendicular to the wall, but an additional requirement establishes that the sprinklers cannot be any more than 3/4 of the maximum allowable distance between sprinklers away from the corner of the room. For example, in a light hazard occupancy with a room corner less than 90 degrees, the sprinkler is not allowed to be more than 7V2 feet from the wall (0.5 x 15) measure perpendicular to the wall, while at the same time, the sprinkler is not allowed to be more than 111/4 feet from the corner (0.75 x 15). See Figure 19-5 for an example. 7.5 ft max 11.25 ft max 7.5 ft max Figure 19-5 Sprinkler Spacing for Irregular Shaped Room There is an exception for light hazard occupancies and the application of the rule that the maximum distance to the wall is 7h feet. In certain, limited circumstances, there is a rule, frequently called the "Small Room Rule", that allows sprinklers to be installed as much as 9 ft from a single wall in the room. The discussion on the Small Room Rule is later in this chapter because there are also considerations in such rooms for the application of the area of coverage, which has not yet been discussed. Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinlders Area of Coverage per Sprinkler In addition to the rules regarding the maximum distance between sprinklers, NFPA 13 also regulates the maximum area that any sprinkler is allowed to cover. The area that a sprinkler is allowed to cover will depend on the hazard classification, the ceiling construction and whether 214

In order to keep the area of coverage within the rules, some dimensions need to be shortened. Table 19-1 summarizes the rules for coverage area per sprinkler. The area of coverage referred to in Table 19-1 needs to be calculated carefully. If all of the sprinklers on the system are uniformly spaced, and each sprinkler does not cover more than half of the actual distance between sprinklers and a wall, then the spacing is quite obvious, But in many circumstances, the spacing is not uniform between sprinklers. To cover this situation, NFPA 13 has developed a set of rules for determining the area of coverage per sprinkler. These rules are commonly called the "S times L Rules" for reasons that will become obvious when they are explained. Each sprinkler needs to be considered separately. When considering the sprinkler, look at the distance between it and the adjacent sprinklers on the same branch line. For sprinklers next to a wall, also look at twice the distance to the wall. The dimension "S" is given to the greatest of the distances to the next adjacent sprinklers or twice the distance to the wall. Similarly, consider the sprinklers on adjacent branch lines and twice the distance to the wall in this direction. The dimension "L" is given to the greatest distance between sprinklers on adjacent branch lines or twice the distance to the wall. The area of coverage for that sprinkler will be S x L. For example, consider the sprinklers shown in the room in Figure 19-6. When trying to detemine the area of coverage for sprinkler 8, the distance to sprinklers 7 and 9 must be determined. Since the distance to sprinkler 9 (12 ft) is greater than the distance to sprinkler 7 (10 ft) the "S" dimension for sprinkler 8 is 12 ft. Likewise, the dimension back to sprinkler 5 (10 ft) is less than twice the distance to the wall (6 x 2 = 12 ft), so the "L" dimension is 12 ft. The coverage area for sprinkler 8 is then 144 sq ft (S x L = 12 x 12 = 144). O O IO ft o 12 ft 6 ft Figure 19-6 Spacing Example 216

Small Room Rule As discussed earlier in this chapter, there is an exception to the lille regarding the maximum allowable distance between a sprinkler and a wall. The normal limit of one-half the allowable distance between sprinklers (7h feet for light hazard occupancies) can be exceeded in certain limited cases. The application of this allowance is frequently called the "Small Room Rule". In order to use the Small Room Rule, all of (he following limitations apply to the room: 1) The room must be a light hazard occupancy 2) The room must be less than 800 sq ft 3) The ceiling must be unobstmcted construction 4) The room must be surrounded by walls and a ceiling. Openings in walls (like those for doors and walkways) are permitted if there is at least an 8 inch deep lintel above the opening to trap heat. Where all of the above limitations are met, sprinklers in the room are allowed to be spaced up to 9 ft away from one of the walls in the room. Note that the 9 ft distance is not limited to a single sprinkler. Many sprinklers are allowed to be 9 ft away from the wall, but it must be the same wall. The Small Room Rule is not allowed to be applied to multiple walls in the same room. The Small Room Rule helps layout technicians place sprinklers in rooms where an obstruction or irregular shape might require additional sprinklers in a very small space. Consider an office that is 15 x 15 with a light fixture directly in the middle. The Small Room Rule allows the office to be protected by a single sprinkler installed away from the light fixture. See Figures 19-7 and 19-8 for examples of the Small Room Rule. Light fixture flush with ceiling 9 ft 7V2ft Sprinkler .<..— 6 ft 71/2 ft Figure 19-7 Small Room Rule Used in Office with Light Fixture in Middle 217

9 ft 16ft 15 ft 5 ft 7 ft i 5 ft 7 ft Figure 19-8 Small Room Rule Used in a Room with Three Sprinklers Where the Small Room Rule is used, a special calculation technique needs to be used along with it to determine that area of coverage per sprinkler. Rather than using the S x L rules discussed earlier, the technician must take the total area of the room and divide by the total number of sprinklers in the room. The area of coverage must be less than the maximum allowed (see Table 19-1) and must be used as the area of the sprinkler for performing hydraulic calculations. The reason that this averaging technique is used has to do with the application of the S x L rule. Part of the S x L rule has the technician compare the distance between sprinklers to twice the distance between a sprinkler and a wall. If a sprinklers is 9 ft from a wall, twice that distance is 18 ft. This will always exceed the distance between sprinklers and will make it difficult, if not impossible, to meet the spacing limitations. Therefore, NFPA 13 allows the user to average the coverage of the sprinklers in the room. For the example in Figure 19-7, the room is 15 ft long by 15 ft wide. The sprinkler is still covering an area of 225 sq ft, even though it is 9 ft from a wall. Note that if the S x L rule was used here, the sprinkler would be considered to be covering 270 sq ft (18 x 15), which would exceed its maximum coverage area. This is the reason that the S x L rule is not used and the averaging technique is employed. For the example in Figure 19-8, the room is 42 ft long by 16 ft wide for a total area of 672 sq ft. With three sprinklers in the room, the area of coverage for each sprinkler is 224 sq ft (672 + 3), just under the maximum of 225 sq ft allowed for each sprinkler. Note that the room could be a little longer to the right side with 6 or 7 ft between the right sprinkler and the wall (instead of the 5 ft shown) and the sprinklers would still meet their rules concerning the maximum distance to the walls. However, the sprinklers in that situation would not be allowed to be installed as shown because the average coverage area for each sprinkler would exceed 225 sq ft, If the room were longer, an additional sprinkler would be required to be installed. 218

Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinklers — Deflector Distance Below Ceiling The sprinklers need to be installed close to the ceiling (for the reasons discussed earlier in this presentation). Exactly where the sprinklers should be located depends on the type of ceiling construction. The nmles that follow apply to spray sprinklers. The design technician is allowed to install sprinklers in locations other than as described here when tests or calculations are performed that show comparable performance as installed to the expected response times of sprinklcrs installed in accordance with these rules. For unobstructed ceiling construction, the sprinkler needs to be between 1 and 12 inches down from the ceiling. The sprinkler is not allowed to be closer than 1 inch to the ceiling so that it can be removed from its fitting without removing a piece of the ceiling. The sprinkler cannot be more than 12 inches down from the ceiling because this will delay the activation of the sprinkler due to the time it will take the hot gases from a fire to bank down from the ceiling and reach the sprinkler. The 12 inch dimension is also important for cooling the ceiling during a fire. Small water droplets from spray sprinklers tend to stay up near the sprinkler creating a cooling effect near the ceiling. This cooling effect keeps the structural members from feeling the heat from a fire and being damaged. This cooling effect is particularly important for combustible ceilings because it prevents the fire from developing into the ceiling. For obstructed construction, the sprinkler needs to be below the structural members (for most situation, some exceptions exist). The general rule is to install the sprinklers from 1 to 6 inches below the structural members, but not more than 22 inches below the ceiling deck, as shown in Figure 15-9. Note that the sprinkler cannot be less then 1 inch below the structural member for the same reason that we do not want the sprinkler too close to the ceiling. We need to be able to remove the sprinkler without moving the structural member. More than I and less than 6 inches Not more than 22 inches Figure 199 Obstructed Construction Sprinkler Placement Below Ceiling There are some exceptions to the rules stated above for obstructed construction. In general, these exceptions have to do with placing sprinkler up in the pockets created by the structural members. In such cases, each pocket needs to be protected, or the "beam Nle" needs to be met so that the spray pattem of the sprinkler is not unduly interrupted. 219

The first exception allows sprinklers to be installed above the plane of the bottom of the structural members if the sprinkler is far enough away from the structural member to spray under the member (needs to meet the Beam Rule). Ln this case, the sprinkler is not allowed to be more than 22 inches below the roof deck. See Figure 19-10 for an example of this situation. In this case, the sprinklers are expected to be within 12 inches of the roof deck, treating each ceiling pocket as a room with an unobstructed ceiling. See Figure 19-11 for an example of this exception. Note that this option requires a great many sprinklers, which will impact the installation cost as well as increase the water supply demands. Concrete tee construction refers to any solid concrete ceiling or roof that has stems (or legs) extending down from a flat deck. The stems are generally longer than they are thick. When the stems are between 3 ft and 7h ft on center, sprinklers are allowed to be installed up to one inch under the ends of the stems without concern to the distance of the sprinkler below the deck. The theory is that the concrete acts as a soft of heat sink that will help activate the sprinklers regardless of how far they are from the roof deck as long as they are not too far below the plane of the bottom of the stems. Of course, the sprinklers are permitted to be above the bottoms of the stems as long as the "Beam Rule" is met with respect to the distance of the sprinkler away from the side of the stem. Due to the combustible nature of composite wood joists, a special rule applies when a building using composite wood joists is protected with sprinklers and the sprinklers are going to be installed below the joists. In addition to the normal rules of placing the sprinkler between one and six inches below the joists and not more than 22 inches below the deck, the joist channels are required to be broken up by firestops into 300 sq ft areas. A firestop is made up of the same type of material as the web member of the joist (plywood or particle board) and installed perpendicular to the web of the joist to the full depth of the joist (see Figure 19-14), The pmpose of the fire stop is to force hot gasses from the fire down under the joists so that sprinklers are activated without having the hot gasses travel the length of the joist channel. 221

Composite Wood Joist Firestops Figure 19-14 Composite Wood Joist Construction In some cases, structural members exceed 22 inches in depth, If none of the exceptions can be met, the owner has two choices: 1) Install insulation in each channel created by the structural members in such a manner that it will not fall out early in a fire scenario. Insulation in this manner materially lowers the effective depth of the channel. 2) Install a drop ceiling below the structural members. The area below the drop ceiling can be treated as unobstructed construction. The area above the drop ceiling may need to be sprinklered depending on the concealed space rules. Sloped Ceilings Sprinklers are required to be installed with their deflectors parallel to the ceiling. When the ceiling slopes, the sprinklers need to be installed so that the deflector is parallel to the slope. At the peak of a roof, the sprinkler is allowed to be installed so that the deflector is horizontal. If the roof slope is less than 2 in 12, the roof slope is considered to be negligible and the sprinklers are allowed to be installed horizontally. Where sprinklers are installed under sloped ceilings, the distances between sprinklers are measured along the slope for the purposes of applying the area of coverage of the sprinklers as discussed above. For the purposes of determining the area under the sprinkler for hydraulic calculation purposes, the distances between sprinklers needs to be measured on the horizontal projection onto the floor. Under some conditions (combination of steep roof slope and sprinkler placement) sprinklers may be placed following the slope of the roof and meeting the spacing rules discussed above, but may still be quite far vertically below the peak of the roof. This would be a problem because the heat from a fire will race up to the peak first and delay the activation of sprinklers until the heat banked down and activated the highest sprinkler. NFPA 13 contains two 222

requirements for the placement of the highest sprinklers in order to minimize this problem. The first rule is that sprinklers need to be placed so that the highest sprinkler near the peak is not more than 3 ft down from the peak (See Figure 19-15). The second rule is an exception to the first. Under steeply pitched roofs (or ceilings), the sprinkler is permitted to be more than 3 ft down from the peak to create a clear distance from the sprinkler to the structural member of two feet (see Figure 19-16). There is no definition of a "steeply pitched roof" under which to apply this exception, but the intent of the standard is to allow this rule to be used any time that a sprinkler cannot bc placed within 3 ft of the peak and still maintain thc 2 ft clearance to the structural members.
