Attics and Other Concealed Spaces Table 19-1 (earlier in this chapter) contains a special entry for light hazard occupancies called, "Wood joist or truss, special attic rules", These rules will be discussed in more detail here, When combustible concealed spaces have significantly sloped roofs and closely spaced truss members, a fire starting in this space will get extremely large and, if sprinklers are not carefully placed, may open too many sprinklers, preventing the system from controlling or suppressing the fire. There are a number of special rules that apply to these combustible concealed spaces (like attics) when they meet certain slopes in order to prevent this from happening. All of the following special rules apply when the slope of the roof or ceiling exceeds 4 in in the concealed space are spaced 3 ft or less on center (see Figure 19-17) if the space is being protected with spray sprinklers: The sprinklers installed in the space must be quick response A row of sprinklers is required to be installed within 12 inches of the peak Sprinklers must be placed along the eave within 6 ft of the outer line of the concealed space. Sprinkler spacing must comply with the line in Table 15-1 for this type of construction, which gives the design technician two choices. Sprinklers can be installed on an 8 ft x 15 ft spacing at 7 psi, or a 10 ft x 12 ft spacing at 20 psi. In both cases, the shorter dimension (8 ft or 10 ft) must be perpendicular to the roof slope and the greater dimension (15 ft or 12 ft) must be measured up the roof slope. In writing the rules for spacing sprinklers in these spaces, the committee also needed to contend with the distribution of water in these spaces. Although not a part of the discussion in this chapter of this text, the pressure at which the sprinklers operate in these spaces is critical to water distribution, hence the requirement for the higher pressure when the 10 ft x 12 ft spacing is selected. The committee did try and minimize the impact of the higher pressure by allowing the use of sprinklers with a k-factor of 4.2 to meet the minimum 20 psi requirement, even for dry- pipe systems as long as the piping in the system is galvanized (or some other fonn of corrosion resistance). This marks the only time in the standard when sprinklers with an orifice having a k- factor less than 5.6 are allowed to be installed on dry-pipe systems inside buildings. 224

Volume of pocket not to exceed 1000 ft 3 Quick response sprinklers completely protecting floor area using spacing rules of NFPA 13 Noncombustible or limited combustible construction Figure 19-18 Ceiling Pockets Allowed to be Unsprinklered Non uniform (or stepped) ceilings are divided into two different categories with different sets of rules for providing sprinkler protection. The first type of situation is where the ceiling does not significantly change elevation. The second situation is where the ceiling significantly changes ceiling elevation. The magic number dividing the two situations is 36 inches, although we need to be careful how we measure the distance. The first situation applies when the distance between the sprinkler deflector at the lower ceiling elevation and the top of the higher ceiling elevation is less than or equal to 36 inches (see Figure 19-19). In this situation, sprinklers can be spaced ignoring the change in elevation as long as the sprinklers at the higher elevation meet the "beam rule". In addition, sprinklers are not required at the higher elevation if the space can meet the pocket rule discussed above. 226

Intermediate Temperature Zone o Airflow B 0.5774 x A c = 1.1547 x A Unit High Temperature Zone ' 'C" Dimension, max 20 ft 30 eater ft radius Figure 19-21 High and Intemediate Temperature Zones Around Unit Heater (Plan View) Summary The placement of sprinklers is a complex and arduous task where the design' technician needs to balance the area of coverage for the sprinklers and the distance of the sprinkler down from the ceiling, while avoiding obstructions and potential heat sources. This chapter has covered the rules for spacing and locating spray sprinklers except for the obstruction rules, which will be covered in the next chapter, Sprinklers are not allowed to be spaced too far apart. The maximum allowable distance between sprinklers varies depending on the hazard being protected. Sprinklers are also not allowed to cover too much area. Most of the time, the area of coverage will be determined using the "S x L Rule", which requires the user to look at each individual sprinkler and determine the distance to the next sprinkler or branch line and compare this to twice the distance to the wall. The dimension "S" or "L" will be determined by the worst case of the comparison. The dimensions "S" and "L" are always measured perpendicular to each other. Distances between 232

## Page 239

sprinklers are never measured on a diagonal. The area of coverage for a sprinkler when the "S x L Rule" is being used is S times L. The exception to the "S x L Rule" is the "Small Room Rule", which allows the area of coverage for each of the sprinklers in a room to be averaged over the total area of the room, ignoring the actual distance between sprinklers and the distances between sprinklers and walls. In order to use the "Small Room Rule", the space must be light hazard, the ceiling must be unobstructed, the room must be surrounded by wails and a ceiling (openings in walls are permitted with an 8 inch lintel) and the room must be less than 800 sq ft in area. Another aspect of the Small Room Rule is that sprinklers are allowed to be spaced up to 9 ft from any single wall. The maximum allowable distance that a sprinkler can be placed below a ceiling depends on the structural elements that support the ceiling and the ability of heat to move through the structural members and for water from the sprinkler to get around the members. Obstnmcted types of construction are those that do not allow heat flow and water distribution, while unobstructed types of construction are those that do allow heat flow and water distribution. For unobstructed types of construction, sprinklers are required to be installed between one and twelve inches below the deck, For obstructed types of construction, sprinklers are generally located one to six inches below the structural members as long as they are not more than 22 inches below the deck, There are a number of exceptions to the obstructed construction sprinkler location rules that allow the sprinkler to be installed in other locations in certain conditions. When sprinklers are installed under sloped ceilings, the distances between sprinklers and the area of coverage (determined by "S X L Rule) are measured along the slope of the ceiling. The highest sprinkler needs to be near the peak so that there is not a significant delay in activation of the sprinklers, but the highest sprinkler also needs some clear space around it so that the spray is not too restricted. Special rules apply to attics and other concealed spaces with steep slopes (over 4 in 12) in terms of spacing and location of sprinklers with respect to the peak and the eaves. Application of the sprinkler rules for rooms with multiple ceiling elevations can be difficult, so rules have been developed to give guidance in three specific situations: skylights, ceiling pockets and ceilings with multiple elevations. In the case of skylights, sprinklers are permitted to be left out of skylights as long as they are less than 32 sq ft. For ceiling pockets, sprinklers can be left out of pockets that are less than 1000 cubic feet in area as long as a bunch of other restrictions are met including that the rest of the room is protected by upright or pendent quick response spray sprinklers or quick response extended coverage sprinklers. When ceilings have multiple elevations, two rules have been established for upright and pendent sprinklers based On the change in elevation that is occurring. For small changes in elevation, sprinkler spacing can ignore the change in elevation as long as the obstmction rules are met. For significant changes in elevation, the change needs to be treated as a wall and sprinklers need to be spaced so that they are not too far from the change in elevation. Sidewall sprinklers are allowed to be installed in light and ordinary hazard occupancies. The rules for spacing standard spray sidewall sprinklers have been presented in this chapter, but 233

## Page 240

not much time has been spent on them because these rules are rarely used. More frequently, when a sidewall sprinkler is used, it is an extended coverage sprinkler. The rules for extended coverage sprinklers will be discussed in a later chapter in this text. Sprinklers should not be located too close to heat sources so that they do not open accidentally. When a sprinkler needs to be in a location where it will be subjected to heating, it should be of an appropriate temperature rating so that it does not open unless there is a fire. In order to determine the correct temperature rating, the ambient temperature in the space needs to be determined. After that, sprinklers near specific equipment need to be of a higher temperature rating than Ordinary. A number of tables outline different pieces of equipment and the correct distance away each kind of sprinkler should be. CHAPTER 20 OBSTRUCTIONS TO SPRINKLERS Sprinklers need to be located far enough away from obstructions to make sure that any fire in the compartment is controlled or suppressed. There are two concerns, making sure that the sprinkler experiences the hot gases from the fire without being in the shadow of an obstruction, and making sure that once the sprinkler opens, the spray pattem can get sufficient water into the compartment. This does not mean that sprinklers need to get water into every square inch of floor space. Instead, the sprinkler needs to get enough water over, under, or to the sides of the obstruction to keep the fire from spreading beyond the area where it started while controlling the temperature in the room to keep the structural members from failing. Spaces in the compartment that are behind the obstruction (on the side opposite the sprinkler) are allowed without getting direct sprinkler spray. It is expected that a fire starting in one of these dry spaces will be limited in its spread by the water spray coming around the obstruction, walls or other sprinklers on the other side of the obstruction. This chapter will focus on the rules for making sure that sprinklers are far enough away from obstructions (or the other way around, making sure that the obstructions are far enough away from the sprinklers). The bulk of the chapter will cover the requirements for spray sprinklers. The rules for determining how far to keep other types of sprinklers away from obstructions will be covered in more detail in the chapter for those types of sprinklers. Organizing the Obstruction Rules The rules for placing sprinklers so that they are not obstructed are scattered throughout NFPA 13 in different sections pertaining to different kinds of sprinklers. There are some general performance criteria in section 8.5,5. The real specific rules are found in each of the following sections of NFPA 13: o Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinklers at Standard Spacing — 8.6.5 o Sidewall Spray Sprinklers at Standard Spacing 8.7.5 245

## Page 252

Upright and Pendent Spray Sprinklers at Extended Spacing — 8.8.5 o Sidewall Spray Sprinklers at Extended Spacing — 8.9.5 Residential Sprinklers 8.10.5 Large Drop Sprinklers — 8.11.5 Early Suppression Fast Response Sprinklers 8.12.5 For sprinkler systems designed and installed under NFPA 13R and NFPA 13D, the rules are much less stringent. These standards only require that the designer try and minimize the effects of obsttuctions. There is no specific distance that a sprinkler needs to be away from any structural member, nor are there any specific distance requirements for objects such as lights or ceiling fans, There will be specific rules in the 2007 editions of NFPA 13R and NFPA 13D. Obstructions to Spray Sprinklers The rules for determining what constitutes an obstruction to a spray sprinkler, and how to minimize the effect of the obstruction, are far from easy to understand. One of the challenges is that the rules have changed with almost every new edition of NFPA 13. Just when people think they have the rules figured out, a new edition comes along and throws another twist into the way we view obstructions. During the 1999 rewrite of NFPA 13, no technical issue received more discussion than the obstruction rules for spray sprinklers. Hopefully, with all the discussion, the committee has finally come to a conclusion on how to treat potential obstructions. The 1999 version of the rules seems to have been effective and no significant changes in philosophy were made in the 2002 edition. Zones of Spray Pattern Distribution By looking at the water spray distribution patterns of many typical upright and pendent spray sprinklers, and by looking at the effect of obstructions of varying size at different places in the spray pattern, the NFPA committee decided to develop rules independently for two separate zones: one close to the sprinkler and one farther below. The zone closest to the sprinkler is the most sensitive. In this zone, even a small obstruction will disturb the sprinkler's ability to develop a complete spray pattern. NFPA 13 calls the potential obstructions in this zone, "Obstructions to Sprinkler Discharge Pattern Development." The rules for minimizing the effect of these obstructions are in section 8.6.5.2. In the zone far below the sprinkler, obstructions are much less important. Once the pattern is fully developed, the only obstructions that are a concern are those that are so large that a significant fire could develop under the obstruction without getting direct 246

## Page 253

water spray from the sprinkler, Such a fire would not be controlled. There are very few obstruction tules that apply in this zone. NFPA 13 refers to potential obstructions in this zone as, "Obstructions that Prevent Sprinkler Discharge from Reaching the Hazard. " The rules for minimizing thc effect of these obstructions are in section 8.6.5.3. The dividing line between the two zones is a horizontal plane 18 inches (46 cm) below the sprinkler extending throughout the room or the area of sprinkler coverage. This plane was selected as the dividing line between the two zones to coincide with the minimum clearance rulc for equipment and storage below sprinklers. See Figure 20-1 for a graphical representation of the two zones in each sprinklered space. Obstructions to Discharge Pattern Development Zone Obstructions that Prevent Sprinkler Discharge from Reaching the Hazard Zone Sprinkler 18 inches (46 cm) Ceiling oor Figure 20-1 Zones of Spray Pattern Distribution (Elevation View) Obstructions to Discharge Pattern Development In the zone closest to the sprinkler, the objectives of the sprinkler committee can be summarized with the performance statement, "sufficient water needs to get under the potential obstruction, over the potential obstmction or to at least two sides of a potential obstruction in order to control or suppress a fire on the other side of the obstruction. " Three different sets of rules are given to locate the sprinkler in relation to the obstruction, one set for each objective (over, under or to both sides). It is only necessary to comply with one of the sets of rules. If sufficient water can get under the obstruction, it makes no difference what is going on above or to the sides. Similarly, if sufficient water is getting to two sides of the obstruction, getting water under the obstruction is not a concern. 247

## Page 254

Getting Water Under Obstructions Section 8.6.5.1.2 of NFPA 13 (frequently called the "Beam" rule) is used to determine if sufficient water can get under the obstruction. ThiS rule is used when obstructions are tight to the ceiling (so water cannot get over) and when obstructions are continuous (so water cannot get to the sides of the obstruction). The objective is to get the sprinkler far enough away from the near edge of the obsttuction that sufficient water will be able to spray under, and beyond, the obstruction, How far the sprinkler needs to be away depends on the distance from the bottom of the obstruction to the sprinkler deflector. The higher the sprinkler is above the bottom of the obstruction, the farther away from the obstruction it needs to be. See Table 8.6.5.1.2 and Figure 8.6.5.1.2(a) of NFPA 13 for more information on exactly how far away sprinklers need to be from these obstructions. Figure 8.6.5.1.2(b) of NFPA 13 is a variation of the beam rule allowed for obstructions against walls like soffits and cabinets. This figure is more liberal than the traditional beam rule distances because the obsttuction is against a wall. There is no need for large amounts of water to get past the obstruction because the wall is there. The sprinkler is not trying to get water any more than 30 inches (80 cm) past the near edge of the obsttuction. If the obstruction is less than 4 ft (1.3m) wide, and the beam lille cannot be met, sprinklers are allowed to be installed on the other side of the obstruction as long as the distance from the sprinklers to the centerline of the obstruction is not more than half the maximum distance allowed between sprinklers. Getting Water to Both Sides of an Obstruction Section 8.6.5.2.1.3 of NFPA 13 (frequently called the "Three Times" rule) is used to determine if sufficient water can get to both sides of an obstruction. This applies to vertical obstructions like columns and to open horizontal obstructions like the bottom chords of uusses and the bottom flanges of bar joist members. See Figure 20-2 and Figure 20-3 for examples of sprinklers spraying to two sides of an obstruction. The "Three Times" rule requires sprinklers to be a distance away from the potential obstruction of three times the maximum dimension of the obstmction up to a maximum of 24 inches (61 cm). Note that the maximum dimension of 24 inches (61 cm) applies to the maximum required distance for the sprinkler away from the obstlllction, not the maximum allowable dimension of the obstruction. In Figure 20-2, a sprinkler is positioned in such a manner that it can spray to both sides of a column with dimensions 3 inches by 4 inches (8 x 10 cm). The sprinkler must be positioned at least 12 inches (30 cm) away form the near edge of the column. Note 248

## Page 255

that the minimum distance is three times the 4 inch (10 cm) dimension even though this is not the dimension closest to the sprinkler. It is the maximum dimension that counts. Also note that the distance is measured to the centerline of the sprinkler deflector. Sprinkler Spray Sprinkler Minimum 12 in (30 cm) Column (10 cm) 3 in (8 cm) Sprinkler Spray Figure 20-2 Plan View of Sprinkler and Column Figure 20-3 shows a similar application of the "Three Times" tule for horizontal obstructions such as the bottom flange of an open bar joist. Since the joist is open, the sprinkler can throw water both over and under the bottom flange. Since water can get to both sides of the obstruction (over and under) the "Three Times" rule is the correct rule to use. If the structural member had been some solid member, or some type of construction defined as "Obstructed" by NFPA 13, then the correct obstruction rule to follow would be the "Beam" rule. edition was changed to clarify that the minimum distance only needs to be measured in a straight line. There are a number of exceptions to the "Three Times" rule in sections 8.6.5.2.1.4 tlÜ•ough 8.6.5.2.1.10 of NFPA 13. Just like the "Beam" rule, if sprinklers are installed on the other side of the obstruction, the "Three Times" rule can be ignored, as long as the sprinkler on the other side of the obstruction is not more than one-half the allowable distance between sprinklers away from the centerline of the obstruction. Another exception allows sprinklers to be installed halfway between wood trusses when they are spaced approximately 24 inches (61 cm) on center. Without this exception, it would be impossible to protect wood ttuss construction 24 inches (61 cm) on center. When the trusses are 24 inches (61 cm) apart, the clear space between the trusses is approximately 20.5 inches (52 cm), assuming that the wood is approximately 3.5 inches (9 cm) wide. With såuctural members 3.5 inches (9 cm) wide, the sprinkler would need to be 10.5 inches (27 cm) away from the near edge of the truss. But with only 20.5 inches (52 cm) of clear space, a sprinkler halfway between the trusses would only be 10.25 inches (26 cm) away from the near edge. The sprinkler misses the "Three Times" rule by 0.25 inches (1 cm). So this exception was written to allow sprinklers halfway between wood trusses 24 inches (61 cm) on center. Another exception allows sprinklers in the centerline of open bar joist and wood tmss structural members. In order to utilize this exception, the bottom piece of the structural member must not be more than 8 inches (20 cm) wide. The sprinkler must be installed at least 6 inches (15 cm) above the bottom part of the structural member and must meet the "Three Times" rule for distances away from the web members. Piping below upright sprinklers can be an obstruction. An exception to the• "Three Times" rule allows piping directly attached to the sprinkler that is less than 3 inches in nominal diameter to be ignored, Any sprinkler branch line pipe more than three inches in diameter would be considered an obstruction. The sprinkler would need to be elevated above the pipe, or installed on an arm-over to the side of the pipe in accordance with the "Three Times" rule. In the 1999 edition of NFPA 13, an important exception was added to the "Three Times" lille and carried forward into the latest editions of NFPA 13. This exception limits the application of the "Three Times" rule in Light Hazard and Ordinary Hazard occupancies to stiuctural members, In other words, people doing sprinkler layout can ignore lights, ducts and exit signs when locating sprinklers. The only things they have to worry about are the structural members in Light and Ordinary Hazard occupancies. It is important to note that this exception only applies to standard spray sprinklers. Other sprinklers, such as extended coverage sprinklers, large drop sprinklers and ESFR sprinklers will still need to consider these other objects as obstructions. The limitation on the application of the "Three Times" rule to structural members in Light and Ordinary Hazard occupancies was not done lightly. The 250

## Page 257

Committee spent a number of hours looking at this issue from all sides. In thc long run, it was agreed that the "Three Times' rule was too difficult to enforce on every object. Too many objects were out of control of the sprinkler contractor or the fire or building official. Many times, long after the sprinkler system was installed and approved, lights or ducts were added to the building, causing an apparent obstruction. Building owners had to pay to move sprinklers away from these objects, but there was no data saying that they were actually a problem. A full search of several insurance company databases showed that minor obstructions due to non-structural elements were not the cause of any significant number of large loss fires. In other words, non-såuctural obstluctions did not affect the sprinkler system's ability to control or suppress fires. Since structural members have to be in place before the sprinklers (or else there would be nothing to hang sprinkler pipe from) and since we can plan for where these elements will be, the committee limited the application of the "Three Times' rule to these structural members. It should be noted that in a Light or Ordinary Hazard occupancy, a non-stmctural element that is tight to the ceiling and long enough that a sprinkler cannot tlu•ow water to both sides still needs to comply with the "Beam" rule even though the "Three Times" lule is not applicable. Similarly, any obstruction in a Light or Ordinary Hazard occupancy more than 4 ft (1.2 m) wide must have a sprinkler installed under it even though the "Three Times' rule does not apply (see 8.6.5.3.2 of NFPA 13). Getting Water Over Obstructions In general, the way to insure that sufficient water can get over the obstruction is to keep a minimum of 18 inches (46 cm) between the top of the obstruction and the sprinkler deflector (measured vertically). However, in Light Hazard occupancies, an obstntction such as a partition or a privacy curtain is allowed to encroach on the minimum clearance. In this case, it is better to have the sprinkler close to the obstruction, so that the water can be distributed over the top. Table 8.6.5.2.2 shows how high the partition can be relative to the plane of the sprinkler deflector. This distance depends on the horizontal distance from the far side of the partition to the center of the sprinkler deflector. Section 8.6.5.2.2 is frequently used with privacy curtains that hang from the ceiling. Frequently these curtains have a rope or twine mesh panel at the top before they become a solid fabric farther down. If the privacy curtain has a close mesh, the vertical distance in Table 8.6.5.2.2 should be measured from the top of the mesh to the sprinkler deflector. If the privacy curtain has an open mesh (0.5 inch or 13mm or greater measured on the diagonal) then the vertical distance in Table 8.6,5.2.2 can be measured from the bottom of the mesh panel to the sprinkler deflector (See A.8.6.5.2.2). 251

## Page 258

Obstructions that Prevent Sprinlder Discharge from Reaching the Hazard In this zone well below the sprinkler, the water distribution pattern has already been established. The only obstmctions to worry about are those that are so large that a significant fire would burn under them, generating large quantities of heat, without getting direct water spray from ceiling sprinklers. The only real obstruction rule in this zone is to put a sprinkler under any permanent fixture that is over 4 ft (1.2 m) wide. Note that furniture is not considered a permanent feature. However, one of the things that is considered a permanent feature is an overhead door. Even though the door is not open 100% of the time, sprinklers need to be positioned so that a fire occurring under an open door can be controlled. In the 1999 edition of NFPA 13, a new exception was added to section 8.42 to allow sidewall sprinklers to protect under overhead doors. It was anticipated that the sidewall sprinklers would be installed at a significant distance below the ceiling, more than the 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) normally allowed for such sprinklers. The sidewall sprinklers should be positioned such that they are 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) below the plane of the overhead door once it is opened. Sidewall Sprinklers The sidewall sprinkler obstruction rules are very similar to the upright and pendent sprinkler rules. There is a different version of the beam rule, and an additional application of a beam rule off to the side of the sprinkler. The "3 times" rule still applies to obstructions where sprinkler discharge is expected on both sides of the obstruction. Extended Coverage Sprinklers The rules for upright and pendent extended coverage sprinklers are the same as the rules for upright and pendent sprinklers at standard spacing with two differences. The beam rule has different values because the spray pattem is higher and broader, and the "3 times" lille becomes the "4 times rule". The rules for sidewall extended coverage sprinklers are the same as the rules for sidewall sprinklers at standard spacing with two differences. The beam rule has different values because the spray pattern is higher and broader, and the "3 times" rule becomes the "4 times rule". 252

## Page 259

Large Drop Sprinklers The Large Drop sprinkler obstruction rules are similar to the spray sprinkler rules, but the upper zone extends down to a plane 36 inches below the sprinkler deflector because it takes more room to develop the full spray pattem. Additional rules apply because the sprinkler is more susceptible to objects inteifering with the development of large watcr droplets. The slides will discuss the rules in more detail. Early Suppression Fast Response Sprinklers Obstructions are extremely critical to this sprinklers ability to achieve fire suppression. An obstruction can cause a loss of vertical water droplet momentum, which will cause the fire to burn out of control. The specific rules will be covered in depth in the slides. CHAPTER 21 EXTENDED COVERAGE SPRINKLERS Extended Coverage sprinklers are also spray sprinklers that are intended to be installed at spacings greater than NFPA 13 allows for standard sprinklers. So, rather than limit the distance between sprinklers to 15 ft or the area of coverage of a sprinkler to 130 sq ft or 225 sq ft, the sprinkler is allowed to cover larger areas. This chapter will cover the special rules applicable to the use of Extended Coverage sprinklers and help the reader understand some of the special considerations when choosing to use Extended Coverage sprinklers. Limitations on Use NFPA 13 (section 8.4.3) allows Extended Coverage sprinklers to be used with the following types of ceilings: o Flat, smooth, horizontal unobstructed constmction o Truss or bar joist construction under horizontal ceilings where web members are less than or equal to 1 inch o Truss or bar joist consåuction under horizontal ceilings where trusses are more than 7.5 ft on center o Smooth flat ceilings with slope not exceeding 4 in 12 where specifically listed for such use o Other unobstructed construction where specifically listed for such use o Noncombustible obstructed construction where specifically listed for such use Areas of Coverage The area of coverage and spacing requirements for Extended Coverage sprinklers are selected by the manufacturer of the sprinkler within limitations placed by NFPA 13 in sections 8.8 and 8.9. In order for the Extended Coverage sprinkler to be used, it must be tested by an independent laboratory (acceptable to the Authority Having Jurisdiction) and must pass its tests at the extended spacing. Once the sprinkler has passed these tests, the laboratory considers the 257

## Page 264

sprinkler to be "listed" for that specific area of coverage and includes the sprinkler on a compilation of "listed" products. One of the limitations that NFPA 13 puts on the sprinkler manufacturers is that the coverage area must be in 2 ft (even number) increments. So a sprinkler could be listed for 16 ft by 16 ft coverage (256 sq ft) or 14 ft by 22 ft (308 sq ft), but there will be no sprinkler listings of 17 ft by 17 ft or 13 ft by 19 ft, Thc reason for the even number increment is to prevent the proliferation of too many different listings. When the manufacturers have been limited to even numbers, they have developed hundreds of different listings (which are difficult enough to keep track of). If the even number limitation was removed, the potential for hundreds more exists, but the NFPA committee did not want to open up the marketplace to that kind of division. One of the reasons that the committee wanted to stick with even numbers is that the typical ceiling tile is 2 ft by 2 ft or 2 ft by 4 ft and many architects want the sprinklers to line up in the same location in the ceiling tile. By sticking with even numbers for spacing and distance requirements, this architectural consideration can be met. Another limitation that NFPA 13 places on Extended Coverage sprinklers is the total area that the sprinkler covers. Although the distance between sprinklers or between sprinklers and a wall is not limited by NFPA 13, the total area that the sprinkler covers is a concem. Manufacturers could make sprinklers that spray plenty of water over 500 sq ft or 600 sq ft areas, the members of the sprinkler committee were concerned about the total size of an area that would be effected if there was a problem with a single sprinkler opening or being obstructed. If the sprinklers are closer together, there is a greater chance that if something goes wrong with one sprinkler, the next sprinkler over might be able to activate and help to control the fire. So, NFPA 13 places a limitation of 400 sq ft for any individual sprinkler to protect any light hazard or ordinary hazard space. For extra hazard or high piled storage, NFPA 13 limits the maximum area that any one sprinkler can cover to 196 sq ft. However, NFPA 13 does not tell the manufacturers how to reach that maximum area. So, for a light hazard occupancy, the manufacturer can make a sprinkler that is listed for 20 ft by 20 ft or a sprinkler could make a sprinkler that is listed for 14 ft by 28 ft. A third limitation that NFPA 13 places on the spacing of Extended Coverage sprinklers has to do with the distance between sprinklers (or the distance between a sidewall sprinkler and the far wall across from where it is placed). Similar to the restriction on areas of coverage, there is also a restriction on the straight line distance that the sprinkler can cover. Upright and pendent sprinklers are limited to 20 ft in any direction for light and extra hazard occupancies and 14 ft for extra hazard and storage occupancies. Sidewall sprinklers are limited to 28 ft in width or length. The last of the special spacing rules that NFPA 13 places on Extended Coverage sprinklers is that the spacing for pendent and upright sprinklers has to be the same in both directions. In other words, the coverage area for a pendent or an upright sprinkler must be square. This does not mean that the sprinkler needs to be used in a square room, but it does mean that the maximum area that the sprinkler can protect must be measured without worrying about which way the sprinkler is oriented. Upright and pendent sprinklers could be made to spray farther in one direction then another, but that would make installation more difficult. It 258

## Page 265

would not be possible to make sure that all such sprinklers would be oriented con•ectly when installed, so Lhe committee insisted that the coverage area be the same. Since sidewall sprinklers do not have the same problem, sidewall sprinklers are not subjected to this limitation. A sidewall sprinkler must always be oriented in the same direction when installed, so it is common to find them listed for one distance in the direction parallel to the wall thal they are installed on and a different distance for the spray into the room. Typically the distance parallel to the wall that they are installed on (called the width) is expressed first and the throw into the room away from the sprinkler (called the length) is expressed second. So, when you see a sprinkler listed for 14 ft by 22 ft, you know first that it is a sidewall sprinkler (because pendent or upright sprinklers wouldn't be allowed to have different distances in the same listing) and you also know that the sprinkler will cover 14 ft parallel to the direction of the wall that the sprinkler is mounted on and it will cover 22 ft deep into the room. When selecting an Extended Coverage sprinkler for a space, the dimensions being covered in both directions are important to consider. A listed sprinkler must be selected that meets all of the coverage area. For upright and pendent sprinklers, the sprinkler must be listed for the maximum spacing in either direction even if the space is not square. For example, to protect a space that is 18 ft x 14 ft (252 sq ft) with a single upright or pendent Extended Coverage sprinkler, a listed 18 ft x 18 ft sprinkler would need to be used. A sprinkler listed for 16 ft x 16 ft would not be acceptable even though it can cover more area (256 sq ft) because it cannot protect the 18 ft distance. When placing upright and pendent sprinklers with respect to the wall, the sprinkler is not allowed to be any more than half the allowable distance between sprinklers away from the wall (see Figure 21-1). The upright or pendent sprinkler can be closer to the wall as long as it is at least 4 inches away from the wall. So, a sprinkler listed to cover a space of 18 ft x 18 ft, can be as much as 9 ft from any (or every) wall. For sidewall sprinklers, the situation for spacing the sprinkler is similar to that for upright and pendent sprinklers, but for the purposes of discussion, we will identify four different walls, The first wall of interest is that wall on which the sprinkler is installed. The second wall of interest is the wall on the far side of the room, parallel to the wall on which the sprinkler is installed. The other two walls are perpendicular to the first two walls and will be referred to as the walls Lo Lhe sides of the sidewall sprinkler. The sprinkler must be selected and placed so that the distance from the sprinkler to the walls on the sides does not exceed one-half of the maximum allowable width. At the same time, the sprinkler must be located so that the far wall is within the allowable coverage length. See Figure 21-2 for a graphical description of these spacing rules. ax hW Notes: 1) W Maximum Allowable Distance Between Sprinklers 2) L = Maximum Allowable Length of Space 3) Sprinkler must be listed for W x L Figure 21-2 Spacing of Extended Coverage Sidewall Sprinklers One question that is frequently asked regarding spacing of sidewall sprinklers has to do with the method of calculating the dimension "L" shown in Figure 21-2. Specifically, the question is, "where does the measurement start, at the sprinkler deflector, or at the wall between the sprinkler?" The answer to that question is not straight forward. The language of Table 8.7.2.2.1 indicates that the measurement must be taken between the walls, not from the sprinkler to the wall. But this language is in section 8.7, which only applies to standard sidewall sprinkler. The same exact language does not exist in section 8.9 for sidewall Extended Coverage sprinklers, so it is not clear exactly what the intent of NFPA 13 is. A case could be made that the intent is to space Extended Coverage sidewall sprinklers from the same location as standard spray sidewall sprinklers, but that case is not explicit. 260

Hydraulic Calculations Specific rules for hydraulic calculations will be covered in more detail in the Hydraulic Calculation chapter of this text. But it is important to understand that when Extended Coverage sprinklers are selected, the sprinkler needs to be used at the flow and pressure demand that conesponds to its listing. Frequently, the flow and pressure necessary for an Extended Coverage sprinkler is greater than the minimum needed to protect the floor area with the density corresponding to the hazard classification. This higher pressure and flow needs to be used Io make the use of the sprinkler legitimate. Special rules also exist for Extended Coverage sprinklers in extra hazard and storage occupancies. These special Jules allow the discharge from the sprinkler to be decreased if it is not protecting its maximum coverage area. This is similar to the S x L rule Chat is used for standard spray sprinklers. See the Hydraulic Calculation chapter in this text for more information. 8 ft 18 ft 18 ft Figure 21-5 Room 18 ft x 18 ft Protected by Extended Coverage Sprinkler Listed for 20 ft x 20 ft Coverage Obstruction Criteria When using Extended Coverage sprinklers, the obstruction rules are similar to those used for spray sprinklers. Extended Coverage upright and pendent sprinkler obstruction rules are very similar to upright and pendent standard spray sprinkler lules. Similarly, Extended Coverage sidewall sprinkler obstruction lules are similar to standard sidewall spray sprinkler rules. For upright, pendent and sidewall Extended Coverage sprinklers, there are different versions of the "beam rule". While the concept is similar to the "beam rule" for standard spray sprinklers, the lille is more stringent. The Extended Coverage sprinkler needs to be farther away from the obstruction so that sufficient water can get under the obstruction, Extended Coverage sprinklers have a broader, flatter spray pattern, so the sprinkler needs to be farther away from the obstruction than would be necessary for standard spray sprinklers. One of the other obstruction rules for standard spray sprinklers is known as the "three- times rule." The "three-times rule" is used when the sprinkler spray needs to get to two sides of an obsttuction such as a column or the web members of a bar joist. Similarly, Extended 263

## Page 270

Coverage sprinklers have a similar rule, however the sprinkler needs to be four-times the dimension of the obstruction away from the obstruction rather than the three times required for standard spray sprinklers. One difference between the three times rule used for standard sprinklers and the four times n-lle used for Extended Coverage sprinklers is the type of obstruction to which the rule applies. For standard spray sprinklers, the three times rule only applies to structural members. For Extended Coverage sprinklers, the four times rule applies to all obstructions including lights and signs. CHAPTER 22 PIPE AND FITTINGS The terms "pipe" and "tube" are going to be used interchangeably in this text. There is a technical difference between the two devices in terms of the methods that are used to manufacture them. But for the purposes of being used in fire sprinkler systems, pipes and tubes perform the same task, conveying water to sprinklers so that it can be discharged over a fire. Therefore, wherever the term "pipe" is used here, the term "tube" could just as well have been applied. According to NFPA 13, there are tfH•ee types of pipe that can be used in sprinkler systems: steel, copper and specially listed. The materials have additional requirements as follows: o Steel pipe is required to be manufactured in accordance with the standards in Table 6.3.1.1 of NFPA 13, or to any standard that exceeds these standards. It is important to note that the pipe manufacturers self-declare that they are meeting these standards and there is no requirement for a third pany listing to prove that the manufacturers are correct. This is the only major piece of equipment in a fire protection system that is not required to be listed. Even though it is not required, many pipe manufacturers do get their pipe listed as a Inarketing advantage over those that have not pursued the listing process. Typical pipes meeting these requirements are ASTM A795, ASTM A53 and ASTM A135. o Copper tube is required to be manufactured in accordance with the standards in Table 6.3.1,1 of NFPA 13, or to any standard that exceeds these standards. Just like steel pipe, this tube is not required to be listed, Type K (thicker wall), Type L (medium thickness wall) and Type M (thinnest wall) copper all meet these standards and can be used on fire sprinkler systems. e Specially listed pipe is only permitted to be used in fire sprinkler systems if it is listed by a third party laboratory, like Underwriters Laboratories (see section 6.3.6 of NFPA 13). Pipes that have received special listings include steel pipes that do not meet the standards discussed above and non-metallic pipe such as CPVC. 267

## Page 274

According to section 6.3.8 of NFPA 13, pipe is required to be continuously marked along its length with the manufacturers name, the model designation and the schedule of the pipe. This helps installers and inspectors identify that the correct type of pipe is being installed. Joining Pipe Each type of pipe has its own method for joining it together. While this textbook cannot deal with all of the possible methods of joining pipe, it will focus on the more this chapter is not to turn anyone into a sprinkler fitter. Instead, the purpose is to make sure that the person responsible for the layout and detail of the sprinkler system makes an informed choice regarding the type of pipe that they will use and the work that it will entail to install the system, along with any special requirements that will be necessary to meet, Steel Pipe There are a variety of methods used to join steel pipe including threaded fittings, roll groove fittings, cut groove fittings, plain-end compression fittings, and welding, Each of these will be explained here in more detail. Cast iron and malleable iron fittings are required to meet the standards listed in Table 6.4.1 of NFPA 13. In order to utilize threaded fittings, the pipe is cut with a threading machine so that it can be screwed into the fitting. When the pipe is cut, the wall thickness is decreased, making the pipe wall weaker and more susceptible to corrosion. Minimum wall thickness information will be discussed later in this chapter. In order to use roll grove fittings, a small indentation is pressed into the pipe near the end. The fitting then slips over the end of the pipe and fits into the groove. Since the pipe wall is not reduced when the groove is pressed into the pipe, the pipe is as strong and corrosion resistant as uncut pipe. Cut groove fittings work the same as roll groove fittings. But, since the groove is cut into the pipe rather than pressed, and some of the pipe wall is taken away, the pipe wall is diminished and considered weaker and susceptible to corrosion, similar to threaded pipe. This type of fitting is acceptable, as long as the pipe wall minimum thicknesses are maintained. Pipe is technically not welded together to put together the sprinkler system. Instead, welding equipment is used to cut a hole (outlet) in the pipe wall. Another (short) piece of pipe is then welded to the outlet and pipe is joined using one of the other types of fittings described here. 268

## Page 275

Steel pipe dimensions are determined by the standards mentioned earlier in Table 6.3.1.1 of NFPA 13. The standard dimensions for steel pipe are given the name "Schedule 40" in the ASTM standards. Pipe with thicker walls is given larger "Schedule" designations, like Schedule 80. Pipe with thinner walls than Schedule 40 is given designations smaller than 40, such as Schedule 30, Schedule 10 and Schedule 5. All steel pipe is manufactured with the same outside diameter in each size, so as the wall thickness gets larger or smaller, the internal diameter of the pipe increases or decreases. Schedule 10 pipe has a thinner wall than Schedule 40, so it has a larger inside diameter. The thinner wall gives it less strength and corrosion resistance, but better weight and hydraulics. Pipe dimensions for Schedule 5, Schedule 10, Schedule 30 and Schedule 40 pipe can be found in Table A.6,3.2 of NFPA 13. The decision as to whether or not to use thinner wall pipe is up to the design technician, as guided by the specifications on the project. NFPA 13 states that the following methods can be used for joining pipe WITHOUT any special listing of the pipe itself up to a maximum pressure of 300 psi, although the grooved fittings (if used) need to be listed as a unit (fitting, gasket and groove): Threaded Schedule 30 (or larger) pipe in sizes 8 inches or larger. Threaded Schedule 40 pipe (or larger) in sizes less than 8 inches. Cut grooved Schedule 30 pipe (or larger) in sizes 8 inches or larger. Cut grooved Schedule 40 pipe (or larger) in sizes less than 8 inches. Roll grooved Schedule 10 pipe (or larger) in sizes up to 5 inches. Roll grooved 6 inch pipe with a minimum wall thickness of 0.134 inch. Roll grooved 8 inch pipe with a minimum wall thickness of 0.188 inch. Roll grooved 10 inch pipe with a minimum wall thickness of 0.188 inch. Steel pipe other than the thicknesses in the bullet points above is allowed to be used in fire sprinkler systems, but the pipe must be listed along with the method of joining the pipe. When threading the pipe, the tlu•eads must be cut to ANSI/ASB/TE B 1,20.1. In order to seal the pipe and fitting so that water does not leak out, joint compound or tape need to be applied. It is important to only apply the joint compound or tape to the male treads of the joint so that too much sealant does not build-up inside the fitting, causing stress on the joint, If pipe is going to be welded, it needs to be welded in the shop. Field welding cuts down on quality control and exposes combustibles in the building to potential 269

## Page 276

ignition sources. You wouldn't want to start a fire by installing a sprinkler system. The two exceptions to the shop welding rule are for tabs on earthquake braces and when design specifications call for field welding. If field welding is conducted, the rules of NFPA 51B need to be followed. Welding methods and procedures are required to comply with American Welding Society (AWS) B2.1. When cutting outlets in the wall of pipe, the holes must be cut to the full inside diameter of the pipe prior to welding on the stub of pipe that will be used to make the connection. The disk that was in the pipe wall needs to be retrieved. In order to prove that they retrieved the disk, some welders actually punch a hole in the disk and attach it to the pipe as evidence. When the stub of pipe is welded in place, it needs to be placed so that it does not penetrate into the inside diameter of the pipe. In order to have a method of comparing different joining methods that have been developed, Underwriters Laboratories has developed the concept of a Corrosion Resistance Ratio (CRR). The CRR mathematically represents the speed at which steel pipe corrodes and compares that corrosion to threaded Schedule 40 pipe at the thinnest point (what is left of the pipe wall after the thread is cut). The formula for CRR is: 3 x CRR = x 40 X = Thickness of the Listed pipe measured under the first exposed thread or at the thinnest wall section for unthreaded pipe. X40 = Thickness of Schedule 40 pipe under the first exposed thread. If the CRR is greater than I, then the pipe will basically corrode similar to Schedule 40 pipe. If the CRR is less than 1, then the pipe will corrode more quickly than Schedule 40 pipe. Just because the CRR is less then 1, the pipe is not a problem. The intent of the CRR is to come up with a percentage as compared to Schedule 40. For example, a CRR of 0.75 is expected to last about 75% of the life of Schedule 40. Since some Schedule 40 pipe lasts longer than 100 years, a pipe with a CRR of 0.75 should also be more than acceptable. The decision as to whether or not to use a pipe with a CRR less than 1 is up to the design technician as guided by the specifications. There are thinwall products, with pipes that are lighter than Schedule 40, but with quality control processes that allow them to come up with CRR ratings that are at least 1.0. These products are considered "Schedule 40 Alternatives". As far as NFPA 13 is concerned, these products can be used as long as they are installed in accordance with their listing. 270

## Page 277

Joining of Copper Tube There are three methods of joining copper tube: brazing, soldering and bonding. Brazing is the strongest and can be used for any sprinkler system. Soldering is not quite as strong, but is still permitted for wet pipe systems that mect the following criteria: Light and Ordinary Hazard Groupl if piping concealed e Light Hazard with piping exposed if sprinklers ordinary or high temperature Soldering is limited to these types of sprinlder systems because there is some concern that the heat from the fire would allow the solder joints to come apart. By limiting the solder joints to sprinkler systems in lower hazard occupancies with water in the pipe, the concern is lessened. There is a special listing for copper tube to be bonded together. Basically, this allows the pipe to be glued to the fitting. The copper bonding product is permitted to be used under the same limitations as the soldering of copper tube. There is also a specially listed product called a "T-drill" that allows a fitting to be installed in copper tube without breaking the pipe apart and brazing in an extra fitting. The drill puts a hole in the pipe wall and uses the copper that was in the hole to make a shallow saddle around the hole. Another piece of copper tube (cut specially to match the hole) can then be attached. Joining of Non-Metallic Pipe At one time, there was a type of pipe listed for fire sprinkler systems called Polybutylene. This type of pipe is no longer manufactured, but it is still in some of our standards. The only type of non-metallic pipe that is currently listed for use under NFPA 13 is Chlorinated Poly Vinyl Chloride (CPVC). CPVC pipe is listed to be joined with a one- step solvent cement. Once joined, the pipe needs time to cure before water can be put into the pipe. Curing time depends on the temperature. In the summer, when temperatures are relatively high, it will only take a few hours for the pipe to cure. Jn the winter, or during colder weather, it might take 24 hours for the pipe to cure, so make sure the curing time is including in any project schedule. There is a Cross-Linked Polyethylene (PEX) pipe that is listed for use in NFPA 13D systems. The PEX pipe is joined by stretching the pipe over the fitting and allowing it to snap back into place on top of the fitting. A band is placed over the pipe and fitting to keep it in place. 271

CHAPTER 23 SYSTEM CONFIGURATIONS In this Chapter, we will discuss the different configurations for sprinkler systems. There are really three basic configurations for sprinkler systems. We choose the system configuration that will best match the building structure while providing efficient delivery of water to the fire sprinklers. Efficient delivery will depend largely on where the water supply enters the building. If you have the luxury of determining this point, then the building's structure will be an important factor in deciding which configuration to use. The three basic types of system configurations are: o Tree Systems o Looped Systems o Gridded Systems In order to understand the specific definitions of these configurations, you will also need a basic understanding of the following definitions from NFPA 13: Branch Lines. The pipes in which the sprinklers are placed, either directly or through risers. (section 3.5.1) Cross Mains, The pipes supplying the branch lines, either directly or through risers. (section 3.5.2) Feed Mains. The pipes supplying cross mains, either directly or through risers. (section 3.5.3) We will use these three names to identify the different types of pipes when describing the basic types of systems. 273

## Page 280

Tree Systems A "Tree System" consists of a single larger main pipe (cross main) supplying many smaller pipes that branch away from it. It is indeed no coincidence that these smaller pipe lines are called branch lines. There are four basic types of tree systems that we will discuss. Each is described first, by the cross main location and, second, by the feed main or supply location. We will talk about these systems in the order of most to least efficient, The first type of tree is the "Center-Center Feed" tree system. Take a look at Figure 23-1 This is the most efficient tree system. Can you see why? The cross main is in the center of the system. The supply, or a feed main, connects to the center of the cross main. This means that water only needs to travel half the distance of the cross main to get to the most remote branch line, Then, when water gets to the branch line, it only need travel half the distance of the branch line to the end sprinkler, Center-Center Feed Figure 23-1 Cent.er-Center Feed Tree System The second type of tree is a "Center-End Feed" tree system. Figure 23-2 shows this type of system. The cross main is in the center of the system. The supply, or a feed main, connects to the end of the cross main, This means that water must travel the entire distance of the cross main to get to the most remote branch line. Then, when water gets to the branch line, it only need travel half the distance of the branch line to the end sprinkler. Can you see how this is usually less efficient than the Center-Center Feed? 274

## Page 281

Center-End Feed Figure 23-2 Center End Feed Tree System The third type of tree is a "Side-Center Feed" tree system, Figure 23-3 shows this type of system. The cross main is on one side of the system. The supply, or a feed main, connects to the center of the cross main. This means that water must travel half the entire distance of the cross main to get to the most remote branch line. However, the reason this system is less efficient than the "Center-End Feed" is that when water gets to the branch line, it must travel the entire distance of the smaller branch line to the end sprinkler. Can you see how this is usually less efficient than the "Center-End Feed"? Side-Center Feed Figure 23-3 Side-Center Feed Tree System The fourth type of tree is a "Side-End Feed" tree system. Figure 23-4 shows this type of system. The cross main is on one side of the system. The supply, or a feed main, connects to the end of the cross main, This means that water must travel the entire distance of the cross main to 275

## Page 282

get to the most remote branch line. The reason this system is less efficient than the "Side-Center Feed" is that when water gets to the branch line, it must travel the entire distance of the smaller branch line to the end sprinkler. Can you see how this is usually less efficient than the "Side- Center Feed"? Side-End Feed Figure 23-4 Side End Feed Tree System Tree systems are a quick and easy way to run the piping for a sprinkler system. The branch lines in a tree system are often typical. There is only one main to install. This makes for a simple installation and that is what will save money on a project. This was the system of choice before the modern era of hydraulic calculations made it simple to calculate more complicated systems. One defining characteristic of a tree sprinkler system is that there is only one path for the water to travel from the water supply to any given sprinkler in the system. While this makes for easy calculation, it makes for an inefficient system because all of the water traveling to the sprinklers has to travel through the same pipes. Looped Systems The other kinds of sprinkler systems we will discuss have a distinct advantage over the tree system. The water can take more than one path to the end sprinkler. How does this help? Well if you were to "be the water", would you move more easily through the pipe if there were less of you to move through that pipe? So, if all the water required to control a fire could split up and take more than one path, wouldn't it be easier for the smaller amounts of water to move through the system to the end sprinkler? In a tree system, the entire amount of water to control a fire must travel through a single main all the way to the branch lines, More water moving through a pipe means there will be more friction. And more friction means we need more pressure to push the water through the pipe. 276

## Page 283

The first kind of system we will discuss that allows the water to take more than one path to the end sprinkler is called a "Looped System" (see Figure 23-5). A loop is efficient because it takes advantage of smaller amounts of water traveling through the main piping than a tree system, Looped. System Figure 23-5 Looped Sprinkler System A "Looped System" has a cross main that connects at both ends. The supply, or a feed main, connects to the cross main at any point around the looped cross main. This means that only a portion of the water must travel around either side of the looped cross main. Even if the water has to travel the entire distance of the looped main to get to the most remote branch line, can you see where this type of system has an advantage over a tree system? Take notice that the water must still travel through the branch line to the end sprinkler on a "Looped System". Typically in Looped Systems, the branch lines are not tied together. The mains share in the water delivery, but once water gets to a branch line, the branch becomes like a tree system in that the water can only get to the sprinkler by traveling down the branch line and all of the water flowing to all of the sprinklers on the branch line must flow in one direction in the same pipe. Gridded Systems The most efficient system for delivering water in a sprinkler system is a "Gridded System" (see Figure 23-6), This type of system takes advantage of several possible paths to send water to the end sprinkler. Not only is there more than one path in the cross mains, the mains are joined by branch lines that create compound loops to carry water through each and every branch line on the system towards the end sprinkler. In a grid, less water travels through every type of piping on the system, creating even less friction loss than any other type of system. 277

## Page 284

Gridded System Figure 23-6 Gridded System In a "Gridded System", water travels from the supply or feed main into the front cross main. As the water travels down the front cross main, some of it splits off and travels through the branch lines to the back cross main. The smaller amounts of water transferring through the branch lines experience very little friction loss. As the branches send some of the water to the back cross main, the water all moves toward the last branch line. By the time the water makes it to the end of the system, it is going into the last branch line from both ends. That means that the most demanding sprinkler is usually somewhere in the middle of the last branch line. With the branch lines connected at multiple places to the main, there is a possibility that the water will travel down a piece of pipe in two different directions towards open sprinklers. This can happen when there is one sprinkler open on a branch line, which means that each part of the branch line only has to handle half of the flow for the sprinkler, or it can happen when multiple sprinklers are open, which will allow individual sprinklers to be fed water from different mains. You may be thinking that it must be more time consuming (and therefore more expensive) to install two mains in a building for a grid than it would be to install one main for a tree. That's a great thought! But you may be surprised to discover that you may be able to reduce the main and branch line piping by two sizes or more each. With that in mind, it is important for you to know that not all buildings are made for gridded systems. If the branch lines are going to be long (100' or more), you should definitely consider a grid. Sometimes buildings with shorter branch lines can benefit from a gridded system, but you will have to analyze every building to determine what the most efficient layout will be. Your goal should be to use the smallest practical pipe sizes, combined with the least amount of lineal feet of pipe, to reduce the total installation time of a system. Remember IT"S ALL ABOUT THE LABOR! ! ! ! 278

This method calculates the water flow and pressure losses through the piping system. In the modern era of sprinkler systems based on hydraulic calculations, it has become very common to create hybrids of the three basic system configurations to produce the most cost effective solution. There will be occasions where you will detail changes to an existing system that has been sized using the "Pipe Schedule Method". You should be familiar with this method and ready to apply it in your work. 280
