CHAPTER 24 BASIC HYDRAULICS Hydraulics is the science that defines the mechanical principles of water at rest or in motion. The term "hydrostatics" applies to the principles of water at rest while the term "hydrokinetics" applies to the principles of water in motion. Since water is the principle fluid used in fire protection, the fire sprinkler technician needs to have a fundamental understanding of what water is and how it moves. This chapter will cover the basic concepts of hydrostatics and hydrokinetics as they apply to fire sprinkler systems. Before getting into the specifics in this chapter it is important to take a minute and talk about units. This textbook is mostly written using the inch-pound system of units common to North America. For pressure, we are going to work in units of pounds per square inch (psi). There are people in the industry that get lazy when talking about pressure and abbreviate the units by using the term "pounds" instead of "pounds per square inch". Technically, this is incorrect. There is no such thing as "pounds" of pressure. The correct units to use for expressing pressure are pounds per square inch, which is abbreviated psi. Hydrostatics The potential energy of the water within a system when no water is flowing is called the "static pressure." The energy is considered "potential energy" because it is stored within the droplets of water and it is not yet doing any work. The energy has the potential to do work, but when it is just sitting in the pipe doing nothing, it is considered "potential energy". Once the energy is used, it will be converted into "kinetic energy" and it will more through the sprinkler system and eventually leave the system to fight a fire. The potential energy (static pressure) can be created by elevating the water (having gravity create the energy) or it can be created mechanically with pumps or pressure tanks. When water is elevated above a reference point, the water has potential energy in relation to that reference point. Consider a droplet of water sitting on a level table. If the water started at the elevation of the table, it will just sit on the table, with no energy, and it will not move. However, if that droplet of water is released from some height above the table, when it arrives at the table, it will have velocity and when it strikes the table, it will continue to move, spreading out and splashing until it has lost its energy. What gave the water energy? 281

## Page 288

The answer is the elevation of the water above the table. Once the water was released, gravity provided an increase to the energy of the water and caused it to pick up speed as it got closer to the table. When the water is being held above the table, the energy is considered potential because the water has not yet been released and gravity has not yet had a chance to provide energy. But we know that gravity won't fail (at least it has not yet) so we consider that the water will eventually get this energy. It is important to remember that the potential energy of the water is only associated with the height of the water above the reference point. In relationship to a different reference point, the water will have a different amount of potential energy. There is a mathematical relationship between the height that water is elevated above a reference plane and the potential energy (static pressure) that the water wilf produce. The relationship is dependent on gravity and the specific weight of water, so this relationship is only true for water near the surface of the earth. Other relationships would hold for other fluids or for water on other planets. In outer space, elevation of water would not create potential energy due to the lack of gravity. The relationship between the elevation of water above a reference point and the pressure that it produces can be expressed by the following formula: P = 0.433 H Where:P = pressure created by the elevation of the water in psi H = the height above the reference point that the water is elevated in feet An example of how to use the relationship between elevation and pressure is as follows. Consider an elevated storage tank connected to an underground water main that has a fire hydrant attached as shown in Figure 24-1. If a gage were to be installed on the fire hydrant, and if the height of the water in the tank is 150 ft above the point where the gage is attached to the hydrant, what would be the (static) pressure reading on the gage if there was no water flowing in the water main? 6' Figure 24-1 Water in Elevated Storage Tank 282

## Page 289

The answer is that the pressure showing on the gage can be calculated from the formula shown above. The height of the water over the gage is 150 ft. Multiplying by the constant 0.433, the pressure reading on the gage should be 65 psi (150 x 0,433 = 65). There is another term used to express the energy created by the elevation of water above a reference point. This term is "head" or ' 'elevation head". No one is quite sure about the origin of the word "head", but it is used to express the energy created by elevating the water and it is measured in tems of distance. In the inch-pound units of measurement common to North America, head is usually measured in feet. For the example shown above, it can be said that an elevation head of 150 ft creates a pressure of 65 psi. Likewise, the expression can be turned around to state that the pressure of 65 psi is equivalent to a head of 150 ft. Both terms (pressure and head) are different ways of expressing the same variable, energy. In the pump industry, pump manufacturers are fond of expressing the energy that their pumps produce in terms of head. While the pump is not physically elevating the water, it is providing energy to the water mechanically that is equivalent to elevating it. So, when a pump manufacturer states that their pump (under some flow condition) creates 150 ft of head, they are really saying that it creates an amount of energy equivalent to elevating the water 150 ft, which as we have calculated is equivalent to 65 psi. Conversions between head and pressure and simple enough with the formula outlined above. The formula can be used in the form above to convert elevation head to pressure. The formula can be turned around to convert pressure to elevation head as follows: H -P + 0.433 Another way of writing the relationship between head and pressure would be to take the division sign out of the formula and replace it with the inverse of 0.433, which is 2.31. Most people are familiar with this version of the formula: H = 2,31P Note that the elevation of water 150 ft above the hydrant in Figure 20-1 gives the pressure of 65 psi at this hydrant. At a different hydrant attached to the same water main, the pressure reading would be different if that hydrant were at a different elevation. By placing a gage on different fire hydrants (attached to the same water mains) and reading these gages simultaneously, the difference in elevation between the hydrants can be determined without knowing the exact height or water in the tank, or the pressure of the water at the source. Consider the following example, a gage is placed on a fire hydrant and found to read 90 psi. At exactly.the same time, a gage is placed on another fire hydrant in the same water distribution system and found to have a pressure reading of 60 psi. What is the elevation different between the two hydrants and which one is higher up? The solution is as follows: 283

## Page 290

90 psi - 60 psi = 30 psi difference between the hydrants H = 2.31P 2.31 (30) = 69.3 ft There is a 69.3 ft difference between the two hydrants in elevation, The hydrant with the pressure of 60 psi must be the one at the higher elevation because the pressure is lower. The water lost pressure as it climbed against gravity to get to the upper hydrant, so this must be the one with the lower static pressure. Before going much further with a discussion of pressure, we need to define a few other tenns to make sure that everyone has the same fundamental understanding. The first of these terms is the "Atmospheric Pressure". Atmospheric pressure is the pressure caused by the weight of the air pressing down on the sulface of the earth. All around the earth is a sphere of air. Even though that air does not weigh much, it does have mass and therefore it does have weight. That air, pressing down on the earth creates a •pressure on everything it touches. Because the atmospheric pressure is based on the air above a surface pressing down on that surface, the amount of atmospheric pressure varies with the altitude. Right at sea level on the earth, one square inch of air weighs 14.7 pounds. That column of air pressing down at sea level creates a pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch (psi) on everything it touches. At higher altitudes, there is less air between a body and outer space, so the value of atmospheric pressure drops below 14.7 psi. At low altitudes, like Death Valley which is below sea level, the value of atmospheric pressure is higher than 14.7 psi because there is more air between a body at this altitude and outer space. Atmospheric pressure is not used directly in many circumstances in fire protection system design, but it is important to know that it exists and that it has an effect on system performance. For example, at higher altitudes, fire pumps do not work as efficiently because of the lower atmospheric pressure, As the combustion air goes into the diesel engine, it does not adequately feed the engine. So, it is imponant for the designer to take into consideration the loss of horsepower due to the lower atmospheric pressure. There is more information on this subject in NFPA 20. The next type of pressure that needs to be explained is "Gage Pressure". It might sound like a bit of a cop-out to define a term by using one of the words in the definition, but the gage pressure is nothing more than the pressure that is read from a gage. The gages that are used for determining pressure in pipes and pressure tanks cannot sense atmospheric pressure. Instead, these gages can only tell the user how much more pressure is inside a piece of pipe or a tank than the atmospheric pressure outside that pipe or tank. If a gage is not connected to anything and is held up in the air, it should read zero psi. This does not mean that there is an absence of pressure. On the contrary, we know from the discussion above that atmospheric pressure is acting on the gage. Instead, when a gage is reading zero pressure, it means that the pressure on the gage is the same as the absolute pressure. 284

## Page 291

When a gage is reading some positive pressure, it means that there is that much more pressure inside of the vessel (pipe or tank) than there is outside that vessel. So, when a gage is reading 30 psi, it does not mean that there is 30 psi inside the vessel. Instead, it means that there is 30 psi more inside the vessel than there is outside the vessel. In order to make this distinction between different kinds of pressures, many engineers will refer to gage pressure as psig, standing for pounds per square inch gage. In fire protection, we deal with gage pressures so often that we tend to drop the "g" and just refer to the pressure in units of psi. That is okay as long as we always remember thal [his is still a gage pressure. When a gage is reading a negative pressure, it does not mean that there is a lack of pressure inside the vessel. Instead, the negative pressure means that there is less pressure inside the vessel than there is outside the vessel. This condition could lead to a serious problem if the vessel wall is not designed to take that kind of stress. While many pipes are very good at holding high positive gage pressures, the same pipes collapse under very small negative pressures because the atmospheric pressure pushing in on the pipe exceeds the pressure of the water inside pushing out. Another type of pressure that needs to be discussed is the "Absolute Pressure". The absolute pressure is the total pressure inside of a vessel (pipe or tank). The absolute pressure can be calculated by adding up the gage pressure and the atmospheric pressure. In order to make a distinction between the different kinds of pressure, absolute pressure is given the abbreviation psia, for pounds per square inch — absolute. Again, in fire protection we rarely worry about any pressure other than gage pressure, so we rarely see this abbreviation, But we should be aware of what it means. One of the places where it is important to know the total pressure is in the sizing of pressure tanks for fire sprinkler systems. In this case, we need to use the total pressure (or absolute pressure) in order to make sure that the water leaving the tank towards the end of the fire will have enough energy to make it through the system and come out the other end to fight the fire. NFPA 13 provides a formula for sizing these tanks in section A.15.2.3.3, and this formula asks the user to provide a pressure, and then adds 15 to it. In this case, the people that write NFPA 13 know that people in the fire protection business tend to work in gage pressure rather than atmospheric pressure. So, rather than ask you to input an absolute pressure (which the formula really needs), they ask you to input a gage pressure and then convert it to an absolute pressure by adding 15 (14.7 rounded up). Hydrokinetics The next subject that we need to study is the science of water in motion, hydrokinetics. In addition to the fundamental concepts discussed above, we are going to add some new terms for discussion. The first new term is the "Residual Pressure" (PR). The residual pressure is the pressure (energy) left over at a given point in a pipe or tube with a specific volume of water flowing. Remember that in the previous portion of this chapter, we talked about the static pressure of the water while it was standing still. Once the water starts to move, it loses some, but not all, of its energy. The energy that is left is the energy still in the water droplets after the 285

## Page 292

energy necessary to move (he water has been taken away. This remaining energy is called the residual pressure. The residual pressure will always be lower than the static pressure. Once the water starts to move, it will always lose energy. The more flow that is created, the lower the residual pressure will go. Any discussion of residual pressure is not complete without some mention of (he flow used Lo create or achieve this residual pressure. Another pressure that is sometimes discussed when water is flowing in a pipe is (he "Normal Pressure" (PN). The normal pressure is the pressure created on the walls of water filled pipe as the water pushes out against the pipe. The normal pressure is always acting in a direction pelpendicular to the pipe wall. Use of the word "normal" is historic in nature. In does not have anything to do with the pressure that is "normally" in the system. Instead, the term "normal" comes from early physics. Any force that acts perpendicular to the surface upon which it acts is considered a "normal force." In this case, the pressure we are trying to describe acts in a direction perpendicular to the pipe wall and is therefore considered in the "normal" direction. The last type of pressure that we will discuss is the "Velocity Pressure" (Pv). The velocity pressure is the pressure associated with the flow of water measured in the same direction as the flow. This is the energy that is responsible for creating the flow of water. As the velocity (or flow) increases, so does the velocity pressure. See Figure 24-2 for information on the directions that normal pressure and velocity pressure act. Water Filled Pipe Flow Direction pv Figure 24-2 Nonnal and Velocity Pressures in Pipe 286

## Page 293

The sum of the normal pressure and the velocity pressure is the total pressure in the water-filled pipe. This can be represented by the formula: When the water is standing still (velocity = 0) there is no velocity pressure and therefore, the total pressure is equal to the normal pressure. When the velocity of the water traveling down the pipe is relatively small, the velocity pressure will be relatively small and there will not bc much of a difference between the total pressure and the velocity pressure. In the design of many fire protection systems, the velocity pressure is small enough to be ignored and the assumption made is that the total pressure is the same as the normal pressure, The process of accounting for velocity pressure is considered advanced hydraulics and will be discussed in greater detail in that chapter of this text. For the basic chapters of this text, wc will work with thc assumption that the velocity pressure is small enough to ignore and that the total pressure is the same as the normal pressure. Another tern that we are going to need to define is the "Flow". The flow is simply defined as the quantity of water that passes by a given point in a given period of time. Flow can be measured in any set of units that contains a volume divided by a time period, and is generally measured in gallons per minute (gpm) or cubic feet per second (cu ft/sec). For mathematical equations, we generally use a letter of the alphabet to represent the variable that is the unknown. For flow, it might seem reasonable to use the letter "F", however, in many mathematical equations, the letter "F" already is used to describe the force applied to an object, Therefore, early hydraulic scientists agreed to use the letter "Q" to describe flow in most equations. It is most probable that the letter "Q" comes from the fact that the flow has something to do with a "quantity" of water. It is important to note that flow and velocity are two different (but related) variables. Flow has to do with the total quantity of water that passes by a given point while velocity deals with only one linear variable. Just look at the units. Flow is measured in cubic feet per second while velocity is measured in feet per second. The difference is subtle, but important, Inside of a piece of pipe, the flow and the velocity are related. As long as the pipe size does not change, the flow will increase as the velocity increases (and decrease as the velocity decreases). But if the pipe size does change as the water flows down the pipe, the flow might stay the same while the velocity changes. This is due to the fact that the same quantity of water is trying to flow down the pipe, but the amount of space in which that quantity has to move has changed due to the change in pipe size. The following formulas illustrate this concept. The relationship between the flow and the velocity of water in a pipe can be explained by the following formula: Q=AxV Where:Q = flow in a pipe in cu ft/sec A = cross sectional area of pipe in sq ft V = water velocity in ft per sec 287

## Page 294

The formula above can be used for a variety of different purposes including calculating the flow of water in a pipe if the velocity is known. Unfortunately, this formula only works with the units that have been described here, which are not customary units for the fire sprinkler industry. Conversion from our customary units will be necessary. For example, the formula above can be used to answer the question, what is the flow in a pipe with an inside diameter of exactly 2 inches when the velocity of the water in the pipe is 5 ft per second? In order to answer the question, the diameter of the pipe needs to be converted from inches to feet because the equation only works in this form when the area is expressed as square feet, A diameter of 2 inches is the same as a diameter of 0.167 ft (2/12 = 0.167). The radius inside the pipe is then half that value, or 0.083 ft (0.167/2 0.083). The area is then nr = = 0.022 sq ft. Q = AV = (0.022)(5) = 0.11 cubic ft per min (ft3/min) While presenting the flow in cubic feet per minute is technically correct, it is not something that people in the fire protection industry easily recognize. So, the value should be converted into a more common unit like gallons per minute (gpm). The conversion from cubic feet per minute to gpm can be accomplished by dividing by 0.002228 (that's how many cubic feet per minute there are in one gpm). So, 0.11 cubic feet per minute is equal to 49.4 gpm 11/0.002228 = 49.4). One of the more difficult statements for many people studying hydraulics to accept is the basic premise that the flow (Q) is a constant for any given closed system. This means that the flow going into the system is going to be the same as the flow coming out of the system. While this sounds simple, it means that if the water flows through any changes in pipe sizes, it automatically speeds up or slows down (changes velocity) in order to keep the flow constant. While this sounds outrageous at first, that the water would know to speed up or slow down, it actually makes more sense the more you think about it. Water is not compressible, and the pipe we use generally does not change shape. So as the pipe size changes, the velocity of the water has to change, otherwise the water would be getting stuck inside the pipe somewhere, and it can't get stuck because there is no where for it to go. Unless the pipe has a leak, the flow going in has to equal the flow coming out. Knowing that, we can amend the flow formula discussed earlier as follows: Q = A x V constant If the pipe is one size at point 1 and then changes pipe size at point 2, the following equation can be written: Once the areas and velocities at the two different points in the system are related to each other, the flow (Q) can be dropped from the equation to show how the variables interact: 288

As long as thc user remains consistent with the units for velocity being the same at both point 1 and point 2 and as long as the units for area are the same at both point 1 and point 2, the formula will work. The following are some examples of how these variables interact with cach other. A1 X VI = A2X V2 0.56 = 0.022V2 = 0.56/0.022 = 25.5 ft/sec Friction Loss Now that we have a fundamental understanding of pressure and flow, we can discuss the concept of friction loss (PL). Friction loss occurs when water flows in pipes or hoses and is caused by contact that the water has with the pipe or hose walls. As the water flows down the pipe, it rubs up against the wall ofthe pipe and loses energy. This loss of energy is called friction loss and needs to be accounted for in every system. The concept of friction loss is also 289

## Page 296

used to account for losses in energy from water making turns or traveling difficult paths. By lumping all of these losses together, the calculations are accurate and simple to perform. As the flow of water in a pipe or hose increases, so does the friction loss. Conversely, as the flow decreases so does the friction loss. The friction loss is also effected by the diameter of the pipe and the smoothness of the pipe. The bigger the pipe, the less the friction loss for any given flow. also, [he smoother the pipe, the less the friction loss for any given flow. There are many different formulas used in the engineering world to calculate friction loss. The formula used most in fire protection was developed at the beginning of the Century by Allen Hazen and Gardner Williams, professors of civil engineering at the University of Michigan. The formula has become known as the Hazen-Williams formula. It is amazing that in the early 190(Ys these men, without calculators or computers, found this relatively simple and accurate formula for calculating friction loss in water flowing down a pipe. Although this formula is not perfect, it is relatively simple to use and has been standardized within the fire protection industry to create acceptable safety factors. The Hazen-Williams formula is as follows: 4.520185 1.85 4.87 Where: PL = friction loss per ft of pipe Q = flow in gpm C = pipe coefficient (Relative to roughness of pipe interior) d = actual internal diameter of pipe in inches Most of the variables in the Hazen-Williams formula are straightforward and are expressed in terms that we generally use in the fire protection industry, so we don't have to make conversions, The flow is expressed in gpm, and the diameter of the pipe in inches. But the "C" factor needs a little bit more discussion. The Hazen-Williams C-factor is an expression of how smooth the inside of the pipe is. As the pipe wall gets smoother, the C-factor increases. One of the questions about using the Hazen-Williams formula has been, "what C-factor is appropriate for different kinds of pipe?" To begin to answer the question, we look at the values for newly manufactured pipe. Tests have shown that newly manufactured copper tube and plastic pipe have C-factors around 150. Similarly, newly manufactured steel pipe also has been tested and found to have a C-factor between 140 and 150. But we want to make sure that when a fire protection system is designed, it not only works when it is new, but it works when the system has been installed for many years as well. As such we do not allow people to use the C-factors for new pipe. Instead, NFPA 13 contains a table explaining the different C-factors that should be used to adequately account for the expected friction loss in an aged system. Table 14.4.4.5 is reprinted here with editorial changes to make it user-friendly for the ease of the reader. 290

Type or Pipe or Tube Unlined cast or ductile iron Black steel dr i es stems) Black steel ( reaction systems) Black steel (wet i es stems) Black steel delu e systems) Galvanized steel (all s stems) Cement-lined cast or ductile iron Asbestos cement Concrete Plastic i e or tube (all listed roducts) Co ertube (t e K, L or M) Stainless steel C-factor to Use Assuming Aging of the Pipe or Tube 100 100 100 120 120 120 140 140 150 150 150 Table 24-1 Hazen-Williams C-factorfor Fire Protection Systems Note that the value of C-factor for steel pipe changes depending on the type of system and the steel's resistance to corrosion. For wet pipe systems, the C-factor is 120 because a wet pipe system is filled with water, which contains a finite arnount of submerged oxygen. In the wet environment, the oxygen and the steel react to form a layer of rust, But after the initial formation of the lust, the air is depleted and there is no more air to promote additional oxidation. So, while the pipe is no longer as smooth as it was when it was new, it does not continue to get worse as time goes on. For dry-pipe systems, the pipe is filled with water during the initial system testing. After that, the system is drained and air is introduced to keep the system dry. The introduction of air into the moist environment of the pipe causes some initial corrosion, which decreases the C- factor. Over the life of the sprinkler system, the constant introduction of moisture followed by air (during the testing and draining of the system) promotes an ongoing corrosion of the pipe, causing a decrease in C-factor. A C-factor of 100 has been found to be conservative for dry-pipe systems utilized black steel pipe, When steel pipe is manufactured, it can be put through an additional galvanization process that coats the interior of the pipe with a corrosion resistant lining. This lining inhibits the chemical reaction between the moisture in the piping and the air. NFPA 13 recognizes this extra protection and allows dry-pipe systems to utilize a C-factor of 120 when such galvanized pipe is used, However, when galvanized pipe is used in a wet pipe system, no additional increase in C- factor is allowed. The system has to be calculated with a C-factor of 120 regardless of whether the pipe is galvanized or not. One of the other variables in the Hazen-Williams formula is the actual internal diameter of the pipe. This value can be found in a number of locations including NFPA 13, manufacturers data and ASTM standards. In Table A-6.3.2 and Table A.6.3.5, NFPA 13 lists the actual internal diameter of different types of steel pipe and copper tube. As the schedule number goes up, the pipe wall gets thicker and the pipe gets stronger, Since the pipe manufacturers keep the outside diameter of the pipe exactly the same for all schedules (published in this list), the inside diameter of the pipe gets smaller as the pipe wall gets thicker. Some pipe manufacturers do not follow the schedules published in NFPA 13 or the ASTM standards and their internal diameter information needs to be obtained from their product literature. Make sure to understand what type of pipe is being used in the fire sprinkler system being calculated and use the corect internal diameter for the pipe being used. Flow From an Orifice Up until now, this chapter has focused on the flow of water in a pipe, Now it is time to introduce the concept of flow from an orifice. Sooner or later, the water will get to the end of the pipe and then discharge from an open sprinkler or nozzle. The formula that is used in fire protection for calculating the flow from an orifice is as follows: Where: Q = flow in gpm leaving the orifice k = constant dependent on to orifice size and configuration P = total pressure in psi at the orifice (note that the value used here is total pressure, not normal pressure, although in advanced hydraulics, normal pressure may be used here) Fottunately, the k-factor is constant and it is known for many different sprinklers. The nominal dimensions were used up until the 1996 edition of NFPA 13. In the 1999 edition, the committee chose to stop using the nominal measurements because there were no parts of the sprinkler that corresponded to these dimensions and they were confusing people. In other words, there is no part of a h inch sprinkler that is actually 1/2 inch in dimension, so there is no reason to refer to the sprinkler by its size. Similarly, the name of the sprinkler (standard orifice or large orifice) has been dropped because the committee was finding it difficult to invent names that indicated sprinkler bigger than "very extra large," Instead, the committee chose to discuss the sprinkler in terms of its k-factor, a known constant value. It is important to note that the k-factor is a function of the opening in the sprinkler flu•ough which water flows. Sprinklers can have the same k-factors, but different operating characteristics and water distribution patterns. CHAPTER 25 HYDRAULIC CALCULATION TIIEORY Hydraulic calculations are used to size piping for fire protection systems, to detennine the needs (demands) of the fire protection system and to determine the necessary size and adequacy of the water supply. This chapter will cover the theory behind the performance of hydraulic calculations and will provide a simple step-by-step procedure for performing those calculations. Basic Principles There are tlu•ee basic principles behind the performance of hydraulic calculations for fire protection systems: 1) Sufficient water must flow from each sprinkler that opens (during a fire) to control or suppress that fire. 2) The water supply must be capable of developing enough flow (at the correct pressure) so that the flow discussed in #1 above is available for all sprinklers that are likely to open during a fire. 3) The pipe size needs to be minimized for cost, but without losing more pressure than the water supply can stand. Items and above will be discussed in more detail in the rest of this chapter. Item #3 is a ftndamental assumption underlying all of the decisions that designers and technicians make. If friction loss did not exist, all of the pipe in fire sprinkler systems would be 1 inch in size because that is the least expensive to install. If the cost of pipe were not an issue, all pipe in fire sprinkler systems would be 6 inch or 8 inch because that would minimize friction loss and allow sprinkler systems to work without the need of high pressure water supplies or fire pumps. But neither of these statements is true. Friction loss does exist and the cost of installing a sprinkler system increases as the pipe size increases. So, the role of the technician or the designer pelforming the hydraulic calculations is to balance friction loss against cost. Keep the pipe sizes small to limit the installation cost while at the same time, not losing more pressure than the water supply can allow, All the time, the 301

## Page 308

designer or technician needs to keep in mind the two questions: how much water do we need to discharge from each sprinkler and how many sprinklers do we think are going to open if there is a fire. Basic Procedure The NFSA has developed the following procedure for performing hydraulic calculations. Some of the steps have been discussed in great detail in previous chapters of this text. The rest of the procedure will be discussed in this chapter. This procedure will work for all fire sprinkler systems, but in order to make sure that it works for all systems, it is not specific to the branch lines and mains. Every sprinkler system will be laid out differently; therefore, every sprinkler system will be slightly different in how it is calculated. By keeping this basic procedure in mind and performing actual calculations, designers and technicians will become accustomed to the application of the actual formulas during each step of the process. See the chapter titled First Calculation Example for more detail on exactly when to apply each of the formulas discussed in this chapter. The procedure is: 1) Select an appropriate hazard category for the building or the area in question 2) Determine the actual spacing for each sprinkler in the system 3) Determine the piping arrangement, making sure that pipe feeds all sprinklers 4) Determine the amount of water that will be needed to discharge from each sprinkler 5) Determine the number and location of the most demanding sprinklers that are likely to open if there is a fire 6) Start at most remote sprinkler and work backwards towards the water supply, calculating the flows and pressures necessary to make sure that each open sprinkler flows a sufficient amount of water 7) Compare the demand calculated in step 6 with the water supply Steps I, 2 and 3 have been discussed in previous chapters. Steps 4, 5 and 7 will be discussed below, A procedure for starting step 5 will be discussed in this chapter, but as stated before, it will be impossible to provide an exact procedure for performing this step because every sprinkler system is different. This is the step performed by computer programs. Even if you are using a computer program to perform your hydraulic calculations, you still need to understand the other six steps in this procedure. 302

## Page 309

Amount of Water Per Sprinlder There are three methods of answering the question, "how much water needs to discharge from the sprinkler to control or suppress the fire?" The three methods are: 1) The Density/Area Method 2) Through the use of specially listcd sprinklcrs, thc listing will contain minimum flow requirements 3) Tables or sections in NFPA 13 or other standards that state a specific flow to be used or a pressure to be applied at the sprinkler. This method is applied to the large drop sprinkler, the ESFR sprinkler and was originally applied to residential sprinklers (although most of the residential sprinklers used today fall under the specially listed category discussed in item above. Density/Area Method The density/area method of determining the flow needed out of the sprinklers has been the most popular for more than 30 years. Although specially listed sprinklers and other types of sprinklers like large drop and ESFR are gaining in popularity, the density/area method is still being used for a majority of fire sprinkler system calculations. In the density/area calculation method, the density is the variable that answers the question, "how much water needs to discharge from the sprinkler to control or suppress the fire?" The density is the measurement of the flow of water that discharges from a sprinkler and lands in a single square foot under that sprinkler. Density is measured in flow divided by unit area. In English units, the density is most often measured in gpm per sq ft. In metric units, the density is given in Liters per minute per square meter (L/min per sq m), which reduces down to millimeters per minute (mm/min). To better understand density, consider it an average of the flow of water coming out of a sprinkler as that water is being spread around to cover the floor area under the sprinkler. For example, assune that a sprinkler is discharging water at a flow rate of 45 gpm and that water is spreading out over a floor space of 225 sq ft under that sprinkler. The amount of water falling in any single square foot of space under that sprinkler will average 0.2 gpm per sq ft (45/225 = 0.2). That average amount of water is the density. Fire sprinklers have been used for more than 100 years. In that time, fire tests have been performed and experience in real fires has been studied and from all of that data, the density needed to control or suppress a fire in different occupancies has been determined. For light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies, the densities necessary to control or suppress a fire have been printed in a figure in NFPA 13 in Chapter 11 (Figure 11.2.3.1.5, reprinted here as Figure 21-1). For other hazards, like storage, NFPA 13 contains density criteria in other locations such as Chapter 12 or Chapter 13. 303

This is a fair question and the answer goes back to the 1960's when hydraulic calculations were first introduced into NFPA 13. At that time, the density/area curves were actually curved, representing the relationship between density and area found during analysis of fire testing and real fire experience. The curves were actually curved all the way up to the 1989 edition of NFPA 13. In the 1991 edition, the NFPA committee decided that the curves were difficult to use and that computer programmers entering the curves into their computers could do so more accurately if they were linear. They straightened out the curves into lines and made some of the points on the curves more conservative. After the curves were made into lines, a few people started to call them "Density/Area Lines" but the name wouldn't stick. There was too much history behind calling them curves. So today, we continue to call them "curves" even though they are lines. In Chapter 12 of NFPA 13, the density/area curves are still curves and have not been simplified into lines (yet). Most of the time when we are calculating a fire sprinkler system, we work backwards tlrough the system. In order to use the curves, a single point is selected off of the correct curve for the hazard being protected, In order to determine the minimum flow necessary from the sprinkler, the density associated with the point that was picked is multiplied by the area of coverage for that sprinkler. There is no need to meet any more than one point from the appropriate curve. The following is an example of the use of the density/area curves: A sprinkler in an ordinary hazard group 2 occupancy covers 130 sq ft, what is the required flow from the sprinkler? 304

The next step in the calculation process is to determine how many sprinklers are most likely to open in case of a fire. As with all aspects of fire protection, we try to be extremely conservative when making this detennination. Although many fires are controlled or suppressed by one or two sprinklers, it is unusual to see a design area this small. More typically, design areas range from a low of four sprinklers to a high of 30 or 40. This is where much of the safety factor is included in the calculation of sprinkler systems. Density/Area Curves As discussed before, the density/area method of design is the most commonly used method of answering the question, "how many sprinklers are going to open?" While the density portion of the curves was used to answer the question about the flow from each sprinkler, the area portion is used to answer the question of how many sprinklers to calculate. The exact number of sprinklers that will be assumed to be open in the a fire will vary depending on the spacing of sprinklers and the placement of sprinklers with respect to walls. In a building where the sprinkler spacing is consistently the same, the number of sprinklers to calculate can be calculated using the following formula: Where:N = the total number of sprinklers to calculate Ac = the area from the density/area curves As = the area of coverage for the typical sprinklers in the system Note that this formula only works when most (almost all) of the sprinklers in the system are installed on the same spacing, When sprinklers are not installed on relatively uniform spacing, other methods must be used to answer the question regarding the number of sprinklers in the design area. These other methods will be discussed later in this chapter. 306

## Page 313

Consider the following example. Sprinklers are installed throughout an ordinary hazard group 2 occupancy at 10 ft x 12 ft spacing. The point of 0.2 gpm per sq ft over 1500 sq ft is selected from the density/area curves. How many sprinklers need to be in the design area? In order Lo answer the question, the design area selected from the curves needs to be divided by the area of coverage for each sprinkler. In this case, the area of coverage for each sprinkler is 120 sq ft (10 x 12 120). The total number of sprinklers in the design area then needs to be 13 (1500/120 = 12.5 rounded up to 13). Note that when this calculation is made, any fraction, no matter how small needs to be rounded up to the next whole number. This is because you can't get a fraction of a sprinkler to open. Sprinklers are either open or they are not. The number of sprinklers in the design area needs to be an integer. The number can never be rounded down, no matter how small the decimal is, because the area covered by the sprinklers will be less than the necessary design area selected off of the curves. The design area needs to be the hydraulically most demanding in the sprinkler system. In most situations, this will include the single sprinkler that is the faithest from the water supply. However, in sprinkler systems with special sprinklers, multiple hazards or in systems with non- uniform spacing, the single most demanding sprinkler may not be the farthest from the water supply. It may be necessary to perform multiple sets of hydraulic calculations to prove that the most demanding situation has been found. For sprinkler systems where the piping is in the configuration of a grid, it is not easy to determine just by looking at the system which is the most demanding sprinkler (or set of sprinklers) so NFPA 13 requires three sets of hydraulic calculations to be performed, the most demanding and the two design areas to either side. Once the number of sprinklers in the design area has been determined, the next step is to determine the shape of the design area. Section 14.4.4.1.1.1 states that the design arga is to be a rectangle and gives the dimension for the length of the rectangle in the direction parallel to the branch lines (1.2 times the square root of the design area). This forces more sprinklers to be calculated on the branch line, which forces the branch line pipes to be slightly larger than they would have been if a perfectly square area were used. Note that some insurance companies, such as Factory Mutual, require the length of the rectangle to be 1.4 times the square root of the area rather than the 1.2 required by NFPA 13. This leads to a more conservative design than what is required by NFPA 13 and forces the branch lines to be slightly larger to accomrnodate the extra flow. In order to find the number of sprinklers that need to be in the design area on the branch line, the following formula can be used on systems where the distance between sprinklers on the branch line is similar: Where NBL = number of sprinklers to calculate on a branch line Arca = the value selected from the density/area curves S = distance between sprinklers on the branch line 307

Note that in the situation shown in Figure 25-2, the design area is not a single rectangle. This is not an unusual situation. Frequently, the total number of sprinklers in the design area does not work out to be divisible by the number of sprinklers on the branch lines to yield a precise integer. Instead, there is frequently a remainder, a few sprinklers that need to be added to make the full design area. When this situation occurs, the designer or technician needs to select the sprinklers that are the most demanding. W"hiie it might seem that the sprinklers farthest from the water supply are the most demanding, this is not the case. The physics of water flowing through the piping actually make the sprinklers closer to the water supply more demanding because they are exposed to a higher pressure and will therefore discharge more water if they open. So, for the third most remote branch line, the tlu•ee sprinklers closer to the main were selected for the design area rather than the 3 sprinklers at the far. end of the main. In summary, the sprinklers in the design area have to be the most demanding for the sprinkler system. Once the most demanding sprinkler in the system (usually the most remote) is included in the design area, every sprinkler closer to the riser operates at a higher pressure, and is therefore more demanding. The design area consist of the correct number of sprinklers per branch line as determined by 1.2 times the square root of the area from the density/area curves. After that, additional branch lines with the same number of sprinklers (in the same location) are added until the design area is reached or the addition of another full branch line will take the total area above that needed. If the addition of another full branch line will take the area over that needed to meet the desired area, then individual sprinklers (starting with the sprinkler closer to the water supply) are added until the total design area is reached. It sounds rather confusing when described in words, but it's actually quite simple. Consider the following example. Sprinklers are installed in a warehouse on a 10 ft x 10 ft spacing. The design criteria is 0.45 gpm per sq ft over 2000 sq ft. How many sprinklers are in the design area and what is the shape of the design area? Since each sprinkler covers an area of 100 sq ft (10 x 10 = 100) there need to be a minimum of 20 sprinklers in the design area (2000/100 = 20). The maximum number of sprinklers that need to be in the design area on each branch line is: 1.2UÖÖÖ = 5.4=6 10 The design area for this example will be 20 sprinklers, 6 sprinklers on the most remote branch line, 6 sprinklers on the second and third most remote branch lines, and only two sprinklers on the fourth most remote branch line, See Figure 25-3 to see a graphic representation of this sprinkler system and its design area. Note how the two sprinklers on the fourth most remote branch line are the ones closest to the water supply (cross main) on that branch line. 309

Most remote branch line Second most remote branch line Third most remote branch line Fourth most remote branch line Design Area of 20 sprinklers IO ft 10 ft Figure 25-3 Storage Design Area Example The density/area cuwes that are shown in Figure 25-1 are just one of the sets of curves that NFPA 13 uses to determine the discharge criteria for sprinkler systems. These particular curves are for light through extra hazard. Other such curves exist for lots of other situations such as storage. In some situations, NFPA 13 provides the user with density/area points rather than curves. Even though the users have no choice, the concept is still the same: use the density for flow and the area for the number of sprinklers that you have to calculate as possibly opening in the event of fire. Area Adiustments Once a point is selected from the density/area curves used for light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies, some adjustment to the area may be necessary. The following adjustments only apply to light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies, similar adjustments may be necessary for other situations (like storage) and will be covered in subsequent chapters of this text. The 310

## Page 317

following situations require that an adjustment be made and will be discussed in more depth following the list: Dry-pipe sprinkler system o Double-interlock preaction system High temperaturc sprinklers (extra hazard occupancies only) Quick response sprinklers (light and ordinary hazard only) Sloped ceilings o Unsprinklered combustible concealed spaces Dry-Pipe Sprinkler Systems For dry-pipe sprinkler systems, the design area selected from the density area curves is required to be increased by 30%. The adjustment is expected to be made without any change to the density. So, if a value of 0.2 gpm per sq ft over 1500 sq ft is selected for an ordinary hazard- group 2 occupancy with a dry-pipe system, the area increase of 30% would bring the discharge criteria to 0.2 gpm per sq ft over 1950 sq ft. The purpose of the 30% increase is to account for the time delay in getting water into a dry-pipe sprinkler system. When a fire occurs in a building protected by a dry-pipe sprinkler system, the first sprinkler opens and drops the pressure enough to trip the dry-pipe valve. Once the valve trips, it takes time for the water to travel from the dry-pipe valve through the piping system to the open sprinkler(s). During that delay in getting water to the fire, it is possible for the fire to grow and open additional sprinklers. The value of 30% for an increase was selected after a review of actual fire data and full- scale fire tests. It has been considered to be conservative for light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies. In recent times, there has been a concern about the use of quick response sprinklers in dry-pipe systems. Some fire protection experts have been concerned that, due to the extra sensitivity of the quick response sprinklers, more sprinklers may open than the 30% increase has accounted for. Research performed by the NFSA has shown that the 30% increase is sufficient, even when a sprinkler system uses quick response sprinklers. Double Interlock Preaction Systems For double-interlock preaction systems, the design area is also required to be increased by 30%. The reason for this increaée is the same as that for dry-pipe systems. In double-interlock preaction systems, the water does not start through the piping system until the fire opens a sprinkler, just as in dry-pipe systems. Traditionally, double-interlock preaction systems keep air in the system at a much lower pressure than a dry-pipe system, so the water should have less 311

## Page 318

resistance as it moves through the pipe and should get to remote sprinklers much more quickly than a dry-pipe system. These traits of a double-interlock system might argue for a smaller increase than 30%, but no research has yet been pelformed to justify any other increase. There are two other kinds of preaction sprinkler systems: single-interlock and non- interlocking. For these two types of systems, no area increase is required (in light ordinary and extra hazard occupancies) because water staffs to flow in the piping system before a sprinkler opens due Co the heat of a fire. The assumption is that the detectors used in preaction systems are more sensitive than the sprinklers and will activate to staff the flow of water before sprinklers open. If a preaction system is being designed with detectors that are not more sensitive than the sprinklers, some area increase should be included in the design. For storage occupancies, all types of preaction systems might be required to take on an area increase depending on the situation. More information is available on this topic in the NFSA publication Sprinkler Protection for Storage and Warehouse Occupancies. High Temperature Sprinlders in Extra Hazard Occupancies The density/area curves for extra hazard are based on the use of ordinary temperature sprinklers. When high temperature sprinlders are used, the design area can be decreased by 25%, but never below the minimum threshold of 2000 sq ft. So, for an extra hazard-group 1 occupancy, the point of 0.3 gpm per sq ft over 2500 sq ft can be selected. If high temperature sprinklers are being used, the area can be decreased. A 25% decrease is the same as multiplying the area by 75% (0.75). Taking 75% of the design area is 1875 sq ft (2500 x 0.75 = 1875). However, the design area is not allowed to go below 2000 sq ft, so the density and area criteria are 0.3 gpm per sq ft over 2000 sq ft. The area decrease is justified by full-scale fire testing that has shown that fewer sprinklers tend to open in extra hazard fires when high temperature sprinklers are used. The reason for this is that the first few rings of sprinklers that open tend to control the temperature of the gasses spreading out from a fire. At some point, the temperature of the gasses from the fire are cooled to the point where they are below 2860F, but above 1650F. These gasses washing over sprinklers that have not yet opened will eventually open ordinary temperature sprinklers, but not high temperature sprinklers. Note that this decrease can only be taken for extra hazard occupancies. For light and ordinary hazard occupancies, the fires don't tend to open enough sprinklers for the difference to be significant. For higher hazard occupancies like storage, there are similar decreases allowed, or high temperature sprinklers are mandated to minimize the number of sprinklers that would open. More recently, some larger orifice sprinklers (k-11.2 or bigger) have been listed for storage occupancies that are ordinary temperature. These sprinklers were listed for their superior abilities to control and suppress fires that tend to happen in storage occupancies. Even though these big orifice sprinklers are ordinary temperature, they perform as well or better than high temperature sprinklers in the same occupancies and are allowed to be used with the high temperature sprinkler density/area curves of the storage chapter of NFPA 13. More information on this issue will be discussed in the Storage chapter of this text. 312

## Page 319

Ouicic Response Sprinklers in Light and Ordinary Hazard Occupancies In light and ordinary hazard occupancies where quick response sprinklers have been used throughout the compartment, the design area can be reduced by a figure between 25 and 40% depending on ceiling height. In order to take advantage of this reduction in area, all of the following conditions must be met: Wet pipe system only 0 20 ft maximum ceiling height No unprotected ceiling pockets Although the design area can be less than 1500 sq ft, it cannot be less than 5 sprinklers For ceiling heights of 10 ft or less, the reduction to the design area is allowed to be 40%. For ceiling heights of 20 ft, the reduction in design area is allowed to be 25%. For ceiling heights over 20 ft, no reduction in design area is allowed. For any ceiling height between 10 and 20 ft, the allowable reduction in design area is defined by a line with the following equation: —3x = + 55 2 Where:y = the percentage of decrease allowed in the design area x = the ceiling height in feet For example, if the ceiling is 18 ft high in an occupancy where quick response sprinklers are used, the design area can be reduced by 28% by the following calculation: -308) —3x +55=55-27-28 y = — + 55 = 2 2 In this example, if the design area had been selected as 1500 sq ft, it could be reduced by 28%, which is the same as multiplying by 72%, to an area of 1080 sq ft as long as it has at least 5 sprinlders (1500 x 0.72 = 1080). The reduction in design area for quick response sprinklers is justified on the theory that the sprinkler will open earlier in the fire, while the fire is still small, and the fire will be controlled before it gets large enough to open too many sprinklers. This theory has been shown to be accurate in both real fires and full-scale fire testing. Some of the fire testing was conducted by the NFSA in the late 1980's where a hazard (with a 20 ft ceiling) that would have been required by NFPA 13 to be protected as extra hazard-group 2 was set on fire and protected by a sprinkler system designed to discharge a density of 0.19 (52% less than what would have been required). In twelve different tests with standard response and quick response sprinklers were performed and the fire was controlled in all cases. On average, 40% fewer sprinklers opened than standard response sprinklers. 313

## Page 320

Sloped Ceilings Roof and ceiling slopes are measured in terms of a ratio in vertical rise over a horizontal run as shown in Figure 25-4. The change in rise is always expressed before the change in run. For hazards where the roof or ceiling above the sprinklers is sloped more than 2 in 12, the design area needs to be increased by 30%. This increase is in addition to any other increase that might be required by any other condition. Rise 6 inches Slope must be expressed in consistent units, So this example would be expressed as 6 in 24 or 3 in 12 or 1 in 4 Figure 25-4 Slope The purpose of the 30% increase for sloped roofs and ceilings is to account for the additional sprinklers that open remote from the fire as heat runs up the slope and along the ridge. These sprinklers take water from the water supply, but are not usually close enough to the fire to actually have an effect. It takes more time for the heat to bank down and open sprinklers directly over the fire. During that delay, the fire will grow larger and require more sprinklers to open to control it. The delay in getting sprinklers directly over the fire to open is similar to the delay that occurs in dry-pipe systems, so the increase is the same. 314

## Page 321

It should be noted that the increase for sloped ceilings applies to light, ordinary and extra hazards, but not to storage. For storage occupancies, the number of sprinklers that might open during a fire under a sloped ceiling is unknown. While the 30% increase might be sufficient to account for the additional sprinklers that will open, the committee is not yet convinced that it is adequate for all circumstances and commodities. Therefore, the lilles in NFPA 13 for storage only cover situations where the ceiling is horizontal or has a slope up to 2 in 12. Ifthe roof for a storage occupancy slopes more than 2 in 12, the owner will have to get a professional engineer to determine appropriate discharge criteria or install a horizontal drop ceiling and sprinkler underneath that ceiling. Unsprinldered Combustible Concealed Spaces Most concealed spaces that are formed by combustible construction are required to be sprinklered, But NFPA 13 contains a list of 13 types of concealed spaces that have combustible constmction that are not required to be sprinklered. Some of these spaces present the potential for allowing a fire to travel through the building. In order to account for additional sprinklers that might open if the fire starts in one sprinklered space and then travels through an unsprinklered (combustible) concealed space and open additional sprinklers, a minimum design area of 3,000 sq ft is required if these spaces exist. The minimum is required to be applied after all other adjustments are made. So, in a building with a dry-pipe sprinkler system, the 30% increase is added and then the minimum 3000 sq ft is applied. This is one of the situations where the user of NFPA 13 might want to slide up the curve to minimize the density while meeting the 3000 sq ft rule. For example, in a light hazard occupancy with unsprinklered combustible concealed spaces that require the minimum 3000 sq ft design area, the point 0.07 gpm per sq ft over 3000 sq ft would make more sense than the 0.1 gpm per sq ft over 1500 sq ft point because the area would have to be increased to 3000 sq ft anyway. Not all unsprinklered combustible concealed spaces require the 3000 sq ft design minimum. The following is a list of the spaces that do NOT require the 3000 sq ft design minimum: Spaces filled entirely with noncombustible insulation Spaces consisting of wood joist construction in light and ordinary hazard occupancies where noncombustible or limited combustible ceilings are attached to the bottom of solid wood joists so as to create enclose joist spaces of 160 ft3 or less in volume, including areas under insulation directly on joists in an otherwise sprinklered attic. All exposed surfaces have a flame spread index of 25 or less Spaces over isolated small rooms 55sq ft in area Vertical pipe chases under 10 ft sq meeting 8.14.1.2.14 315

Any combustible concealed space that is not sprinklered and that does not appear as one of the five exceptions directly above requires the sprinkler system in that building to be designed with a minimum design area of 3000 sq ft. 3 ft IOft 12 ft Design Area of 14sprinklers The 14 sprinklers in Che design area actually cover 1530 sq ft Figure 25-7 Actual Floor Area Example — Sprinklers Closer to Wall, Correct Floor Area Room Design Method An alternative to the room design method for determining the number of sprinklers that will open during a fire is called the Room Design Method. Basically, this method assumes that all of the sprinklers in the room will open during the fire and confine the fire to that room. For the design of the sprinkler system, all of the sprinklers in the most demanding room (usually the largest room farthest from the water supply) will need to be calculated. The person performing the calculations must be careful to make sure that they look at all of the possibilities. A room farther from the water supply may be more demanding because of the arrangement of sprinklers or a room close to the water supply may be more demanding because of its size. In order to qualify for this design method, the room must be a compartment surrounded by walls and a ceiling. The walls are required to have a fire resistance rating equal to water supply duration applicable to the hazard classification (Table 11,2.3.1.1). Compartments are allowed to have openings to other compartments as long as there is a lintel over the opening at least 8 inches deep. The lintel helps the hot gasses from a fire stay in the room and build up in order to activate the sprinkler. 319

## Page 326

Openings in walls generally need some SOIt of protection (like a door) in them in order to help keep the heat in during a fire. For light hazard occupancies, the doors must have some sort of closing capability (automatic or self closer) or the calculations must include two sprinklers in the adjoining space. For ordinary and extra hazard occupancies, the doors must have automatic or self closers with appropriate fire resistance ratings for the walls they are set in, Corridors arc rooms and need to be considered when deternmining what the i00St demanding room is. It is entirely possible that a conidor might be the most demanding room in a building. However, most corridors are long and narrow and protected with a single row of sprinklers. A fire starting in a corridor is not likely to set off all of the sprinklers in the con•idor since the sprinklers will cool the gasses from the fire and prevent other sprinklers farther down the hall from opening. Therefore, a special set of rules exist for the room design method where the room in question is a corridor protected by a single row of sprinklers. For light hazard occupancies, a maximum of 5 sprinklers are calculated regardless of the number of sprinklers in the corridor or whether or not the openings onto the corridor have the correct fire resistant doors with closers or not. For ordinary and extra hazard occupancies, the doors are required to have the correct fire resistance and closers, so the design will also be 5 sprinklers for the corridor. Narrow rooms that can be protected by a single row of sprinklers are similar to corridors in that it is unlikely that all of the sprinklers in such a room would open. However, the amount of combustibles in a room are likely to be more than what is found in a corridor (considering that corridors are generally kept clear for egress) so the number of sprinklers that are required to be calculated is 7 if the room is narrow enough to be protected by a single row of sprinklers. The room design method is a completely separate method of determining how many sprinklers will open during a fire; therefore the rules from the density/area method do not apply. There is no requirement under the room design method to increase the number of sprinklers for a dry-pipe system nor is there any allowance for decreasing the number of sprinklers if quick response sprinklers are used, Quite simply, the room design method states that all of the sprinklers in the room will open, unless that room is long and narrow like a corridor. There is one unusual situation with the room design method. Even though none of the rules of the density/area method apply to the room design method, there is a combination of sections in NFPA 13 (11.2.3.1.8 and 11.2.3.1.8(3)) that requires the 3000 sq ft minimum for qualified unsprinklered combustible concealed spaces (the same as the density/area method). So, even if the room design method is used, the 3000 sq ft rule has to be followed if there are unsprinklered combustible concealed spaces of the type that require the 3000 sq ft rule. Frequently, when using the room design method, there will be many different rooms, each with unique flow and pressure demands. If one single room has the highest pressure and flow demand, that will be the single most demanding room to use for the hydraulic calculations. If there is one room that has the highest flow demand, and a different room that has the highest pressure demand, then both rooms are considered the most demanding and two sets of hydraulic calculations need to be performed. The water supply will need to be capable of supplying both of the rooms (individually, not added together). 320

Other Sprinklers For some sprinklers, the answer to the question, "How many sprinklers will open if there is a fire?" is answered by the very type of sprinkler being used. By definition, certain sprinklers have a set number of sprinklers in the design area either by statements in NFPA 13 or by the listing of the sprinkler. Each of the sprinklers in this category will be discussed in the following section. Extended Coverage Sprinklers For extended coverage sprinklers, the number of sprinklers to calculate comes from the area portion of the density area curves divided by the area of coverage per sprinkler, but cannot be below 5 sprinklers. For example, if an extended coverage sprinkler is being used in an ordinary hazard occupancy at 14 ft x 14 ft spacing, the number of sprinklers in the design area will be 1500 sq ft divided by 196 sq ft per sprinkler (14 x 14 = 196) yielding 8 sprinklers in the design area (1500/196 = 7.6 rounded up to 8). Since this special design method for extended coverage sprinklers references the area portion of the density/area method, all of the area adjustments also apply to this method of design. So the design area must be increased for dry-pipe systems and is allowed to be decreased for the use of quick response sprinklers. If the example in the above paragraph had utilized quick response sprinklers and had a 20 ft ceiling, a 25% reduction in design area would be permitted. The design area would be 1125 sq ft and the number of sprinklers would be 6 (1125/196 = 5.7 rounded up to 6). As another option, the room design method can be used with extended coverage sprinklers. If this is the case, the same rules apply as those discussed for the room design method above. When extended coverage sprinklers are used with the room design method, it can be very difficult to determine the most demanding situation, so many different possibilities usually need to be explored. Large Drop Sprinklers The tables in Chapter 12 of NFPA 13 declare how many sprinklers to calculate for a variety of different commodities. More information on these sprinklers can be found in the NFSA publication Sprinkler Protection for Storage and Warehouse Occupancies. Specific Application Control Mode Sprinklers The tables in Chapter 12 of NFPA 13 declare how many sprinklers to calculate for a variety of different comrnodities. More information on these sprinklers can be found in the NFSA publication Sprinkler Protection for Storage and Warehouse Occupancies, 321

Assuming that the pipe is I-inch schedule 40 steel pipe, the friction loss is as follows: 4.5201 85 x10=1.8 1.85 4.87 The pressure loss between the most remote sprinkler and the second most remote sprinkler is 1.8 psi. This means that the pressure necessary at the second most remote sprinkler is 20.2 psi in order for the system to work. The figure of 20 psi is obtained by adding the 18.4 psi necessary at the first sprinkler to the 1.8 psi of friction loss between the sprinklers. If a pressure of 20.2 psi exists at the second most remote sprinkler, it will discharge more water than 24 gpm when it opens during a fire. We need to calculate that amount of water using the formula: 25.2 The second most remote sprinkler will discharge 25.2 gpm. The pipe feeding this sprinkler will need to flow a minimum of 49.2 gpm. This figure is calculated by adding the flow of 24 gpm necessary for the first sprinkler to the 25.2 gpm necessary for the second sprinkler. The sprinkler coming from thethird most remote sprinkler to the second most remote sprinkler needs to carry this total flow (49.2 gpm). The rest of the sprinkler system is calculated working back toward the water supply adding the flow of open sprinklers and calculating the pressure loss in the pipe between the sprinklers. At each sprinkler, the total pressure necessary to make the system work is used to calculate the discharge of the water from that sprinkler. Once all of the flow from all of the sprinklers in the design area have been added in, the friction loss from the design area to the water supply needs to be calculated. This total flow and pressure is the demand of the sprinkler system. 7) Compare the demand calculated in step 6 with the water supply. For this example, we don't have water supply information, but if we did, this is the step where it would be compared to our demand (calculated in step 6). If our demand was greater than our supply, we would need to go back and change something about our sprinkler system to lower the demand, such as increasing our water pipe 325

sizes. Note that when pipe sizes are increased in the design area, it lowers friction loss, which lowers the pressure at each sprinkler. So, increasing the pipe size in the design area has the effect of lowering the pressure demand as well as the flow demand. Increasing the pipe size outside the design area will lower the pressure demand, but will not lower the flow demand. CHAPTER 26 HYDRAULIC CALCULATION FORMS, NFPA 13 RULES AND FIRST HYDRAULIC CALCULATION The process described in the previous two chapters provides all of the basics for understanding how to perform hydraulic calculations for sprinkler systems. But the actual process is difficult to teach and without specific information, it is difficult to grasp. Part of the difficulty is that there is no set step-by-step procedure that will work for every sprinkler system (although we have tried to put something together in the next few paragraphs). In order to help understand how to perform hydraulic calculations, this chapter will provide a specific example and walk the reader through the process of calculating this system step-by-step. Although the exact process used in this example will not work for every sprinkler system, it will provide a basic philosophy that can be implemented in all sprinkler systems. In addition to outlining a process and proving an example, this chapter will also discuss many of the specific rules of NFPA 13 and how they apply to specific situations within the example. The example has been specifically chosen to present many of the common features of fire sprinkler systems so that these important points can be discussed, So many people have asked over the years for a specific step-by-step procedure to follow for every sprinklers system, that it is worth trying to put something together. The following procedure (from the previous chapter, but expanded) is the closest that can be developed in terms of a step-by-step procedure that would work for all sprinkler systems: 1) Select an appropriate hazard category for the building or the area in question. 2) Determine the actual spacing for each sprinkler in the system. 3) Determine the piping an•angement, making sure that pipe feeds all sprinklers. 4) Determine the amount of water that will be needed to discharge from each sprinkler (start with the most remote sprinkler). Using the flow required for the most remote sprinkler and the k-factor of the sprinkler, also calculate the pressure that will be necessary to make sure this flow can be pushed out of the sprinkler when it opens. 333

## Page 338

5) Determine the number and location of the most demanding sprinklers that are likely to open if there is a fire (the size and shape of the design area). 6) Start at the most remote sprinkler with the flow and pressure necessary for that sprinkler (calculated in step 4). a) Calculate the friction loss between the most remote sprinkler and the second most remotc sprinkler. b) Add the friction loss (and any elevation loss) between the first and second most remote sprinklers to the pressure necessary at the most remote sprinkler to determine the demand pressure at the second most remote sprinkler. c) Use the preesure at the second most remote sprinkler and the k-factor for that sprinkler to calculate the flow from that sprinkler. d) Add the flow from the second sprinkler to the flow from the first to determine the total flow that has to come down the pipe from the third sprinkler to the second. e) Continue down the branch line calculating the friction loss (and elevation loss) between sprinklers to determine what the pressure will be at the sprinkler and use that pressure and the k-factor of the sprinkler to calculate the flow. Add the flow from the sprinkler to the total flow and calculate the friction loss back to the next sprinkler, Continue repeating this procedure for all of the sprinklers on the branch line, f) Calculate the friction loss (and elevation loss) from the last sprinkler on the branch line that is in the design area to the cross main. Add this loss to the pressure at the last sprinkler on the branch line to get the pressure demand at the connection of the branch line to the cross main. g) Using the flow and pressure demand at the connection of the branch line to the cross main, calculate the k-factor for the most remote branch line. h) Calculate the friction loss for the flow between the most remote branch line and the second most remote branch line (as well as the elevation loss). Add the loss to the pressure demand at the remote branch line to get the pressure demand at the second most remote branch line. i) If the number, location and arrangement of sprinklers on the second branch line are identical to the first, including the number of sprinklers in the design area, the k-factor calculated in step 6(g) can be used along with the pressure at the second most remote branch line, calculated in step 6(h), to calculate the flow going up into the second branch line. 334

j) Add the flow from the second branch line to the first to get the total flow. k) Continue down the cross main adding additional flow for additional branch lines with sprinklers in a similar manner as adding sprinklers along the branch line. The k-factor calculated in step 6(g) can be used for any branch line with the same number, location and anangement of sprinklers as the first branch line (including the number of sprinklers in the design area). Add the loss to the pressure demand back at the cross main to determine the total pressure demand for the system at the water supply. 7) Compare the demand calculated in step 6(1) with the water supply Hydraulic Calculation Forms When performing hydraulic calculations by hand, the best way to keep track of the information is to use a form. The most popular form is published in the annex to NFPA 13 (Figure A. 14.3.3 in the 2002 edition). Another version of the form is available in pads of 100 du•ough the NFSA Resource Center, an example of which is shown in Figure 26-1. This section of the book will be an explanation of the columns in the form and how to use the form. Hydraulic calculation forms are used for many purposes. The original user needs them to keep track of the multiple pieces of information necessary to correctly perform the hydraulic calculations. Once finished, the calculation forms are turned over to plan review officials, who use them as a method of verifying that the correct procedures were followed in calculating the system. Additionally, the calculations serve as a back-up to the system drawings so that information such as distances between nodes, locations of sprinklers and positions of equipment can be double checked. Due to this multiple use of the forms, it is incumbent on the original user filling out the forms to provide as much information as possible for the future readers. Think of these forms as a forest of information. The data that you put down on the forms is the trail of breadcrumbs that leads the reader through the forest and helps them follow your path. You have to give them as many breadcrumbs as possible so that they can follow (understand) what you did, so provide as much detail as possible to make your calculations understandable. 335
