The top of the form contains some basic information about the sprinkler system being calculated ("Contract Name"). It is a good idea to use this portion of the form to keep straight which system (or portion of a system) is being calculated. In the upper right This poltion of the form is corner of the fonn is a section labeled "Sheet of used for systems needing multiple pages of calculations. The user can use this portion of the form to keep track of pages by using the first blank to note the page they are working on and the second blank to note the total number of pages in the calculation. The first column of the form is a reference column or step number. This column is rarely used unless iL is not easy to determine the order of the calculations. Most calculations start at the top and work their way down the form. In this case, the first column is not necessary. But if the form is not used from the top down, the user should give some clue to future readers as to what order they performed each step. Node Identification The second column of the form is titled "Nozzle Type and Location" or "Nozzle Identification and Location". It is used to declare the nodes being calculated in each step. Each row is considered one step. Within each row, some of the columns are split into two or three lines of information. The "Nozzle" column is used to state the nodes at the beginning and ending of each step. Since the information at the top of each row is usually associated with the node at the beginning of the step, while the information at the bottom of the row is usually associated with the end of the step, some people use this column by putting the beginning node at the upper left of the column and the ending node at the lower right of the column. This helps to keep the information straight. Some people use the "Nozzle" column by just stating the sprinkler (usually the starting node of the step) and its location without actually stating the ending node of the step. The terminology might be, "sprinkler 2 on branch line 1". While this terminology complies with the name of the column, it is less helpful to future readers because it is not clear where the beginning and end of the step actually takes place. Therefore, this practice is not recommended. Flow Summary The third column is "Flow" and is divided into two lines for every step. The top line is labeled with a small "q" while the bottom line is labeled with a capital "Q". The area with the small "q" is used to describe the flow discharging from the system at the beginning node of the step. This usually occurs as the flow from a sprinkler. The area with the large "Q" is used to record the total flow in the pipe between the two nodes of the step. This flow is usually greater than the flow discharging from the sprinkler, so it is represented by the larger "Q". The "Q" in many steps is calculated by adding the small "q" from the current step to the large t 'Q" from the previous step. 337

## Page 342

Pipe Size The fourth column is labeled "Pipe Size" and is used to record the actual diameter of the pipe. Some people use this column by just writing in the nominal pipe size (such as I-inch or inch), however, this policy does not provide much information to future readers of the calculations. Use of the actual inside diameter of the pipe is required for calculations. Different kinds of pipe have different internal diameters even though their nominal sizes are the same. so) I-inch pipe is not descriptive enough to determine if the calculations were performed correctly. Instead, the actual inside diameter of the pipe being used should be entered in this column. For example, 1.049 should be used for 1- inch schedule 40 pipe and 1.097 should be used for I-inch schedule 10 pipe. Equivalent Lengths for Fittings and Devices The fifth column is labeled "Fittings and Devices". This column is used to list any device, valve, tee or elbow that causes extra friction loss in the system between the nodes in the step. Some people just use this step to list the fittings, others try to squeeze in the equivalent length of the fitting, which can be difficult given that the equivalent length may take a great deal of calculation by itself. The concept of an "equivalent length" for fittings deserves some discussion. There are many different ways that could be used to account for the friction loss that occurs as water flows through a fitting. The method that the fire protection industry has settled on is to express the energy loss that occurs through the fitting as an "equivalent length" of pipe. The "equivalent length" of the fitting is the length of the same size pipe that would create the same amount of friction loss as what occurs in the fitting. For example, if water flowing through a 2-inch 90 degree elbow at 100 gpm loses 0.5 psi, then the equivalent Jength of the elbow will be the length of straight 2-inch pipe that has the same friction loss of 0.5 psi. Calculations show that this is 5 ft of pipe. The beauty of using the "equivalent length" method of calculation is that the length is the same regardless of flow, making it easier to use consistent information in the calculations even when the person doing the calculations is making changes that cause the flow to change. There are a number of ways to obtain the equivalent length for a fitting or valve. The most common is to look the fitting up in a table. For example, see Table 14.4.3.1.1 in NFPA 13. While this Table is convenient, the user needs to recognize that it has limitations. This particular Table is only valid for Schedule 40 steel pipe with a C-factor of 120. For other types of pipe, adjustments need to be made to accurately calculate the • equivalent length of the pipe. There are two types of adjustments that may need to be made, The first is for pipes with C-factors different than 120. Table 14,4.3.2 in NFPA 13 contains a multiplying factor for common C-factors. For example, the multiplying factor for pipe with a C-factor of 100 is 0.713. A 90 degree elbow on a 2-inch piece of pipe with a C-factor of 120 has an equivalent length of 5 ft of pipe. For a pipe with a C- factor of 100, the elbow has an equivalent length of 3.6 ft of pipe (5 x 0.713 = 3.6). 338

## Page 343

It may sound counter-intuitive that the equivalent length for pipe with a C-factor of 100 is shoner than the equivalent length for the same fitting on a pipe with a C-factor of 120, but as you think about it, it will make sense. The friction loss through the fitting does not change based on the pipe it is connected to. For our example of an elbow on 2- inch pipe, the friction loss through the elbow is the same 0.5 psi regardless of the type of pipe connected to the elbow. But when comparing that 0.5 psi to a length of straight pipe, it will take a different amount of straight pipe to equal the same amount of friction loss (0.5 psi in our example). Since the pipe with the C-factor of 120 is smoother on the inside than the pipe with the C-factor of 100, it will take a greater length of pipe with a C- factor of 120 to achieve a friction loss of 0.5 psi than it will a pipe with a C-factor of 100. The second adjustment that needs to be made is when the pipe has a different internal diameter than Schedule 40 steel. Instead of a table in NFPA 13 describing the multiplying factor that needs to be applied, there is a formula in NFPA 13 that provides Lhe factor as follows: Factor = 4.87 d 40 where: CIA = the actual diameter of the pipe being used d40 = the inside diameter of the same nominal size of schedule 40 steel For example, the equivalent length of a 4 inch tee is 20 ft of schedule 40 steel pipe. Since schedule 10 pipe has a different internal diameter, a multiplying factor would need to be found using the internal diameters of the pipe as follows: Factor = 4.87 d 40 4.87 4.26 = 1.32 4.026 The multiplying factor needs to be applied to the equivalent length from the Table in NFPA 13 to obtain the equivalent length of the fitting for schedule 10 pipe. In this example, the equivalent length to use for a 4-inch schedule 10 tee is 26.4 ft (20 x 1.32). Many people find it difficult to remember or use this formula. For these people, the NFSA has developed a table that has already performed the calculation for you for many of the common different internal diameters of pipe. Feel free to utilize this table to find the multiplying factor rather than the formula described above. 339

This will be necessary any time the pipe being used does not have a C-factor of 120 and does not have the same internal diameter as schedule 40 steel. For example, if 6-inch lined ductile iron pipe (Class 52) is being used (with an actual internal diameter of 6.03 inches) and a C-factor of 140, the equivalent length of a tee can be found by using the Table in NFPA 13 and applying two multiplying factors. The equivalent length of a 6- inch schedule 40 steel tee is 30 ft (see Table in NFPA 13). A multiplying factor of 1.33 needs to be applied for pipe with a C-factor of 140. A multiplying factor of 0.97 needs to be applied for the different internal diameter (use formula or table above). This makes the equivalent length for this tee 38.7 ft (30 x 1.33 x 0.97). As an alternative to calculating or looking up these equivalent lengths, another approach that is acceptable is to use information from a manufacturer. Many different pipe, fitting and valve manufacturers publish equivalent lengths for their materials. If the manufacturer's product is being used in accordance with its limitations, the published values by the manufacturer can be substituted for the Table and multiplying factors of NFPA 13. For example, manufacturers of CPVC pipe provide their own tables of equivalent lengths of fittings, which can be substituted for the Table and multipliers of NFPA 13. For some types of valves like pressure reducing valves, dry-pipe valves, alarm valves and internally loaded check valves, there is no information in NFPA 13 regarding the equivalent length of the fitting. For these devices, the manufacturer's information must be consulted to find the cotTect equivalent length. Be careful when applying the information from manufacturers to make sure that the information they provide matches the type of pipe in your system, If the type of pipe they provide information for does not match the type of pipe being used in your system, the conection factors of NFPA 13 still need to be applied. For example, if a manufacturer of check valves tells you that their 4- inch check valve has an equivalent length of 30 ft (for schedule 40 steel pipe with a C=120) and we were using schedule 10 pipe in our system (with a C-factor of 120), we would need to convert the equivalent length of the fitting for the different diameter of the schedule 10 pipe by multiplying the equivalent length by 1.32 making the correct equivalent length 39.6 ft (1.32 x 30 = 39.6). 340

## Page 345

For some types of valves, such as backflow preventers, the manufacturer does not provide friction loss in terms of equivalent length. Instead, the manufacturer provides the friction loss in terms of actual loss (usually in psi). For these situations, the friction loss must be taken at a different point in the calculations (usually in the pressure summary column discussed later in this chapter) since there is no known equivalent length. The sixth column is labeled "Equivalent Pipe Length" or "Pipe Equivalent Length" and is divided into three lines labeled "L", "F" and "T". The "L" line is used for the actual length of pipe between the beginning and ending node in the step. The "F" line is used for the total equivalent length of all of the fittings between the beginning and ending node for the step after all correct adjustments have been made. The "T" line is intended to be the total length of pipe and fittings. "T" should always be equal to "L" + F for each step. Friction Loss and Pressure Summary The seventh column ("Friction Loss psi/ft") is used to record the friction loss per foot of the flow (Q from the third column) through the pipe with the diameter (from the fourth column). The friction loss per foot is calculated using the Hazen-Williams formula as discussed in previous chapters of this text. The eighth column ("Pressure Summary" or "Required psi") is broken up into three lines per step. The first line is labeled "Pt" and is intended to be used to describe the total pressure required at the beginning node of the step. The second line is labeled "Pe" and is intended to be used for the change in elevation between the beginning and ending nodes in the step. The third line is labeled "P/' and is intended to be used for the total friction loss between the beginning and ending nodes in the step. For each step, Pf will be equal to the total length of pipe and fittings (T from the sixth column) times the Hazen-Williams friction loss per foot in the seventh column. All tlu•ee of the pressures in the Pressure Summary column are intended to be added with the sum placed in the Pt line in the next step down, which is usually the starting pressure for the next node and the next step. The ninth column is labeled "Normal Pressure" and will not be discussed or used in this text. This column is used for an advanced procedure in hydraulic calculations where the effects •of velocity in the pipe are accounted for to fine tune the calculations. NFPA 13 does not require the use of this column or this procedure. Additional information on using this column can be found in advanced hydraulics information available from the NFSA. 341

Notes The last column of the calculation form is labeled "Notes". The person pelforming the calculations should use this column to describe everything that they do including the formulas and equations used to determine the flow from sprinklers and other steps in the calculation. First Hydraulic Calculation The use of the calculation form will become second nature after a little practice. Let's start getting some practice by looking at a specific example in-depth. The rest of this chapter will be an example of how to perform hydraulic calculations on a specific sprinkler system. The sprinkler system in this example is for an electronics processing plant, which will be protected as an ordinary hazard group 1 occupancy. The building is 18 ft high from floor to ceiling. The sprinklers on the system will be upright standard response standard spray sprinklers with a k-factor of 5.6 and will be installed 12 inches down from the (unobstructed type of construction) ceiling. The sprinklers will be spaced at 130 sq ft per sprinkler with 10 ft between branch lines and 13 ft between sprinklers on the branch lines. The cross main will be installed 2 ft below the ceiling and a 1 ft riser nipple will connect each branch line to a cross main. The plan view of the sprinkler system is shown in Figure 26-2. An elevation view of the sprinkler system is shown in Figure 26-3. An isometric view of the sprinkler system is shown in Figure 26-4. The water supply has been determined to have the following characteristics once it has been adjusted for the reasonable worse-case conditions: Static Pressure: 90 psi Residual Pressure: 60 psi at a flow of 1000 gpm Step 1 — Hazard Classification We have already been told that this building is being used as an electronics processing plant and that it will be treated as an Ordinary Hazard-Group 1 occupancy. Step 2 — Sprinkler Spacing We have already been told in this case that a uniform 130 sq ft spacing has been selected with 10 ft between branch lines and 13 ft between sprinklers on the branch lines. The sprinklers are located so that they are 5 ft from the East and West walls and 6.5 ft from the North and South walls. 342

Step 4 — Flow and Pressure for Sprinlders A point of 0.15 gpm per sq ft over 1500 sq ft is selected from the density/area curve for Ordinary Hazard Group 1 from Figure 11.2.3.1.5 in NFPA 13. Note that other points on the curve would be acceptable, but this is the one that has been selected for this example. A density of 0.15 gpm per sq ft applied to a sprinkler covering 130 sq ft results in a flow of 19.5 gpm (0.15 x 130 = 19.5). This means that each sprinkler that covers 130 sq ft must discharge at least 19.5 gpm. Since all of the sprinklers in this example cover 130 sq ft, this•will be the minimum flow necessary from each sprinkler. Of course, many sprinklers in this system will end up flowing more than 19.5 gpm as the pressure at each sprinkler increases. This minimum flow is called a "demand" flow because this is the amount of water that we have determined to be necessary in order to fight a fire in this building. In essence, we are demanding that the system supply this minimum amount of water: For a sprinkler to discharge water there needs to be some pressure in the water in the pipe in order to push the water out of the sprinkler. How much pressure is necessary will depend on how much flow is needed and how easy it is for the water to get through the orifice in the sprinkler. The k-factor is a measurement of how easy it is for the water to get through the hole. The k-factor is a function of the shape and the size of the orifice of the sprinkler. We can calculate the pressure necessary to discharge 19.5 gpm from a sprinkler with a k-factor of 5.6 with the following formula: 2 2 Q k 19.5 = 12.1 5.6 The equation above shows that we will need a minimum of 12.1 psi in order to push 19.5 gpm out of a sprinkler with a k*factor of 5.6. This pressure is also called a "demand" pressure because it is a minimum necessary to make the system work. 345

## Page 350

Step 5 — Size'and Shape of Design Area We have already determined that the area component of the density/area point that was selected from the density/area curve is 1500 sq ft (from Figure 11•.2.3.1.5). At this step, we should determine if there are any adjustments that need to be made to the area selected from the table. Since standard response sprinklers are being used, the decrease in area allowed for the use of quick response is not appropriate. Since the system is a wet-pipe system, the increase Lo the design area for dry-pipe systems is not appropriate. Since the roof is flat, the increase for sloped ceilings is not appropriate. Since ordinary temperature sprinklers are being used to protect this ordinary hazard occupancy, the reduction for high temperature sprinklers in extra hazard is not appropriate, In summary, there are no adjustments that would be appropriate and the design area should be 1500 sq ft. The next decision that needs to be made is the total number of sprinklers in the design area. With uniform spacing, this can easily be calculated by taking the design area (1500 sq ft) and dividing by the area of coverage per sprinkler (130 sq ft) as follows: 1500 -—=11.54-12 130 Note that the total number of sprinklers in the design area needed to be rounded up to 12 sprinklers from 11.54, This is because you can not have a fraction of a sprinkler open. Any fraction, no matter how small would have to be rounded up otherwise the number of sprinklers would not be sufficient to cover the required design area. In order to determine the shape of the design area, the maximum number of sprinklers to include on each branch line needs to be calculated from the following formula: = 3.58 — 4 13 Note that the formula calculates that we need a minimum of 3.58 sprinklers per branch line. Since we can't have only a fraction of a sprinkler open, we have to round that up to 4 sprinklers. Even if this had come out to a very small number after the decimal point, we would always have to round this number up. For example, 3.1 would also round up to 4 sprinklers because we would need that small fraction of the area covered by the fourth sprinkler and once you need the sprinkler open to cover that small fraction, you have to consider the flow from the entire sprinkler. In summary, the design area will consist of 12 sprinklers (see the cross hatched portion of Figure 26-2) with four sprinklers on the most remote branch line, four sprinklers on the second most remote branch line and four sprinklers on the third most remote branch line. The sprinklers on the North end of the branch lines have been selected in order to show an area, Since the system is exactly symmetrical in the way that it was placed in the building, the sprinklers on the South side of the branch lines would be equally correct. Not every sprinkler system will work 346

In many cases, the number of sprinklers on the last branch line will be less than the number of sprinklers on the other branch lines, In this case, the sprinklers to select are those that arc the most demanding and are adjacent to the ones being selected on other branch lines. The most demanding sprinklers are going to be those closest to the water supply because those are the sprinklers that will operate at the higher pressures and therefore would flow more water. First, let's look at the flow discharging from sprinkler S4 (24.3 gpm). Sprinkler S4 covers the same area (130 sq ft) as all of the other sprinklers in the system; however it is discharging more than the required flow to meet the required density, What is the density of the discharge from sprinkler S4? The density can be calculated by dividing the flow by the area covered by the sprinkler. For sprinkler S4, the density is 0.19 gpm per sq ft (24.3/130 = 0.19). This is 27% more than the 0.15 gpm per sq ft density required for this occupancy. This concept, that more water will discharge from sprinklers closer to the riser, is called "overage" and creates a significant safety factor for sprinkler systems, Even if the fire starts in the worst possible corner of the building, if it spreads out along the branch line, all of the other sprinklers will discharge more water than what is needed to control the fire. A sprinkler only 39 ft away from the worst corner of the building is already discharging 27% more water than what is necessary to control the fire. Another reason worth pausing here and examining the sprinkler system is to consider where the next node (point in the system) is that we need to take into account. We only need to worry about locations where there is flow exiting the system, locations where pipe diameter changes or locations where the type of pipe changes, In this case, there is a sprinkler between sprinkler S4 and the riser nipple that connects the branch line to the cross main. But this sprinkler is not in our design area and we don't have to worry about it discharging any water. As long as we use the same type of pipe and the same pipe size (lh inch) starting at sprinkler S4 and continuing all the way to the tee at the top of the riser nipple, we don't have to stop our hydraulic calculations. In fact, if we use the same size pipe (lh inch) for the riser nipple, we 354

don't need to stop until we get to the bottom of the riser nipple. We do need to stop there because the pipe size at the main changes to 2 inch pipe. A few paragraphs earlier, we calculated that the total flow coming into sprinkler S4 needs to be 86.4 gpm. Since there are no other openings in the first branch line creating flow, this is the same flow that needs to come out of the cross main and up the riser nipple to the first branch line. If we label the node at the bottom of the riser nipple (where it connects to the cross main) as BRN We can calculate what happens to the water between BRN and S4 in one step, The friction loss per foot in this section of lh inch pipe (1.61 inches actual inside diameter) can be calculated using the Hazen-Williams formula as follows: 4.5201 85 - 0.242 1.85 4.87 The friction loss per ft is 0.242 psi per ft and the total distance of pipe is 20.5 ft (13 ft between sprinkler S4 and the other sprinkler on the branch line plus 6.5 ft between that sprinkler and the riser nipple plus 1 ft in the riser nipple). In this step, we do have some equivalent lengths to add for fittings. There is a lh inch tee at the top of the riser nipple and another lh inch tee at the bottom of the riser nipple. Note that we have ignored the tee at the sprinkler that is not discharging water. Section 14.4.4.5(5) of NFPA 13 allows us to ignore flow that goes straight through a tee or cross. According to Table 14.4.3.1,1 of NFPA 13, the equivalent length of one lh inch tee is 8 ft (assuming schedule 40 pipe and C=120). Since we have two tees, we have to add 16 ft to our pipe length to get our total equivalent length of pipe and fittings of 36.5 ft (20.5 + 16 = 36.5). This makes the total friction loss between BRN and S4 8.8 psi (0.242 psi per ft x 36.5 ft). In this step, we also change elevation for the first time. The riser nipple is a total of 1 ft in length (straight up/down) making the elevation pressure loss 0.4 psi (0.433 x 1 = 0.4). With friction loss of 8.8 psi between BRN and S4 and an elevation loss of 0.4 psi, the total pressure necessary at BRN is 28.1 psi. (18.9 psi from S4 plus 8.8 psi plus 0.4 psi = 28.1). See Figure 26-15 for a picture describing this last step. See Figure 26-16 for how this would be represented on hydraulic calculation paper. 355

Once the first branch line (including the riser nipple) has been calculated to the cross main, it is wolfh stopping and asking the question "are any other branch lines that need to be calculated that are exactly the same as the first branch line?" If the answer to this question is "yes" then the next step is to calculate an equivalent k-factor that represents the branch line. The k-factor will rely on the flow and the pressure demand at the point where the branch line connects to the main (node BRN in our example). The following formula is used to calculate the k-factor for the branch line: Q 86.4 16.3 The k-factor of 16.3 represents the situation of the branch line and riser nipple that we just calculated and can be used to represent any branch line thal has the some number of sprinklers, the same pipe sizes and lengths and the same configuration of equipment (as do all of the other branch lines on this sprinkler system). We do not need to use the k-factor right now, but we calculated it right now because the information that we needed to calculate the k-factor was right at our fingertips. The next step is actually to calculate the friction loss as the 86.4 gpm flows down the 2 inch cross main (real inside diameter of 2.067 inches). In reality, the cross main would probably not have three different sizes of pipe (2 inch, then 2h inch then 3 inch) but they were included here to give the reader some experience working with different size pipe. In reality, this system would have probably had 3 inch pipe for the entire main. The friction loss between the first and second branch lines (BRN and BL2) can be calculated using the Hazen-Williams formula as follows: 4.5201 85 1.85 4.87 = 0.072 Note that the friction loss in the cross main is very small (0.072 psi per ft). Does this make sense? Yes it does. The flow in the cross main is small compared to the size of the main. Look at the Hazen-Williams formula. The pipe size is raised to the 4,87 power. This is incredibly powerful in reducing the friction loss per ft when the pipe size is increased, With a friction loss per ft of 0.072 and a distance of 10 ft between the branch lines (length of the cross main) the total friction loss between BRN and BL2 is 0.7 psi (0.072 x 10 = 0.7). This means that the total pressure at BL2 needs to be 28.8 psi (28.1 psi needed at BRN plus the 0.7 psi friction loss). See Figure 26-17 for how this would be represented on hydraulic calculation paper. 357

## Page 368

The next to the last step is to calculate from the base of the riser (BOR) out [hrougli lhe underground to the city main. While this is fundamentally like the previous steps, it will be made slightly more difficult by the fact that the interior diameter of the copper tube is not the same as the schedule 40 pipe we have been using. Additionally, the copper tube has a different C-factor, so we will have to make some adjustments to the equivalent lengths for the fittings. The copper tube has a length of 55 ft (50 ft horizontally from the riser to the street main and 5 ft vertically underground to connect with the riser in the building). There are three fittings in the copper tube, a long-turn elbow (an equivalent length of 5 ft from Table 14.4.3.1.1 in NFPA 13), a tee at the connection to the city main (equivalent length of 15 ft) and a gate valve (not shown on the drawing but very common in underground to isolate the underground pipe, equivalent length of 1 ft) for a total equivalent length of 21 ft if this were schedule 40 pipe. However the pipe is not schedule 40, so two different adjustments need to be made. The first is the adjustment for the C-factor. The C-factor for copper tube is 150, so according to Table 14.4.3.2 in NFPA 13, the correction factor that needs to be applied is 1.51. Also, a correction factor for the diameter needs to be taken from the Table earlier in this chapter or calculated from the following formula: 4.87 4.87 d pipe 2.907 = 0.77 3.068 So the true equivalent length that needs to be used for the fittings is 24.4 ft (21 ft from the schedule 40 Table times 1.51 times 0.77). This length needs to be added to the actual length of the pipe (55 ft) to achieve the total equivalent length of pipe and fittings of 79.4 ft (55 + 24.4 = 79.4), The friction loss can now be calculated, starting with the Hazen-Williams formula to obtain the friction loss per foot. Note that now the C-factor has changed to 150: 4.5201 85 1.85 4.87 - 0.071 (2.907)487 With a friction loss per ft of 0.071 and a total equivalent length of pipe and fittings of 79.4 ft, the friction loss in the copper underground can be calculated as 5.6 psi (79.4 x 0.071 = 5.6). Adding the 5.6 psi friction loss to the 64.6 psi demand at the base of the riser (BOR) yields the final pressure demand of 70.2 psi. See Figure 26-23 for how this information would be represented on hydraulic calculation paper. Note that there is no elevation change here even though the copper tube goes down 5 ft. This is because the water supply data was not obtained at the elevation of the copper tube. Instead, the water supply data was obtained from a fire hydrant several feet above the copper tube. In this case, the assumption is that the fire hydrant where the water supply data was obtained is at the same elevation as the base of the riser. When calculating this final step, always include the change in elevation between the base of the riser and the location of the fire hydrant where the water supply data was obtained. If the hydrant is below the base of the riser, the loss will be positive and a positive number should be entered in the calculation form. But if the hydrant is above the base of the riser, the loss will be negative (pressure will increase) so a negative number needs to be entered into the calculation form. 364

## Page 371

Step 7 -z Compare to Water Supply We have determined (at the end of Step 6) that this sprinkler system needs 513 gpm at a pressure of 70.2 psi in order to control a fire in this occupancy. Note that there are significant safety factors that have been incotporated in these figures. As a reminder, a few of these safety factors are: 1) The calculation included 12 sprinklers even though the overwhelming majority of fires are controlled or extinguished by 4 or fewer sprinklers. 2) The calculation assumes that all 12 sprinklers will open at once. In a fire, this rarely happens. It is much more likely that a few sprinklers will open with less total flow resulting in much lower friction loss in the system. Therefore, the density being discharged from these first sprinklers will be much more than the 0.15 gpm per sq ft required for this occupancy. This concept is known as "hydraulic increase" or "hydraulic lift". 3) The hose stream demand will not be used by the fire department early in the fire scenario, again saving water and pressure for fire sprinklers to discharge more Lhan the required minimum. 4) The C-factor of the pipe has been degraded in consideration of the fact that conditions inside the pipe deteriorate over time. In reality, the pipe is usually smoother on the inside than it has been calculated, which will result in less friction loss and more discharge from the sprinklers. 5) The sprinklers closest to the water supply will discharge more than the required density even when all 12 sprinklers in the design area are open. Only the single most remote sprinkler in the corner will flow at the density of 0.15 gpm per sq ft. 6) The water supply data given earlier (static pressure of 90 psi and residual pressure of 60 psi at 1000 gpm) has already been degraded, taking into account worse-case conditions for the daily and seasonal fluctuations in accordance with section 15.2.1.2 of NFPA 13. For all of these reasons, and more (see the article "Water Supplies -- How Low Should You Go" in the Summer 2002 edition of Sprinkler Quarterly, Issue 119), there is no specific safety factor required for our fire sprinkler system. We are allowed to plot the water supply data and use all of that flow and pressure for our sprinkler system, In our example, the water supply data (reduced for worse-case scenarios) is: Static Pressure: 90 psi Residual Pressure: 60 psi at 1000 gpm flow 367

Figure 26-26 shows the water supply information along with the sprinkler system demand point, With the demand well below the water supply curve, there is no problem using this sprinkler system with this water supply. Figure 26-26 System Demand Compared to Water Supply Another way to look at the water supply data is to use formulas rather than graphs. The beauty of the formula is that it allows more precise analysis rather than relying on the interpolation of points on a graph. As discussed in the Water Supply chapter of this text, the water supply can be represented with the following formula: 1.85 where: P = Pressure at any given flow PR = Residual pressure given in the water supply data PS = Static pressure given in the water supply data Q = Flow at which you want to know the pressure QR = Flow at the residual pressure (PR) 369

## Page 374

For the water supply in this example, PR is 60 psi, Ps is 90 psi and QR is 1000 gpm. Plugging these numbers into the equation yields the following formula Io describe this specific water supply: 1.85 P = (60-90 + 90 1000 This formula can be further reduced as follows: I .85 p 30 + 90 1000 1.85 1 (Q -l- 90 1000 P = +90 P = 8.46 +90 This last version of the formula can now be used to provide the pressure available from the water supply at any given flow. Right now, we know that at 1000 gpm, this water supply will deliver 60 psi (given from the data). But the biggest question we need answered is "how much pressure is available from the water supply at a flow of 513 gpm (the system demand including hose streams)?" To answer this question, we plug 513 in for Q and solve for P: P +90 p = —8.7+90 p = 81.3 So, with the graph, we estimated the pressure available to be about 82 psi. With the formula, we have actually calculated it to be 81.3 psi. Either way, for this sprinkler system, this water supply will do just fine. 370

CHAPTER 27 HANGERS AND HANGING Requirements for proper hanging of sprinkler systems have been included in the NFPA sprinkler rules since the publication of the first edition in 1896. Among the original acceptable types of hangers wcrc U-typc hangers made of round wrought iron or malleable cast iron, ring clips and approved adjustable hangers. Flat U-type hangers were permitted if at least 3/16-inch thick. Hangers were required to be placed at least 12 inches from sprinklers to avoid intelference, except that round hangers were permitted as close as 3 inches. For concrete construction, cast iron inserts were recommended, but expansion bolts could be used in existing buildings, preferably in a horizontal position. More than a century later, some of these same mles are still in place, such as the 3-inch minimum distance between upright sprinkler deflectors and the common hanger rod. For expansion shields in concrete, the standard continues to favor their use in the horizontal position. But those simple rules have been expanded over the decades. Today, the proper hanging of sprinkler systems and other water-based fire suppression systems relies on a combination of Lules for hangers and rules for hanging, These rules are found in separate but adjacent sections of NFPA 13, and are referenced for use by other NFPA standards such as NFPA 13R, NFPA 14 on standpipe and hose systems, NFPA 15 on water spray systems, NFPA 16 on foam-water sprinkler systems and NFPA 750 on water mist systems. They are not referenced for use by NFPA 13D since, as part of the objective of low-cost systems for dwellings, piping support methods used in local plumbing codes are considered acceptable except for special listed pipe, which must be supported in accordance with the requirements of its listing. Because piping support is used in other industries as well, and is considered a well-developed area of engineering, it is no surprise that hanging of sprinkler piping was one of the first aspects of sprinkler system design that was opened to perfotmance-based alternate approaches. A performance option is presented within NFPA 13 that allows the used of the standard to bypass the specific rules for hangers if a professional engineer certifies some other approach as meeting the following four provisions: o capable of supporting five times the weight of the water-filled pipe plus 250 lbs (114 kg) at each point of support o the points of support are adequate the spacing limitations for the piping material are not exceeded e the hanger components are ferrous (i.e. iron or steel) Detailed calculations must be submitted to the Authority Having Jurisdiction as required to prove the performance-based alternate. Performance-based approaches are most likely to be encountered in unusual buildings and structures, such as fabric-supported structures. They have also been applied in historic structures to avoid damaging the historic fabric of buildings, and have included concepts such as a self-supporting piping network that stands independent of the ceiling. 375

## Page 380

Hanger Requirements A general rule of the NFPA 13 hanger requirements is that the components of hanger assemblies that directly attach to the building structure must be listed. There are two exceptions to this rule: mild steel hangers formed from rods and fasteners (screws, bolts, etc.) as specifically allowed by the standard. When listing these components, the product approval laboratories apply the same "five times the weight of the water-filled pipe plus 250 pounds" criterion that was mentioned above for the performance-based alternate approach, As such, each listed hanger component is listed for the maximum nominal diameter pipe it can support, and the listing assumes the maximum allowable distance between hangers, The 250 lb (114 kg) additional load is sometimes misunderstood by architects and structural engineers to be a dead load to be added per system hanger, but that is not the intent. It is intended as an individual load that might be added to any individual hanger in the system at any time on a random basis. It is an additional bit of conservatism that many believe can represent the weight of a sprinkler fitter that might be grabbing onto a section of pipe while working on the system, but it could just as easily represent some other worker, perhaps a ceiling cleaner in a paper corrugation facility. Another general rule is also reflective of the performance-based criteria: hangers and their components must be ferrous. The intent if to provide hangers that will hold up to fairly intense heat from a fire that might develop prior to sprinkler operation and control. This would especially be the case with a dry pipe system awaiting water arrival to open sprinklers, Again, there are several exceptions. Nonferrous components are considered acceptable if their adequacy can be proven through fire tests reasonable for the hazard, as established through a listing and if otherwise in compliance with the standard. Another exception recognizes that holes through structural members such as solid wooden beams are permitted to serve as hangers if permitted by the applicable building codes. The various types of hangers are defined by how they attach to the building structure and to the sprinkler piping. However, if low-strength cinder concrete is used, expansion shields are permitted only for branch lines where alternated with through bolts or beam hangers. If installed vertically, expansion shields must be installed in holes drilled to provide uniform contact with the expansion shield over its entire length. Powder-driven studs and welding studs must also be listed, along with their installation tools. Once installed, powder-driven studs in representative samples of concrete must be tested for minimum loads in accordance with the standard. Section 9.1.3.9.3 (2002 edition) requires the following test loads: 0 750 lb (341 kg) for 2-inch (50 mm) or smaller pipe 0 1000 lb (454 kg) for pipe between 2-inch (50 mm) and 4-inch (100 mm) 1200 lb (545 kg) for 4-inch (100 mm) or 5-inch (125 mm) pipe An annex section suggests that steel used for attachment of powder-driven studs not be 3/16 inch (4.8 mm) thick. Steel must be not less than US standard 12 gauge for welded attachment of welding studs or other hanger parts. Increaser couplings must be directly attached to powder- driven studs or welding studs. Rods, U-hooks and eye rods are among the most common hangers and components due to their simplicity. The minimum allowed diameters allowed depend on the pipe size to be supported, but 3/8-inch diameter is the absolute minimum for rods and eye rods, 5/16-inch for U-hooks, unless they are part ofa listed hanger assembly. Most rods used as hanger components today are all-thread rods, but NFPA 13 does not permit threaded sections of rod to be bent or formed. This is due to concenl for stress cracking and subsequent corrosion as a result of the work hardening that takes place as the rod is threaded. For ceiling flanges as well as U-hooks, NFPA 13 specifies minimum screw options and dimensions in Table 9.1.5.2.1 (2002 edition). For coach screw rods, Table 9.1.5.7.2 (2002 edition) specifies minimum plank thickness and beam or joist face width. As an example, to support 3-inch pipe, the minimum plank thickness t is 4 inches, and the minimum beam or joist width W is 2 inches. plank tt Beam or joist w NFPA 13 contains some additional rules relating to hangers: Nails are not acceptable for fastening hangers Holes for lag screws and coach screw rods must be pre-drilled 1/8-inch less in diameter than screw thread maximum root diameter Bolts must be provided with a flat washer and nut, and holes for bolts must not be more than 1/16 inch larger in diameter than the bolt. Eye rods must be secured with lock washers to prevent lateral movement, with flat washer also provided for wood structural members 378

Hanging Requirements NFPA 13 contains some specific rules relating to the installation of hangers, such as maximum spacing. However, there are other considerations not specifically addressed by the standard. Most significant is the concept that it is most efficient to run branch lines perpendicular to the close-spaced structural members such as joists or purlins. This provides the opportunity for the most hanger attachment points for most of the system piping. A basic installation rule is that piping be supported independently of the ceiling sheathing. There are, however, two exceptions: e Toggle hangers are permitted under hollow tile or metal lath and plaster for pipe 1-1/2 inch (38 mm) or smaller. o Branch line hangers can support pipe I-inch (25 mm) and smaller by drilling or punching vertical members and using through bolts. Piping in storage racks to be suppoffed from the rack structure. As opposed to the requirement for hangers discussed earlier, the requirement for the structure is that it must be capable of supporting the weight of the water-filled piping plus 250 lb (114 kg). Because only one times the weight of the water-filled pipe is used instead of five times the weight, this is a less conservative requirement. The requirement recognizes that some structures may not have the additional strength, and suggests that the hanger will not be the weak part of an installation. Not all hangers are required to exclusively support the sprinkler piping. Piping under ducts can be supported from the ductwork supports, provided they are capable of supporting the sprinkler system loads in addition to those of the ductwork. Maximum hanger spacing is based on the type of pipe and nominal pipe size and is given in Table 9.2.2.1 (2002 edition). Steel pipe is assigned a maximum 15 ft spacing, but with a 12 ft maximum for pipe up to 1-1/4 inch and for threaded light wall steel pipe. Other maximums are assigned for copper, CPVC, and ductile iron pipe. A basic rule of hanging is that each pipe section must have its own hanger, although branch line starter lengths less than 6 ft do not generally require a hanger. For cross mains, the general rule is that there be at least one hanger between each two branch lines. There are a special set of exceptions for the use of steel pipe mains in bays whereby some hangers can be eliminated. Where hangers are attached to purlins on all branch lines as near to the cross main as possible, intermediate hangers are permitted to be omitted from steel cross mains in bays: o For 2 or 3 branch lines per bay, 1 hanger can be omitted o For 4 or more branch lines per bay, 2 hangers can be omitted 379

The example below shows an omission with 3 branch lines per bay Branch lines Permitted omission Cross main For special listed pipe special hanger requirements are often developed during the investigation and listing process. Beam strength of the special listed pipe is a primary consideration. As an example, special hangers are now available that are intended to avoid harm to nonmetallic piping through the elimination of sharp edges. NFPA 13 contains some special requirements relative to hangers and hanging in areas subject to earthquakes. For hangers in earthquake areas, retaining straps are required for all C-type clamps, which includes beam and large flange clamps. The retaining straps are either required to be listed or can meet the minimum dimensions specified in the standard: a steel strap of not less than 16 gauge thickness and not less than 1 in (25 mm) wide for pipe diameters 8 inch (200 mm) or less and 14 gauge thickness and not less than 1-1/4 inch (32 mm) wide for pipe diameters greater than 8 inch (200 mm). In absence of an adequate lip on the flange, the retaining strap is to be secured with a bolt or a screw. Also, powder-driven fasteners are not permitted where systems are required to be protected against earthquake accelerations greater than 0.5g unless specially listed. At the present time there are none listed for such service. Sometimes it is necessary to provide a point of attachment for the system piping where no st•uctural member is convenient. If branch lines are run perpendicular to the closely-spaced structural members as suggested earlier, the lack of a proper point of hanging is more likely to be for a cross main. In this case, trapeze hangers are often used to span between two structural 380

## Page 385

members to provide a suitable point of attachment. Trapeze hangers can therefore be considered an extension of the building structure; used to transfer loads to appropriate structural members. In the illustration below, a manufacturer of composite wood joists provides a detail of how an additional wood member can be attached between two composite wood joists to form a trapeze from which to attach a U-hook. O 4 NFPA 13 contains a simplified approach to the selection and sizing of trapeze hangers through the use of two tables. One table (Table 9.1.1.6.1(b) in the 2002 edition) specifies the minimum required "section modulus" of a trapeze hanger based on the size of the pipe to be supported from the trapeze and the total span of the trapeze. The other table (Table 9.1.1.6. I(a) in the 2002 edition) specifies the section moduli available from pipe sections and angle irons conmmonly used as trapeze members. The criteria on which the tables are based include the assumption of a simple center-loaded steel beam supporting 15 ft of water-filled pipe plus 250 lbs with maximum allowable bending stress of 15 ksi. Where it is known that the load will not be at the center of the trapeze span, a formula can be used to calculate an "effective length" of trapeze. The effective length will be smaller than the actual length, since the trapeze is more capable of carrying a load that is located to one side of the span. The effective length is calculated as: L = 4ab / (a + b) where a and b are the distances from the two end supports to the load of the suspended pipe. Example: For a 6-8 span for 8-inch Schedule 10 pipe located at the center of the trapeze, the required section modulus from the table is 0.97. If pipe is 1 ft from one support, a=l and b=5, making effective length 3.33 and required section modulus = 0.64 As the NFPA Committee on Hanging and Bracing of Water-Based Fire Suppression Systems worked on changes to the 2007 edition of NFPA 13, trapeze hangers were among the items that came up for discussion. There are three hanging points associated with a trapeze hanger, consisting of both ends of the trapeze plus the suspended load. Each of these points of hanging has two potential points of attachment, one at top and one at bottom. This section has been changed in the 2007 edition to require that all three hanger assemblies, and hanger components associated with all points of attachment, be sized on the basis of the suspended load. Typically, the suspended pipe is larger in diameter than a pipe section used as the trapeze member. There 381

CHAPTER 29 PROJECT SCHEDULING In the chapter on Contracts we learned that there are five bases for the agreement are Quality, Quantity, Arrangement, Time, and establishment of the level of Risk, Once the price is agreed to, it appears that the most important thing to an Owner becomes completing the job on time. It is not only of concern to the Owner, but it is of critical importance to the Contractor. What is a Schedule? There are a number of definitions we could consider, but it's best to keep it simple. A project schedule is a systematic procedure of planning that brings all required resources together to accomplish a task, or group of tasks, within a specific period of time. Benefits and Value of Scheduling When we consider the benefits and value of scheduling we need to view these ideas from the perspective of the person who is looking at the schedule. The primary purpose according to the Owner would be to track overall progress of the job. For the contractors at all levels there are a number of purposes: To measure the trade contractors conformance to contract requirements. To document job progress to support change order requests. To fonn the basis for customer communication and a central point of reference. To promote and increase productivity of the installers since they have a plan to work to that includes measurable objectives. To act as an internal communication device. It provides each department within a contractor's office an opportunity to see how their part of the job relates to the project as a whole. It also enables each person to plan his or her work against measurable objectives. 387

## Page 394

Types of Schedules Contractors use a number of different types of schedules. The choice of which type will be based on thc complexity of the project and the decision of the Owner/Architect/Contractor as to what level of control, measurement and reporting they want. Bar Chaff — The most common schedule for overall planning, and the easiest to understand is a type of schedule called a Bar Chart. It is a traditional management device on which the tasks are listed vertically and the corresponding time planned for cach task is represented by a horizontal bar or line. It is a good display of the general segments and trades involved in the project. The disadvantages of this type of schedule are: The schedule does not show the interdependence or priority of the various segments or tasks o The Bar Chart is not adequate for detail planning o The Bar Chart makes no distinction between critical or non-critical operations Shown below is an example of a simple Bar Chatt regarding format and content: 2005 2006 ACTIVITY Structural steel Walls Roof Sprinklers SEP OCT NOV DEC {JAN FEB MAR APR MAY JUN JUL Critical Path Method (CPM) — This type of schedule is the most effective of those commonly used in the construction industry. This type of schedule provides a number of features that give the users a complete picture of how a project goes together. It shows when each event (task or activity) is supposed to happen and how each task relates to another. It shows the order in which the tasks are required to take place. The CPM uses arrow notation or flow diagram symbolism. Each activity in the project is represented by an arrow or line. In scaled diagrams the length of the arrow will correspond to the duration of the activity. The flow diagram model uses text and numbers on the lines to describe the task and how long is allotted for its performance, There are boxes or geometric shapes called nodes that can indicate either a time or a task. For instance, a number in the node symbol indicates how much time has elapsed since the project started. 388

## Page 395

All activities to completely build the project should be on the CPM. These would include not only installation activities, but purchasing lead times, shop drawing preparation, permit lead times, and other support activities that are incorporated in the contractor's work. Another major feature of the CPM is that it establishes precedence. In other words, it shows in the flow diagram, which activities must come first, which activities can occur simultaneously, and where certain activities came together. Here are some other characteristics of a CPM: Progress through the network goes from one node to another There are no gaps in the network All activities must have another following, except the last Each path from node to node is a single activity. The CRITICAL PATH is defined as the time to complete the longest path through the network from start to finish. Likewise, the CRITICAL PATH is the shortest amount of time it can take to build the building without premium time or lengthened workdays. There are other terms used in conjunction with CPM' s. The most interesting if FLOAT, which is the flexible time allotted to tasks that will not delay completion of the building. Shown below is an example and a brief explanation of a portion of a CPM which, hopefully, will help clarify this material. 1 1 A 7 9 8 c 15 7 10 Duration 7 10 7 5 5 5 H 17 1 16 23 6 5 J 7 11 Path ABEK ACDEK FGHEK FIJK Time 25 Days 27 Days 30 Days 29 Days Activity c Activity 1 Duration 9 7 6 6 11 3 389

## Page 396

In the above example the CRITICAL PATH would be activities FGHEK which result in a 30 day completion time. It is the longest time to get through the network. An example of FLOAT would be the activities represented by paths AB and ACD which both end at day 23 which is on the CRITICAL PATH. If we add up activities ACD they add up to 19 days, while activities FGH that are on the CRITICAL PATH add up to 22 days. That means that Activity A could be started three days later than Activity F and still not hold up the job. The absolute fact is that whenever A B C and D start they must be finished so that they arrive on the CRITICAL PATH at day 23. It also means that A must be finished in time for C and D to do their work in the time allotted. Knowing where the FLOAT occurs can help contractors schedule around tight situations. They must be aware of their obligations, but understanding the CPM and FLOAT provide opportunities to help smooth work flow. SHORT DATER VAL SCHEDULE — A third type of schedule we use in our daily lives is called a Short Interval schedule (SIS). This is a working document used by field supervision that shows what is expected to be accomplished on a project on a daily basis for the immediate future. Most SIS do not extend for more than tlu•ee weeks. The Foreman/Field Supervisor would revise this schedule on a weekly basis by dropping the week completed and adding another week, The primary focus is on the week coming up. SIS looks at time segments required for individual tasks to complete a single activity. By breaking the job down into these individual tasks it is easier for field management to use. This type of schedule is based on time rather than activity, and it provides an organized way to look at labor, equipment, and material needs for the short term. See below for an example of one week of a typical SIS. ONE WEEK SEGMENT OF SHORT NTERVAL SCHEDULE Project manager: Prep D re by: Description of Work subcontractors Alternate Work Available Summary Mon. Tues. Week Starting Date: Wed, T ur s. Date: job Number: Sat./ Sun. E St. Phase Comp. Date Job Name; Resources Neede on the Job materials TOO Equip. Remember that scheduling serves a number of purposes. First, it is used to make sure we keep track of our subcontract requirements. It is a planning tool to communicate to all departments in a company as it outlines when various tasks and activities are required to be done. A well though-out schedule represents the current thinking on the most efficient and economical manner 390

CHAPTER 31 RESIDENTIAL SPRINKLER SYSTEMS The first concept to discuss is "what do we mean when we say residential?" Basically, we mean any place where people live either on a temporary or permanent m•rangement to include sleeping, cooking, and conduct of daily living activities. With this in mind the occupancies would include single-family homes, condos, apartment and townhomes, hotels, dormitories, board and care facilities, and lodging and rooming homes. This is a wide variety of merangements and includes everything from single story to hi-rise living. We are concemed about fires in residential stmuctures because of the 80% statistic. This translates into the facts, according to NFPA, that 4 out of five structure fires, or about 400,000 per year occur in residential occupancies. The other statistic is that 80% of all fire deaths also occur in residential occupancies. It is obvious that attention must be paid to this problem. Fire deaths occur due to heat and toxic gasses. Fires in residences grow fast and temperature build-up is rapid. The fuel loading from furniture and carpets provides the basis for large quantities of carbon monoxide and other toxic gasses. Flashover can occur in as little as five minutes from the first appearance of flames. Since the response time for fire department target arrival is five to six minutes from notification, you can see that the fire department usually an•ives on-scene when the situation is at a critical stage. Therefore, the goal of a residential system is to do something when the fire is at the incipient stage, prior to flashoVer and usually prior to fire department arrival. The focus of the residential sprinkler system is to enhance life safety even in the room of fire origin, and new technologies have been employed to accomplish this. We shifted our primary concern to where people will be when a fire breaks out. We devised new technology to specifically look at controlling fires in the residential scenario. NFPA statistics show that fires start in living rooms 40% of the time, in the bedroom 26% of the time and in the kitchen 15% of the time. There's that 80% figure again. The serious drive toward reducing loss of life umrough sprinkler system installation began in the late 1970's with a series of tests in Los Angeles. The goals were to keep temperatures and toxic gasses below critical levels, get water on the fire as soon as possible and provide a safe path of egress for the occupants, and at a cost that would encourage adoption of the sprinkler concept. Key to the accomplishment of these goals was the development of the fast response link 395

## Page 402

and a change in spray pattern to provide high wall-wetting characteristics. As you can imagine, initial fire spread takes place up the walls due to curtains, and fumiture placement in typical residential situations. Components of Residential Sprinlder Systems The primary components of the residential sprinkler system are the water supply, meters and valves, piping and sprinklers One of the features of the residential fire sprinkler system is the economy of the water supply demand. As part of the effort to keep costs down it was determined that the life enhancing performance of the system could be accomplished without large volumes of water. The sources of water can be from street mains, a tank with a pump, a pressure tank or tank with water that is pressurized by an external source such as a nitrogen cylinder. For residential portions of NFPA 13 occupancies and for NFPA 13R occupancies the water supply needs to be 30 minutes while for NFPA 13D residential systems the water supply duration needs to be only 10 minutes. The flow and pressure needs to meet the demand of the hydraulically calculated sprinklers within the residential compartment under consideration. Meters and valves can have a large effect on pressure reduction of the incoming water supply. For NFPA 13D and NFPA 13R systems the incoming supply is usually a combination line, serving both domestic and fire sprinkler needs. If the sprinkler system is separately piped, most local water authorities will require backflow preventers. This device could have as much as a 4-6 psi pressure drop at the sprinkler flow rate. Additionally, since the combination line is for domestic uses also, the local authority will require a water meter. Again, the pressure drops are significant, depending on flow rate and meter size. As an example, with 26 gpm flowing through a 5/8" meter, the pressure drop could be 18 psi. The same flow through a 3/4" meter would be 9 psi. It is important for a FPET to obtain equipment cuts of the meters and valves being used on the system so that correct pressure losses can be assigned within the calculations. Piping materials can be •steel, copper, chlorinated polyvinyl chloride (CPVC), or for a special type of system only in NFPA 13D installations called a network system, piping can be cross-linked polyethylene (PEX). All materials used for residential fire sprinkler systems must be specifically listed for fire protection. Most technicians and installers are familiar with steel, copper and CPVC materials. It is important to note that each material has its own unique way of being joined and separate rules for hangers for the material, aé well as, the requirements within the respective standards. Additionally, manufacturers list the friction losses for their respective materials for use in hydraulic calculations. Another consideration is that for use in combination and network piping systems, where water for both domestic and fire purposes is in the same piping, all material and fittings and joining techniques must be approved by the national Sanitation Foundation (NSF) and be approved in the plumbing code. Residential sprinklers employ the use of a fast response link, that with a RTI of 50 or less. The spray pattern is designed to wet the wall higher than commercial sprinkler, approximately 18" down from the ceiling juncture. U.L standard 1626 is the basis for testing

## Page 403

and acceptance of residential sprinkler. This standard has been modified over the years, with the latest change occurring on July 12, 2002 regarding density of water delivery. Essentially, the test employs a rectangular room into which three sprinklers are placed according to their intended spacing and coverage goals. A fire is set in a wastebasket that is under a table, next to a simulated sofa and chair with wood paneling on the walls. Two of the sprinklers are placed for room coverage and the third is placed near an open door that provides a vented fire condition. A successful test occurs when no more than two of the three sprinklers open and control the fire. Two sprinklers flowing in the room must be capable of providing 0.05 gpm/sq ft to be listed for NFPA 13R and NFPA 13D systems and 0.1 gpm/sq ft to be listed for NFPA 13 installations. All sprinklers operate with a minimum of 7.0 psi. There are a great many coverage and spacing options offered by manufacturers. The original requirement of 12' X 12' spacing and 18 gpm for a single sprinkler and 13 gpm for two flowing sprinklers is no longer valid for new installations. In essence each residential sprinkler has its own special listing. Residential sprinklers are the preferred type of sprinkler to use due to their fast response and distribution characteristics. However, other types of sprinklers are allowed depending on the standard and the application. For instance, NFPA 13 allows Quick response and QR extended coverage sprinklers, as well as, residential sprinklers in the dwelling units. NFPA 13R allows QR and QR extended coverage within mechanical closets and outside the dwelling unit, and if the entire dwelling unit contains 4 sprinklers they can be used there also. Residential sprinklers are the preferable sprinkler within dwelling units. NFPA 13D requires residential sprinklers within the dwelling unit and allows QR and QREC within mechanical closets. A discussion is now appropriate on the highlights of residential systems as covered by NFPA standards 13D and 13R or residential areas within structures covered by NFPA 13. We all have a good idea of what a garden apartment building looks, as well as, a single family home. NFPA standards discuss certain requirements and options within an entity called a dwelling unit. Here is the NFPA definition, "One or more rooms ananged for the use of one or more individuals living together as in a single housekeeping unit normally having cooking, living, sanitary and sleeping facilities. Includes hotel rooms, dorm rooms, apartments, condominiums, sleeping rooms in nursing homes and similar living units." NFPA 13 NFPA 13 covers all instances wherea fire sprinkler system is to be inStalled. NFPA 13 states that, "Residential sprinklers shall be permitted in dwelling units and their adjoining conidors located in any occupancy provided they are installed in conformance with their listing. If a bathroom is in a nursing home or opens onto a public corridor, it must be sprinklered. Sprinklers are also not required in closets that are less than 24 sq. ft' in area with the least dimension not exceeding 3 ft. as long as the walls and ceilings are of noncombustible or 397
