CHAPTER 32 STANDPIPE SYSTEMS We have discussed much about fire sprinklers in this textbook. Not only do sprinklers protect the occupants of a building, they aid the firefighter that must enter the building during fl fire emergency. As a practical matter, wouldn't it be great if a firefighter could just carry one hose into the building, attach to a water supply, and extinguish the fire that is being held in check by the sprinkler system? The NFPA created the Committee on Standpipe and Hose Systems in the early 1900's to create rules for standpipes in buildings. Standpipes are just an extension of the fire hydrant system into the building to aid firefighters during fire operations or to provide water to hoses for building occupants. In 1912, their report was approved and accepted to create the document known today as NFPA 14, Standard for the Installation. of Standpipe and Hose Systems. Around 1940, the Committee added guidance for hose stations that could be used by the building occupants during a fire emergency. This required guidance for regulating the pressure so occupants could use the systems without injuring themselves or others, In the 1950's, high-rise construction was increasing in popularity. The NFPA 14 Committee began examining the available pressure at hose outlets. A minimum pressure of 50 psi was needed to flow 250 gpm from a hose tip. With the friction losses through the hose, the Committee realized that at least 65 psi was needed at the standpipe connection. In the 1970's, the Committee began requiring 500 gpm from the remote standpipe. This would allow a firefighter to connect to the hose valve on the topmost floor and flow 250 gpm, while another hose was run from the hose valve on the floor below also flowing 250 gpm. The maximum height for a standpipe was raised in 1973 from 275 ft to 400 ft. This caused high pressure at lower floors to become an increased concern. So in 1974, the Committee recognized pressure regulating devices and gave guidance for their use and installation, In the 1990's, catastrophic fires caused the Committee to examine the minimum pressures required at hose nozzles. Developments in the design of nozzles led to the requirement to provide 100 psi at the top of standpipes that would be used by fire departments in 1991. And these requirements are in effect for today's standpipe systems. 401

## Page 408

Standpipe Requirements While we have talked a lot about the NFPA 14 standard, this standard only tells us how to layout and install standpipe systems. NFPA 14 does not tell us when standpipes are required. The requirement for a standpipe system comes from the model building codes or from the Life Safety Code. These codes will require a standpipe in a building based on the building's height, area, and occupancy, and whether fire protection systems are in place. Once the Codes have determined a standpipe is required, NFPA 14 should be used to layout and install the standpipc system. System Components and Hardware When it comes to the parts and pieces we can use to create the standpipe system, the requirements for system components closely parallel the requirements from NFPA 13. As we did not discuss hose valves in the earlier chapter on piping and components, you should be aware that the hose valves are required to be listed and to be compatible with the local fire department's apparatus. Types of Systems There are five basic types of standpipe systems and they are described by their water supply and whether the system piping is filled with water or not (wet or dry). The five different types of standpipe systems are: Automatic-Dry standpipe -- very similar to a dry-pipe sprinkler system. The system has air under pressure in .the pipes. When a hose valve opens, the pressure drops, opening a dry-pipe valve and delivering water to the hose valve connection. Automatic-Wet standpipe — very similar to a wet pipe sprinkler system. Has water under pressure available at the hose valve. When the hose valve is opened, water immediately flows to the hose nozzle at the correct flow and pressure necessary to make the hose useful in fighting the fire. There is no need for the fire department to use their own pumper trucks if the system is working correctly. Semiautomatic-Dry standpipe — very similar to a preaction sprinkler system. There is air under minimal pressure in the pipe. When a hose valve is opened, loss of air pressure will not send water to the hose valve. The firefighter must push a button or activate a pull-station in order to get water to flow. The electronic signal back to the automatic control valve (preaction or deluge valve) is what starts the flow of water. The purpose of the Semiautomatic system is to prevent damage from false trips of the system due to air leakage. Manual-Dry standpipe — A system with no water in the system piping. The system will not have any water in it until the fire department arrives and pumps water into the Fire 402

## Page 409

Department Connection (FDC). Manual-dry systems are a maintenance concern because there is no way to monitor the integrity of the piping. Air pressure and water pressure are not kept in the system. o Manual-Wet standpipe — A system with a water supply under pressure, but with insufficient flow or pressure to reach the demand of the fire department until (he fire depattment anives with their pumper truck. Once the fire department pumps in to the FDC with their equipment, the pipe is sized to accommodate their needs and provide the demand flow and pressure, Manual-wet standpipe systems are common in fully sprinklered buildings. The water supply is sized to automatically meet the demand of the fire sprinkler system, which also uses the standpipe risers as sprinkler system risers. However, the water supply does not need to meet the demand of the standpipe system automatically, saving the building owner from a fire pump in many cases. Manual-dry and manual-wet standpipe systems are not allowed to be used in high rise buildings and can only be used by the fire department. Each hose connection on a manual standpipe must have a sign stating that the connection is a manual connection. NFPA 14 requires the sign to read, "Manual Standpipe for Fire Dept. Use Only". Additionally, dry standpipes are only allowed where the piping is subject to freezing. Classification of Standpipes There are three classifications of standpipes. The classifications describe how the standpipe will be used and by whom. Class I standpipes are intended to be used solely by the fire department. A Class I standpipe has a 2h" Connection (see Figure 32-1). The 2 h" hose connection may have an 1 h" adapter on it in case the fire department wants to use a smaller hose for mop-up operations. All hose valves are required to have a cap on them. Firefighters carry a 'spanner' wrench that enables them to remove the cap easily. Figure 32-1 Class I Outlet with 21/2 inch Outlet and 11/2 inch Adapter 403

## Page 410

Class II standpipes are intended Lo be used by trained building occupants or by the fire depaltment during initial response. A Class II standpipe has an lh" Connection (see Figure 32- 2). There may or may not be an lh" hose on a rack attached to the hose valve. NFPA 14 allows 1" hose in Light Hazard Occupancies when the AHJ approves. Figure 32-2 Class II Hose Station Class III standpipes are a combination of Class I and Class II standpipes. They have 1 1/2" hose stations to supply water for use by trained building occupants and 2h" hose connections to supply a larger volume of water for use by fire depattments. NFPA 14 allows 1" hose stations instead of 1 h" when the AHJ approves. NFPA 14 also allows omitting the smaller hose comection when the occupancy is protected by an approved fire sprinkler system. In the past, the rules for Class III were accommodated by installing a single 2h inch outlet with a lh inch reducer connected to lh inch hose. If the building occupant needed to use the hose to fight a fire, they would have the hose available. Ifthe fire department wanted to connect their larger diameter hose, the could uncouple the reducer, swing the hose out of the way, and have access to the 2h inch outlet. However, in recent years, with the rules for Class I systems and Class II systems changing so dramatically, it is very hard, if not impossible, to install a single system that meets all of the rules of Class I and Class II at the same time. Given the different requirements for pressure at the outlet, and given the different requirements for placement of the outlets, the easiest way to install a Class III system in a building today is to install separate Class I and Class II systems tlu•oughout the building. All classes of standpipe systems must have a listed 3 h" gauge installed as follows: At each discharge pipe from the fire pump At the pressure tank At the air supply to the pressure tank At the top of each standpipe (only a single gauge is required when multiple standpipes are interconnected at the top). 404

## Page 411

All standpipes must have a listed water flow alarm installed. The sensing mechanism must be appropriate to the type of standpipe. Similar to sprinkler systems, paddle-type water flow alams are only allowed to be used on wet standpipe systems. Design Criteria As we think about where to begin in the layout of a standpipe system, we must consider whcrc thc fircfightcr will begin thcir attack. They must enter the building and connect their hose to the hose valve, so our first consideration is the hose station location. Hose stations must be located so the firefighter is safe and able to connect without impediment. The logical place to begin would be in a fire rated exitway or stairwell, since these are the most protected locations in the building from a construction standpoint. For Class I standpipes, the 2 h" hose connections must be located: At intennediate landings in required exit stairways (unless there are no intermediate landings, in which case they need to be on the main floor landings), At each side of wall adjacent to horizontal exit openings, In required exit passageways at entrances from building areas, At public entrances and at entrances to exit corridors or passageways in malls, and At the highest landing of staiLway or on a roof. For more information on horizontal exits, exit passagways, exit corridors and other "means of egress" terms, see the article "An Up-To-Date Standpipe Vocabulary" in the Fall 1994 edition of Sprinkler Quarterly magazine available from the NFSA. Back issues of articles are free to members and can be downloaded from the NFSA website at www.nfsa.org in the Members Only section. If the travel distance from the hose station to any part of the building exceeds 150 ft, you must install additional hose connections. In sprinklered buildings the travel distance is allowed to increase to 200 ft. For Class II standpipes, the 1 h" hose•connections must be located so that all portions of each floor level are within 130 ft of a hose connection. If the hose is smaller than 1 h" the distance is reduced to 120 ft. The assumption is that 100 ft of hose will be connected to the outlet and the rest of the distance will be made up as the water leaves the nozzle, For Class III standpipes, you must meet the combined requirements for Class 1 & II standpipe locations simultaneously. 405

## Page 412

NFPA 13 - Inside I-lose Connections When placing hose connections directly on sprinkler systems, 1 h" connections are permitted if connecting to a pipe at least 2h" in size on a wet pipe system. The size can be as small as 2" pipe if the hose connection has been included in and proven by the hydraulic calculations. The piping going to the hose connection can be 1" pipe for runs up to 20 feet, 1 1/4" pipe for runs between 20-80 feet, and 1 h" pipe for runs greater than 80 feet. When dropping down to feed an 1 h" hose connection the vertical pipe is allowed to be l" in diameter. When detailing 1 1/2" hose connections, it is important to know that the pressure at these outlets may not exceed 100 psi. If the pressure at the connection is greater than 100 psi, a pressure reducing device must be installed. NFPA 13 also allows 2 h" hose connections on wet pipe systems in Light and Ordinary Hazard Occupancies. These types of hose stations must be fed from the riser and must be under a separate control valve. If these hose connections are on a common riser, the sprinkler system must be controlled separately. The common riser must be at least 4" pipe, unless hydraulic calculations show smaller pipe is appropriate. NRPA 14 Standpipe Requirements There has to be at least one standpipe in every required exit stairwell. The standpipes must be interconnected at the bottom of the building, with a control valve for each individual standpipe. The standpipes must be interconnected at the top of the building if the supply comes from tanks on top of the building. In this case, check valves are required at the base of the standpipe to prevent circulation. Class I and III are required to be at least 4" in size unless they are part of a combined standpipe/sprinlder system. When part of combined system, the pipe must be at least 6 in. in size unless hydraulic calculations show smaller pipe is appropriate. In no case can the piping be smaller than 4" on a combined system. The hydraulic calculations must provide at 100 psi at the top of Class I standpipes and 65 psi at the top of Class II standpipes. The AHJ may approve lower minimum pressures. The pressure at any hose valve can never exceed 175 psi for Class I standpipes and 100 psi for Class II standpipes. The pressure may not exceed 350 psi at any location on any standpipe. The hydraulic calculations must prove that Class I standpipes can flow 500gpm from the remote standpipe while an additional 250gpm is flowing from every additional standpipe. The most the hydraulic calculations have to prove is a flow of 1250gpm, unless the building is protected with sprinklers. Then the most the calculations have to prove is 1000gpm. The hydraulic calculations must prove that Class II standpipes can flow 100gpm from the remote standpipe, with no other required flows at any additional standpipes. The water supply to all standpipes must have a thirty-minute duration. 406

## Page 413

Combined Systems Standpipes in fully sprinklered buildings are required to have the standpipe and the sprinkler system hydraulic calculations perfonned separately. The design technician must show which system is more demanding without combining them. However standpipes in buildings with partial sprinkler protection, must add the sprinkler demand to the standpipe flow for the hydraulic calculations. Drain & Test Risers NFPA 14 recommends a 3" drain riser be adjacent to each standpipe that has pressure regulating devices, This allows the disposal of water during the required inspection and testing of these types of devices. This drain riser is required to have 2 h" inlets with an internally- threaded, swivel fitting located on every other floor. NFPA 14 also requires that each standpipe be capable of draining. Fire Department Connections NFPA 14 requires a Fire Department Connection for each standpipe system. One or more fire depaflment connections are requiréd for each zone in Class I and III systems. Each zone in a high rise building is required to have at least two remotely located fire department connections unless the fire department specifies otherwise. NFPA 14's requirements for FDC's closely mirror that of NFPA 13, as discussed previously in this text. There is one exception that must be noted. The FDC is required to be sized to deliver the entire standpipe demand. This would require a 2 h" inlet for every 250gpm of flow calculated for the standpipe system. Standpipe System Zones Standpipes are limited to 350 psi at any point in the system. Therefore, very tall buildings must have their standpipe systems broken into zones vertically to meet this requirement. Each zone requiring pumps is required to be equipped with separate pumps. If the pumps that supply two or more zones are on the same level, each zone is required to have separate and direct supply piping not less than the standpipe it serves. (see Figure 32-3) Where supply for each zone is pumped from the immediate lower zone, and standpipes are used to supply higher zones, these standpipes fall under supply line definitions. In the system shown in Figure 32-3, the discharge from one fire pump is directly connected to the suction for a second pump. This mrangement is permitted by NFPA 14 and NFPA 20 and is called "pumps in series". While the arrangement is permitted, there is one concern. If the upper zone pump starts before the lower zone pump, the upper zone pump will not get sufficient flow and will become damaged as it tries to suck water up hundreds of feet, In 407

## Page 414

order for this kind of installation to be successful, the controllers for the two pumps need to be interconnected so that the upper zone pump never starts before the lower zone. A different installation for multiple zone standpipe systems would be to have the lower zone pump fill a tank on the upper zone. Then, the tank can supply a pump on the upper zone by itself. By making sure that the tank in the upper zone is adequately supplied, the pump in the upper zone never has to worry about running out of water and does not need to be interconnected with the pump in the lower zone. This is a more reliable fire protection system, but will cost the building owner more to install and maintain, not to mention having the building owner give up the space that the tank needs to be placed in. Two Zone Configuration Two Pumps with Seiies Layout Figure 32-3 Two Zone Standpipe System With Pumps In Series Zones with two or more standpipes are required to have at least two direct supply pipes not smaller than the largest standpipe in the zone. For systems in which second or higher zones cannot be supplied by the residual pressure required through fire department pumpers, a secondary supply is required ürrough high-level storage, Summary The layout and detailing of Standpipe Systems will be a major part of your job description. It is important to follow the requirements of NFPA 14 when working on these types of systems. Remember that NFPA 13 also calls for hose stations in certain situations. Understanding these two standards will be enough to assist the fire department in the important work that they do every day, and will make you a valuable commodity! 408

I' CHAPTER 33 INTRODUCTION TO FIRE PUMPS The subject of fire pumps is much too expansive to cover in a single chapter of a textbook. In fact, the entire subject has been covered in great detail in a textbook of its own titled Pumps for Fire Protection Systems authored by Milosh Puchovsky of the NFPA staff and Kenneth Isman of the NFSA staff. The book is available from the NFPA and can be ordered through their catalog or by calling 1-800-344-3555. Instead of covering everything that the technician needs to know about fire pumps, this chapter of the textbook will review the need for pumps, some basic hydraulics related to pumps, the different types of pumps that are available, the components of centrifugal pumps, the requirements for pump rooms and pump houses, the piping and equipment around the pump, and the sizing fire pumps. This will be an excellent study guide for NICET work elements 13025 (Fundamentals of Hydraulics), 14002 (Selection of Fire Pumps) and 14010 (Fire Pumps and Systems). Information on work element 14004 (Pump Flow Test) will also be covered, although this is covered in more detail in the above mentioned book dedicated to pumps and other NFSA seminars. The term "fire pump" is used to describe any kind of pump used in a fire protection system as a part of the water supply or fluid supply for fighting a fire. A fire pump might supply fire sprinklers, standpipes, foam systems, water spray systems or water mist systems or any combination of these systems. Fire pumps are required to be listed for fire protection service in order to be used, Pressure maintenance pumps (devices placed on systems to prevent the fire pump from turning on just to make up small losses in pressure that have nothing to do with a fire) are not considered fire pumps and are not required to be listed, Pressure maintenance pumps (also called jockey pumps) are not covered in this text, but are covered well in the textbook discussed above. 409

## Page 416

The Need for Pumps Centrifugal fire pumps have been installed on fire protection systems since the middle of the century. Yet for most people they remain a mysterious portion of the fire protection system, Traditionally, each company had a single individual dedicated to knowing what was needed for fire pumps, and there was just enough work to keep that individual busy throughout the year. But recently, there has been an explosion of the use of fire pumps. We are seeing fire pumps being used in ever increasing numbers around the country, forcing more people to need to know how to deal with these pieces of equipment. There are a number of forces driving the need for fire pumps: o The increasing demand for fire sprinkler systems. As the number of systems being installed increases, the number of fire pumps needed to supply those sprinkler systems also increases. Between 1986 and 2002, the fire sprinkler industry in the United States doubled in size. Even if there were no other situations leading to increasing the number of fire pumps, the demand would still have risen as the sprinkler industry got bigger. o In 1990, the demand for the pressure at a Class I standpipe outlet was increased by the NFPA Standpipe Committee from 65 psi to 100 psi. Water supplies that may have been strong enough to provide the 65 psi at the hose station on their own could not supply the 100 psi without a pump. o Use of ESFR sprinklers is on the rise. Many ESFR systems need fire pumps to achieve the high pressure necessary to protect the high hazard storage contents that make these sprinklers desirable. More sprinkler systems are being installed in rural areas where there is no water supply, Many fire protection professionals are recognizing that structures in mral communities with volunteer fire departments are especially in need of fire sprinkler protection. These buildings in rural communities usually use fire pumps in conjunction with stored water supplies to provide adequate pressure for the fire protection systems. o More speculative buildings are being built. When you don't know how the building is going to be used, you need to make some worse-case assumptions, which generally need more pressure, hence the need for more fire pumps, o High rise retrofit requirements are becoming more common. Many of these buildings have not had automatic water supplies until the fire sprinkler system came along. So, due to the factors discussed above, the number of fire pumps being installed is now greater than ever. It would be a worthwhile exercise to discuss exactly what a fire pump can do for a fire protections system. It is important for everyone to remember that fire pumps cannot create water! There is no magical device inside of a pump taking hydrogen molecules and oxygen molecules out of the air and smashing them together to make water. A fire pump cannot make up for the fact that there is insufficient flow available at a site for fire protection. All that a fire pump can do is take the water that is given to it from a water supply and increase the pressure (energy) of the water. 410

## Page 417

If the hydraulic calculations are performed for a fire protection system and the water supply is analyzed, the fire pump will not be able to help if the water supply does not have the flow available that the fire protection system needs (demand flow). The only time that a fire pump is useful is when the water supply has the demand flow available, but does not have the demand pressure. Then a fire pump can take the flow from the water supply and increase the pressure to meet the demand of the fire protection system. If the water supply can not provide the flow required for the fire protection system, then an additional water supply needs to be found. A fire pump might be involved in getting the water from this secondary supply to the fire protections system, but it can't make the water on its own. The most frequently used example of this situation is when a ground level water storage tank is added to increase the flow of water available to a site and a pump is added to take the water from the tank and push it into the fire protection system. To illustrate the concept of a pump only being used to increase pressure (not flow), consider Figure 33-1, which shows the results of a water supply test. This water supply has a static pressure of 75 psi and a residual pressure of 25 psi at 800 gpm. If you continue this line all the way down to the bottom of the graph (as it is shown in Figure 28-1) the pressure from the water supply reaches 0 psi at a flow just under 1000 gpm (989 gpm to be exact). If a 750 gpm fire pump (rated at 60 psi) were installed on this water supply with a churn (net) pressure of 70 psi and a net pressure at maximum flow (1125 gpm) of 45 psi, the discharge pressure from the pump as a function of flow would look like the curve on the top of Figure 33-2. Note that the curve cuts off at 989 gpm and does not continue to extend beyond this point. This is because the water supply cannot produce any more water than 989 gpm and the pump cannot make water. In reality, most water utilities would require that the graph be cut even shorter than what is shown in Figure 33-2. Most water utilities don't want the pressure in their mains drawn down below 20 psi (some allow pressure as low as 10 psi, so check with your local utility), so they will want you to cut off the graph at whatever flow is equal to 20 psi in their main. In this case, 20 psi occurs in the water main at a flow just under 850 gpm (837 to be exact), so the discharge curve for the pump should be cut off at that point as shown at the top of Figure 33-3. 411

This chapter will expand upon those topics and introduce some new concepts that are unique to fire pumps. The first topic that we are going to discuss was introduced in an earlier chapter on hydraulics, the difference between gage pressure, atmospheric pressure and absolute pressure. The first of these terms is the "Atmospheric Pressure". Atmospheric pressure is the pressure caused by the weight of the air pressing down on the surface of the earth. All around the earth is a sphere of air. Even though that air does not weigh much, it does have mass and therefore it does have weight. That air, pressing down on the earth creates a pressure on everything it touches. Because the atmospheric pressure is based on the air above a surface pressing down on that surface, the amount of atmospheric pressure varies with the altitude. Right at sea level on the earth, one square inch of air weighs 14.7 pounds. That column of air pressing down at sea level creates a pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch (psi) on everything it touches. At higher altitudes, there is less air between a body and outer space, so the value of atmospheric pressure drops below 14.7 psi. At low altitudes, like Death Valley which is below sea level, the value of atmospheric pressure is higher than 14.7 psi because there is more air between a body at this altitude and outer space. 413

## Page 420

Atmospheric pressure is not used directly in many circumstances in fire protection system design, but it is imponant to know that it exists and that it has an effect on system performance. For example, at higher altitudes, fire pumps do not work as efficiently because of the lower atmospheric pressure. As the combustion air goes into the diesel engine, it does not adequately feed the engine. So, it is important for the designer to take into consideration the loss of horsepower due to the lower atmospheric pressure. There is more information on this subject in NFPA 20. Thc next type of pressure that needs to be explained is "Gage Pressure". It might sound like a bit of a cop-out to define a term by using one of the words in the definition, but the gage pressure is nothing more than the pressure that is read from a gage. The gages that are used for determining pressure in pipes and pressure tanks cannot sense atmospheric pressure. Instead, these gages can only tell the user how much more pressure is inside a piece of pipe or a tank than the atmospheric pressure outside that pipe or tank. If a gage is not connected to anything and is held up in the air, it should read zero psi. This does not mean that there is an absence of pressure. On the contrary, we know from the discussion above that atmospheric pressure is acting on the gage. Instead, when a gage is reading zero pressure, it means that the pressure on the gage is the same as the absolute pressure. When a gage is reading some positive pressure, it means that there is that much more pressure inside of the vessel (pipe or tank) than there is outside that vessel. So, when a gage is reading 30 psi, it does not mean that there is 30 psi inside the vessel. Instead, it means that there is 30 psi more inside the vessel than there is outside the vessel. In order to make this distinction between different kinds of pressures, many engineers will refer to gage pressure as psig, standing for pounds per square inch — gage, In fire protection, we deal with gage pressures so often that we tend to drop the "g" and just refer to the pressure in units of psi. That is okay as long as we always remember that this is still a gage pressure. When a gage is reading a negative pressure, it does not mean that there is @ lack of pressure inside the vessel. Instead, the negative pressure means that there is less pressure inside the vessel than there is outside the vessel. This condition could lead to a serious problem if the vessel wall is not designed to take that kind of stress. While many pipes are very good at holding high positive gage pressures, the same pipes collapse under very small negative pressures because the atmospheric pressure pushing in on the pipe exceeds the pressure of the water inside pushing out. Another type of pressure that needs to be discussed is the "Absolute Pressure". The absolute pressure is the total pressure inside of a vessel (pipe or tank). The absolute pressure can be calculated by adding up the gage pressure and the atmospheric pressure, In order to make a distinction between the different kinds of pressure, absolute pressure is given the abbreviation psia, for pounds per square inch — absolute. Again, in fire protection we rarely worry about any pressure other than gage pressure, so we rarely see this abbreviation. But we should be aware of what it means. One of the places where it is important to know the total pressure is in the sizing of pressure tanks for fire sprinkler systems. In this case, we need to use the total pressure (or 414

## Page 421

absolute pressure) in order to make sure that the water leaving the tank towards the end of the fire will have enough energy to make it through the system and come out the other end to fight the fire. NFPA 13 provides a fonnula for sizing these tanks in section A.15.2.3.3, and this formula asks the user to provide a pressure, and then adds 15 to it. In this case, the people that write NFPA 13 know that people in the fire protection business tend to work in gage pressure rather than atmospheric pressure. So, rather than ask you to input an absolute pressure (which the formula really needs), they ask you to input a gage pressure and then convett it to an absolute pressure by adding 15 (14.7 rounded up). Suction Pressure With respect to fire pumps, there are three very important pressures that we want to discuss: the suction pressure, the discharge pressure and the net pressure. The "Suction Pressure" is a gage pressure that measures the energy of the water immediately before the water enters into the pump (at the suction flange of the pump). The suction pressure is not a function of the pump itself. Instead, the suction pressure is a function of the water supply and its ability to deliver water to the suction flange of the pump. Fire pump manufacturers all make a few assumptions when the make their pumps. The first assumption that we will discuss in this text is that the water arriving at the pump suction flange will always be at a positive gage pressure. If this rule is violated, not only will the pump probably suffer some damage, but the suction pipe is also at risk of collapse. Remember that when the gage pressure is negative, it means that there is more atmospheric pressure outside the pipe than there is water pressure inside the pipe. With higher atmospheric pressure on the outside pushing in, and less water pressure on the inside pushing out, the pipe wall might collapse under the strain. In recognition of the concerns discussed above, NFPA 20 requires that the water supply be analyzed to make sure that under all flow conditions, the suction pressure at the pump is always a positive gage pressure. This means that at the maximum flow of the pump (generally 150% of the rated flow of the pump) the water supply has to have enough energy to overcome all of the friction losses and elevation losses between the water supply and the pump. Before settling on a fire pump for installation, a calculation will have to be performed to make sure that the water supply can get the necessary flow to the pump at a positive gage pressure. The following is a procedure that has been developed to help perform such a calculation. 1) Determine the pressure available from the water supply at the maximum flow of the pump, which is usually 150% of the rated flow of the pump. Make sure that this pressure is the reasonable•worse-case as required for use by NFPA 13 (section 15.2.1.2). 2) Calculate all of the friction losses between the water supply and the pump. 3) Calculate the elevation losses (or gains) between the water supply and the pump. Remember to consider the change in elevation from where the water supply data was obtained, not from the elevation of the water main itself. 415

## Page 422

4) Subtract all of the losses (or add the gains) from the water supply pressure to achieve the suction pressure at the pump. The following formula shows this subtraction: Where:Ps = Suction pressure, the pressure of the water at the suction flange of the pump PR = Residual pressure at the water supply at the maximum flow of [he pump in psi PFL = Sum of the friction losses between the water supply and the pump, measured in psi PE = Change in elevation between the location where the water supply data was recorded and the suction flange of the pump, measured in psi The following is an example of how to calculate the suction pressure. A water supply (city water main) has been analyzed and it has been determined that the reasonable worse-case is that the water supply will be capable of providing a pressure of 37 psi at a flow of 1500 gpm at the proposed location where a fire pump is going to be installed. A 1000 gpm fire pump is proposed to be installed at an elevation of 50 ft above the elevation where the water supply data was obtained. The following components will be between the water supply and the fire pump: 900 ft (includes the equivalent length of fittings and valves) of 8-inch Class 52 lined ductile iron pipe (I.D. = 8,14 inches), an 8-inch backflow preventer with a friction loss of 6 psi, 15 ft (includes equivalent length of fittings and valves) of 8-inch schedule 30 steel pipe (I.D. = 8.071). Given that we already know the water supply data, the next step is to calculate the friction losses in the suction pipe. Using the Hazen-Williams formula, the friction loss in the lined ductile iron is 0.013 psi per ft times 900 ft of pipe gives us a total friction loss in the ductile iron of 11.7 psi. In the steel pipe, the Hazen-Williams formula indicates that the friction loss will be 0.018 psi per ft times 15 ft for a total friction loss of 0.3 psi in that piece of pipe. The total friction loss in the entire suction pipe, including the backflow preventer, is then 18 psi (11.7 + 0.3+6 = 18). The next step is to incorporate the elevation difference. Since the pump is above the water supply, the energy will be lost from the water and the elevation pressure will need to be subtracted from the water supply pressure. If the fire pump had been below the water supply, the water would have gained energy moving from the water supply to the pump and the elevation change would have been added. With a change in elevation of 50 ft, the elevation pressure is 22 psi. The suction pressure of the pump can now be calculated using the formula discussed earlier: Ps = PR — PFL ± PE Ps=37-18-22 PS = -3 psi Note that the suction pressure in this example is negative, which violates the rules of NFPA 20. This fire pump installation would not be allowed. Some change would need to be

## Page 423

made in order to achieve a higher pressure at the suction flange of the pump. One possibility would be to lower the pump. If there is any way to get the pump 7 ft lower in elevation, it would only lose 18.6 psi due to elevation) which would yield a suction pressure of 0.4 psi. While this is not a very big number, it is positive and would meet the requirements of NFPA 20. Instead of lowering the fire pump, another option for the example above would be to replace some (or all) of the 8-inch lined ductile iron pipe with 10 inch pipe. If all of the pipe were changed, Lhe friction loss would be lowered to 0.005 psi per ft. When multiplied by 900 ft, the friction loss in the lined ductile iron pipe would only be 4.5 psi. Adding all of the other losses, the total friction loss would be 10.8 psi (4.5 + 0.3 + 6 = 10.8) and the suction pressure at the pump would be 4.2 psi (37 — 10.8 — 22 = 4.2). Again, this is not a high pressure, but it is sufficient for the pump to work properly. Here is another example of a suction pressure calculation. A 1500 gpm fire pump is proposed to be installed and connected to a public water supply. The water supply graph is shown in Figure 33-4 and can provide 24 psi at a flow of 2250 gpm. The analysis will be pelformed at 2250 gpm because this is 150% of the flow rating of the fire pump (1500 x 1.5 = 2250). The arrangement of the pipe and pump are shown in Figure 33-5. Friction loss calculations show that the friction loss in the underground is 2.4 psi and in the above ground pipe in the pump room the friction loss is 1.2 psi. According to the manufacturer of the backflow preventer, the friction loss is 8.0 psi through that device. The elevation between where the pump is being installed and the fire hydrant where the water supply data was obtained is the same. What is the suction pressure at the pump when a flow of 2250 gpm is move through the pump? R 40 s 30 s R 20 IO s 10 400 800 1200 1600 2000 2400 Flow (GPM) 2800 3200 3600 Figure 33-4 City Main for Second Suction Pressure Example 417

Residua) pressure 24 psi at 2250 gpm (i .63 bar at 8516 L/min) •Illßlll• (24.4-m) equivalent Pump house Pump Figure 33-5 Arrangement for Second Suction Pressure Example The answer is that the suction pressure is 12.4 psi. This is obtained by taking the residual pressure at the water supply (24 psi) and subtracting the friction losses (24 — 2.4 — 1.2 — 8 = 12.4). If the water utility had stated that they never want the pressure in their mains to get below 20 psi, is this situation acceptable? The answer is that it should be, even though the suction pressure is 12.4 psi at the pump. Remember that the suction pressure is the pressure of the water at the pump, not at the street main. While the pressure is 12.4 psi at the pump, the pressure at exactly the same moment is 24 psi in the street main, so this should still be acceptable to the water utility. Discharge Pressure The discharge pressure is the gage pressure of the water as it exits from the fire pump. This pressure is measured by a gage at the discharge flange of the pump. The discharge pressure is a function of the pressure of the water coming form the water supply, plus the energy that the pump added to the water. There is no maximum or minimum requirement for the discharge pressure, however, the components downstream of the fire pump need to be rated to handle the pressure produced by the pump. For example, if the pump produces a discharge pressure of 180 psi, the discharge piping, check valve, and control valve downstream of the pump must be rated to handle this pressure. The maximum discharge pressure will occur at the lowest flow situation, which is when there is no flow going into the fire protection system. With no flow going into the fire protection system, the water supply is at its static pressure and the fire pump is producing the most pressure that it can produce. This combination of events makes the no-flow condition the highest possible discharge pressure. 418

## Page 425

The lowest possible discharge pressure will occur when the pump is operating at its maximum flow while at the same time; the water supply is at its lowest available pressure. The lowest possible discharge pressure may never occur because the pump may not turn on during a time of peak water usage. Net Pressure The net pressure is the pressure (energy) that is actually produced by the pump and given to the water. The net pressure is a measurement of the work that the pump performs. This is the purpose of the fire pump, to create net pressure. The net pressure is independent of the suction pressure. Regardless of how much energy is coming form the water supply, the pump will always produce the same net pressure at the same flow and speed. For example, if a certain pump produces 45 psi of net pressure at a flow of 500 gpm, it will always produce 45 psi regardless of whether the suction pressure is 20 psi or 100 psi. The difference will be in the discharge pressure. If the pump produces 45 psi at 500 gpm and if the water supply provides a suction pressure of 20 psi, the discharge pressure will be 65 psi. Ifthe pump conditions remain the same, but the water supply provides a suction pressure of 100 psi (at the 500 gpm flow) then the discharge pressure will be 145 psi. On a fire pump, there is no net pressure gage. There is no way to just read the net pressure. Instead, a little bit of math needs to be done. The net pressure is always equal to the difference between the discharge pressure and the suction pressure. In other words, the energy that the pump puts into the water can be determined by subtracting the energy that the water had going into the pump from the energy that they water had coming out of the pump. This concept is illustrated with the following formula: Where:PN = Net pressure PD = Discharge pressure PS = Suction pressure There should always be a gage on the suction side of the pump and on the discharge side of the pump. By simple reading these two gages and subtracting the suction pressure from the discharge pressure, the net pressure can be found. For example, if a fire pump is running and is reading 90 psi on the discharge gage and 50 psi on the suction gage, the net pressure of the pump at this flow is 40 psi (90 — 50 = 40). This version of this formula is used when testing fire pumps in order to eliminate the variable of the water supply. By figuring out the net pressure, the person testing the pump is able to isolate the performance of the pump from other factors that might effect the results of the test. There are variations on this formula that can be useful in other situations. For example, the suction pressure can be added to both sides of the equation to produce the formula below. What we are saying is that the discharge pressure is always equal to the suction pressure plus the 419

## Page 426

net pressure. Another way of saying this is that the energy of the water coming out of the pump is equal to the energy of the water that went into the pump plus the energy that was added by the pump. This concept can be expressed with the following formula: This version of the formula is used in two ways, First, it is used to calculate the discharge pressure at any flow in order to make sure that the correct pressure is being created and that the system is not being ovelvressurized. Second, this formula is used when sizing a fire pump to determine whether or not the fire pump can supply the right pressure at the fire protection system demand flow. More on this topic in the Pump Sizing portion of this chapter. Pump Speed All of the discussion so far has been about the pressure that the pump can produce and the flow of water going through the pump. Each of these variables is affected by the speed at which the pump turns. Most pumps are designed to at a single speed. Ifthe pump speeds up or slows down, it will effect the amount of water that can move tlu•ough the pump and the pressure created by the pump. In general, the faster that the pump turns, the more water will move through it (higher flow) and the more pressure it will produce. The opposite is also true, the slower the pump turns, the lower the pressure produced by the pump and the lower the flow through the pump. In fact, the pressure produced by a pump (net pressure) is proportional to the speed at which a pump turns squared. This means that if the pump tums twice as fast as you thought it was going to, it would produce four times as much pressure. • If the pump turned three times faster than you thought it was going to, it would produce nine times as much pressure, This very powerful relationship can be summarized in a series of formulas that assume that you know the pressure and flow conditions for at least one speed at which the pump will tum. These formulas are often called the "affinity laws" and are as follows: 2 1)N2 = Flow through the pump at the second speed Where: (22 = QI = Flow through the pump at the first speed N2 = Second speed Nl = First speed Net pressure created by the pump at the second speed Net pressure created by the pump at the first speed PNI = 420

## Page 427

The affinity laws are most frequently used when testing a fire pump if the fire pump does not turn at its rated speed. The formulas help determine what the results of the test would have been if the pump had turned at the correct speed. By utilizing these formulas, the person running the test can determine if the speed of the pump is the problem or if there is something else wrong with a pump that needs to be investigated. This text will not spend any additional time discussing pump testing, but will leave that subject to other NFSA learning activities. Recently, manufacturers of drivers for fire pumps have developed ' 'variable speed drivers" that take advantage of the affinity laws to make sure that fire pumps don't overpressurize fire protection systems. The drivers can be set to maintain a constant pressure at the discharge of the pump. Under low flow conditions, Che pump will turn slow. If the demand for water increases (more sprinklers Open, increasing the flow) the pump can speed up to deliver more flow and keep the pressure at its target. Laminar and Turbulent Flow Another hydraulics concept that needs explanation before going further into fire pumps is a description of the manner in which particles of water travel through a pipe. The flow of water in a pipe can be described as either laminar or turbulent, Laminar flow consists of very straight streams of water all flowing through the pipe in the same direction, all parallel to each other. See Figure 33-6. If you were to look inside a piece of pipe while water was flowing through in a laminar fashion, you would see flat plats of water all sliding down the pipe in a uniform direction. Laminar flow can only occur in slow moving water. The faster water tries to move, the more disturbed its flow becomes and it loses the ability to stay laminar. If laminar flow were compared to music, it would be considered the "easy listening music" of water flow. It is very calm, very smooth, very gently moving water. Figure 33-6 Laminar Flow Sticking with the music analogy, turbulent flow is the "acid rock" of water flow. Turbulent flow is very mixed up, jumbled up water. At any given time, water can be moving in any direction within the pipe. Flow streams can impinge on one another and two different particles of water that start next to each other might be completely separated when they get to the end of the pipe. See Figure 33„7, 421

## Page 428

Figure 33-7 Turbulent Flow Turbulence natufally occurs in swiftly moving water, Turbulence also occurs when water is forced to change direction. If the flow of water in a pipe is laminar and becomes turbulent due to a change in direction (such as traveling through an elbow), it will become laminar again after the change in direction if it is given enough straight pipe before any additional changes in direction. The reason that this discussion of turbulence is necessary is that fire pump manufacturers make two assumptions when they make their pumps. The first assumption we have already discussed, that the water entering the suction flange of the pump will be at a positive gage pressure. The second assumption is that when the water arrives at the pump suction flange, it will be moving in a laminar fashion. The reason for this assumption will become clearer after we examine the parts of a centrifugal pump, but for now, take it on faith that we need to provide laminar flow at the suction flange of the pump. In order to achieve laminar flow, the goal is to keep the velocity of the water down and to limit the number of turns and bends that the water goes through on the suction side of the pump. Velocity is controlled by the size of the suction pipe (remember Q = AV = a constant). As the cross sectional area of the pipe increases, the velocity of the water flowing in the pipe decreases. The critical velocity for water arriving at a fire pump is 15 ft per second (see section 5.14.3.3 of NFPA 20). This is the only place in an NFPA standard where the velocity of the water is regulated in any way, and it only applies to a small length of pipe attached to the suction flange of the pump (a distance of 10 times the diameter of the pipe). Luckily, we do not need to perform the velocity calculation. Instead the NFPA committee has already taken care of that for us. Table 5-25(b) ofNFPA 20 provides the correct size pipe for several different common sizes of fire pumps. Note that not al of the suction pipe needs to be sized in this manner. Only that short length of pipe attached to the suction flange that is 10 times the diameter of the pipe needs to be this size. For example, Table 5-25(b) states that suction pipe feeding a 750 gpm pump needs to be 6 inch in diameter. This means that the portion of the suction flange within 5 ft (6 x 10 = 60 inches, which is 5 ft) of the pump neéds to be 6 inch diameter pipe. Closer to the water supply, the pipe is permitted to be smaller (or larger) as long as the water at the supply has sufficient 422

## Page 429

encrgy to still deliver water to the suction flange at a positive gage pressure (see the suction pressure discussion above), See Figure 33-8. Pipe can be smaller diameter than shown in Table 5- 25(b) as long as suction pressure is at least 0 psig at maximum flow Must be 10 times diameter shown in Table 505(b) of NFPA 20 to minimize turbulence at suction flange or pump Figure 33-8 Suction Pipe Size In addition to controlling the velocity, the key to limiting turbulence is to also limit the turns and bends that the water is forced to travel on the way to the pump. Devices such as elbows and tees cause the water to change direction and increase the turbulence of the water as it exits from these devices. For this reason, such devices are not permitted to be close to the pump's suction flange. A deeper discussion of the rules will be included in this text in the Suction Piping section later in the chapter. Elbows and tees are not the only devices in the suction pipe that might cause water to change direction. Butterfly valves, check valves and backflow preventers all force the water to travel around obstructions in the waterway. While these devices are not prohibited in the suction pipe, they are regulated in how close they can be to the pump. See the Suction Piping section of this text for more detail. Types of Pumps There are two mechanical methods that can be used to increase the pressure of water, positive displacement and centrifugal force. Positive displacement pumps were the first kinds of pumps used and date back several thousand years. A simple definition of a positive displacement pump is "a device that increases the energy of a fluid by pushing that fluid through a known path within a confined volume." The most conunon forms of positive displacement pumps are piston pumps and rotary gear pumps. Piston pumps, like the one shown in Figure 33- 9 were common on antique fire trucks in the 1700's and 1800's. Those big handles that people pushed up and down were piston pumps with multiple pistons that pushed water as people moved the handles. Rotary gear pumps, like the one shown in Figure 33-10, move the fluid through the rotation of the gear teeth. 423

Today, the most common applications of positive displacement pumps are for foam concentrate and water mist systems. Foam concentrate (the viscous fluid that has not yet been mixed with water to make foam solution) is most easily moved through the use of rotary gear pumps. Water mist systems use positive displacement pumps because they can generate much higher pressure than centrifugal pumps of the same size and horsepower. Water mist systems sometimes need pressures greater than 1000 psi, which can be difficult for a centrifugal pump to generate. Since 99% of the fire pumps used in the United States are centrifugal pumps, the rest of this chapter will be dedicated to centrifugal pumps. Anyone wishing more specific information on positive displacement pumps can find much more detail in the NFSA Academy (www.nfsaacademy.org) where there is a recorded lecture on this subject. Centrifugal Pumps Centrifugal Pumps utilize centrifugal force to increase the energy of the water droplets. In general, centrifugal force works as follows: 1) An object dropped in the center of a rotating disk will pick up energy from the rotation 2) As the object picks up energy, it will move toward the outside of the rotating disk 3) If unrestrained, the object will be tlu•own off of the disk when it reaches the outer edge. The speed at which it will leave the disk is proportional to the energy that it has picked up while in contact with the disk. This immediate use of the energy picked up from the disk is called "kinetic energy" because the energy is being used to move the object, 4) If restrained, the energy picked up by the object is stored as potential energy (an increase in pressure in the case of water). At some future point in time, when the restraint is released, the potential energy will be converted to kinetic energy and the object will do some work at that time. Consider a small weight tied to the end of a string. If you just hold the sting up in the air, the weight will hang down at the end of the string and not move at all. If you provide rotation by swing the string around your head in a circle, the weight will pick up energy from the rotation and will rise up and start moving in a circle around your head. In this case, energy has been given to the weight. Some of the energy is being used as kinetic energy to move the weight, but most of the energy is being stored as potential energy due to the restraint of the weight by the string. The string itself is restraining the weight, keeping it from flying off. What would happen if you let go of the string? The restraint would be released, the potential energy stored in the weight would convert to kinetic energy and the weight would fly off in whatever direction it was headed the instant you let go of the string. 425

## Page 432

Components or Centrifugal Pumps Centrifugal pumps work just like the glescription of rotation of a weight and a string. Water droplets are placed between two rotating plates. Individually, each of these plates is called a "shroud". Together, two shrouds are called an "impeller." The impeller is mounted to a shaft in its center and the shaft is attached to a motor or engine to provide the rotation. Around the shaft is an opening that allows the water to enter the impeller called an "eye." Once the water droplets enter the eye of the impeller, they are squeezed between the shrouds where they pick up energy from the rotation. As thc water droplets pick up energy, they rotate to the outside edge of the impeller. Once they reach the outside, they are restrained within the "casing" of the pump. By restraining the water droplets inside the casing, the energy picked up by the rotation is stored as potential energy. As long as the water stays inside the piping system, the energy is held as potential energy. Once the water gets to an open sprinkler or hose nozzle, the restraint is released and the potential energy converts to kinetic energy and the water performs some work, fighting tlu•ough the fire plume to absorb heat and control or suppress a fire. The amount of energy that a water droplet will pick up is a function of how fast the impeller is turning and the efficiency of the contact between the shrouds and the water droplet. If the shrouds and the water droplets slip past each other, the transfer of energy is not very efficient and the water's pressure will not increases significantly. In order to increase the efficiency of the pump, "vanes" are added between the shrouds to make sure that the water droplets rotate along with the shrouds. See Figure 33-11 for examples of shrouds, vanes and the eye of an impeller. In Figure 33-11, the shroud closest to the observer has been partially broken away so that the vanes inside can be clearly seen. Front shroud Vane Back shroud Shaft Impeller eye Figure 33-11 Pump Impeller 426

## Page 433

Figure 33-12 shows a water droplet traveling through an impcllcr starting at the eye and working its way to the outside. This figure has also had the top shroud removed so that the observer can look inside and see the vanes. o O o o Eye Vane Figure 33-1214 Water Droplet Travels Through an Impeller One of the key components of the centrifugal pump is the casing. The casing surrounds the impeller and makes sure that the water stays inside, restraining the droplets and keeping the energy added to the water by the rotation as potential energy. Without the casing, water droplets would spray all over the pump room, rather than stay in the piping system. If the casing had a hole in it, the transfer of energy between the shrouds and the water droplets would not be as efficient as it would be with the casing complete. Water would leak out of the hole and allow much of the energy in the water droplets to turn from potential energy to kinetic energy before the water has a chance to get into the piping system, The casing is made from an extremely strong material so that accidental holes don't develop in the casing. However, there is one intentional hole that is put in the casing, and we need to seal this hole so that we don't lose efficiency. The hole is where the shaft (bringing rotation from the driver) penetrates the casing to be connected to the impeller inside the casing. This shaft penetration of the casing needs to be sealed in order to maintain the efficiency of the pump. The material that is wound around the shaft in order to seal the penetration of the casing is called "packing". Different materials have been used over the years to make packing. One characteristic that all packing materials have had in fire pumps is that they all need to be kept moist. If the packing is allowed to dry out, it flakes off of the shaft and then allows water to exit the casing, causing the pump to lose efficiency. Keeping the packing properly lubricated is the key to maintaining an efficient pump. 427

## Page 434

The unfortunate situation is that nobody knows exactly how much water the packing material will need at any given time, It depends on how long the pump will be running, the temperature in the pump room and even the humidity in the pump room. Rather than try and figure out how much water the packing material will need, the pump manufacturers design the pumps to deliver more water than the packing will ever need to keep moist, and the excess is designed to drip out of the bottom. Let me repeat that because it is important. Packing glands (the area around the packing material) are designed to discharge water! We are not talking about a large volume of water here, but packing glands will drip water. This means that when you are designing a fire protection system, you must plan on having a drain so that the packing discharge can be taken safely from the pump room. Water Delivery to Impeller There are two different ways that a fire pump can be designed to deliver water to the impeller, single suction or double suction. In a single suction pump, the water is only delivered to one side of the impeller. In a double suction pump, the water is split with half of the water going into the impeller on one side and half of the water going into the impeller on the other side. See Figure 33-13 for a single suction pump and figure 33-14 for a double suction pump. Discharge Impeller Suctior Impeller shaft Figure 33-13 Single Suction Pump Discharge Impeller Pump shatt Suction Figure 33-14 Double Suction Pump 428

## Page 435

Consider the double suction pump for a moment. In order to work correctly, exactly half of the water must go in one side while exactly half of the water goes in the other side. Ifthe flow were to be split unevenly, with more water going in one side of the pump than the other, the impeller would be out of balance, With more weight on one side of the impeller than the other, the impeller would wobble as it rotated and cause damage to the shaft. With rotational speeds of several thousand revolutions per minute, an impeller that is out of balance could do serious damage to the pump. This is thc reason that the pump manufacturcrs want to minimize the turbulence on the suction side of the pump. Turbulence in the wrong direction could cause more water to enter a double suction impeller on one side and cause the impeller to be out of balance. For single suction pumps, thc balance situation is already a concern. With the water only entering the impeller from One side, there is already a tendency to have the impeller out of balance. To make up for this situation, the manufacturers of single suction pumps make the transition of water into the impeller much smoother Chan what is shown in Figure 33-13. But the reality is that any additional turbulence at the suction flange could cause balance problems for the impeller. Single suction pumps tend to only be used for low flow situations. As the flow increases, it is easier (and more efficient) for the water to enter the impeller from both sides, so double suction pumps are more common for larger flow pumps. Types of Centrifugal Pumps There are a number of different kinds of centrifugal pumps that are used for fire protection. The following is a partial list of the most common types of pumps that are used. One of the descriptive terms with respect to fire pump names has to do with the orientation of the shaft running from the driver to the impeller. When the shaft running from the driver to the impeller is in the horizontal plane, the pump is considered a "horizontal pump." When the shaft between the driver and the impeller luns in the vertical plane, the pump is considered a "vertical pump." These two terms are mixed with other descriptors to form the name of many common types of pumps used in fire protection. A "split case pump" is one where the casing sun•ounding the impeller is divided into two pieces (a bottom and a top) with the two pieces bolted together (see Figure 33-15). The beauty of the split case pump is that the top half of the casing can be removed to expose the packing and the impeller without disturbing the driver or the alignment of the shaft. When the pump is of the split case design and the shaft between the driver and the impeller is running in the horizontal direction, the pump is called a "horizontal split case pump." Horizontal split case pumps are the most common type of pump found in fire protection due to its ease of repair and the wide variety of sizes that are available. 429

## Page 436

Casing split into two pieces and bolted together at this point Figure 33-15 Horizontal Split Case Pump An "in-line pump" is one where the centerline of the suction and discharge flange and the centerline of the impeller (lengthwise) are on the same plane (see Figure 33-16). Most in-line pumps have a motor mounted directly on top of the pump with a shaft running down to the impeller. Since the shaft runs in the vertical direction, the pump is called a "vertical in-line pump." Vertical in-line pumps used to be limited to very small sizes due to the concem that if there was a problem with the impeller, the intake or the discharge, Lhe motor would have to be lifted off of the pump in order to correct the problem, The concern was that as the pumps and motors got bigger, they would reach a point where they were too heavy to lift and they would be too difficult to maintain. However, several cycles of NFPA 20 ago, the committee decided that it would be up to the owner if they wanted to accept this risk. Meanwhile, manufacturers of in-line pumps have designed the in-line pumps so they don't need to be taken completely apart to fix problems with the impellers. It is quite possible that in the near future we will see some extremely large in-line pumps. The third type of pump [hat will be described here is the "ventical shaft turbine pump" also called the "vertical line shaft turbine pump." This is the only type of pump that can draw water up from a standing source like a river, pond or reservoir. The vertical shaft turbine pump has a shaft that drops well below the discharge. At the bottom of this shaft is an intake for the water to go in (usually covered by a screen so that only water goes in). Immediately inside the shaft are a series of impellers that increase the energy of the water and send it up the shaft. At the top, the water discharges from the pump and enters the system piping. Verica! turtüto rxe pump releaso Oischatgo Sump waler kvet Surro Figure 33-17 Vertical Shqft Turbine Pump The vertical shaft turbine pump is considered "vertical" because the shaft bringing rotation to the impeller is in the vertical plane. When electric motors are used to drive vertical shaft turbine pumps, the motor sits right on top of the shaft that drops down into the water. However, when diesel engines are used to drive vertical shaft turbine pumps, they cannot sit directly on top of the pump because there are no diesel engines that produce vertical rotation. All diesel engines produce horizontal rotation, So, in order to get a diesel engine to drive a vettical shaft turbine pump, the engine has to be set off to the side and a device called a "right angle gear drive" needs to be placed on top of the pump. The right angle gear drive takes the horizontal rotation from the engine and transfers it to vertical rotation for the pump. 431

Multiple Stage Pumps Most of the time, stationary fire pumps will only have one impeller inside the casing. However, it is possible to place multiple impellers inside the casing to boost the performance of the pump. When more than one impeller is placed inside the casing, the pump is called a "multiple stage pump," The number of stages is equal to the number of impellers. So, a "two- stage pump" is a pump with two impellers inside the casing. A "four stage pump" is one with four impellers inside the casing. The impellers can be set for parallel or series pumping. In parallel pumping, the water is split and sent to the two impellers at the same time. The pressure is increased as the water goes through the impellers and the flow is put back together on the discharge side of the impeller. Each droplet of water only goes through one impeller. Parallel pumping is good for getting large quantities of water through a fire pump. See Figure 33-18 for an example of a multiple stage pump set in parallel. 1000 gpm. 170 psi Discharge 500 gpm 170 PSI Impeller Pump shaft 500 gpm 500 gpm 170 psi impeller 500 gpm 1000 gpm 20 psi Inlet Figure 33-18 Two Stage Pump in Parallel When a multiple stage pump is set for series pumping, all of the water that goes into the pump goes into one impeller first, After the water has increased in pressure, it goes into the next impeller. The water continues to go through impellers, increasing its net pressure. Series pumping is good for increasing the pressure of the water. See Figure 33-19 for a multiple stage pump set in series. 432

500 gprn 170 psi Impeller Pump shaft Discharge 500 gpm 320 psi Impel!er 500 gpm 170 500 gpm 20 psi Inlet Figure 33-19 Two-Stage Pump in Series Fire trucks usually have two-stage pumps and can be set to switch back and forth between parallel and series pumping. This is because fire fighters don't know from one day to the next where the trucks will be used. One day they may be at a one story warehouse and may need lots of flow, so they set the trucks in parallel. The next day they may go to a high-rise building fire and may need to pump water up to the floor, so they need series pumping. Fixed fire protection systems rarely need this kind of flexibility. They are designed for specific fire protection systems and will be set by the pump manufacturer in either series or parallel pumping as required. Centrifugal Pump Ratings All centrifugal pumps are given a net pressure and flow rating by their manufacturers. The purpose of the rating is solely to allow a discussion and comparison of the pumps. The rating is not intended to be a limit on the performance of the pump, although NFPA 20 does set some limits that are based on the rating information. It is common for pumps to exceed both their net pressure and their flow ratings. NFPA 20 allows pumps to be used to supply flow demands up to 150% of the rated flow of the pump (see section 5.8.1). So, for example, a fire pump rated at 1000 gpm can easily supply demands for fire protection systems in excess of 1000 gpm all the way up to 1500 gpm. Likewise, a pump with a net pressure rating of 60 psi might easily (and often) produce pressures of 75 or 80 psi. As stated earlier in this text, fire pumps are designed to run at a rated speed. When the pump is turning at its rated speed and when the pump has its rated flow going tlu•ough it, the pump will produce.at least as much net pressure as its rated net pressure. The importance of the 433

## Page 440

rated flow and pressure of the pump is to link this information. So, when a pump rated at 1000 gpm and 60 psi actually has 1000 gprn going through it, it should be producing at least 60 psi if it is turning at its rated speed. NFPA 20 goes on to establish some other performance limits for fire pumps in section 6.2. At maximum flow (150% of rated flow), the pump is not allowed to produce any less than 65% of its rated net pressure. The pump is allowed to produce more pressure than this (and always will) but the pump will not be allowed to be listed as a fire pump if it cannot meet this minimum criteria. Another performance limit for a fire pump is also expressed in section 6.2. The maximum pressure that a pump is allowed to produce is not allowed to exceed 140% of the rated nct pressure of the pump. This maximum pressure will always occur in the lowest flow condition (when there is no flow at all going into the fire protection system). This no-flow condition is also called "churn" or "shutoff'. The limit in NFPA 20 is a maximum, meaning that pumps can (and often do) create much less pressure at churn than 140% of the rated net pressure. The important thing to remember about these performance points that we have discussed here is that the limits discussed by NFAP 20 are a minimum and a maximum. Fire pumps are allowed to perform anywhere in between. This subject will be discussed much more in-depth in the Sizing Fire Pumps section later in this text. Pump Houses and Pump Rooms NFPA 20 does not require that the fire pump be installed in doors. However, section 5.12.1 does require that the pump be protected from a long list of problems, and most designers choose to comply with this rule by putting the pump in a pump room or pump house. If the pump is going to be installed outside, it still needs to be protected from the same problems; the designer will be expected to state how they are going to protect the pump from each of the items. The list of concerns for which the pump, driver and controller need protection is: Explosion Fire Flood Earthquake Rodents Insects Windstorm Freezing Vandalism Other adverse conditions 434

## Page 441

Once it has been determined that the pump will be placed inside, the next decision that needs to be made is whether the pump will go in a pump room or in a pump house. A "pump room" is a space inside of the building being protected by the fire protection system that is dedicated to the fire pump, driver, controller and other equipment necessary for the fire pump. Other devices that are not related to the fire pump are allowed in pump rooms (like domestic water tanks or other pump equipment), but they are not allowed to add Lo the combustibility or the hazard of the space. A "pump house" is a separate building housing the same type of equipment as the pump room. A pump house needs to be made of substantial construction so that it will not be damaged, especially during a fire incident. A pump house is required to be at least 50 ft away from the building it provides fire protection for unless the walls are rated for a specific fire resistance. If the pump house is closer than 50 ft to the building, it needs to have 2-hr rated walls. The rating is allowed to go down to I-hr if both the building and the pump house are sprinklered. Separation of the pump room is even more important. During a fire, a person is supposed to be standing by the pump in order to monitor how it is working and make adjustments if necessary to keep thc fire pump working. Put yourself in the shoes of the person standing by the pump. If the building is on fire, wouldn't you want there to be some substantial separation between you and the fire? NFPA 20 has not always required separation for pump rooms, but it does now. Walls are required to have a 2-hr rating unless the whole building (including the pump room) is sprinklered. If the whole building is sprinklered, the walls are allowed to have a I-hr rating. Another concern regarding the pump room is accessibility. At this time, NFPA 20 does not require that the pump room be accessible directly from the outside. However, once again, you should set yourself in the shoes of the person who is being sent to standby the pump while it operates during a fire. You don't want to have to go through the fire to get to the pump! There needs to be a protected, accessible, route from the outside of the building to the pump room. While this might not mean a door directly from the outside to the pump room, it might mean special fire resistance ratings and better control of combustibles along the route from the outside to the pump room. This way, a person can comfortably exit from whatever portion of the building they are in if a fire occurs and then get to the pump room safely from the outside. Pump rooms and houses need to be heated to at least 400F so that the water in the pump does not freeze. If a diesel engine is being used, the pump room will need to be warmer in order to make sure that the diesel engine will start. Most diesel manufacturers have different requirements for their engines, but it is not uncommon to see the minimum temperature requirement at 560F or higher. It is also important to provide ventilation for a pump room or pump house. While a person is in the room, they will need air. Also, diesel engines take air out of the room in order to perfonn combustion, This air needs to be replaced or the engine will not be able to run efficiently. Many designers forget this simple fact and end up starving a diesel engine and not 435

## Page 442

getting the horsepower they need to meet the demands of the fire protection system. Check with the engine manufacturer to make sure that sufficient ventilating louvers or other air handling systems are provided to get sufficient air to the engine. Pump rooms and houses need both artificial and emergency light. We can't just put a window in the pump room and assume that all fires will happen during the day. Some artificial light is required so that we can see the equipment. For now, a flashlight on an automatic charger by the door is allowed as emergency lighting. In the next edition of NFPA 20, this is likely to change with emergency lighting similar to what is found in a means of egress under the Life Safety Code also required in pump rooms or pump houses so that the pump can be operated if the power is out in the building (something that happens during a fire). While a pump is running, water is often being discharged in the pump room or pump house. As discussed earlier in this section, the packing glands are designed to discharge water. Other devices around the pump are also designed to discharge water such as pressure relief valves, circulation relief valves, diesel engine cooling lines and pressure sensing lines. The floor of the pump room or pump house should be pitched towards a drain and the drain needs to be capable of handling the total flow from all of these devices. Needless to say that the drain should be at a low point in the floor. Pump rooms and pump houses must be sized such that they can fit in the pump, driver, controller and any other piece of equipment that is associated with the fire pump. This might include diesel fuel tanks, relief valves and/or metering equipment. In addition, there needs to be room to bring in the suction pipe without making significant turns and bends in order to minimize turbulence, as discussed in the Basic Hydraulics portion of this chapter. Turns or bends in the pipe (elbows and tees) that would cause more water to enter one side of the impeller than another must be far away from the pump. Turns or bends (elbows or tees) that would not cause the water to divide unevenly are permitted close to the pump (even on the pump suction flange) because even though they cause turbulence, it is a kind of turbulence that will not affect the pumps performance. There is more discussion on suction pipe requirements in the next section of this chapter. Suction Pipe There are three different ways that water could come into the suction flange of a horizontal split case (double-suction) fire pump. The first way is illustrated by Figure 33-20 with the piping coming directly into the suction flange of the pump without making any turns or bends. This is the ideal scenario and keeps the flow laminar as it gets to the pump. 436
