Suction pipe enters pump room and goes straight to suction flange with no tees or elbows Figure 33-20 Suction. Pipe Straight Into Suction Flange Unfortunately, it isn't realistic to believe that all water supplies in the world line up directly with where we want to install our fire pumps. We have to understand that there are times when we are going to have to put a tee or an elbow into the suction pipe. The two other ways that water can get to the suction flange of a pump are handled with two different rules that cover how far from the pump the elbow or tees need to be. An elbow or tee that only makes a veltical turn is not required to be any distance away from the pump. See Figure 33-21 (parts a and b) for examples of acceptable tums in the suction pipe. As long as there is no horizontal component to the turn, there is no requirement for the elbow or the tee to be any distance from the pump's suction flange. When water is flowing along and suddenly changes direction, its forward momentum tends to push more water to one side. If this water then goes into the suction flange, there is a tendency for more water to go into the impeller on one side. As previously explained, this could do great damage. The only way that NFPA 20 allows •a turn with a horizontal component to the change in direction of the water is if there is a 437

distance of straight pipe at least 10 times as long as the diameter of the pipe. See Figure 33-22 for an example. This turn is only acceptable if "X + Y is greater than or equal to IO times the pipe diameter Driver Pum Plan View Elevation View Figure 33-23 Example of Acceptable Vertical Turn With Horizontal Component in Suction Pipe Aside from the concerns about the changes in direction of the suction piping, there are also concerns about other devices and situations. One of these concerns is having air in the suction pipe. While centrifugal pumps are very good at moving fluids (like water), they are very bad at moving gasses (like air). A combination of liquid and gasses in the same impeller while it is turning is a bad combination. The fluid will slosh around as the impeller turns and cause an imbalance in the system, which will cause damage to the pump. The designer must do everything possible to avoid the introduction of air on the suction side of the pump. This means designing the system with as little change in direction vertically as possible so that there is no where for the air to collect. Also, suction pipe should be joined properly and hydrostatically tested prior to connection it to the pump. Ifthe joints are not good and tight, they may let air in under low suction pressure conditions. Some designers place automatic air release mechanisms on the top of the pump and at the top of any vertical change in direction so that air that sneaks into the system has a way of getting out without going all the way through the pump. 439

## Page 446

For some reason, fire pump manufacturers frequently don't provide the same size flange on the pump as we need to connect the suction pipe. Often they provide a flange that is smaller than the suction pipe. For example, according to Table 5-25(b) of NFPA 20, we need to use a suction pipe size of 8-inch for a 1000 gpm fire pump, yet most pump manufacturers only provide us with a 6 inch suction flange on the pump. How do we connect an 8-inch piece of pipe to a 6- inch flange? We need to use a reducer. There are two kinds of reducers in the world, an eccentric and a concentric reducer. Concentric reducers have a common centerline all the way through and the reduction in diameter occurs around the whole device. When concentric reducers are installed, there is a possibility of trapping air in the pipe, which would be bad for the pump if this air ever made it into the pump, so concentric reducers are not allowed. The other kind of reducer is called an eccentric reducer. These reducers only change diameter across once side of the device, with the other side being completely flat. When•we install a reducer in the suction piping, we are required to use a concentric reducer and we are required to install it so that the flat side is on top. This prevents the possibility of trapping air as the system is filled with water. See Figure 33-24 for the correct and the incorrect way to install reducers. Right O Eccentric Reducer Wrong Alr pocket o Concentric Reducer Figure 33-24 Reducers The suction piping must also be protected from freezing. This is usually accomplished by burying the pipe below the frost line. If burying the pipe is not possible or practical, some other method of keeping the pipe warm is required. It will be up to the Authority Having Jurisdiction to determine if the method is reliable enough to be acceptable. Once inside the pump room or pump house, the heating system should keep the water in the pipe from freezing. There are a number of devices in the suction piping that must be discussed. The first of these is the control valve. NFPA 20 requires a control valve in the suction piping in order to be able to isolate the pump for repair or maintenance. The suction control valve is required to be an OS&Y gate valve in order to minimize the turbulence in the suction pipe. When a gate valve is open, there are no obstructions in the waterway to interrupt the flow of water. Although there are butterfly valves listed for fire protection, they are not permitted to be used as suction control valves because they force water to flow around parts of the valve and cause turbulence on the suction side of the pump. 440

## Page 447

Other devices that cause concern in the suction piping are backflow preventers and check valves, These devices also cause turbulence and need to be far enough away from the suction flange of the pump that the water has a change to calm down before entering the suction flange of the pump. Section 5.26.3 of NFPA 20 requires that check valves and backflow preventers be installed a distance of at least 10 times the diameter of the suction pipe away from the suction flange. Also, these devices cause friction loss to occur as the water moves through them, A calculation must be performcd if check valves or backflow preventers are used in the suction pipe to make sure that the water at maximum flow will still get to the pump suction flange at a positive gage pressure. A couple of sample calculations were pelformed in the earlier portion of this chapter where suction pressure was discussed. Another device to be concerned with on the suction side of the pump is a "low suction cut-off' device. These devices are installed in the suction pipe and sense the pressure on the suction side of the pump and if that pressure gets too Iow, they swing closed, cutting off the flow of water to the pump. If this happens while the pump is running, it will destroy the pump to have the water flow suddenly stop while the impeller is turning at several thousand RPM. There are versions of this device that do not starve the pump for water, but instead send a signal to the controller to stop the pump if the suction pressure gets too low. While these versions of the low suction cut-off valves do not destroy the pump, they do shut down the pump while it is running, which would be a bad situation if there was a fire, especially if the pump were supplying fire fighters with flow for hose streams that they are using for interior fire attack. When a fire fighter enters a building to fight a fire, the water coming from their hose is there only protection. No fire fighter wants some automatic valve to decide that there is not enough suction pressure and shut down the pump. Section 5.14.9 of NFPA 20 prohibits the installation of suction cut-off devices. Water utilities have a legitimate concern that suction pressures might get low as fire pumps work during a fire. The designer is supposed to calculate this in advance and make sure that the suction pressure is not going to get below the water utility's stated minimum, but the utilities are still concerned about unknown conditions during a fire. Many of them want some sort of low pressure monitoring device. There are two alternatives to the low pressure cut-off device that NFPA 20 allows. The first is a device that monitors the suction pressure and sounds an alarm if the pressure gets too low. This alerts fire fighters to the situation and allows them to decide on the safest way to decrease their flow and allow the public water supply to recover. The second alternative to the low pressure cut-off device is the "low pressure throttling device". A low pressure throttling device is installed in the discharge piping, but it senses the pressure in the suction pipe. If the suction pressure gets too low, the throttling valve closes a little bit (not all the way) on the discharge side of the pump. This decreases the flow of water through the pump, but does not shut the pump down. The device is harmless to the pump and allows the water supply to recover by decreasing the flow demand. It is not great for fire fighters to have less water, but at least they still have some water: left to protect themselves. In every community where they used to require low pressure cut-off valves, the NFSA has been successful in getting them to accept one of the alternatives discussed above (alarms or 441

## Page 448

low suction throttling valves) except in the state of Ohio. For some reason, Ohio still requires the low pressure cut-off device even though NFPA 20 prohibits such devices. The NFSA has not been able to find anybody in the state of Ohio in a position of authority that is willing to listen to reason. If you install fire pumps in the state of Ohio, never sign any document that says that you installed the pump in accordance with NFPA 20. All of the fire pumps in Ohio (that are connected to public water supplies) are required to have low pressure cut-off devices and these devices violate NFPA 20. Bypass Piping All fire pumps connected to a water supply that has "sufficient pressure to be of material value without the pump" are required Lo have a bypass (see section 5.14,4.1 of NFPA 20). The bypass should begin in the suction pipe between the water supply and the suction control valve and end on the fire protection system piping, downstream of the discharge control valve for the pump. By placing the bypass pipe in this position, the pump can be isolated by closing the control valves on the suction and discharge sides with the bypass still able to feed water to the fire protection system around the pump. Unfortunately, there is no definition of how strong the water supply needs to be to have "sufficient pressure". Some authorities consider the ability to provide 7 psi to one sprinkler anywhere in the building to be sufficient enough to warrant a bypass. Others think that the bypass only has value if it can supply 3 or 4 sprinklers on the top floor of the building without the pump. There area wide range of opinions anywhere between these two points. In practice, it would seem that bypass piping is generally installed on all fire pumps taking water from a public water utility. Bypass piping is generally not provided for fire pumps taking suction from standing ponds, reservoirs or even ground level storage tanks. The bypass piping should have a check valve that only allows the water to flow in the direction from the water supply towards the fire protection system. Without this check valve, the water coming out of the pump under normal conditions would flow backwards to the pump suction and recirculate through the pump. Since the check valve is going to be installed, there needs to be two control valves in the bypass piping, one on each side of the check valve so that it can be serviced. These control valves are required to be left open so that the bypass can take over if the pump fails to start or jams up due to an obstruction. The valves need to be supervised consistent with the method of supervision for all of the other control valves associated with the pump. See section 5.16.1 of NFPA 20 for information of the supervision requirements and the position (open or closed) that the valve is required to be maintained in. 442

## Page 449

Discharge Piping The discharge piping is the small portion of pipe, valves and equipment that run from the discharge flange of the pump to the discharge control valve for the pump, The discharge pipe will always contain a check valve and a control valve. There may or may not be other equipment in the discharge piping as well. The above ground portions of discharge piping (which is the entire length of the discharge piping in most installations) is required to be steel pipe, regardless of what other kind of pipe is used aboveground or underground in the fire protection system (see section 5.15.3 of NFPA 20). The sprinkler system might be using some other kind of pipe for the riser, main(s) and branchlines (such as copper or CPVC), but the discharge pipe is still required to be steel. The discharge check valve is required in the discharge piping in order to trap the higher pressure created by the pump in the fire protection system. After the pump shuts down, the pressure in the pump itself will return to the suction pressure. It is valuable to trap the higher pressure in the fire protection system to give the first device that opens (sprinkler, hose station or spray nozzle) an initial charge of water before the pump kicks on. Also, by monitoring this pressure, decisions can be made about when to start the pump automatically. Any significant loss in pressure (that a pressure maintenance pump cannot keep up with) in the fire protection system is viewed as an opening of a device and a reason to start the pump. The control valve exists to make it possible to isolate the pump for repair or maintenance. The control valve is permitted to be any kind of valve listed for fire protection, even butterfly control valves. Once the water is on the discharge side of the pump, there is no longer a concern about turbulence. Pressure Relief Valves Another device that might be found on the discharge piping is a pressure relief valve. Over the years, NFPA 20 has had different requirements for when to install pressure relief valves, so identical systems may have different equipment based on when they were designed and installed. For the 1993 edition of NFPA 20 and most of the editions previous to that one, there were two conditions under which pressure relief valves were required as follows: 1) For all pumps driven by diesel engines, regardless of what pressure the pump would create under normal conditions. The concern was for what would happen• during an overspeed situation. The pressure relief valve was not intended to open under normal operating conditions, but was a safety device in case of a failure of the engine. 2) For all pumps driven by electric motors that created more pressure than the rating of the components in the fire protection system. In this case, the relief valves generally would open under normal operations (at least during the churn test) and discharge large volumes of water. 443

## Page 450

For the 1996 edition of NFPA 20, item 1 above was eliminated as a requirement. The argument was that diesel engines have overspeed shut-off devices that automatically shut down the pump if it turns at more than 120% of its rated speed. The proponents of this change convinced the committee that pressure relief valves were not necessary because they were never going to be used, They would not open under normal conditions and they would not open under overspeed conditions because the pump would simply shut down. So, under the 1996 edition of the standard, pressure relieve valves were only required for any pump (electric motor or diesel engine driven) that created more pressure than the rating of the components in the fire protection system. While writing the 1999 edition of NFPA 20, the committee was asked to readdress the issue of relief valves as a safety device on diesel engine driven systems. While many people agreed that the pump would shut down when it turned 20% faster than it was supposed to, they were concerned with what would happen if the pump turned 10% or 15% faster than it was supposed to and created more pressure without shutting down the engine. Remember that the pressure produced by a pump varies with the speed squared. So if the pump turns 10% faster than normal, it will produce 210/0 more pressure (1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21). Also during the discussion on the 1999 edition of the standard, the rules for using the pressure relief valve as a method for overpressuring the system were reexamined. There was a general concern amongst the committee members as to the advisability of designing the pump under normal operating conditions to open the relief valve and discharge large quantities of water. Ultimately, the committee decided that it would be better to pick a pump that did not produce that much pressure in the first place, or to design the fire protection system so that the components could withstand the pressure created by the pump. The provision for using a pressure relief valve to make up for the fact that the system was being overpressuized by the pump was eliminated. So, for the 1999 edition of the standard (and all editions since then) the only requirement for a pressure relief valve to be installed is for all pumps driven by diesel engines where the static pressure from the water supply plus 121% of the churn (shut off) pressure exceeds the rating of the components in the fire protection system. Circulation Relief Valves Circulation relief valves are very different devices than pressure relief valves. Just because a system has one, it does not eliminate the need for the other. A circulation relief valve (also sometimes called a casing relief valve) is a device attached to the casing of the pump or somewhere very close to the pump that opens up and discharges a small amount of water to a drain. This discharge of a small amount of water causes some new water to travel from the water supply to the pump, creating a circulation of water (hence the name of the device) even when no water is flowing into the fire protection system. Think about what is happening when a fire pump is operating in the churn condition (there is no water flowing into the fire protection system). The impeller is turning inside the casing rubbing up against the water. The friction caused by this motion is heating up the water. If allowed to continue, the water would heat up to the point where it is trying to boil, When it 444

## Page 451

reaches the point that it is trying to boil, it will try and tum to steam. When water converts from a liquid to a gas, it wants to expand tremendously (the ratio is about 1700 to 1 in volume), but the steam vapors cannot expand because they are restrained inside the casing, so the pressure goes up instead. If left on its own, the pressure would increase to the point where the casing would fail catastrophically. In order to prevent the scenario described above from happening, the circulation relief valve takes a little of the warm water from the casing of the pump and dumps it in a drain. Fresh cool water comes from the water supply and mixes with the water in the casing, keeping the temperature down and the pump from overheating. The circulation relief valve is very small (3/4 or 1 inch) and creates a flow under 25 gpm in most cases. But this small flow is enough to make sure that the water in the pump casing never gets too hot. There are two types of fire pumps that need circulation relief valves: 1) Electric motor driven pumps. 2) Diesel engine driven pumps with radiator recirculation coolant systems. Both of the types of pumps described above need the circulation relief valve because [here is no water being exchanged in the casing of the pump while they are operating in the churn condition. One common type of pump does not need a circulation relief valve, the diesel engine that uses water from the pump to cool the engine. This is the most common type of diesel engine. Most diesel engines used to drive fire pumps take water from the discharge side of the pump and circulate it through a coolant loop and heat exchanger that cools the diesel engine. Since this water is drawn off from the discharge side of the pump (even during churn conditions) there is already fresh cool water coming from the water supply and mixing in the casing, therefore, additional water from a circulation relief valve is not necessary. For many years, these were the only types of diesel engines listed on the market. More recently, there has been a concern about diesel engines that use water from the discharge side of the pump because of the amount of water that runs through the coolant system and gets dumped in a drain. Diesel engines that use this kind of cooling system can spend 900 to 1000 gallons every week during the regular churn test. In areas of draught, when people are being told to conserve water, it seems like quite a waste to put 1000 gallons down the drain to test a fire pump. So, radiator recirculation diesel engines were developed and liéted for fire protection to eliminate this concern. While these engines use less water, they do still use some water during a churn test because the circulation relief valve is required. 445

## Page 452

Testing Arrangements Somewhere on the discharge side of the pump must be a mechanism for testing the pump. The mechanism must be capable of allowing the pump to flow enough water to achieve 150% of the rated flow. NFPA 20 recognizes three different mechanisms for testing a fire pump: 1) A test header — A device with a number of hose connections that can be used to flow water. The hose is not required to be permanently attached to the header; it is assumed that the person doing the test will bring their hose. Generally, the water from a test such as this will flow to a drain, storm drain or sewer system. See Figure 33-25 for an example of a test header on a fire pump system. 2) Metering devices where the water is returned to the original source of supply. See Figure 33-26 for an example of this metering arrangement. 3) Closed Loop Metering -- This is different than item 2 above in that the water goes tlu•ough a meter and then immediately back into the suction flange of the pump. See Figure 33-27 for an example of closed loop metering. Control Valve (normally closed) Test Header Drip Drain Figure 33-25 Test Header Arrangement 446

Throttling Valve Normal (normally Water closed) Level Water Check Valve Flow Meter Storage Tank Figure 33-26 Flow Meter Discharge to Water Supply Check Flow Meter El III. Throttling Valve (normally closed) Figure 33-27 Closed Loop Metering Although NFPA 20 recognizes each of these as an acceptable method of testing a fire pump, NFPA 25 does not give the same credit to each method. The third method (closed loop metering) is considered a less than desirable method of testing a fire pump because it does not provide a method of testing the ability of the water supply to deliver water to the suction flange of the pump. Using the first and second method discussed above, the water going into the pump comes from the water supply. Eventually, it may get returned to the supply tank, but it comes from the supply to get to the pump. Closed loop metering does not provide this same benefit. NFPA 25 allows closed loop metering to be performed for the annual pump test, but not for more than two years in a row. After the second year of doing closed loop metering for a pump test, the 447

## Page 454

pump is required to be tested using a method that brings the water from the water supply. This means that as a person planning out a fire protection system from the beginning, if you want to use closed loop metering, you must include another method of testing the pump that is not closed loop metering so that three years after the system is installed, it can still be tested. When a test header is used, there must be sufficient hose outlets on the header to create enough flow to achieve 150% of the rated flow of the pump. Table 5-25(b) of NFPA 20 contains the information for how many hose connections need to be provided for each common size of fire pump. If the test header is going to be installed in an area subject to freezing, a control valve needs to be installed in the piping to the test header in .a location that is not subject to freezing, At all times when the system is not being tested, this control valve is kept closed and the piping between the control valve and the test header should be designed to drain so that there is no standing water left in this pipe. The size of the pipe going from the pump to the test header is also controlled by a column in Table 5-25(b) of NFPA 20. However, this table assumes that the distance from the pump to the test header will be relatively sh01t, If the pipe between the pump and the test header is more than 15 ft long, the next larger size than that indicated in the table is required to be used or a set of hydraulic calculations needs to be performed to prove that the pipe size proposed will work. This calculation can be difficult, See the NFSA Sprinkler Quarterly article in the Fall 2003 edition on this subject for more information as to how to perform this calculation. If a flow meter is going to be used, the meter must be listed and it must be capable of sensing at least 175% of the rated flow of the pump. The minimum size for the meter and the pipe for the meter bypass are listed in Table 5-25(b) for common sizes of fire pumps. The meter needs to be calibrated when it is installed and then again on a regular basis in order for the readings to be considered accurate. If the test header is being used, there will need to be some method of determining the flow from the hoses once they are connected to the header. The most frequently used tool for this measurement is the pitot gage. The pitot gage is named after a French scientist Henri Pitot, who lived in the 18üi century and conducted experiments in hydraulics including calculating velocity pressures in flowing streams. The pitot gage that we use today (shown in Figure 33-28) is startlingly similar to the pitot tube that he used in 1730. 448

50 40 70 30 20 0 0 80 90 10 100 hij Orifice Pressure gauge Pitot tube Handle Figure 33-28 Pitot Gage A pitot gage measures the velocity pressure of the water exiting a nozzle. Using a fonuula, we can convert this velocity pressure into a flow in gallons per minute (gpm). When using multiple hose nozzles, the total flow going through the pump can be calculated by using the pitot gage to determine the flow in each nozzle and then adding up all of the flows to get the total flow. the formula used to convert a pitot gage reading in psi to a flow in gpm is as follows: Q = 28.93cd2NFp Where: Q = flow in gpm c = nozzle coefficient (0.97 for straight-bore nozzles) d = the diameter of the nozzle opening in inches Pp = the velocity pressure read from the pitot gage in psi Sensing Lines The sensing line is the pipe that runs from the controller to the discharge piping. The purpose of the sensing line is to allow a pressure switch in the controller to be exposed to the pressure in the fire protection system. When the pressure in the fire protection system drops below a preset point, the pressure switch in the controller assumes that water is flowing to a fire and starts the fire pump. The sensing line is a critical piece of equipment because the fire pump will never stmt if there is a problem in the line. The sensing line is required to be connected to the fire protection system in the discharge piping of the fire pump. Specifically, the sensing line is required to be connected in between the discharge check valve and the discharge control valve for the fire pump it controls. It is important to note that each fire pump has its own controller and that each fire pump has its own sensing line. When multiple pumps are installed, the sensing lines need to be completely independent and they need to be tied into the discharge piping for their own pump. 449

## Page 456

The requirement for sensing lines to be completely independent not only applies to all fire pumps, but also applies to all jockey (pressure maintenance pumps). Each jockey pump has its own controller. Each jockey pump controller has its own sensing line that luns from the controller to the piping in between the jockey pump discharge check valve and the jockey pump discharge control valve. The jockey pump sensing line is not allowed to be combined with the main firc pump sensing line because such a combination would require that the whole system be shut down if there was a problem. Ifthe lines are kept separate (as required by NFPA 20, see sections 10.5.2.1.6 and 12.5.2.1.6) and there is a problem with the fire pump, the jockey pump can be kept in service as a partially effective bypass. Likewise, if there is a problem with the jockey pump, the main pump can be kept in service without the jockey pump, See Figure 33-29 for an example of the jockey pump sensing line and the main fire pump sensing line urangement. Rated pressures for fire pumps vary between 40 and 200 net psi. Rated flows vary from 25 to 5000 gpm. Also mentioned previously in this text, and important to this discussion, is the fact that these ratings only mean that at the rated flow, the pump will produce at least its rated pressure. Higher pressures and flow will occur during different times with the same pumps and the ratings are not limits to the pump's performance. NFPA 20 allows the maximum pressure that the pump will produce (this will occur during the no-flow or "churn" condition) to be 140% of the rated pressure of the pump. However, this is a maximum pressure that few pumps actually achieve. Many pumps only produce a maximum pressure of 120% of the rated pressure. Some only produce a maximum pressure of 110% of the rated pressure. •You must never assume that the pump you want to use 450

## Page 457

will achieve 140% of its rated pressure just because this number is in NFPA 20. The pump may never produce that kind of pressure and you will be over-predicting the pressure available from the pump, a dangerous assumption. Likewise, NFPA 20 states that the minimum pressure that the pump is allowed to produce at maximum flow (150% of rated flow) is 65% of the rated pressure. Once again, this pressure is a minimum below which pumps are not allowed to perform. But they are allowed to perform at higher pressures and almöst all of them do. Never assume that thc fire pump you want to use performs at this minimum, it will be an incon•ect assumption that will lead you to incorrect information about how much pressure is being produced by the pump. Just to show the wide variation in pump performance, Figure 33-30 shows the performance curves of two different pumps (both rated at 1000 gpm and 80 psi) as compared to the NFPA 20 limits of 140% of rated pressure at churn and 65% of rated pressure at maximum flow. Note that neither of the pumps follows the NFPA 20 ctuve, Assume for a minute that you are going to use a fire pump rated at 1000 gpm and 80 psi and you have a sprinkler system connected to that pump that is going to need 100 psi from the pump at 500 gpm. If you follow the NFPA 20 curve, you would assume that any pump rated at 1000 gpm and 80 psi would meet your demand. However, if you purchased the pump represented by the dashed line, you would only get about 89 psi at 500 gpm. If you purchased the pump represented by the dotted line, you would only get about 85 psi at 500 gpm. Neither of these pumps would give you the 100 psi that you need. So, if we can't use the limits discussed in NFPA 20 to determine how a pump will perfonn, what are you supposed to use? Well, since each pump is different, the best way to size a pump is to get the actual performance curve from the manufacturer for the pump that you want to use. This way, you are not making assumptions about how a pump might perform. Early in a project, it might be difficult to get exact information on a specific model pump, so it is possible to make some conservative assumptions, but those will not be discussed here. Once a sprinkler contractor is developing working plans, a specific model pump should be selected and verified as meeting the demand of the system. One of thc concerns regarding the selection of fire pumps is the use of computer programs. A computer program is only as good as the perspn providing the input data. If the data going into the calculation is bad, the results of the calculation will be bad. Be careful when using a computer program for hydraulic calculation along with a fire pump. Many computer programs assume the limits of NFPA 20 for fire pumps; the exact opposite of what you now know is the correct thing to do. Some programs will allow you to enter the data for the real pelformance curve of the fire pump, but it is a feature that has to be turned on. If you don.'t activate the feature, it does not calculate the system correctly. How do you know which programs are which? The answer is that if a program asks for only one data point to describe the pump, you know that it is assuming the other data points, which is a bad situation. If the program is asking for at least three data points to describe the curve, you can input tlu•ee points from the manufacturer's curve and know that the program is working correctly. It only takes three points to define a curve for a computer. When selecting a fire pump, there are two concerns. The first is making sure that the pump can provide you with the pressure you need at the demand flow for the fire protection system. The second is making sure that the pump does not over-pressurize the system at maximum pressure. The following is a procedure for sizing a fire pump for any fire protection system: 1) Calculate the fire protection system demand to pump discharge flange. 2) Calculate the suction pressure at the pump suction flange for the static (no flow) condition, the demand flow of the fire protection system and the maximum flow. The suction pressure at the maximum flow must be positive in order to move on to the next step. 3) Select a pump so that the system flow demand is less than 150% of the rated flow of the pump (less than 140% is recommended, but not required by NFPA 20). 4) Using the manufacturer's performance curve for the pump that you want to use, find the pump's net pressure at the system demand flow. 452

## Page 459

5) Add the suction pressure (at the demand flow) to the net pressure (at the demand flow) to get the discharge pressure (at the demand flow). 6) If the discharge pressure is greater than the demand, okay. If not, select new pump and go back to step 2. Only move on to step 7 when everything up to step 6 is okay. 7) Add the suction pressure at no-flow to the maximum churn pressure of the pump. If this is less than the pressure rating of the components downstream of the pump, you are done. If not, make changes to the components or the arrangement, or select a new pump. The following is an example of how to size a fire pump for a standpipe system in the five story building shown in Figure 33-3L Although it is not dimensioned on the Figure, the suction pipe in this example is a total of 150 ft of pipe and fittings of 8-inch pipe. The standpipe system has been calculated back from the most remote outlet to the discharge flange of the pump and will require a flow of 1010 gpm at 125 psi. The water supply for the system is an elevated tank where the bottom of the tank is 75 ft above the suction flange of the pump. Note that the measurement is made to the bottom of the tank because the pump needs to work near the end of the fire when the tank is nearly empty. There are two fire pumps under consideration to supply this particular standpipe system, a 750 gpm pump with a performance curve as shown in Figure 33-32 and a 1000 gpm fire pump as shown in Figure 33-33. The task will be to determine which of these pumps is conect for this fire protection system. At worse-case (bottom of the tank) this is 32.5 psi (0.433 psi/ft x 75 ft = 32.5 psi). b) The demand flow of the fire protection system -- This will be the elevation head from the tank minus the friction loss in the pipe between the tank and the pump. Using the Hazen-Williams formula, the friction loss when 1010 gpm is flowing tlu•ough the suction pipe is found to be 1 psi, so the suction pressure at 1010 gpm is 31.5 psi (32-1 = 31.5). c) The maximum flow (1125 gpm) — Once again the suction pressure will be the elevation head minus the friction loss. Using the Hazen-Williams formula, the friction loss when 1125 gpm is flowing through the suction pipe is found to be 1.3 psi, making the suction pressure at maximum flow 30.2 psi (31.5 — 1.3 = 30.2). The suction pressure at each of these flow conditions is positive, so we can move on to the next step. 3) Select a pump so that the system flow demand is less than 150% of the rated flow of the pump. The discharge pressure at 1010 gpm will be 123.5 psi (31.5 + 92 = 123.5). 6) Ifthe discharge pressure is greater than the demand, okay. If not, select new pump and go back to step 2. Using the Hazen-Williams formula, the friction loss when 1500 gpm is flowing through the suction pipe is found to be 2.2 psi, making the suction pressure at maximum flow 30.2 psi (31.5 — 2.2 = 29.3). The suction pressure at each of these flow conditions is positive, so we can move on to the next step. 3) Select a pump so that the system flow demand is less than 150% of the rated flow of the pump. We have already selected a 1000 gpm pump to try as shown in Figure 33-33. 4) Using the manufacturer's performance curve for the pump that you want to use, find the pump 's net pressure at the system demand flow. From Figure 33-33, the net pressure created by the pump at a flow of 1010 gpm is 112 psi (see the "X" on the Figure). 5) Add the suction pressure (at the demand flow) to the net pressure (at the demand flow) to get the discharge pressure (at the demand flow). The discharge pressure at 1010 gpm will be 143.5 psi (3115 + 112 143.5), 456

## Page 463

6) Ifthe discharge pressure is greater than the dentand, okay. If not, select new pump and go back to step 2. Only move on to step 7 when everything up to step 6 is okay. Our discharge pressure when using this pump is much greater than what we need for thc fire protection system. The pump will discharge 143.5 psi at a flow of 1010 gpm and we only need 125 psi to make the system work, so we can move on to step 7. 7) Add the suction pressure at no-flow to the maximum churn pressure of the pump. If this is less than the pressure ratin.g of the components downstream of the pump, you are done. If not, make changes to the components or the arrangement, or select a new pump. At the no-flow (static) condition, the suction pressure of the pump was calculated at 32.5 psi and the churn pressure of the pump will be 129 psi (see Figure 33-33). This will make the discharge pressure 161.5 psi. Since fire protection equipment is rated for a minimum of 175 psi, this pump does not overpressurize the system and will work just fine. Note that this step was performed with the worse-case pressure from the water supply of 32.5 psi, which was based on the water being in the bottom of the tank. For this particular calculation, the worse-case condition is actually when the water is in the top of the tank, creating the highest possible suction pressure on the pump. Assuming that the tank itself is 30 ft tall, the top of the tank would be 105 ft above the suction flange of the pump, creating a suction pressure of 45.5 psi (0.433 psi/ft x 105 ft = 45.5 psi. With a chum pressure from the pump of 129 psi, the discharge pressure in this case would be 174.5 psi (45.5 + 129 = 174.5), which is acceptable. Ifthe tank were any taller, the components downstream would have to be rated for pressure greater than 175 psi, which is not a problem for standpipe system components. Pump Drivers There are three possible drivers for fire pumps: electric motors, diesel engines and steam turbines. Although steam turbines are reliable, they are not generally used to drive fire pumps unless there is some other reason that large quantities of steam are already near the facility, which is a rare occurrence. Due to the fact that they are extremely rare, they will not be covered in this text. Prior to 1974, gasoline engines were also used to drive fire pumps. When writing the 1974 edition of NFPA 20, the comrnittee decided that gasoline was too volatile a fuel to store for use in a fire protection system. Diesel engines are just as reliable as gasoline engines, but are much safer to use. So, in the 1974 edition of NFPA 20, gasoline engines were eliminated from consideration as acceptable drivers. However, the requirement was never made retroactive, so it is still possible to find gasoline engines being used on systems installed prior to 1974. There is no requirement in any NFPA code or standard to replace these engines as long as they still create the horsepower necessary to tum the pump. However, the storage tanks for these engines must store the gasoline in accordance with any local flammable liquid storage code. Electric motors are very common drivers for fire pumps. The advantages of electric motors are that they are clean, quiet, small and efficient. An electric motor is usually smaller than a diesel engine of the same horsepower. The drawback of the electric motor is that it will 457

## Page 464

only work when there is electric power to the motor. During a power outage, the electric motor will not work unless there is some sott of back-up power. While electric motor driven pumps might cost less than diesel engine driven pumps of the same horsepower, the demand for back-up power might make the electric motor more expensive. NFPA 20 does not require back-up power for all fire pump installations. Instead, NFPA 20 requires a single reliable power supply for the electric motor that is driving the pump. If the power supply is not "reliable" then a back-up power supply is' required. Unfortunately, there is no definition of what a "reliable" power supply is. It would be nice if the NFPA 20 committee could say that a "reliable" power supply is one where the average power outage is "X" number of hours and the maximum amount of time that people have been without power is "Y" number of hours. But the cornmittee has never been able to agree on what the values of "X" and "Y" should be. So, it is up to the building owner and the AllJ to decide whether or not a local power utility is "reliable" or not. Diesel engines are also very common drivers for fire pumps. The advantages to diesel engines include the fact that they do not need to have continuous electricity in order to work. a power outage, a diesel engine will still be able to detect a fire and start. However, the drawbacks of the diesel engines include the noise that they create and the maintenance that they require. In order to keep the engine operational, it needs to be started at least once each week and run for at least 30 minutes. After several weekly tests, the fuel needs to be refilled. There are some insurance companies that give greater discounts to fire protection systems that utilize diesel engines over those that they give for systems that utilize electric motors. The basis for this greater discount is that the diesel engine is more reliable because it does not require constant electrical service. However, if a building owner is going to make the decision to have a diesel engine, they are also going to have to make the commitment to maintaining that engine, An engine that is not maintained is not going to start, which does not make that engine reliable at all. Controllers and Equipment for Electric Motor Driven Pumps The controller for an electric motor driven fire pump will generally have two switches (or handles) on the outside: the isolation switch and the circuit breaker. The isolation switch breaks the electrical circuit and stops the flow of electricity through the controller, The purpose of the isolation switch is to allow safe work on the controller after the pump has been stopped by other means. The isolation switch should never be used to stop the pump from running because it is not rated for the maximum current that might be flowing tlu•ough a controller to a pump motor, making it dangerous to touch this switch if there is any possibility that there is power going to the pump. The isolation switch should only ever be touched after the circuit breaker has already been turned off. The isolation switch should have a sign on it warning the user not to touch it unless the circuit breaker is already off. The circuit breaker is the second of the switches or levers on the outside of the controller for electric motor driven pumps. The circuit breaker is rated for the maximum current that might 458

## Page 465

be flowing through the system and can safely be touched under any current situation. Since it is impossible to look at a motor and tell what the current situation is, the corect sequence for turning off an clectric motor driven firc pump is to always throw the circuit breaker first, then turn off the isolation switch. When turning the pump back on, always start with the isolation switch and then turn on the circuit breaker. By following the order, you are never touching the isolation switch mless the circuit breaker is in the off position. Some controller manufacturers have taken this important concept one step further. They have designed the lever on the outside of the pump Lo work both the isolation switch and the circuit breaker by designing the lever to have üu•ee positions. When the lever is in the top position, both the circuit breaker and the isolation switch are on. When the lever is moved down to the middle position, the circuit breaker is disengaged. When the lever is moved to the bottom position, the isolation switch is disengaged. Moving the lever up through the positions engages the devices in the conect order, Since you can't go from the top to the bottom without going through the rniddle position, you are always moving the switches in the correct order. This type of controller only has this single lever on the outside, but it is connected to the two individual switches on the inside. Each controller is required to be labeled "Electric Fire Pump Controller". If there are multiple pumps installed, each pump needs its own controller and the controller need to identify which pump it controls. If the different pumps control different portions of the system, the controller needs to be labeled as to which portion of the system it controls. The controller is required to have two signals that indicate whether or not a specific condition is present or has occurred. The two signals are power available and phase reversal. The "power available" light should always be on. This indicates that the pump has sufficient power to operate. Before going into the phase reversal signal, it is important to discuss the concept of electricity and three-phase power. The fire pumps that are currently listed all use three-phase electrical power. Without going into a big (and difficult) discussion of electricity, let us just summarize three-phase power by saying that there are three big wires brining the electricity to the controller. As long as the correct wires are connected to the correct terminals, the motor will turn. If the wrong wire is connected to a terminal, the electricity will arrive, and the motor will turn, but it will turn backwards. Fire pumps that turn backwards will not created very much pressure and will not serve the fire protection system well at all. Therefore, we must make sure that the power arrives in the correct phase. A legitimate question to ask is why we need to constantly monitor the phase at which the power is arriving? Can't we just test the pump after it is installed and make sure that the motor turns in the correct direction? The answer is that we can (and do) test the pump as soon as it is installed and make sure that it turns in the correct direction. However, we do not generally control the power utility, nor do we control the cables and wires that deliver the electricity. Therefore, even after a pump has been installed and the system tested to verify that it was installed correctly, it is possible for the electric generating system or thc electric distribution 459

## Page 466

system to change what they are doing and mess up the phase of our motors so we must constantly monitor the situation to make sure that we have electricity arriving al the proper phase. Under normal circumstances (the pump having the correct power in the correct phase) the "phase reversal" indicator may be on or it may be off. The problem is that there are two different types of phase indicators and there is no requirement as to which kind of indicator manufacturers are required to use. One kind of indicator is called the "normal phase indicator". The normal phase indicator will light up when the power to the controller is in the correct phase and the pump will work properly. If there is a phase problem with the power supply, the light will go out. Many manufacturers (and controller users) like the normal phase indicator because it is positive confirmation that everything is okay. Ifthe light is out, there is a problem that needs to be investigated. It might just be that the light bulb has burned out, or it might be that the electric phase has experienced a problem. The other kind of indicator is the "reversal of phase indicator", which only lights up if there is a problem with the electrical phases. This kind of indicator is frustrating at times because the normal condition is with the light off. The only time that the light comes on is if there is a problem, If the light bulb has burned out, the user might think that everything is okay, but then find out later that phase reversal had occurred but no one knew because the light was out. When looking at a phase monitor on a fire pump controller, always figure out what kind of phase monitor you are looking at. It should say on it that "on is the normal condition" or "a light indicates phase reversal". There should be some indication of what the normal condition should be. Another device that will either be on the controller or on the sensing line that runs from the controller to the discharge piping will be a pressure recorder. This device will tell the user what the pressure has been in the fire protection system for the last seven days. Many of these devices are spring loaded mechanical devices that rotate a piece of paper in a circle and indicate the pressure with a pen moving across the paper. The device is only accurate if the paper is changes once each week. More recently, digital pressure recorders have been installed that can print out a list of the pressure in the system over a given time period. Some of these can connect to portable computers or handheld devices and provide the pressure information in spreadsheets. The requirement for pressure recorders on electric motor driven pumps was new to the 1996 edition of the standard, so it is possible that existing installations will not have this feature. In addition to the signals on the controller, there are three signals that are required to be sent to a constantly attended location. These three signals are pump running, loss of phase, and phase reversal. The pump running signal is intended to let someone know that the pump is running. That person is required (section 5.3 of NFPA 20) to dispatch a person that knows about the operation of the fire pump to the pump room to monitor the pump. It is important to know that this is not a signal that should be used to call the fire department, but it is a signal that needs to be responded

## Page 467

to immediately because the pump is worth a great deal of money and if it does not operate properly, it may get damaged. The loss of phase signal indicates when one of the tlu•ee wires is disconnected from the source or is not receiving electricity. Again, this is not a reason to call the fire department, but it is a condition that needs to be fixed as soon as possible because the fire pump will not be able to run correctly until it is repaired. The phase reversal signal has already been discussed, but it is included in the list of items that need to be monitored at a constantly attended location so that immediate action can be taken if a problem occurs. Controllers and Equipment for Diesel Engine Driven Pumps Diesel engines are generally equipped with govemors that attempt to keep them tuming at a constant speed. The governor should be set to keep the engine turning at rated speed at maximum flow (150% of rated flow). At lower flows, the ideal condition would be for the pump to maintain a constant speed, but that is next to impossible with current engine technology, so NFPA 20 allows the motor to increase speed as much as 10% at any flow condition (including the no-flow condition which is where the least load is on the engine). Recently, diesel engines have been listed for use with fire pumps that have variable speed controls. These engines slow down when high discharge pressure conditions occur. These engines are subject to the 10% variance requirement. If the engine ever turns at more than 20% over its rated speed, the engine has an automatic switch that will shut it down. This is a safety feature that is built into the engine so that systems do not become overpressurized. Remember that the pressure produced by the pump is related to the speed it turns squared. If a pump turns 20% faster than it is supposed to, it produces 44% more pressure than it is supposed to. For example, if a pump is rated to produce a net pressure of 140 psi at a speed of 3000 rim, it would produce a net pressure of 202 psi at 3600 rpm (20% faster speed). This dramatic increase in net pressure might do serious damage to the equipment on a fire protection system, or to a person trying to handle a hose line, so the pump is required to shut down. The engine is required to have an oil pressure indicator, a temperature indicator and a run-time meter. The oil pressure and temperature indicators just let the operator know that the engine is able to operate properly. These are similar to the gages that you scan every few minutes while driving your car, The run-time meter gives an indication of when the engine will need maintenance. For the engine in your car, you decide when to perform maintenance based on how many miles you drive. But fire pump engines don't go anywhere, so a different method needed to be found to determine when maintenance procedures need to be performed, The method that has been standardized is to have a meter on the engine giving an indication of how many hours it has run. The maintenance is then performed based on the number of hours, not the number of miles. 461

## Page 468

Diesel engines are generally started by batteries (although there are air pressure and water pressure starting mechanisms for spark free environments, bul they won't be covered here due Io their being relatively scarce). According to NFPA 20, there need to be two sets of batteries connected to the engine, each capable of starting the engine on their own. When the engine gets a signal from the controller to staff, the first battery set cranks the engine for 15 seconds or until it starts, whichever is shorter. Ifthe engine does not stmt after 15 seconds, the engine rests for 15 seconds and then tries to start from the second set of batteries. If the engine still does not start, it rests for 15 seconds and goes back to trying to start from the first set of batteries. The engine keep going back and forth with periods of 15 seconds of cranking and 15 seconds of rest for 3 minutes (6 total attempts to start with 3 from each battery set). If the engine has not started at that point, a failure to start signal is sent to a constantly attended location and the controller no longer tries to start the engine. The switching back and forth between two different sets of batteries with 15 seconds of cranking and 15 seconds of rest is called a "cranking cycle". When batteries are used to start the diesel engine, they are required to be recharged from the engine by an alternator or a generator. There is also required to be an ammeter installed on the controller or engine to monitor the charging state of each battery set. Diesel engines need to be cooled while they are running. There are two different types of diesel engine coolant systems that are listed for fire protection systems. The most common diesel engine coolant system takes water from the discharge side of the pump and circulates that water flu•ough a heat exchanger to keep the engine cool. The water is then discharged to a drain, somewhat warmer than when it went into the engine because it has absorbed heat from the engine. Engine coolant lines typically discharge about 30 to 40 gpm while the engine is running. Since engines have to be run for a minimum of 30 minutes per week, these types of engines are not real popular in areas subject to water shortages. The other type of coolant system uses a radiator and a fan to recirculate the same coolant fluid (usually not plain water, but some kind of efficient heat transfer fluid). The fluid goes through a heat exchanger and takes heat from the engine; it then circulates past a fan, which uses ambient air to cool the liquid down again. These types of engine coolant systems are popular where water shortages frequently occur. However, they have additional concerns in that they need to be in well ventilated spaces because they rely on the air being cool enough to bring the temperature of the fluid back down. They also need circulation relief valves (see the discussion on this subject in the Discharge Piping section of this chapter). If the pump is using a coolant system that is discharging to a drain, the drain needs to be in view of the person operating the pump or there needs to be a sight glass in the drain line so that the operator can be sure that water is moving in the coolant line. If the operator can't see movement in the coolant line, they need to take action because the engine will overheat and be damaged. Diesel engines need fuel in order to run. NFPA 20 requires the fuel tank to be in the pump room or pump house. This is not a violation of the code regarding the storage of combustible liquids, although some local codes require a dyke around such liquid storage, which is easy enough to do in a pump house or room. The tank is required to be sized for at least one 462

## Page 469

gallon per horsepower of the engine plus 10% (5% for sump at the bottom and 5% for expansion allowance at the top), see Figure 33-34. The value of one gallon per horsepower is arrived at by assuming that engines burn approximately one pint of fuel per horsepower pcr hour and the NFPA 20 committee wants the tank sized for at least 8 hours. Note that NFPA 25 does not require that the tank be kept full, so even though the tank is sized for 8 hours, it may not always have 8 hours of fuel. If the duration of the fire protection system and/or the refill abilities of the tank are such that the required testing of the fire pump cannot be performed without leaving enough fuel in the tank in case of fire, the tank may need to be oversized. 5% for expansion I gallon per horsepower 5% for surnp Fill Line Figure 33-34 Di.esel Fuel Tank Sizing Diesel engine driven pumps need fresh air in order to operate properly. In addition to the issue already discussed with keeping the room cool so that the engine does not overheat, the engine also needs fresh air for combustion. Without sufficient quantities of fresh air, the engine cannot combine oxygen with fuel in order to keep turning efficiently, A lack of air to the engine will cause it to lose power output, which would affect the pressure produced by the pump. Ventilating louvers need to be designed to bring plenty of air into the pump room or pump house. There are two types of louvers that can be used: free convection louvers and motorized louvers. "Free convection louvers" swing freely on a hinge. When the engine starts, it takes air from the room and creates a negative pressure in the room. Air from outside presses against the louvers and caused them to open, letting air in and causing the pressure to equalize. As long as the engine is running and taking pressure from the room, the louvers will stay open. As soon as the pump stops, the pressure will equalize and the louvers will close. The problem with free convection louvers is that they also swing open when the wind blows. Many building owners have a hard time heating the pump room because the louvers swing open in the breeze and let cold air in. Over time, many owners, not knowing the importance of the louvers, obstruct them or stuff them with insulation so that they don't open. While they have solved a potential heat problem, they have impaired their fire protection system. The louvers need to be kept clear to open so that the engine can get all the air it needs. 463

## Page 470

Motorized louvers are much better for the owner. The louvers stay closed until a signal comes from the controller thal the engine is going to start. The louvers then open and allow the air to come in while the engine is running. After the engine shuts down, the louvers close again. The louvers are operated on low voltage electricity that is easily back-up up from the same source as the controller and will operate even during power outages. In the worse-case condition of a power outage lasting so long that the back-up power dies, the louvers end up opening because the electricity keeps them closed, so they are fail-safe. If you are going to use a diesel engine, consider using motorized iouvers for the pump room or pump house. In addition to getting the air into the pump room for combustion, you have to get the exhaust out of the room safely so that people are not overcome with carbon monoxide. If there are multiple engines in the same pump room, the exhaust has to be independent for each engine. You cannot manifold the exhausts together because the exhaust might go up from one engine and come back down into the room through the other engine if that second engine is not running. The exhaust needs to be connected to the engine with a flexible coupling. The purpose of the flexible coupling is to absorb the vibrations created by the engine without transferring them to the building structure, Diesel engines Vibrate quite a bit and the exhaust is usually attached to part of the building (while it penetrates a wall or ceiling) so we need to make sure that we don't vibrate the building when running the pump. If the wall or ceiling that the exhaust penetrates is combustible, there needs to be 9 inches of clearance around the exhaust pipe to insure that the warm exhaust does not set the building on fire. There are two exceptions to the 9 inch clearance rule both involving metal thimbles installed around the exhaust as it penetrates the building (wall or ceiling) as follows: Exception 1: Penetrate combustible roofs with ventilated metal thimble at least 6" in diameter larger than the exhaust pipe. Must extend 9" above and below the roof. Exception 2: Penetrate combustible walls with Metal thimbles at least 12" larger than pipe diameter; or Metal or burned clay thimbles built in brickwork providing at least 8" of insulation Controllers for diesel driven fire pumps are required to have the following signals directly on the controller as well as also sending these signals to a constantly attended location: Position (Automatic, or on) Low Oil Pressure High Engine Jacket Temperature Failure of Automatic Start Overspeed Shutdown Battery and Charger Failure Low Air or Hydraulic Pressure Low Diesel Fuel 464

The following signals are not required for controllers of diesel engine driven pumps, but they are recommended by NFPA 20 in annex material as being a good idea to monitor: o Low Pump Room Temperature Relief Valve Discharge o Flow Meter bypass "on" Water Level or Pressure in Suction Pipe Just like the situation with controllers for electric motor driven fire pumps, controllers for diesel engine driven fire pumps are also required to have a pressure recorder or the pressure recorder needs to be installed in the pressure sensing line between the controller and the discharge piping. This requirement has been in the standard for a long time on for diesel driven equipment, so they should be on all pump systems in the field. Starting the Pump Every pump is required to have a starting two mechanisms, one automatic and the other one manual. The automatic method is usually a pressure monitoring device in the controller that is attached to the discharge piping of the fire pump tlu•ough a pressure sensing line. When a sprinkler opens, or someone opens a hose valve) the flow of water form the open device causes a drop in pressure in the system. The pressure sensing device responds to this drop in pressure by turning on the pump. The manual method of starting the pump is generally a "staff' button on the controller or a switch that can be turned from "automatic" to "manual start". In order to make sure that the pump's weekly test is performed, many controller incorporate a weekly programmed timer to automatically start the pump at the same time each week. Although this timer is allowed to automatically start the pump, it may not be allowed to automatically stop the pump. See the discussion below for more details. Stopping the Pump Every pump is required to have a manual method of stopping the pump, which may be a switch that is moved to the "stop" position or a button marked "stop" that needs to be pushed. A pump is allowed to be automatically stopped (turned off without human intervention) but in order for the pump to be stopped this way, it needs to meet all of the following rules: 1) All starting conditions have returned to normal, for electric motors) 3) The pump is not the sole source of supply for a sprinkler or standpipe system. 4) The AHJ has not mandated "manual-only" shut-down. 465

## Page 472

The cause for concem regarding automatic shutdown is that the pump will decide to turn itself off even though there is a fire. Once the pump is shut off, the fire would get a chance to grow again and do more damage. Most members of the NFPA 20 committee want a human being to decide that the fire is out and that the pump can tum itself off. However, there are people in the fire protection community that believe in technology and are concerned about the damage that a pump running a long period of time could do if there were not a fire, but a break in a pipe or a problem with a drain. These people point to instances of flooded basements and water damage when people ignored "pump running" signals and a pump ran for a long period of time causing a great deal of water damage. These people want pumps to shut themselves down after the conditions discussed above are met. The most difficult condition is that the pump is not allowed to be the only water supply for a sprinkler or standpipe system. Since FDC's don't count as water supplies, most sprinkler and standpipe systems don't have more than one supply, so they can't use the automatic shut-down feature of NFPA 20. However, in some jurisdictions, they override this provision of NFPA 20 and mandate automatic shutdown. Understand the rules in the local jurisdiction so that you install the fire pump the way that the local AHJ wants it.
