CHAPTER 34 WATER TANKS FOR FIRE PROTECTION There are a number of occasions where the water for a fire protection system is going to be stored in a tank. This chapter will discuss the different times when tanks are needed, the different kinds of tanks in use and some of the basic installation and design considerations for tanks. The most basic question will be answered, "How big does the tank need to be?" This chapter will be an excellent study guide for NICET work element 14011 (Storage Tanks) and will provide background material helpful for understanding work elements 13007 (Water Supply Requirements) and 13008 (System Connections). The rules discussed in this chapter apply to private tanks that are used for the purpose of providing water to one or more fire protection systems. While similar rules might apply to tanks that are a part of a public water supply, such public tanks are outside the scope of fire protection standards and are under the control of the water utility. The water utility should be consulted if there are any questions about the reliability, duration or flow from any tank that is a part of a public water supply. Need for Tanks There are five different conditions that might exist that would lead to the need for a tank to hold water for one or more fire protection systems. These conditions are: Rural area - no public mains Public main produces insufficient flow Building divided into vertical zones Second supply for redundancy Second supply for seismic zone Each of these situations will be discussed in more detail here starting with the lack of public mains. Buildings in areas where there are no public mains still need water available to 473

## Page 480

fight Tire. Unf01tunately, many times building owners tend to try and exempt themselves from built-in fire protection (like fire sprinkler systems) when they are in litral areas with no public water supplies. These building owners think that putting the sprinkler system in will be a hardship because there is no public water supply. In reality, buildings in rural areas with no public water supplies are the ones that need sprinkler protection the most! When a fire occurs in a building that does not have a public water supply, the fire depattment will have to find water somewhere to fight that fire. Often the fire department has to bring that water in tank trucks, or set up long relay stations from a pond or other remote source like a public utility far from the fire. Getting sufficient quantities of water can be a challenge for any fire depaltrnent in these circumstances, but in nu•al communities, these departments tend to be volunteer and often don't have the manpower and the resources to get sufficient water to a fire. Also, these volunteer departments may have difficulty in getting water to the fire in the early stages of fire development, when it is easiest to extinguish. Fire protection systems with their own tanks help buildings in mral communities by getting the correct amount of water to the fire in the early stages of fire development, minimizing the damage to the building. By getting water to the fire early, the fire protection system helps to conserve water because it takes less water to extinguish a fire in the first few minutes from a fire protection system than it does from fire department hoses. A light hazard occupancy (such as a school) can be protected with a flow as low as 120 gpm for a duration of 30 minutes (a total demand of 3600 gallons of water). Compare that to the flow from a fire department hose. The typical hose used for primary attack on fires by fire fighters flows 250 gpm. Considering that multiple hoses are in operation at any given time, and that it takes hours to fight a fire, it is easy to see how fire departments might need tens of thousands of gallons of water to fight a fire in an unsprinklered property. Given the choice of putting in sprinklers and a 3600 gallon tank or putting a 30,000 gallon water supply for the fire department, it would seem to make much more sense to choose the sprinkler system. Another situation under which a tank might be found is where a public main exists, but is not capable of producing the flow necessary for the fire protection system. This might happen in a rural community, but is also possible in any community as the demand flow for fire protection systems increases as the hazard increases. In these cases, the tank is just as important as the discussion above for tanks in rural areas. The third situation under which tanks are found occurs in extremely tall buildings. When a building is so tall that the static head of the water in the vertical pipes creates excessive pressures, the system is broken into multiple vertical zones. Many times, a tank is used to feed the upper vertical zone(s). For example, consider a building 700 ft tall (shown in Figure 34-1). If a vertical pipe fed a standpipe system from the bottom all the way to the top, it would take a pressure of 403 psi at the bottom of the standpipe to make sure that the required pressure of 100 psi was available at the top of the pipe. A pressure of 403 psi is excessive and above the rating of many of the pipes and fittings typically used in standpipe systems. Rather than try and work with this high pressure, systems are frequently broken into multiple vertical zones with pumps and tanks used within the building to feed the zones as shown in Figure 34-2. 474

## Page 481

For Figure 34-2, the system was broken into 2 vertical zones. In order to keep 100 psi at the topmost portion of the pipe, the maximum pressure at the bottom of one of the vertical pipes is 252 psi. While this pressure is still high (pressure rcducing valves will still be required at the hose outlets since the pressure exceeds 175 psi) there are components that are conunon to standpipe systems that can handle this pressure. Breaking this system into even more vertical zones can continue to decrease the pressure even more so that pressure reducing valves will not be needed. In order to make the concept of multiple vertical zones work, Lhere must be an air gap (a physical separation) between the pipe from the lower zone that feeds the upper zone and the tank in the upper zone. If the tanks are not pressure tanks, a pump will also be needed in the upper zones to pressurize the water from the tanks. The pumps have been removed from Figures 34-1 and 34-2 for simplicity. 100 psi (required by NFPA 14) 403 psi (700 x 0.433 + 100) Figure 34-1 Pressure in Vertical Pipe in a Tall Building 475

## Page 482

100 psi (required by NFPA 14) Upper Zone Tank 252 psi 100 psi (required by NFPA 14) Lower Zone 247 psi (340 x 0.433 + 100) Figure 34-2 Tall Building with Two Vertical Zones The foulth situation where tanks are found as a portion of the fire protection for a building is where a second water supply is desired for redundancy. NFPA 13 (and most building a fire codes) only requires one water supply for any fire protection system. However, many insurance companies give substantial discounts to buildings that have two or more water supplies (as long as both supplies are independently capable of supplying the demand for the fire protection system). The general consensus in fire protection is that a single water supply is reliable enough, but that an additional water supply provides an extra level of protection. Tanks are frequently used as a portion of the second water supply. 476

## Page 483

The last situation where tanks are found as a portion of thc fire protection system for a building is in an extremely active seismic zone. There are some building codes that require a second water supply for impottant buildings in areas of high seismic activity, The concern is that a big earthquake might take out a city main and render a sprinkler system ineffective. These secondary supplies are only found in areas of extreme earthquake activity, usually only refer to celtain types of buildings and generally do not require storage of the entire demand of the fire protection system. Most building codes only require 30 minutes worth of water supply. For example, the Lnternational Building Code (IBC-2003 edition) only requires the secondary water supply for high-rise buildings in Seismic Design Categories C, D, E and F and only requires the tank to hold a total of 30 minutes worth of water for the sprinkler system (including hose stream demands). Types of Tanks There are two types of tanks, atmospheric tanks and pressure tanks. Atmospheric tanks are those that are open in some location (it might just be a vent hole) and free to exchange air between the outside and the inside of the tank. Atmospheric tanks are filled with water and allowed to sit without any additional pressurization of the water. The water at the top of the tank will be at atmospheric pressure. The water at the bottom of the tank will be at a pressure based on the depth of the tank. Pressure tanks are sealed from the outside and pressurized after the water has been placed in the tank. The most common form of pressurization that occurs is the use of an air compressor to pressurize air in the tank. The pressurized air pushes on the water and increases the total pressure in the tank. The volume of air in the tank and the pressure of the air determine what pressure will occur inside the tank. Since the volume of air plays a role in determining the pressure in the tank, it is important not to overfill pressure tanks. Pressure tanks tend to work best when the volume of air in the tank is approximately 1/3 the total volume of the tank (the water being in the other two thirds of the tank). See Figure 34-3 for an example of a pressure tank. 477

## Page 484

Air genera!!y 1/3 of volume Water - generally 2/3 of volume Control Valve Figure 34-3 Pressure Tank System Riser Site Glass Check Valve Atmospheric tanks are generally divided into two different categories, elevated tanks and ground level tanks. Elevated tanks are placed above the fire protection systems that they serve to take advantage of the elevation head and increase the available pressure in the fire protection system (see Figure 34-4). The pressure created by elevating the tank is only as effective as the height difference between the bottom of the water in the tank and the highest sprinkler in the fire protection system. Water higher in the tank is useful, but the fire protection system needs to work towards the end of the fire when the water is at the bottom of the tank. The system also needs to work all the way to the top floor of the building. 478

## Page 485

Useful Height "IT' Static Pressure at sprinkler equals 0.433 x H Figure 34-4 Elevated Tank Feeding Fire Sprinkler System Ground level atmospheric tanks will require some device to increase the pressure of the water so that the water can get into the fire protection system and actually fight the fire. In most cases, a fire pump will be used to provide this increase in preséure. Most of the time, the fire pump will be a fixed part of the fire protection system, however, it is possible to rely on the fire department pumper trucks to provide this increase in pressure in some manual types of systems. Where the tank is being used to feed a fire pump, it is typically called a suction tank. See Figure 34-5 for a typical suction tank. If the tank is being used as a suction tank, it is required to have a device at the bottom of the tank called an "anti voltex plate". The anti vortex plate is a flat plate parallel to the bottom of the tank with a hole in the middle. An elbow is connected to the hole and the elbow is connected to the discharge pipe for the tank. When water leaves the tank, it 479

## Page 486

flows under the anti vortex plate, up through the hole, into the elbow and int.o the discharge pipe of the tank. by forcing the water to flow through this path, it prevents (he water from forming a voltex in the tank as the water goes out. This vortex, if it were allowed to form, would damage the fire pump. By forcing the water to flow through this path, we protect the fire pump from the turbulence and air pockets that would form in the water without the anti vortex plate. Fire Pump Anti Vortex Plate Figure 34-5 Suction Tank Another type of ground storage tank is the Embankment Supported Rubberized Fabric (ESRF) tank. The idea with an ESRF tank is to build some barriers of earth (usually by digging a hole in the ground) and line the eatth with rubber (so that the water won't leak out). The area is then filled with water and covered. The concept is not much different than a covered rubber lined swimming pool, While these kinds of tanks are easy to build, they do require that space be available to the property, which may be difficult in an urban environment. Tank Materials In addition to the ESRF tanks discussed above, tanks can be made from wood, steel, concrete or fiberglass. Some of the oldest tanks in the world are wood tanks. These durable and reliable tanks have been in service for years and provide excellent fire protection as long as they are maintained. Steel tanks are available in two different varieties, welded and bolted. For most large atmospheric tanks, individual sections are shipped out to a job site and then assembled. The sections are either bolted or welded together to form a steel tank. For pressure tanks, the tank is assembled at the factory and welded together, then pressure tested. Once it passes the pressure 480

## Page 487

test, it is shipped as a unit to the job site and cannot be altered there unless the manufacturer comes out and performs another pressure certification test. For this reason, extremely large pressure tanks are rare in fire protection. The practical limit is what will fit on the back of a flatbed truck for shipping pulposes. Fiberglass tanks are a concern in fire protection because of the possibility that they will become involved in the fire itself. There are also concerns about mechanical damage to the fiberglass. For these reasons, fiberglass tanks are generally stored underground so that they will not be subjected to damage and so that they cannot be involved in a fire in the building. For small residential systems, fiberglass tanks are sometimes used indoors as a concession to cost. Installation Rules The installation standard for tanks is NFPA 22 —e Standard for Water Tanks for Private Fire Protection. The most recent edition of this standard is the 2003 edition. This standard has sixteen chapters and three annexes, which is too much material to include in an introductory chapter such as this one. All we will cover in this text are the location requirements, the sizing requirements, the necessary connections for the tank, and the need for heating systems. For other issues, please consult NFPA 22. Tank Location The tank needs to be located so that it will not be subjected to fire expose and so that the water in the tank will not freeze. In order to protect the tank from fire exposure, NFPA 22 requires that the tank be located at least 20 ft from combustible structures, or that the tank be protected in some way. If the tank is within 20 ft of combustible structures, it must be made from noncombustible and fireproofed materials (steel itself is not sufficient because it loses its integrity too early in a fire scenario) or it must have an exposure protection system (open sprinklers in a deluge anangement) built into the support structure for the tank as well as protecting the tank itself. In order to protect the water in the tank from freezing, the tank needs to be located in space that will not freeze or a heating system needs to be installed. The water in the tank is required to be maintained at a temperature of at least 420F. NFPA 22 contains a map of the United States with the lowest one-day mean temperatures (Figure 15.1.4 of NFPA 22). Jn order to put a tank above ground and not install a heating system, the tank has to be in a portion of the United States where the lowest one-day mean temperature is 420F or higher, There are very few areas of the United States that fall into this category. Everywhere else in the country needs to have some sort of heating system, or the tank needs to be located in a heated space. Burying the tank underground below the frost line does count as locating the tank in a heated space. See the tank heating system requirements at the end of this chapter for more details on tank heating systems. 481

## Page 488

Tank Sizing There are commercial tanks available for fire protection systems in all kinds of sizes between 3,000 and 500,000 gallons. Smaller tanks, all the way down to 100 gallons are available for residential (NFPA 13D) sprinkler systems. How do you know which is the correct size to use for any specific fire protection system? This portion of this chapter will help answer that question. It is impoltant to note that NFPA 22 does not contain the answer to this question. Instead, each of the NFPA standards contains a statement about the expected duration requirement for the water supply. For example, NFPA 13 has a chart that states the expected duration for different hazard classifications (Table 11.2.3.1.1 of NFPA 13-2002 edition). For other hazards, or other fire protection systems, similar information is contained in the applicable NFPA standard. Table 11.2.3.1.1 of NFPA 13 can be confusing to some people because it contains a range of durations for ordinary hazard and extra hazard occupancies. The duration requirement for light hazard occupancies is clear enough (30 minutes). But the question is frequently asked, "which duration am I required to use for ordinary hazard, 60 or 90 minutes?" Similarly, people frequently ask which duration they are supposed to use for extra hazard, 90 or 120 minutes. The answer to these questions is found in section 11.2.3.1.8(10) of NFPA 13 (several pages away from the Table). This section states that the lower duration values are only to be used where the sprinkler system is monitored by remote station or central station service. Taking this rule into account and including some information from other NFPA standards, the following table can be set up to explain what the water supply duration requirements are of NFPA 13, NFPA 13R and NFPA 13D. Standard NFPA 13 NFPA 13 NFPA 13 NFPA 13 NFPA 13 NFPA 13 NFPA 131k NFPA 131) NFPA 13D Occupancy Light Hazard Ordinary Hazard with Remote Station or Central Station Service Ordinary Hazard without monitoring service as mentioned above Extra Hazard with Remote Station or Central Station Service Extra Hazard without monitoring service as mentioned above Stora e All Not meeting situation discussed below One-stor buildin 2000 s ft or less Water Supply Duration 30 minutes 60 minutes 90 minutes 90 minutes 120 minutes Varies, see Cha ter 12 30 minutes 10 minutes 7 minutes Table 34-1 Duration Requirements from Popular NFPA Standards 482

## Page 489

Another important note regarding NFPA 13 and storage tanks is that the tank is not required to hold the entire amount of water for the area of the sprinkler system closest to the riser. The tank is only required to hold the duration specified in the table for the most remote area. There is a significant difference between these two concepts. The remote area is the most demanding for the water supply in terms of pressure. However, portions of the fire protection system that are closer to the water supply will flow more water (because they operate at higher pressure). So, a tank sized to provide 30 minutes for the most remote area will not provide 30 minutes worth of water for a fire close to the tank's location, which is acceptable to NFPA 13. Safety factors have been built into the calculation technique as well as the duration requirement to make up for the fact that the water will not last as long for fires close to the water supply. Another factor in sizing the tank is the presence of hose stations. Ifthe tank does not supply hose stations, then the tank is not required to be sized to include hose stream demand. If the tank does supply hose stations, then the hose stream demand needs to be added to the sprinkler demand before the tank size can be appropriately determined. So, how do you size tanks properly? The answer depends on whether the system is hydraulically calculated or pipe schedule. The answer also depends on whether the tank is elevated or at ground level and whether it is an atmospheric tank or a pressure tank. The following procedures are recommended for different situations, Procedure for Sizing a Tank for Systems With Elevated Tanks 1) Determine system demand (flow and pressure for remote area) a) Hydraulic Calculations b) Pipe Schedule 2) Determine duration (see table above) 3) Tank size = flow demand x duration 4) Calculate elevation height necessary to provide system pressure Example #1: For an elevated tank connected to a sprinkler system that has been designed in accordance with NFPA 13R. The tank is in a warm location (like Honolulu, HI) so there is no concern over having the water in the tank freeze. The hydraulic calculations have been performed to the base of the tank and the system demand (for the remote area) is 80 gpm at 45 psi. What are the requirements for the elevated tank? How large does it need to be and how high above the ground does it need to be? Answer to Example #1: The tank needs to hold at least 2400 gallons. This is calculated by knowing that NFPA 13R requires 30 minutes worth of water and that the remote area requires a flow of 80 gpm. Multiplying the flow by the duration gives us the size of the tank (80 gpm x 30 min = 2400 gallons). The tank needs to be elevated by at least 104 ft. This can be found by taking the pressure demand for the remote area (45 psi) and dividing by 0.433 (the relationship between elevation and pressure). The result is 104 ft (45 psi/0.433 psi per ft = 104 ft). 483

## Page 490

Procedure for Sizing a Tank for Systems With Suction Tanks Feeding Fire Pumps I) Determine system demand (flow and pressure for remote area) a) Hydraulic Calculations b) Pipe Schedule 2) Determine duration (see table above) 3) Tank size = flow demand x duration 4) Make sure that the friction loss between the tank and the pump does not exceed 3 psi The procedure outlined above for suction tanks is the same as for elevated tanks except that the height of the tank is not a concern and has been eliminated. However, it ié important to deliver water to the suction flange of a fire pump at a positive gage pressure (see the Fire Pump chapter of this text for more information on this subject). For suction tanks, the only pressure in the suction pipe to the pump is created by the elevation of the water in the tank. When a fire has occurred and water has flowed for a long period of time, the water level in the tank will drop to the point where it will not be able to overcome the friction loss in the suction pipe anymore. NFPA 20 allows this situation to occur as long as the bottom of the tank is on the same elevation as the base of the pump and as long as the friction loss does not exceed 3 psi. If the friction loss exceeds 3 psi, the bottom of the tank needs to be elevated so that the total loss of energy at the pump suction flange does not bring the suction pressure lower than -3 psig as the last water empties out of the tank. Procedure for Sizing Tanks for Hydraulically Calculated Sprinkler Systems With Pressure Tanks 1) Determine system demand 2) Determine duration 3) Tank Size (water portion) = demand x duration 4) Choose total tank size 5) Calculate pressure using formula P = (PHC + 15)/A - 15 P = pressure in psi PHC = Pressure demand for remote area from hydraulic calculations A = proportion of air in tank (expressed as a decimal) 6) If pressure is unreasonable, pick larger tank 484

## Page 491

Example 112: A hydraulically calculated light hazard sprinkler system is being supplied by a pressure tank, The hydraulic calculations have been performed from the remote area to the location of the pressure tank and the system will require a flow of 182 psi at a pressure of 40 psi. What size should the tank be and at what pressure should the tank operate? Solution to Example With a flow demand of 182 gpm and a duration requirement of 30 minutes for light hazard systems, the water portion of the pressure tank will need to be at least 5,460 gallons (182 x 30 = 5,460). The tank will need to be larger than this fto allow some room for the pressurized air, For the first time wc are attempting this solution, let us try a 7,000 gallon tank. If we take a 7,000 gallon tank and put 5,460 gallons of water in the tank, there will be 1540 gallons of space left for air (7,000 — 5,460 = 1540). The space left for air represents 22% of the volume of the tank (1540/7000 = 22%). The decimal form of 22% is 0.22, so for the equation we need to use, the value of A is 0.22. Plugging into the formula, we find that the pressure we need for this pressure tank will be 235 psi: +15 40+15 -15 = 250-15 = 235 0.22 A pressure of 235 is too high for most fire protection systems. Most components of fire protection systems are only rated for maximum pressures of 175 psi. Even if components could be found for all of the system parts that are rated for 235 psi, many people are uncomfortable with extremely high pressures in tanks such as this. A larger tank will help bring the pressure down. Instead of using a 7,000 gallon tank, let us evaluate what would happen with an 8,000 gallon tank. If we were to take an 8,000 gallon tank and put 5,460 gallons of water in it, the volume of the tank left over for air would be 2540 gallons, or 32%. The pressure necessary for the tank can then be calculated with the formula as follows: +15 40 + 15 0.32 A pressure demand of 157 psi is much more reasonable and the 8,000 gallon tank is the better option for the fire protection system in Example #2. Note that the volume of air and the volume of water in the tank is critical to these calculations. In Example #2, we figured out that we need an 8,000 gallon tank filled with 5,460 gallons of water. The problem is that once we have the tank, there is no line on the tank to let us know when exactly 5,460 gallons of water has gone into the tank. Yet this water level is critical to know since we need at least this much water, but we cannot put more water in the tank and take away the room we need for air. The solution is to make sure that you know where the correct water level in the tank is. This can be found in two ways: 1) Carefully monitor the water going into the tank with a calibrated meter the first time that the tank is filled. Make sure to mark that water level in a permanent way so that the owner will know how full to keep thc tank. 485

## Page 492

2) Using geometry and the shape of the tank, calculate the height of the water level in the tank equal to the capacity that you need. Make sure to mark this water level petmanently so that the owner will know how full to keep the tank. This is fairly easy for a cylinder standing on its end, the formula for volume is TCI'2h where r IS the radius of the cylinder and "h" is the height of the water (note that this formula only woLks whcn h and r are expressed in ft and the volume of the tank is in cubic feet, but that is a fairly easy conversion from gallons). However, if the tank is a cylinder sitting on its side, there is no simple formula for calculating the height of the tank that equals any specific volume. A computer program or spreadsheet might be the best way to calculate the volume of water in these cases. Tank Connections The tank needs to have a number of connections so that it can function properly. For atmospheric tanks, the ports available for these connections can be cut into the tank once it has been assembled. But for pressure tanks, the manufacturer has to know about all of these connections in advance so that the holes for the equipment can be cut prior to the pressure testing of the vessel. Once the tank has been pressure tested and certified, it cannot be cut for any reason, even if another piece of equipment needs to be installed. The following connections are necessary for tanks: Water Level Gage (could be a sight gage, an altitude gage or a closed circuit high and low level alarm) Discharge Pipe (Control Valve & Check Valve) Fill Pipe (could be bypass around discharge pipe check valve with its own control valve if there is a method of pressurizing the system) Overflow Piping Cleanout Hole Riser Drain Air Pressure Gage (Pressure Tanks Only) The different water level gages are worthy of some discussion, A site gage is a glass tube that is connected to the tank above and below the water line. The water level in the tank seeks the same level in the glass tube and allows the user to look at the glass tube to determine the water level in the tank instead of opening up the tank. Be careful with pressure tanks and site gages because it is possible for air pressure to trap water in the tube at a different level than water in the tank. Once in a while, the pressure should be taken off of a pressure tank so that the water level in the site glass can equalize with the water level in the tank and then the pressure can be brought back up again. 486

## Page 493

An altitude gage is usually used on large ground level tanks. A target on the outside of the tank is attached to a float on the inside of the tank by a rope through a pulley. As the water in the tank rises, the target drops towards the bottom of the tank. As the water level sinks, the target is pulled to the top of the tank. The outside of the tank is usually marked with a big F for full and a big "E" for empty. Since the target is being pulled by a rope over a pulley, the '(F" will be at the bottom of the tank and the "E" will be at the top. This is the exact opposite of the fucl gagc in your car, so it looks funny to the observer, but it is conect. See Figure 34-6 for an example of an altitude gage. Float Water Level Target Figure 34-6 Altitude Gage on Ground Level Water Storage Tank Heating Systems As discussed previously in this chapter, the tank needs to be protected from freezing. If the tank is not installed in a location that is protected from freezing, then a heating system needs to be installed inside the tank. Generally, it is not the intent for the heating system to try and heat all of the mass of all of the water in the tank simultaneously. Instead, the heating system will heat a small portion of the water and circulate it through the tank. By heating and circulating the water, it is prevented from freezing. Tanks with heating systems must maintain the water at a temperature of at least 420F. In addition, tanks with heating systems need to have water temperature thermometers and low temperature alarms (set at 400F) installed, Heating systems that are covered by NFPA 22 include: 487

## Page 494

e Steam Water Heaters o Gas Fired Water Heaters o Oil Fired Water Heaters Coal Burning Water Heaters Electric Water Heaters o Vertical Steam Radiators Steam Coils Inside Tank e Solar Heating For Embankment Supported Rubberized Fabric (ESRF) tanks, there are some special requirements. If the tank is located anywhere that the lowest mean temperature for one day is lower than 50F, a special recirculating heating system is required to be installed in accordance with the manufacturers instructions. When the temperature of the air around the tank drops to 420F, the system must start circulating the water. If the water temperature drops to 440F, the heating system is then turned on. Summary In summary, tanks are used when there is no public supply, when it is not practical to count on the public supply, or when the owner is looking for redundancy to the public supply. Tanks must be sized to meet the remote area demand for the intended duration. Tanks need operational equipment so that they work properly and can be inspected to verify that they are in working condition. Lastly, the water in tanks needs to be protected from freezing. CHAPTER 35 SYSTEM ALARMS AND SUPERVISION Requirements relating to sprinkler system alarms and supervision are found not only in the NFPA sprinkler standards (13, 13D and 13R)•, but also in NFPA 72 — National Fire Alarm code, NFPA 70 - National Electrical code, and ANSI/ASNIE A117.1 - National Elevator Code. The adopted building code may also contain requirements in addition to those contained in the standards. The basic requirements differ between the three sprinkler standards. For most systems, NFPA 13 simply requires a local alarm, meaning an alann that sounds at the protected premises. A continuous alarm is required within 5 minutes of a sprinkler activation. With regard to minimum water supply durations, NFPA 13 (Section 11.2.2.7 in the 2002 edition) does permit lower durations where remote station or central station waterflow alarm service is provided. When NFPA 13D was developed for dwelling protection in the 1980's, a basic premise was to encourage the installation of these systems by reducing cost as far as practical. Because applicable dwelling codes generally required at least one smoke detector per dwelling, it was believed that the requirement for a sprinkler system water flow alarm could be waived where smoke detection was provided. As such, NFPA 13D continues to allow omission of a system water flow alarm where the dwelling contains at least one smoke detector, although a number of jurisdictions that require dwelling sprinklers have found it useful to also require system water flow alarms. When NFPA 13R was first published in 1989, it required local water flow alarms like NFPA 13, but also required that the system flow alarm be comected to the building alarm system where provided. Historically, the NFPA 13 alarm was most often a mechanical water motor gong, powered by a stream of water diverted through an alarm line when the clapper of the system alarm valve or dry alarm lifted in response to a loss of downstream water pressure due to sprinkler operation. Today the alarm is more frequently activated electrically by a paddle-type water flow switch for wet systems and a pressure switch for dry pipe systems. The official requirement in NFPA 13 is that a wet pipe system must contain a listed alarm check valve or other listed waterflow detecting device. A dry pipe system 491

## Page 498

must be equipped with listed alarm attachments for the dry pipe valve, but paddle-type waterflow switches are nol allowed. This is due to some adverse experience with early paddle-type switches, in which the impact of the water column detached the paddle from the switch. Detection Systems for Preaction and Deluge Systems For pre-action and deluge type systems, alarms must be actuated independently by both the detection system and the flow of water the system. Compared to wet and dry pipe systems, relatively little information is provided within NFPA 13 on preaction and deluge systems. The features these two types of systems have in common are that they both employ a deluge valve and a supplemental detection system. At least one manual means of operating the deluge valve must also be provided, resulting in hydraulic, pneumatic or mechanical release of the valve. The systems are listed by the product listing laboratories, and various types of detection devices and their spacings are controlled by the listings and the manufacturer's specifications. This includes the use of automatic sprinklers as part of a wet pilot line or dry pilot line detection system. There is a difference in the manner in which the two product approval organizations list the detection devices for use in preaction and deluge sprinkler systems. Underwriters Laboratories lists "special system control valves — deluge type" including the various acceptable types of detection devices that can be used with each manufacturer's model. FM Global maintains a table of approved or compatible devices that can be used with any manufacturer's model of "automatic water control valve." There are four basic types of detection devices: o Pneumatic rate of rise detectors o Wet pilot line sprinklers o Dry pilot line sprinklers o Electrically-signaled detectors The maximum height of wet pilot line sprinklers is controlled in the valve listing since it is important to prevent water columning, whereby the weight of the water due to excessive elevation could prevent the clapper of the valve from opening. The. category of electrically-signaled detectors can take in a wide range of types, including heat detectors, smoke detectors, fire gas detectors, or radiant energy / flame detectors such as ultraviolet or infrared. Heat detectors can be fixed temperature or rate of rise or a combination of both. 492

## Page 499

NFPA 13 Alarm Requirements The basic NFPA 13 requirement is that an alarm unit be either mechanical or electric. Specific wording calls for a listed mechanical alarm, horn or siren, or a listed electric gong, bell, speaker, horn or siren. Not all of these devices are available in the marketplace. NFPA 13 also requires that piping to a water motor operated device be galvanized steel, brass, or other corrosion-resistant material and at least 3/4-inch nominal diameter. This is intended to avoid clogging over time duc to intemal corrosion, since thc alarm line is only periodically wet. Basic rules for the electrical components of system alanns are contained in one of two standards. For electrically operated alam attachments that form part of an auxiliary, central station, local protective, proprietary, or remote station signaling system, NFPA 72 is referenced. If the sprinkler system is not part of such a system, then the more basic provisions of NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code apply, and NFPA 13 clarifies that the sprinkler system does not need to be supervised. NFPA 72, which is essentially an installation standard that parallels NFPA 13, nevertheless carries the title National Fire Alann Code. It addresses the application, installation, performance and maintenance of fire alam systems and their components. The standard includes requirements for both "alatm service" and "supervisory service," and addresses the various types of fire alarm systems mentioned above: Protected premises alarm system — this system provides alarms only at the protected premises, essentially a "local alarm" Proprietary supervising station system — this system provides alarms at a constantly manned station at the protected property. Remote supervising station system — this system provides alarms to a remote station, which is responsible to take appropriate action Central station alarm system — this system proves alarms to a constantly manned facility that is listed to provide this type of service Both alarm service and supervisory service can be provided with any of these atrangements, although the reliability of service would naturally be expected to increase with the degree to which the receiving point is manned by properly trained personnel. The only special requirement for any of these levels contained in NFPA 13 is the requirement (Section 8.16.1.7 in the 2002 edition) that systems protecting rack storage be provided with "central station, auxiliary, remote station, or proprietary sprinkler waterflow alarm service". A local waterflow alarm is permitted for installation where recorded guard service is provided. The only applications for which NFPA 13 specifically requires supervisory service are for high-rise buildings (Sections 8.15.1.1.2.2 and 8.16,1.6 in the 2002 edition). 493

## Page 500

The services are defined in NFPA 72 as follows: Alarm service — the service required following receipt of an alarm signal, defined as a signal indicating an emergency requiring immediate action Supervisory service — the service required to monitor, , ,the operative condition of fixed fire suppression systems or other systems for the protection of life and properly The use of the term "supervised" to indicate a fire suppression system that is provided with supervisory service can be confusing due to the fact that NFPA 13 uses the term differently. NFPA 13 for decades has required that system water supply valves be "supervised" by one of the following methods (Section 8.15.1.1.2.1 in the 2002 edition): (1) Central station, proprietary or remote station signaling service (2) Local signaling service that will cause the sounding of an audible signal at a constantly attended point (3) Valves locked in the correct position (4) Valves located within fenced enclosures under the control of the owner, sealed in the open position, and inspected weekly as part of an approved procedure Only the first two "supervision" options satisfy the definition of the term "supervisory service" within NFPA 72. The chaining and locking of valves in the open position or allowing the valves to be sealed open if within a fenced enclosure under the control of the building owner do not qualify as supervisory service within the intent of NFPA 72 since they do not fully monitor the operative condition of the system. What conditions are required to be monitored in order to provide supervisory service? NFPA 72 specifies (Section 6.8.5.7,3 in the 2002 edition) "the conditions that are essential for the proper operation of sprinkler and other fire suppression systems." The standard specifically omits conditions relating to water mains, tanks, cisterns, reservoirs, and other water supplies controlled by a municipality or a public utility." In doing so, the standard makes it clear that all such water supplies under the control of the property owner would need to be monitored. Monitoring takes place through the transmission of signals. Alarm signals are essential to alarm service, and supervisory and trouble signals provide the basis of supervisory service. As indicated above in the definition of alarm service, an alarm signal would indicate an emergency requiring immediate action. For sprinkler and other suppression systems, detection of system operation is considered detection of a fire, i.e. a fire emergency. A signal that indicates water flow in a sprinkler system is therefore considered an alarm signal. 494

## Page 501

A supervisory signal is a signal indicating the need for some type of action in connection with a fire suppression system or piece of equipment. A trouble signal is a signal initiated by the fire alarm systems itself, indicating a fault in a monitored circuit of system component. Both alarm signals and supervisory signals rely on initiating devices, defined as system components that originate transmission of change of state conditions. Initiating devices can range from smoke detectors to manual fire alarm boxes to supervisory switches. Supervising signal initiating devices include devices whose change of state signal indicates an off-normal condition, or the return of that condition to normal. Typical supervisory switch initiating devices are valve supervisory switches, water level indicator switches, and low air pressure switches for dry pipe systems. A basic requirement of NFPA 72 is that alarm signals, supervisory signals and trouble signals be distinctively and descriptively annunciated, so that they cannot be confused. As might be expected, alarm signals have priority ranking. Actuation of alarm notification devices or emergency voice communications must occur within 90 seconds after the activation of an alarm initiating device. For supewisory signals, 90 seconds is also the time limit for visible and audible signals as well as visible indication of a return to the normal state. The locations for these indications must include: Control unit for local fire alarm systems - Building command center for emergency voice / alarm communications systems - Supervising station location Trouble signals have the lowest priority ranking. Such signals, and their restoration to normal, must be within 200 seconds at the: - Control unit for local fire alarm systems Building command center for emergency voice / alarm communications systems Supervising station location Trouble signals and their restoration must also be visibly and audibly indicated at any proprietary station. 495

## Page 502

Sprinlder System Initiating Devices Based on the general rules described above, NFPA 72 requires that initiation of an alarm signal must occur within 90 seconds of water flow at the initiating device when flow takes place equal to or greater than that from a single sprinkler of the smallest orifice size installed in the system. This appears more stringent than the NFPA 13 requirement noted earlier, but NFPA 13 refers to a "continuous" alarm within 5 minutes. It is recognized that discontinuous alarms can result from "bouncing" as water entering a sprinkler system compresses trapped pockets of air at the ends of branch lines. This can lead to intermittent sounding of mechanical alarms such as water motor gongs, but can also prevent paddle type water flow switches from operating, especially when such switches are provided with a time delay to prevent false alarms due to occasional pressure surges. There are a number of different types of initiating devices that could be needed to properly monitor the conditions necessary for proper operation of the sprinkler system, depending on the type of system and water supply arrangements: Control valve supervisory switches — movement must initiate an off-normal signal during the first two revolutions of a hand wheel or 1/5 of the travel distance from normal. The restoration signal must sound only when returned to normal position. Pressure supervisory switches — a signal must be initiated for pressure tanks or pressure devices on dry pipe systems when the pressure increase or decrease 10 psi (70 kPa) from the normal pressure Water level switches — the off-normal signal is required for pressure tanks when the water level falls or rises more than 3 inches (75 mm) from normal. For all other types of tanks, the signal is required when the water levels drops more than 12 inches (300 mm) below normal. Water temperature switches — one signal must indicate if the temperature drops to 400F (4.40C) and another for restoration above this temperature. Room temperature switches — one signal must indicate if the temperature drops to 40 OF (4.40C) and another for restoration above this temperature. Water temperature or room temperature switches would be appropriate only where there is concern for freezing. For exterior tanks, water temperature switches would be appropriate, but room temperature switches can be substituted used where tanks are located inside a building. Such switches are also appropriate for heated dry pipe valve enclosures and pump houses in areas otherwise exposed to freezing. 496

## Page 503

Pump Supervision A common question is whether a pump mnning signal is considered an alarm signal or a supervisory signal. Although the pump would be expected to operate in a fire condition, the pump running signal is considered a priority supervisory signal. NFPA 20 is the standard referenced for proper supervision of a fire pump. In addition to the pump running signal, NFPA 20 requires electric pump power to be supervised for all phases and for possible phase reversal. Central Station Responsibilities A central station has different responsibilities depending on what type of signal il receives from the system. Alarm signals are of the highest priority, requiring that the central station immediately transmit the alarm to the public fire service communications center such that firefighters are dispatched. The central station must also dispatch a runner or technician to the protected premises to arrive within 1 hour where equipment needs to be manually reset, notify the subscriber by the quickest available method, and provide notice to the subscriber or authority having jurisdiction or both For supervisory signals, the central station is required to communicate immediately with the person(s) designated by the subscriber, dispatch a runner or maintenance person (arrival time within 1 hour) to investigate (except where an abnormal condition is restored to normal in accordance with a scheduled procedure), notify the fire department or law enforcement authority or both, and notify the authority having jurisdiction when fire suppression systems are out for 8 hours or more Other NFPA 72 Requirements NFPA 72 contains several other requirements related to sprinkler systems that must be observed for systems where NFPA 72 is applicable: • Piping between the sprinkler system and a pressure actuated alarm-initiating device shall be galvanized or of nonferrous metal or other approved corrosion- resistant material of not less than 3/8 in. (9.5 mm) nominal pipe size o A maximum of 5 waterflow switches can be connected to a single initiating device circuit. e A maximum of 20 supervisory devices can be connected to a single initiating device circuit. 497

## Page 504

Conflicts Between Sprinkler and Alarm Standards Inevitably, conflicts can arise between different codes and standards, A true conflict is a situation in which both standards cannot be satisfied, which is rare. Most of the time one standard is simply more demanding. One example involves testing and maintenance of alarm initiating devices. Traditionally, for the fire sprinkler industry, the inspector's lesl was considered more than an alarm test connection. It also sewed as a check on continuity of flow through the system, the same way the main drain test connection serves to ensure that all underground valves from the water supply are open. NFPA 25 traditionally required quarterly testing of waterflow alarms, whereas NFPA 72 allows semi-annual testing of alarm initiating devices. Palt of this difference can be attributed to the fact that the water- based standards utilize waterflow alarrn initiating tests to ensure that all valves are open and that the automatic water supply is available, whereas the alarm standard simply contemplates a test of the alarm devices. In recent years, a compromise of sorts has been reached, whereby waterflow switches are tested semiannually, but mechanical water motor gongs and pressure switches continue to require quarterly testing. The NFPA 25 Committee holds to the quarterly test schedule for these devices on the basis that they contain small orifices more prone to clogging, and require a greater degree of attention than paddle-type waterflow switches. As another example, consider the possibility of a dry pipe or preaction system downstream of a wet pipe system. NFPA 72 requires that where such a system is supplied downstream of the wet pipe system alarm initiating device, a separate pressure switch or other alarm initiating device be provided to initiate a waterflow alarm. NFPA 13 specifically permits connection of the alarm actuating device for a downstream dry system to be connected to the alarms for the wet pipe system, clarifying that a separate alarm device is not needed. Where a sprinkler system is supervised in accordance with NFPA 72, another small but troublesome conflict for many years involved the valve in the connection to the system alarm device. NFPA 13 required that this valve be of the indicating type and that it be locked or sealed in the open position. NFPA 72, however, states that any valve in the connection between the fire suppression system and its alarm initiating device be fully supervised in accordance with the regular provisions of the standard related to valve supervision. An appendix note specifically points out that sealing or locking the valve, or removing the handle, does not meet the intent of supervision. Beginning with the 2002 edition of NFPA 13, this section (8.16.1.4.2) was changed to allow electrical supervision of these valves as an alternate to sealing or locking, and special trim valves with built-in supervisory switches are now available in the marketplace. 498

CHAPTER 36 INSPECTION, TESTING AND MAINTENANCE OF FIRE SPRINKLER SYSTEMS Once a fire sprinkler system has been designed and installed (hopefully correctly), it needs to be maintained in proper working order. Maintenance activities include inspections to insure that the equipment appears to be in proper working order, testing to prove that the equipment will operate appropriately, repairs to any equipment that is not in acceptable condition and preventative work to make sure that equipment does not break down. This chapter will concentrate on the requirements for maintaining common components of fire sprinkler systems. Many other types of fire protection systems have similar equipment and are maintained in a similar manner, but will not be covered in this text for the sake of space. This chapter will be an excellent study guide for NICET Work Element 14007 Sprinkler System Maintenance and will also assist with Work Element 15007 System Acceptance Tests since many of the acceptance tests are similar to the regular maintenance routines. Development of NFPA 25 The NFPA standard that describes the minimum work that needs to be performed in order to maintain a sprinkler system is NFPA 25, Standard for the Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Water-based Fire Protection Systems. The first edition •of NFPA 25 was released by the NFPA in 1992 and subsequent editions have been released in 1995, 1998 and 2002. Since fire sprinkler systems have been around for more than 100 years, a common question is, ' 'why did it take the NFPA so long to write a standard for maintenance of sprinkler systems?" The answer to this question is mired in the history of the NFPA and the typical enforcement of fire and building codes. As we discussed in the Rules Governing Installation chapter of this text, there are three different kinds of NFPA documents; codes, standards and recommended practices. Codes and standards are legally enforceable, while recommended practices are written in language that is more of a suggestion of good practice rather than a legal mandate. During the early days of the NFPA, there was some question as to whether or not a standard could be written regarding inspection of private premises. The Fourth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States promises that no unreasonable searches will be carried out 499

## Page 506

without a walTant. Mandatory inspections then were questionable since building officials and fire marshals rarely get a search warrant prior to conducting an inspection, The best that the NFPA could do was to write a recommended practice, which they did for many years. NFPA 13A was the Recommended Practice for the Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Sprinkler Systems. Similarly, the NFPA wrote NFPA 14A, Recommended Practice for lhe Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Standpipe and Hose Systems. In addition to these two documents, the NFPA also published requirements in the last chapter of NFPA 20 for the care and maintenance of fire pumps. Although this information was in the body of a standard, it was rarely enforced by individual fire marshals or building officials, but was relied upon by the insurance community as a good practice similar to a recommended practice for testing of fire pumps. In 1967, the Supreme Court of the United States addressed the issue of fire inspections and warrants directly in the case of See vs. the City of Seattle. The Seattle Fire Department had attempted to enter a warehouse owned by a man with the last name "See." Mr. See had refused to allow the fire marshal to enter the property and had been arrested for violating the city code that gave the fire department authority to conduct inspections. Mr. See appealed his conviction all the way to the Supreme Court saying that the fire department violated his Fourth Amendment rights. The fire department argued that the Fourth Amendment only protects against "unreasonable" searches and that it was reasonable and necessary to look for violations that affected public safety. In a split decision (4-3), the court ruled in favor of Mr. See and gave individuals the right to refuse entry to the fire department if the fire department did not have a warrant. The court also established some pretty easy guidelines by which fire departments could obtain warrants if they needed them to enter. But given the legal climate, it seemed that the decision to write recommended practices rather than standards was a good one. Since 1967, a number of changes have occurred in the legal climate in the United States that have opened the door to a standard or code addressing the care and maintenance of fire protection systems. More recent coult decisions have chipped away at the protection offered to building owners under See vs. Seattle. At the same time, the fire protection community has come to the realization that we cannot depend on the fire department to inspect every building with a fire protection system. Instead, the building owner must be charged with the responsibility for caring for the fire protection system (just as they are responsible for caring for the electrical and plumbing systems). Ifthe building owner takes care of the system, no entry should be needed on the part of the fire department, so there is no concern for obtaining warrants. Given these changes, the time was right in the late 1980's to start thinking about changing the recommended practices to standards. In the late 1980's, at the request of a group of fire marshals, the NFPA Standards Council appointed a task group to study the current state-of-the-art in the care and maintenance of water- based fire protection systems and report back to the Standards Council with recommendations for how the NFPA documents should address this issue. The task group was chaired by Bill Testa of Grinnell, who was the chairman of the NFPA 13A committee and included fire marshals, code enforcement officials, sprinkler contractors and manufacturers, building owners and insurance officials. In 1990, this task group reported back to the Standards Council that the 500

## Page 507

NFPA needed to consolidate all of its documents on the inspection, testing and maintenance of water-based systems into a single document and that document should be a standard rather than a recommended practice. The Standards Council agreed and established the first Committee for Inspection, Testing and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems and placed Bill Testa as the chailnan of the committee. That group worked throughout 1990 and 1991 to write the first edition of NFPA 25, which was approved by the NFPA membership in November 1991 (at the Fall Meeting in Montréal, Canada) and issued by the Standards Council in February of 1992. In the beginning, many members of the NFPA 25 committee believed that the document would be relatively thin. Just making sure that people kept control valves open and preformed regular main drain and alarm tests would cover most of the perceived issues regarding usual malfunctions of sprinkler systems. But a study conducted in 1991 started to change many people's minds. The study, conducted by Cigna (a large insurance company) found that there were many more problems with sprinkler systems than just closed valves and alarm bells that didn't ring. Cigna selected at random 368 of their Highly Protected Risk (HPR) propelties. These are special properties that get extremely low insurance rates because of their extra special attention to fire protection, including extra attention given to the design, installation and care of fire sprinkler systems. What Cigna found in these HPR properties was that there were deficiencies in 59% of the fire protection systems. These properties included: Health Care, hotel, mercantile and offices (22% of the properties) Petrochemical and manufacturing facilities (42% of the properties) Utility and warehouse buildings (30% of the propeffies) Other buildings (6% of the properties) The problems in these buildings were not limited. to closed valves and non-working waterflow alarms. The following list shows the problems that were encountered and the frequency with which these problems existed: Design deficiencies (25%) Fire pump problems (18%) Water supply deficiencies (14%) Alarms didn't function (11 %) Water supply valves shut (8%) Fire door failures (6%) Fire detection system problems (6%) Other (12%) Note that shut valves only constituted 8% of the problems. While the fire protection community has been led to believe for a long time that closed valves are the most frequently found problems with fire sprinkler systems, this Cigna study did not conelate with that assumption. Additional information can be deduced by looking at the deficiencies found in each type of building as shown in the following table. 501

## Page 508

Fire Pum Valve Closed Alarms Design Water Su ly Fire Door Detection Other Manufacturing 9 9 16 21 22 8 2 13 Warehouse 18 6 8 35 15 6 2 10 Petrochemical 35 9 9 13 13 4 17 Office 26 5 17 32 5 5 5 5 Hotel 6 11 17 22 33 11 Table 36-1 Cigna Study Percentage of Deficiency by Occupancy Looking at Table 36-1, we can see that valves being closed in hotels and offices are less of a problem than in petrochemical and manufacturing. One of the reasons for this might be that hotels and offices are generally required to have electronic supervision of valves where petrochemical and manufacturing facilities tend to have more mechanical methods of supervision (padlocks with chains or tamper-evident seals). Similarly, the Table shows that warehouse systems are three times more likely to have a design deficiency than hotels, possibly because the commodity being stored changes the hazard in a warehouse more often than the hazard changes in a hotel. One of the scary issues surrounding this survey is that it only looked at the properties that had been designated as HPR. These were special properties getting a reduced insurance rate because of their extra attention to fire protection. If these facilities were having problems 59% of the time, how many problems would we find in the buildings that are ordinary risks that have not received any special attention? After looking at the results of this survey and after checking with other sources to determine if this survey was an anomaly or not, the committee responsible for writing NFPA 25 decided that the standard needed to have a lot more information in it regarding the inspection, testing and maintenance of all water-based fire protection systems. This decision almost derailed the standard when it first came up for a vote at the Fall 1991 meeting. Building owners thought that the standard had gone too far in what it proposed needed to be done at regular intervals. After a long debate on the subject and some amendments from the floor, the standard was adopted by the NFPA membership. Since that first contentious meeting, there has been little debate regarding the specific rules in NFPA 25 and the 2002 edition of the standard looks very similar to the 1992 edition. Chu-rently, there are many building and fire codes that directly reference NFPA 25 as a mandatory standard for maintaining fire protection systems. But even if you are in a jurisdiction that does not legally enforce NFPA 25, its requirements still affect you. NFPA 25 has been adopted by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) as an American National Standard. That means that NFPA 25 has been adopted as the minimum accepted standard of care for fire sprinkler systems in the United States. Any building owner who does not care for their fire protection system in accordance with the ANSI National Standard might be open to liability if a 502

## Page 509

loss occurs in their building. In addition, fire sprinkler contractors that offer inspection and testing serv'ices should indicate which of the requirements within NFPA 25 they are helping building owners comply with, since it establishes a minimum set of actions that need to be performed. Organization of NFPA 25 NFPA 25 is written so that there is a different chapter for each type of fire protection system. Rules .for fire sprinkler systems are found in Chapter 5, while rules for other types of systems are found in other chapters (for example Chapter 6 covers Standpipe and Hose Systems). But in addition to Chapter 5, you will also need to use some additional chapters to make the inspection, testing and maintenance complete. Some components in fire protection systems are common to many systems. Rather than repeat the rules for these common components in each chapter, they have been given their own chapters. The following chapters apply to all fire protection systems that have these pieces of equipment: o Chapter 8 applies to fire pumps o Chapter 9 applies to water storage tanks o Chapter 12 applies to valves, valve components and trim (including fire department connections) So, at the very leaét, a fire sprinklers system would need to comply with the rules of Chapter 5 and Chapter 12. If that system incorporated a pump and/or a tank, Chapters 8 and 9 would also need to be used. It would be a fundamental mistake to think that you could just follow the requirements in Chapter 5 and think that you were providing proper care for a fire sprinkler system. In addition to the chapters dealing with components and their inspection, testing and maintenance rules, there are also two chapters of NFPA 25 that deal with specific problems. The lilles in these chapters need to be followed in order to make sure that these conditions don't exist, or to deal with these problems if they do occur. The first of these special chapters is Chapter 13 for Obstruction Investigations. The chapter outlines a basic rule for looking at the inside of piping on a sprinkler system at a few locations once each five years to make sure that there isn't a problem. In addition to this fifth-year test, there is also a section that lists 14 conditions that might lead to obstructions being present in a fire protection system. If any of these 14 situations is encountered, an investigation needs to be conducted. Lastly, this chapter provides procedures for finding and clearing obstructions. The second chapter to deal with situations rather than components is Chapter 14 on Impairments. This chapter explains what to do when systems, or portions of systems, are shut down. This chapter will be described in much more detail later in this text. 503

## Page 510

Responsibility for Performing Work The fundamental philosophy in NFPA 25 is that it is the building owner's responsibility to make sure that the inspection, testing and maintenance work gets done at the con•ect intervals. The owner may hire a contractor to get the work done, but ultimately it is the owner's responsibility to make sue that each of the respective items is taken care of. Through a written agreement, it is possible for the owner to transfer this responsibility to a tenant. This is usually done through a clause in a lease. Just like a lease specifies who is to pay for electricity and water, it should specify who is going to be responsible for maintaining the fire protection system. In the absence of any specific written agreement, it is the owner that will be held responsible. It is also the responsibility of the owner to maintain the records that the system has been maintained correctly. Many fire officials were concerned when NFPA 25 first came out because they thought that they would be required to keep all of the records on all of the buildings in their jurisdiction, but that is not how NFPA 25 was written. With some requirements for daily inspections, that would be an incredible burden on a public authority, to send them copies of such frequent inspections for all of the buildings in their jurisdiction. Instead, NFPA 25 requires that the records be made available to the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) when they are requested by the AHJ. Every AHJ has a different way of looking at this requirement, and they are all correct given the current language. Some AHJ's want to see a copy of a repolt annually (from each building in their jurisdiction) that shows that the system is being properly maintained. Others do not want such volumes of paperwork and only will go looking for documentation if some other problem arises (other violations are found) or if there is a fire and the system fails to operate correctly. Still a third group of AHJ's notify building owners at random that they want to see records as a spot check of what is happening in the community. Since the work is required to be done and kept on file, it should be a minimal burden for owners to produce these records. The NFSA has been encouraging AHJ's to collect the records of annual system care so that a database of protected properties can be established. If AHJ's wait until a fire has occurred before asking for records, building owners have the opportunity to say "my records burned up in the fire." It is better to establish compliance (or lack therein) prior to any possible fire. It is also more urgent for the building owner to fix problems that are found if they know that the fire marshal is going to get a copy of the report form. The NFPA 25 committee is working on a future edition of the standard as this text goes to press and will address this issue. The acceptance tests that are performed when the fire protection system is new need to be maintained by the owner for the life of the sprinkler system. These acceptance tests contain vital information on the performance of the system that helps to establish the pass/fail criteria for future tests. For example, the results of a main drain test cannot be evaluated if the results of the original acceptance test are unknown. For regular periodic, testing and maintenance once the system has been placed in service, the records must b? kept one year past when the next interval of activity takes place. For example, records of an inspection that are conducted daily have to be kept for one year and a 504

## Page 511

day. Records for a test Chat occurs once every three years need to be keptfor four years. The rule is to keep the records for one year past when Che next intewal for that activity will occur. This way, the previous test will always be available to use when interpreting the data and determining if the system is still in acceptable operating condition. As discussed previously in this section, it is the owner's responsibility to make sure that the inspection, testing and maintenance get performed properly. One way to do this is to hire a contractor. Another way to complete this requirement is for the owner to do the work or to have trusted employees perform the tasks. Whichever choice the owner makes, it is important to make sure that the people performing the work are trained and knowledgeable in the tasks that they are performing. One way to determine if contractors offering this service are knowledgeable is to look for a contractor's license. In some states, contractors have to prove that they know something about the work they do by passing a test or meeting other technical knowledge. However, a license is not always a sign that the contractor is knowledgeable. In some jurisdictions, the only requirement for a license is to pay a fee. In some jurisdictions, a test is given, but it is only a test of administrative and business issues, not the technical field of the license. So, a license is not a guarantee that the contractor knows their subject. Another method that can be used to determine if the people doing the inspection, testing and maintenance are knowledgeable is certification. NICET has a program for people to prove that they know how to inspect, test and maintain fire protection systems through a series of tests and a demonstration of experience. You do not need to be a contractor to get certified. If you work for a building owner and want to perform the inspection, testing and maintenance on that building, you can also go through the NICET certification program. Most building owners use some combination of performing the work themselves and hiring contractors. In general, most building owners perform the frequent tasks of making sure that valves are open and making sure that tanks stay full while contractors perform the less frequent tasks like dry-pipe valve trip tests and main drain tests. This is why it is important for the sprinkler contractor to make clear what tasks they are pelforming, so that the owner can determine what else needs to be done. System Impairments An impairment of a sprinkler system is the shutdown of that system or a portion of that system. When any sprinkler system is impaired, the building and the occupants of the building are at a higher risk and precautions need to be taken to minimize that risk There are two different types of impairments; emergency and preplanned. An emergency impairment is one that occurs without warning or preparation. Examples include pipes bursting of freeze-ups of systems. The other type of impairment is a preplanned impairment, which is an impairment that is scheduled. Preplanned impairments occur when a system needs to be turned off and drained so that work can be done. Regardless of whether an impairment is an emergency or a preplanned impairment, the procedures to follow are the same because the risk to the building and its occupants is the same whether the impairment was planned or not. 505

## Page 512

Every building owner must designate an Impairment Coordinator for the fire protection systems in their building. If the owner has not specifically designated an Impairment Coordinator, then it should be assumed that the building owner is the Impairment Coordinator. The job of the Impairment Coordinator is to prepare for planned impairments and to deal with emergency impairments. The Impairment Coordinator is expected to minimize the risk to the building and occupants of the building, limit the time of the impairment, and authorize any preplanned impairments. If an impairment does occur, NFPA 25 requires the use of an Impairment Tag to announce the fact that the system is out of service. One Impairment Tag is required to be placed on the affected (closed) control valve while a second tag is required on the fire department connection. By placing the tags in these locations, appropriate people will know what they should be doing if a fire occurs while the system is out of service. See Figure 36-1 for an example of an Impairment Tag (available for purchase from the NFSA Resource Center). Fire Protection Valve SHUT This valve/connection controls fire protection in building(s): Site: Shut by: Signature: Date: Note: After valve is opened, perform a main drain test. Main Drain Test Results: Static Pressure Flowing Pressure psi Drain Test By: psi Date: Form 25-TAG 02002 NFSA P.O. Box 1000 Patterson, NY 12563 Impairment Tag Instructions 1) Use this tag when a system is to be removed from service. 2) Place tags at the closed control valve and the fire department connection. 3) Fill in information requested on the front of the tag. 4) Follow the procedures in NFPA 25 for Impaired Systems and any locat requirements. 5) Repair system promptly. 6) Follow the procedures in NFPA 25 for Restoring System to Service and any local requirements. 7) Conduct Main Drain Test. 8) Record results on front of tag. 9) Compare results to previous main drain tests. 10) If 0K, remove tags and file. 1 1) If not 0K, check for closed valves and/or conduct obstruction investigation. Repeat steps 7 to 11 until system is 0K. Figure 36-1 Impairment Tag Front and Back 506
