The procedure that an Impairment Coordinator must follow if a fire protection system becomes (or is going to become) impaired is as follows: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6, Determine the duration of the impairment Evaluate the risk to the building and its occupants and submit recommendations to the building owner to mmimize these risks Notify the fire depattment, other AHJ's and supervisors of workers in the affected areas Insure that the impairment tags are in place Assemble the tools and materials necessary for repair Make sure that the repair is made in a timely fashion Once the reason for the impairment has been resolved and the system has been restored to service, the Impairment Coordinator needs to conduct the following procedures: 1. Conduct all required inspections and tests to make sure that the system is operational (including a main drain test after opening the control valve) 2. Notify everyone that the system is back on (fire department, other AHJ's, supervisors) 3. Remove the impairment tag, filing it with the information from the main drain test Sprinkler contractors frequently ask if they can offer (as a service to their customers) to be the Impairment Coordinator for the building owner. The answer to this question depends on the sprinkler contractor's knowledge of the building and what goes on in the building. Part of the job of the Impairment Coordinator is to submit recommendations to the building owner about how to limit the risk to occupants of the building while the system is out of service. If the building is an office building or hotel, chances are good that a sprinkler contractor can figure out what's going on in the building. But if the building is an industrial facility with all kinds of chemicals and different manufacturing processes going on, the contractor should only be the Impairment Coordinator if they know and understand these chemicals and processes completely. Terminology Up to this point in the chapter, the terms "inspection", "testing" and "maintenance" have been used without any specific definition. While their dictionary definitions might suffice for a general introduction, their specific definitions in accordance with NFPA 25 are much more important for the rest of the chapter. NFPA 25 defines these terms in the following manner: Inspection: "A visual examination of a system or portion thereof to verify that it appears to be in operating condition and is free from physical damage" (section 3.3.19 of NFPA 25 — 2002). 507

## Page 514

Testing: "A procedure used to determine the status of a system as intended by conducting periodic physical checks on water-based fire protection systems such as water-flow tests, fire pump tests, alarm tests, and trip tests of dry-pipe, deluge or preaction valves. These tests follow up on the original acceptance test at intervals specified in the appropriate chapter of this standard" (section 3,3.36 of NFPA 25 - 2002). Maintenance: "Work pelformed to keep equipment operational or to make repairs" (section 3.3.22 of NFPA 25 - 2002). As these three definitions show, the terms "inspection", "testing" and "maintenance" are intended to be different and not to overlap. The inspection is a visual check of an item. You should be able to perform an inspection without ever touching the item. You should also be able to perform an inspection without having to get too close to an item. The is clarified in some of the inspection requirements that actually mention that the inspection of sprinklers and other components is from the floor level. There is no intent to require that people get up on ladders to inspect each sprinkler. Tests are generally performed by touching components. Tests also sometimes employ the use of tool, either in directly performing the test or in resetting the equipment after the test. By its very nature, the concept of a test implies that when you are done with the test, you will be able to say if the component "passed" or "failed" the test. In NFPA 25, the pass/fail criteria are not always explicit and it takes knowledge and experience to interpret the data. It is also necessary to have the original acceptance test information to refer back to in order to help determine if the component has passed or failed. Maintenance is also performed by touching an object (sometimes with tools). But the difference between testing and maintenance is that there is no pass or fail criteria with maintenance. Generally, maintenance falls into two categories: 1) The corrective work that is performed when a test or an inspection reveals that there is a problem with a component. 2) The preventative work that is done to keep the system operational. For example, lubricating the stem of an OS&Y valve is considered maintenance because it will keep the valve easy to open and close when needed. Inspection Requirements The following components of fire sprinkler systems are required to be inspected at the frequency discussed for each item. 1, Control Valves — The inspection needs to be performed weekly if the valves have been sealed shut with the tamper-evident seals. Otherwise, this task needs to be performed monthly (for control valves that are locked and chained or electronically supervised), During the inspection, it should be verified that the valves are in their normal (open or 508

## Page 515

closed) position, properly supe,1Wised and identified, accessible, provided with appropriate wrenches (if special wrenches are needed to open or close the valve) and are free from leaks. 2. Check Valves —The valve nccds to be inspected internally once every five years to make sure that water can flow through in the appropriate direction. Note that this requires the valve to be opened, which may mean taking the valve out of the system. Also note that this means that the valve needs to be opened, which generally requires touching the valve and using tools. This somewhat bends (if not breaks) the definition and discussion about the differences between "inspection" and "testing". It would probably be better to move this requirement to the testing section of NFPA 25, however, it has remained in the inspection section because once the valve is opened, the check of lhe conditions is just meant to be visual. 3. Backflow Preventers — The assembly needs to be inspected either weekly or monthly depending on the supervision of the control valves at either end of the assembly. If the control valves are sealed, then the inspection is weekly. If the control valves are supervised with a lock and chain or an electronic supervision switch, then the inspection requirement is monthly. The inspector needs to verify that the isolation valves are open and supervised and that Lhe relief POLI (on reduced-pressure type devices only) is not discharging. 4. Pressure Regulating Valves — Need to be inspected quarterly to verify that the valves are in the open position, they are in good condition and not leaking, and that they are maintaining a reasonable downstream pressure, For many years, NFPA 13 has required a pressure gage on the downstream side of the valve so that this inspection could be performed. However, NFPA 13 did not always require that this gage be installed, so older systems may not have it in place. If such system is found, a recommendation should be made to the building owner to add a gage in this location so that the inspection can be conducted. 5. Fire Department Connections — These devices are required to be inspected quarterly to make sure that the connections are visible and accessible, that the. caps are in place and are free to rotate, that the gasket inside is in place and in tact, that the sign or identification is in place, that the check valve does not appear to be leaking, and that the automatic drain appears to be operating. 6. Alarm Valves (exterior) —The outside of the valve is required to be inspected quarterly to make sure that the gages are reading reasonable pressures, that the valve is free of damage and that there is no leakage from the trim, and that all trim valves appear to be in appropriate condition. When inspecting the gages, it is often found that the top gage (reading the system pressure) is slightly higher than the bottom gage (reading the water supply pressure). This is a good sign as long as the higher system pressure does not exceed the pressure for which components on the system are rated.. It means that at some point in time there was a higher pressure from the water supply and that pressure got trapped in the sprinkler system. Once the pressure dropped in the water supply, the check valve in the alarm valve closed and trapped the higher pressure in the system. The fact 509

## Page 516

that the pressure remains higher in the system means that the check valve is not leaking and is not letting water from the sprinkler system back into the water supply. 7, Alarm Valves (interior) — Since there is a check valve inside the alarm valve, it needs to be inspected on the inside once every five years, just like the check valve. See the discussion above for the check valve for more information. While the alam valve is open) check any strainers, filers and orifices and clean them as necessary while also looking at the general condition of the valve, 8. Enclosures for Dry-Pipe, Preaction and Deluge Valves — During cold weather (below freezing) the enclosures around dry-pipe, preaction and deluge valves need to be inspected either daily or weekly to make sure that they are maintaining an acceptable temperature (at or above 400F). The daily inspection is required if there is no low temperature alarm in the enclosure. The weekly inspection is required if there is a low temperature alarm, If you find a valve enclosure with no low temperature alarm, you might want to offer to sell the owner a low temperature alarm and reduce their inspection frequencies by seven times. 9. Gages on Dry-Pipe, Preaction and Deluge Systems — The gages need to be inspected on the same frequency as the enclosure (daily or weekly). The water supply gage should be showing a reasonable static pressure from the water supply while the system gage should be showing a reasonable air pressure. If there is a gage on a quick opening device (QOD) associated with the dry-pipe valve, it should be reading the same pressure as the air pressure gage on the dry-pipe valve. If the gage on the QOD is reading a different pressure than the air pressure gage on the dry-pipe valve, it is a sign that there is an obstruction inside the QOD. Remember that most dry-pipe valves are differential valves, so it only takes a small amount of air pressure to hold back considerable water pressure. Many dry-pipe valves have a 6:1 differential, meaning that 1 psi of air pressure can hold back 6 psi of water pressure. NFPA 13 (and NFPA 25) says that the air pressure should not be more than 20 psi above the air pressure needed to hold back the maximum expected static pressure from the water supply. This means that the air pressure in a dry- pipe system that has a 6:1 ratio valve should only be 40 psi when the maximum expected static pressure from the water supply is 120 psi (120 + 6 + 20 = 40). 10. Dry-Pipe Valves (exterior) — The valves need to be inspected monthly to make sure that they are free from physical damage, that the trim is in appropriate condition and that there is no leakage from the intermediate chamber. 11. Dry-Pipe Valves (interior) — Each year, after the trip test of the dry-pipe system, the dry- pipe valve needs to be opened and inspected on the inside. While the device is opened, strainers, filters and orifices should be cleaned. This lille holds true for all dry-pipe valves, even those that can be reset from the outside. 12. Sprinklers — Annually, all sprinklers in the system that are visible from the floor level need to be inspected to make sure that they are free from corrosion and physical damage, that there is no obstruction to the spray pattern, and that any paint was the original paint applied by the manufacturer. The inspection is only required to be from floor level, 510

## Page 517

regardless of the height of the ceiling. Sprinklers in concealed spaces are not required to be inspected. The space above a drop ceiling is considered a concealed space even though it might be very easy to lift up the tiles. •Any sprinklers that are found with paint (not applied by the manufacturer), corrosion, damage or loading of foreign material must be replaced. 13. Spare Sprinklers — Annually, the spare sprinkler cabinet must be inspected to make sure that the proper number of sprinklers of each type is in place. A sprinkler wrench must be included for each type of sprinkler. NFPA 25 requires a minimum of 6 sprinklers in the spare sprinkler cabinet. For facilities with more than 300 sprinklers and 1000 or less sprinklers, NFPA 25 requires a minimum of 12 spare sprinklers in the cabinet. For facilities with more than 1000 sprinklers, NFPA 13 requires 24 spare sprinklers in the cabinet. There must be one of every type (and temperature rating) of sprinklers in the system in the spare sprinkler cabinet except for dry-type sprinklers. 14. Pipe --- Annually, all pipe that is not installed in a concealed space is required to be inspected to make sure that it is in good condition, free from mechanical damage and free from misalignrnent. The piping also cannot be leaking or corroded. Piping in concealed spaces is never required to be inspected. 15. Piping Obstruction Investigation Once every five years, the system is required to be opened and the interior of the piping is required to be checked for the presence of foreign material or build-up. The flushing connection at the end of one main and a sprinkler at the end of one branch line are required to be opened. The intent is to pick these points in the system at random so that many different points are checked during the life of the system. If any material is found, a complete obstruction investigation should be conducted. 16. Hangers and Braces — Annually, the system's hangers and braces need to be checked to make sure that they are still attached to the sprinkler pipe and the building sttucture. As with sprinklers and pipe, the hangers and braces in concealed spaces are not required to be sprinklered. Any missing hangers or braces need to be replaced and any damaged or loose hangers or braces need to be refastened correctly or replaced. 17. Building — Annually, the building itself must be inspected to make sure that adequate heat will be provided to any area with wet piping. Adequate heat is defined as enough heat to keep the space at a minimum temperature of 400F. The best time to conduct this inspection is just prior to the onset of freezing temperatures so that any problems can be identified and repaired before any damage occurs to the system. 18. Alarm Devices — On a quarterly basis, all alarm devices (water motor gongs, bells, pressure switches, flow switches) need to be inspected to make sure they are free from damage and that all electrical connections are secure. This inspection is not a test to see if the bell rings, it is just a visual observation to see if the alarm looks like it is capable of Working. 511

## Page 518

19. Hydraulic Nameplate — All systems that have been hydraulically calculated (as opposed to being installed in accordance with the Pipe Schedule mles) are required to have a hydraulic nameplate attached to the riser. The name plate gives information about the assumptions that were made in order to conduct the hydraulic calculations. This information can be extremely useful for people trying to go back and figure out what hazard classifications were assumed in thc design of the system and can provide clues about possiblc changes in occupancy. However, the intent of NFPA 25 is not to determine if the sprinkler system is adequate for the hazard in the building. The purpose of NFPA 25 is served by just making sure that the sign is present so that other people can conduct design reviews if they so choose. Testing Requirements NFPA 25 requires that the following tests be run at the intervals specified: 1. Control Valves — Post Indicator Valves (PIV's) and road-box valves need to be tested qualterly to make sure that they are in the open position. This test is frequently called the Torsion Test because the wrench is placed on the valve and pushed in the open direction until spring (or torsion) is felt pushing the wrench back. This is the indication that the valve is completely open. The valve should then be turned one-quarter tum back in the closed direction so that valve gate is not compressing the spring inside the body of the valve. 2. Backflow Preventers (backflow) — There are two tests that need to be performed at lest annually on backflow preventers. The first is a backflow test to make sure that water will not flow from the fire protection system back to the water supply. this test is performed in accordance with local plumbing codes and manufacturers instructions. Generally, this test consists of closing the isolation valves on the backflow preventer and attaching some equipment to the test cocks on the backflow preventer. Different parts of the backflow preventer are pressurized and the change in pressure should not go back through the device. 3. Backflow Preventer (forward flow) — The problem with the backflow test described above is that the device will pass the test with flying colors if the internally loaded check valves are stuck in the closed position. This would prevent water from flowing backwards, but would also prevent water from flowing forwards tlu•ough the device if there was a fire. Since fire sprinkler systems sit for long periods of time without water flowing through them, and since backflow preventers have internally loaded check valves with rubber seats, it is entirely possible that the check valves will get stuck in the closed position. Since the 1996 edition of NFPA 13, every time a backflow device is installed on a fire sprinkler system, a means of testing the device at the full flow demand of the sprinkler system has been required to be installed downstream. This will generally be more than the 2-inch main drain can provide, so some other method of flowing water must be available. NFPA 13 recommends hydrants, test headers or even the use of the fire department connection line, although you would have to have a temporary or 512

## Page 519

permanent method of bypassing the check valve. If the system does not have any possible means of flowing the sprinkler system demand, NFPA 25 requires every drain connection downstream of the backflow preventer to be opened at the same time to achieve the maximum flow possible. On many old systems, this may only be the main drain and the inspector's test connection. 4. Pressure Regulating Valve — A flow test is required annually. The objective is to achieve the flow rate that is required downstream of the device and make sure that the pressure upstream and downstream of the device is reasonable. This test also requires that there be some method downstream to create the flow such as a test header or other opening. 5. Main Drain — The purposes of the main drain test are to help determine whether or not significant changes to the water supply have occurred, to make sure that valves truly opened after they were closed and to flush any build-up of pipe scale from the system. The frequency with which to conduct the tests has changed over the years as people have sought to exercise different pieces of equipment. For the 1992 and 1995 editions of NFPA 25, the requirement for the main drain test was quafferly. In 1998, the quarterly test was seen as being too frequent by some building owners, and they successfully petitioned the committee to change the requirement to annually conducting the test as well as conducting the test after each time that any valves had been closed. While writing the 2002 edition, the committee was asked once again to look at this lule because the internal springs on backflow preventers were not getting as much exercise when the test went to annual for the main drain, so the committee put the rule back to a quarterly test when there is a backflow preventer between the main drain and the water supply. the procedure for a main drain test is as follows: a. b. c. d. e. f. g. Read the static pressure on the water supply gage. Open the main drain to the fully open position. Observe flow from the drain. Read the residual pressure from the water supply gage with the water flowing. Shut down the main drain. Observe the water supply pressure gage and watch how long it takes for the pressure to return to the original static pressure. See the discussion at the end of the testing section on the pass/fail criteria. 6. Alarm Device — On a regular basis, the alarm must be tested by flowing water (equal to the flow of a single sprinkler in the system) and making sure that the device can sense that flow and cause an alarm to sound within a appropriate time. For mechanical alarms (like water motor gongs) the appropriate time is 5 minutes. For electronic alarms, the appropriate time is 90 seconds. The frequency with which this test needs to be run has changed over the years, For the 1998 edition (and all previous editions), the requirement was to perform this test quarterly. This was successfully challenged by some building 513

## Page 520

owners with large buildings that found this requirement expensive to comply with and generally not necessary given how infrequently they found problems with paddle-type flow switches. For the 2002 edition of NFPA 25, the frequency for testing paddle-type flow switches was changed to semi-annually (once every 6 months) but for other types of alarms (water motor gongs and pressure switches) the requirement stayed at quatterly. Note that this test requires water to flow in order to be properly performed. Some alarm testing companies will usc a wire to complete an electric circuit and ring the bells, While this might prove that the bell will ring, it does not prove that the alarm is sensitive to the flow of water, so this procedure is not allowed. 7, Sprinklers (from before 1920) — Any sprinkler that is found on a system that was manufactured prior to 1920 is required to be replaced. The types of solder used in these sprinklers was subject to problems and the manufacturers from that time just want them to be replaced. While this is technically not a "test", this rule fits in with the other rules about testing and replacing sprinklers, so it appears in the testing section of NFPA 25. 8. Sprinklers (50 to 70 years old) — When sprinklers are found on a system that are between 50 and 70 years old, the sprinklers are required to be sample tested or replaced. If all of the old sprinklers are replaced, no testing is required. But if the building owner intends on keeping these older sprinklers in place, they need to test a randomly selected sample. If the sprinklers pass the test when they are 50 years old, they need to be tested again when they are 60 years old and then again when they are 70 years old. If any one of the sprinklers does not pass the test, all of the sprinklers that sample represents need to be replaced. A representative sample is defined as one-percent of the sprinklers in the system or four sprinklers, whichever is greater. The sprinklers should be selected randomly from the system, removed from the system and replaced with new sprinklers. The old sprinklers that have been removed need to be sent to one of the testing labs (either UL or FM) and tested. The testing is destructive, so the sprinklers will not be placed back in service after the test. The test is similar to the response test that is carried out on new sprinklers. Care should be used in selecting samples to test because if any one of the sprinklers fail, all of the sprinklers that sample represents need to be replaced. For example, in a four story building, it might be smart to make each floor a separate sample and remove one-percent (or four) sprinklers from that floor, label them, and get them tested separately from the other three floors rather than just treat all four floors in the building as one big sample. This way, if one sprinkler fails•the test, only the sprinklers on that floor need to be replaced rather than all of the sprinklers in the building. If there are different environments in the building (a freezer, an attic, a basement, a clean room, a manufacturing area, a storage area, etc.) these areas should be treated as different sampling areas. 9. Sprinklers (75 years old or more) — For sprinklers 75 years old or more, the same tests discussed above have to be conducted on the sprinklers, but now the interval is once every 5 years instead of the 10 year interval for sprinklers 50 or 60 years old. As before, to avoid the testing requirement, replace all of the sprinklers. 10. Sprinklers (fast response) -- For fast-response type sprinklers, the testing requirements are the same as discussed above for the 50 year old sprinklers, but the testing needs to start 514

## Page 521

sooner. Representative samples of fast-response sprinklers need to be tested when the spcinklers axe 20 years old and then again at every 10 year interval. Since the first fast- response type sprinkler was used in 1981, the labs are just staffing to get data on these sprinklers now. It will be some time before any conclusion can be drawn about the life of these sprinklers. As before, to avoid the testing requirement, replace all of the sprinklers. 11. Sprinklers (extra high temperature) — For extra high temperature sprinklers that are normally exposed to temperatures clogc to their operating temperature, a representative sample needs to be tested every five years or the sprinklers need to be replaced. 12. Gages — Every gage needs to be tested against a calibrated gage every five years or the gage needs to be replaced. Ifthe gage is not accurate to within 3%, it needs to be recalibrated or replaced. Given the inexpensive nature of gages, it is generally more cost effective to replace the gages every five years than to worry about testing and recalibration. 13. Antifreeze — At least once each year (hopefully prior to the onset of freezing weather) the strength of the antifreeze system is required to be checked. The most common method is to check the specific gravity of the solution. In recent years there has been a significant debate regarding the procedure to use for this test. Should all of the solution be drained in order to test the concentration of the antifreeze, or will a small amount of antifreeze be sufficient. For small antifreeze systems, a small amount of solution is probably sufficient for the test. But for larger systems, a small amount of solution taken at only one location is not sufficient to insure that all of the antifreeze is at the same concentration everywhere in the system. For larger systems, small amounts of solution should be taken from multiple points, or the whole system should be drained and tested at one time. Regardless of the size of the system, if the solution is found to be under strength, the whole solution should be drained, antifreeze should be added to bring the solution up to strength, the whole solution should be completely mixed, and the solution should be pumped back into the piping. Note that it is important not to add too much antifreeze for two reasons. The first is that the higher the concentration of antifreeze (above 60%) the higher the freezing point. So, putting in too much antifreeze can actually cause the system to freeze. Second, it needs to be pointed out that most antifreeze concentrates are combustible liquids. When mixed with water, they will not readily burn, but if the concentration has too much antifreeze, it will not have the desired effect when sprayed on a fire, 14. Dry-Pipe Systems (priming water) — The level of water above the clapper in the dry-pipe valve (called the priming water) is required to be tested quarterly. The test is conducted by opening a valve on the trim that is at the correct level. If water flows from this connection, then the con•ect amount of priming water is in the dry-pipe valve. If air spits from this connection, immediately close the valve so that it does not trip the dry-pipe valve and add water to the priming chamber. Note that the trim set-up for many dry-pipe valves does not have an adequate way to get water into the priming chamber. If the priming chamber is only connected to a fill cup with a single valve (see Figure 36-2), it will be impossible to get water into the priming chamber without taking the whole valve out of service and releasing all of the air pressure from the piping. Instead, the priming 515

chamber should have trim attached to it with a small tank and a valve at each end of the tank (see Figure 36-3). Close the valve at the bottom of the priming water fill connection tank, Open the valve at the top of the priming water fill connection tank. Pour water in the fill cup until the tank is full. Close the top valve. Open the bottom valve. Water will flow down in to the priming chamber even though the air is under pressure because the water is heavier than the air. You should be able to hear the water draining into the priming chamber. When the water has stopped draining into the priming chamber, close the bottom valve. Open the valve to the priming water leveldreck and see if water comes out. If water comes out, you are done, if air spits out, shut the valve immediately and repeat the procedure, 15. Dry-Pipe Systems (QOD) — The quick opening device (either accelerator or exhauster) if installed, must be tested semi-annually (once every 6 months). This is done without tripping the dry-pipe system. See the manufacturer's instructions for the procedure for this test. 17. Dry-Pipe Systems (full flow trip test) — The full flow trip test is only required to be run once every three years. The basic idea is to open the inspector's test connection at the end of the system and fill the entire system up with water. Since this introduces water into an environment that normally has air, this can cause corrosion in the system piping. The test only needs to be run once every three years to minimize the corrosion situation. The procedure for a full-flow trip test is as follows: a. b. c. Record air and water pressure from gages. Open the main drain and allow water to flow until clear to clean out any scale that may have accumulated. Close the main drain. 516

d. e. f. g, h. i. j. k. l. m. n. o. Open inspector's test connection (usually takes a second person in communication with the first). Start a timer as soon as the valve is opened. Note (he air pressure when the valve trips. Record the time When water flows from the inspector's test connection. Let water flow until clear, then close the inspector's test connection. Close main system control valve. Open all drains including low point drains and auxiliary drains. When water is no longer discharging from the drains, close all drains. Reset the dry-pipe valve and the quick opening device making sure to check the latching equipment for the clapper inside the dry-pipe valve. The latching equipment is important since the main drain is below the clapper. If the clapper is not held open, the system cannot drain properly because the water will not be able to get past the clapper. Attach a card or tag to the dry-pipe valve that includes the date of the trip test and the name of the organization that performed the test. Make sure that the records to the owner include the initial air and water pressures, the valve condition, the tripping pressure and the tripping time. See the discussion at of this section on interpreting the data from the full- flow trip test to determine pass/fail criteria. 18. Dry-Pipe Systems (partial flow trip test) In the years when the full flow trip test is not being performed (two out of every three years) a partial flow trip test will be performed. The objective of the partial flow trip test is to trip the dry-pipe valve with enough force to latch the clapper open, but to not allow the water to get past the riser. The procedure for the partial flow trip test is as follows: a. Record the air and water pressures. b. Open the main drain to flush out pipe scale. c. With the main drain open, start to close the main control valve. Continue to close the main control valve until there is only a small amount of water discharging from the main drain. d. Close the main drain valve. 517

But those that do need to be checked on a quarterly basis to make sure the proper amount of water is in the valve. The check should be similar in procedure to that required for the dry-pipe valve. 20. Preaction and Deluge Systems (low pressure alarms) — The alarms need to be tested quarterly to make sure that they sense a drop in pressure. Preaction and Deluge Systems (air maintenance devices) The devices need to be tested annually to make sure that they sense the low pressure and activate the compressor (or other air/nitrogen provider) to pump up the pressure and tum off at an appropriate high pressure. The site needs to be checked to make sure that water runoff will be safe (drains are clear, ground slope has not changed, etc.) and anything in the area that might be damaged-by the water needs to be removed or made safe for discharge. There are four exceptions to the annual trip test rule for preaction and deluge valves as follows: a. C' Where the nature of the protected property is such that water cannot be discharged for test purposes, the trip test shall be conducted in a manner that does not necessitate discharge in the protected area" (Section 12.4.3.2.2.1 of NFPA 25- 2002). 518

In all cases, the test frequency shall not exceed 3 years" (Section 12.4.3.2.2.2 of NFPA 25-2002). "Preaction or deluge valves protecting freezers shall be trip tested in a manner that does not introduce moisture into the piping in the freezer" (Section 12.4.3.2.2.3 of NFPA 25-220). Note that this does not excuse a system in a freezer from being tested, it just means that the water is not required to fill the piping in the freezer after the valve is tripped. The water is generally sent through a testing bypass line to a drain in a warm section of the building. Main Drain Test Pass/Fail Criteria As discussed in item #5 above, the main drain test is an important test for determining the long-term situation with a water supply and for insuring that valves have been opened after they were closed. One might think that the indicating mechanism on the valve was enough to insure that it had been opened, but that is not the case. It is possible for a valve to be indicating that it is open, when in fact the valve will not allow water to pass through. The most common type of valve used in fire protection is the OS&Y .valve, which consists of a stem attached to a gate. When the valve is open, the gate is in the "up" position and the stem sticks out of the valve. When the valve is closed, the gate is in the "down" position and the stem is inside the valve. It is possible (though rare) while the valve is in the closed position for the stem to become disconnected from the gate. If this happens, when the valve is turned to the open position, the stem will rise out of the valve, but it will not pull the gate up with it. Therefore, it is important to run the main drain test after each time that the valve has, been closed and then opened again. 521

## Page 528

Even if we never had to WOITY about the gate and the stem becoming separated, we would still want to perform periodic main drain tests to make sure that the water supply was not deteriorating and that the supply pipe was not getting plugged up. In order to determine these problems from the results of a main drain test, the person analyzing the data needs to use. some judgment and experience. looking at thc data from a main drain test, the first concern should be to find the results from the previous test and the results from the acceptance test. Without at least one of these sets of numbers, the rest of the data is useless, The objective is to compare the results from this test to the results of the previous tests. If the static pressure during the most recent test is 60 psi and the residual pressure with the main drain open is 40 psi, this information by itself does not tell us much, But if we know that the static pressure the last time the test was run was 60 psi and the residual pressure was 55 psi, then we have more useful information. We know that under flowing conditions, a change has occurred that is causing 15 psi more friction loss today than last time the test was run. The only explanation for this would be an obstruction between the water supply and the main drain or some change to the system between these points (like the addition of a backflow preventer). So, you can see that the whole analysis depends on the comparison of the data to the previous tests. There are some people that try to place some significance on the residual pressure and comparing that number to the pressure demand on the hydraulic nameplate. They want the residual pressure during the test to be at least as high as the sprinkler system demand. However, that practice is not fundamentally sound and may lead to serious errors. On one hand, it can cause people to accept systems that have problems, and on the other hand, it can cause authorities to reject systems that have no problem at all. The problem is that there is no way to determine how much water is discharging from the main drain while the test is being run. A pressure without an associated flow is no help at all. Over the years attempts have been made to estimate the flow from the main drain, however, all such attempts have been fraught with difficulties and have never been successful. The variables are too great to quantify considering that the results are affected by the number of turns in the drain pipe, the size of the drain pipe, the type of drain control valve, the arrangement of the drain and many other variables. Advocates of using this data have suggested putting a Pitot gage in the flow stream to determine the flow, but this will not be accurate either. The use of the Pitot gage assumes that the full cross-sectional area of the discharge pipe will be comprised of fluid discharging the pipe, but in a main drain pipe, this is rarely happening, making the formula for converting the Pitot pressure into a flow unusable. Consider a sprinkler system with a large flow demand and a 6 inch riser. The main drain will be 2 inches in size. With the main drain fully open, the flow of water from the drain will always be less then the sprinkler demand. So if the residual pressure during the test is greater than the demand pressure for the sprinkler system, does this mean that the water supply is okay? No, because the flow is not anywhere near the demand of the sprinkler system, so you can't say that the pressure has any meaning. All you can say is that the water supply is providing a pressure greater than what is needed for the fire protection system at a flow that is less than what 522

## Page 529

is needed for the fire protection system. You can't tell from this data what the pressure would be when the flow from the water supply was equal to the flow demand for the sprinkler system. Next, consider a small sprinkler system for a high-rise apartment with a 4 inch riser and a 2 inch main drain. The main drain test might easily flow more water than the sprinkler demand, which would cause a great deal more friction loss than the sprinkler demand. If the residual pressure during the main drain test was less than the pressure demand for the sprinkler system, should the sprinkler system fail thc test? No, because the fiow is greater than the dcmand of the sprinkler system. Al a lesser flow, thc residual pressure would be expected to be higher and the sprinkler system could be fine. There is no way to tell from looking at the data of the main drain test. 1. 2. 3. 4. The following procedure is recommended for evaluating the data from a main drain test: Compare the static pressure from the most recent test to the previous tests. Are they similar? Are they very different? A difference by itself is not a problem and may reflect the test being run at a different time of day or a different season than the previous tests. Given your knowledge of this water supply, does the difference (if there is any) make sense? Compare the residual pressure from the most recent test to the previous tests. Are they similar? Are they very different? Once again, a difference by itself is not a problem. But if the static pressures are similar and the residual pressures are not, then there is a problem that needs to be investigated. If both the static and the residual pressures are different from the previous years, then they should be different by the same (or a similar number). For example, if the static and residual pressures were 60 psi and 55 psi one time, and then 50 psi and 45 psi the next, the sprinkler system is probably still okay. It is showing the same relative difference between the values of static and residual pressure. But if the static and residual pressures are 60 and 55 psi one time, and then 75 and 60 psi the next, there is probably a problem even though the residual pressure has gone up from one test to the next. The problem is that the first time the test was run the difference between static and residual was 5 psi while the next time that the test was run, the difference was 15 psi. This is worth additional investigation to see if significant changes have happened to the sprinkler system. Did the gage take a long time after shutting the drain valve off to get back to the original static pressure? If the gage takes a long time to get back to the original static pressure, it is a sign that there is partial blockage in the line. The system is letting water through and the pressure is going up, but it should happen very quickly on most sprinkler system, simultaneous with the closing of the valve. Did the pressure make it back to the original static pressure? Usually, the water pressure in a water supply will not change during the running of a main drain test, so the pressure should go back to where it started before you opened any valves. However, this won't always be the case. In some circumstances, the flow from the main drain will cause pumps to start and increase the pressure in the system, thereby affecting your final pressure result. Know the water supply before drawing conclusions. 523

Trip Test Passmail Criteria The two key pieces of data from the full-flow trip test are the time that it took the valve to open and the time that it took water to merive at the most remote portion of the system (inspector's test connection). Other pieces of data are collected and can be useful, such as the water pressure or air pressure at which the valve tripped, but this data is less important than the time. The time that it takes to trip the valve is a function of the water gupply pressure, the air pressure in the system, the differential of the valve (surface area in contact with water pressure compared to the surface area in contact with air pressure) and the maintenance that has been performed on the valve. There is no direct pass or fail criteria for the trip time of the valve, but it should be very similar from year to year, only varying by any changes in the water supply pressure. A higher water supply pressure will allow the valve to trip sooner while a lower water supply pressure will slow down the action of the valve. Assuming that the valve has been maintained well and there is not a build-up of foreign material inside the valve, the time that it takes to trip that valve can be calculated using a process and formula outlined in the SFPE Handbook of Fire Protection Engineering. If there are any questions about whether the trip time is acceptable or not, this formula can be used to determine how far off the valve is from operating correctly. While this formula is not exact, it should be able to predict tripping of the valve within 20%. The variable that everyone spends a great deal of time worrying about is the time it takes to deliver water to the inspector's test connection. This variable deserves a great deal of discussion. First, we need to discuss how the variable is measured. When water gets to the inspector's test connection, it is often mixed with air. The first few bits of water will be a combination of water and air spitting from the connection like a mist on the breeze. This will be followed by brief flows of water interrupted by short volumes of air. Eventually, the water will begin to flow in a continuous stream, NFPA 13 and NFPA 25 say that this first continuous stream is when you stop the timer. From time to time, you may get a pocket of air that interrupts the flow of water for a second or two, but these minor air pockets are not a concern. The time for water delivery to the inspector's test connection is measured from when the comection is fully open to when the water first becomes a continuous stream. The next logical question is, "What is an acceptable water delivery time?" Unfortunately, there is no direct answer to this question for most sprinkler systems. From a design perspective, NFPA 13 does not require that all sprinkler systems deliver water to the inspector's test connection in any specific period of time. There are only two rules in NFPA 13 that specify any water delivery time and they are as follows: 1) For sprinkler systems that do not have quick opening devices (accelerators or exhausters) and are greater than 500 gallons in volume, but less than 750 gallons in size, water must be delivered to the inspector's test connection in 60 seconds or less. (See sections 7.2.4.1 and 7.2.4.2 of NFPA 13-2002.) 524

## Page 531

2) For sprinkler systems that are greatcr than 750 gallons in volume, water must be delivered to the inspector's test connection in 60 seconds. These two sections are the only requirements in NFPA 13 for any specific water delivery time. For dry-pipe systems that are 500 gallons or less in volume and for dry-pipe systems that are 750 gallons of volume or less with a quick opening device, there is no requirement in NFPA 13 fog any specific water delivery time. Therefore, there is also no specific requirement for any specific water delivery time for the periodic full-flow test unless you are in a cornmunity enforcing a fire code that has a specific time limit of its own, Even if the sprinkler system is one of those that is required to deliver water to the inspector's test connection under NFPA 13 (large systems or medium size systems with no quick opening devices) there is no requirement in NFPA 25 that says that the water must get to the inspector's test connection in 60 seconds for every periodic test in the future. The 60 second rule is for the sprinkler system when it is new. There is an expectation that performance may get slower as the system gets older, so the system is not required by NFPA 25 to pelform exactly like it did when it was new. There are some local codes that have mandated their own water delivery times and they are too numerous to mention here. However, the BOCA National Fire Prevention Code was widely used in the Mid-Atlantic States and New England during the 1980's and 1990's. This code did require all existing dry-pipe sprinkler systems (regardless of size) to deliver water to the inspector's test connection within 60 seconds. This code no longer exists and has been replaced by the ICC International Fire Code, which no longer contains this provision, But there are still communities enforcing the old BOCA Fire Prevention Code, so this rule may still be on the books in some portions of the country. More important than the 60 second rule is a comparison of the water delivery time during the most recent test to the performance of the dry-pipe sprinkler system during its last full-flow trip test (probably three years earlier). By looking at the performance of the sprinkler system over time, it is easier to spot when there is a dramatic change in performance. If there is a dramatic change in performance, without a corresponding change in water and air pressure, then there is a serious problem that needs to be investigated. Beginning with the 2002 edition of NFPA 13, there are many dry-pipe systems that have 50 second, 45 second, 40 second and even 15 second water delivery times (see section 11.2.3.9.1). Many of these sprinkler systems are not required to deliver this water to the inspector's test connection. Instead, these systems are required to be calculated in order to deliver this water to multiple open sprinklers. Tests have shown that the water gets out to sprinklers much faster when there are multiple sprinklers open, rather than just the inspector's test that simulates a single open sprinkler. Sprinkler systems can be designed with a computer program that predicts this water delivery, or they can be rigged with a manifold with multiple outlets that simulates multiple sprinklers flowing. Either way, water will get to the inspector's test connection at a different time than it would to multiple openings. For these types of systems, having the acceptance test records is critical. After the system has been accepted, a test of the time it takes to get water to the inspector's test should be conducted, That time then becomes the 525

## Page 532

baseline for that system and all subsequent tests should be compared back to this original test. Even though water may get to 4 sprinklers in the system in 40 seconds, it may take 90 or even 150 seconds to get that water to the inspector's test, so there is no hard and fast rule that dictates an acceptable time, everything needs to be compared back to the original test. Also, there is no requirement to build a manifold to test the systems that were calculated by a computer for their water delivery times, the computer programs are accepted as accurate. Of course, the input needs to be reviewed Lo make sure LhaL clae computer calculated the con•ect sprinkler system. Maintenance For most fire protection system components, the correct maintenance is just to repair or replace any items that are damaged or no longer working. There is very little periodic maintenance that needs to occur. The following paragraphs outline the few regular maintenance items that need to be taken care of. The stem of OS&Y valves needs to be lubricated annually. Once the lubricant has been applied, the valve should be closed and opened again to distribute the lubricant. Since this closes the valve, then a main drain test should also be run. Since the main drain test needs to be run annually anyway, these procedures should be coordinated so that the testing and maintenance is done in an efficient manner. For dry-pipe systems, if the system is losing more than 10 psi per week, the leaks are required to be found and repaired. This is the amount that most compressors can keep up with without allowing the dry-pipe valve to trip accidentally. For preaction systems, any air leaks that cause low pressure alarms need to be taken care of. There is no specific rule for how much air loss is considered unacceptable as there is with dry-pipe systems. For dry-pipe, preaction and deluge systems, low point drains must be opened and drained of water annually, before the onset of freezing weather. Even if the system has not been tripped in a while, it is possible for condensate to develop in the pipe and pool in the low points. This condensate has the ability to expand if it freezes and damage pipe and fittings. It is necessary to get this condensate out of the system before freezing weather occurs. For dry-pipe systems, low- point drains that act as an air-lock should be installed so that the water can be drained without letting the air out of the System (see section 8.15.2.5.3 in NFPA 13-2002 for more detail). If sprinklers are ever replaced on a system, they need to be replaced with new sprinklers that have the same characteristics as the old sprinklers, or the system needs to be reviewed for the acceptability of the new sprinklers. The characteristics that need to be the same for replacement sprinklers are: Style and deflector type (upright, pendent or sidewall) Orifice size and k-factor Temperature rating Coating (if any) Design requirements 526

## Page 533

Only new sprinklers can be used to replace old sprinklers, This has been the cause of some discussion leading to the question, "can sprinklers be reused?" The answer is that a sprinkler can be taken out of a system and put back in approximately the same place on that system (this covers moving a sprinkler during tenant renovations and when a new obstruction causes a coverage problem) but sprinklers are not allowed to be removed from a system and stock piled for later installation in that same system or any other system. The storage conditions (temperature) and the physical well being of the sprinkler (possible damage to bulbs or links) are too large of a problem to allow sprinklers to be stockpiled for reuse. Where special sprinklers have been installed (such as the attic sprinkler or the concealed space sprinkler) any replacements are required to be with the same model sprinkler from the same manufacturer IUIless such sprinklers are no longer being manufactured. It is interesting to note that when this rules was first written in NFPA 25, extended coverage sprinklers and residential sprinklers were considered as "special sprinklers". But times have changed and NFPA 13 no longer considers them"'special". They are just two different kinds of sprinklers that have their own installation sections in Chapter 8 of NFPA 13. Therefore, they are no longer subjected to the rule of having to be replaced with the same model. Now, if you want to replace an extended coverage sprinkler or a residential sprinkler, you can do it with any sprinkler from any manufacturer, but you need to make sure that the new sprinkler has the same k-factor and has the same (or less) pressure and flow demands at the spacing in which it is being used. As discussed previously in this chapter, the stock of spare sprinklers in the spare sprinkler cabinet is required to be at least 6 sprinklers, but might be more depending on thc number of sprinklers in the building. In addition, at least one of every kind of sprinkler in the system must be represented in the sprinkler cabinet except for dry-type sprinklers. The following are the number of spare sprinklers that are required as a minimum: 6 sprinklers for facilities with less,then 300 sprinklers 0 12 sprinklers for facilities with between 300 and 1000 sprinklers (inclusive) 24 sprinklers for facilities with more than 1000 sprinklers Sprinklers that protect spray coating areas are required to be covered by a bag to protect from overspray. The bag is required to be plastic or paper. Plastic bags have to be 0.003 inch thick or less. Paper bags do not have any specific minimum size or thickness) but should not be much larger than the sprinkler to avoid delaying the activation of a sprinkler if there is a fire. The bags need to be replaced whenever the deposits or residue accumulates on the bags. While the bags to slightly delay the activation of the sprinklers, it is much easier to replace the bags on a regular basis than to replace the sprinklers. Sprinklers used for commercial cooking equipment and ventilating systems generally need to be replaced annually. If the sprinklers are glass-bulb type sprinklers and they show no sign of grease build-up or build-up of other materials, they can stay in place after being inspected on an annual basis. 527

CHAPTER 37 STORAGE Even though this subject is quite advanced, no discussion of fire sprinkler systems would be complete without some mention of how to protect storage occupancies. For more than 100 years, sprinkler systems have been installed in storage occupancies and they still continue to be the majority of some sprinkler contractors' work today. Everyone in their sprinkler industry career will be faced with sprinklering many storage occupancies, so the demand for protecting them correctly is significant. A brief outline will be given in this text for dealing with sprinkler systems for storage occupancies, which is a good introduction for NICET Work Elements 14005 High Piled Storage and 14006 Rack Storage. Additional material will be presented in the next chapter for actually putting sprinklers into rack structures. A more in-depth discussion of protecting storage occupancies can be found in the NFSA publication Sprinkler Protection for Storage and Warehouse Occupancies, which is available from the NFSA Resource Center. In this chapter, the classification of different storage commodities will be discussed along with the basic procedures for protecting these commodities when they are stored in various configurations. This chapter is intended to be a brief overview of the organization of chapters 5 and 12 of NFPA 13. It will not be possible to describe in-depth how to protect every conceivable combination of commodity and storage configuration in this text. Commodity Classification There are seven types of commodities in storage occupancies; Class I, Class II, Class III, Class IV, Group A Plastics, Group B Plastics and Group C Plastics. As we will see in the definitions, two of these classifications will drop out and there will only be five different categories to use for determining the rules for sprinkler protection. In each category, a benchmark commodity will be discussed. These benchmark commodities are the products that would be used in a fire test if such a test was going to be used to determine protection criteria for a specific configuration of this commodity. The benchmark commodities not only help to establish rules for fire protection, but they also give people a specific image of what each specific commodity is intended to be. 533

## Page 540

Commodity classifications are covered in Chapter 5 of NFPA 13. In the annex to Chapter 5, there are a series of extremely useful tables, The tables contain a great deal of commodities that have been evaluated over the years and placed in specific categories by either full-scale fire tests, medium-scale tests under a fire products collector, or engineering judgment. The first table in the annex (Table A.5.6.3 is an alphabetic listing by commodity that contains all of the commodities and lets you know the classification for each one. The rest of the tables (Table A,5.6.3.i through Tabie A.5.6.4.i) show each of the commodity classifications together, so you can get a feel for the kind of products that fall into Class I, Class IL etc. Class I Commodities Class I commodities are noncombustible products stored in ordinary single layer cardboard cartons. This includes metal and glass products, noncombustible foods and noncombustible products placed directly on wooden pallets and noncombustible produ•cts shrink wrapped or paper wrapped as a unit load (with or without pallets). An example of a Class I commodity familiar to most of the people in this industry is sprinklers in cartons. Factory Mutual considers glass jars in compartmented cardboard cartons to be a benchmark Class I commodity. Other examples of Class I commodities are: Alcoholic Beverages (up to 20% alcohol) in metal, glass or ceramic Appliances (stoves, refrigerators) not packaged with no appreciable plastic trim Batteries (dry Cell) Batteries (automobile-filled) Bottles/Jars (glass filled with noncombustible liquids) Bottles/Jars (glass filled with noncombustible powders) Bottles/Jars (plastic less than 5 gal [19L] filled with noncombustible liquid) Cement (bagged) Fertilizer (bagged-phosphates) Frozen foods (nonwax nonplastic packaging) Nuts (canned and cartoned) Paints (friction top cans, waterbased [latex]) Poultry Products (canned and cartoned) Poultry Products (frozen with nonwax nonplastic containers) Transformers (dry and oil filled) 534

Class II Commodities Class II commodities are the same as Class I, but in more substantial packaging such as wooden crates, solid wooden boxes or multiple thickness cartons. Factory Mutual considers metal lined double tri-wall cartons (6 layers of cardboard) to be a benchmark Class II commodity. Examples of Class II Commodities include: o Alcoholic Beverages (up Io 20% alcohol) in wooden containers Appliances (stoves, refrigerators) in conugated cartons with no appreciable plastic trim Baked Goods (cookies, cakes and pies) frozen and in plastic coated package Batteries (dry cell in blister pack) in cartons Fertilizers (bagged-nitrates) Frozen Foods (waxed paper containers, cartoned) o Pharmaceuticals (pills and powders in glass bottles and cartoned) o Pharmaceuticals (nonflammable liquids in glass bottles and cartoned) e Plastic Containers (Noncombustible liquids in larger than 5 gal [1910] containers) Poultry Products (frozen on paper or plastic trays) o Wood Products (solid pile of lumber or plywood) Class III Commodities Class III commodities are products fashioned from ordinary combustibles such as wood, paper, cloth and leather, Group C Plastics are also defined as Class III commodities. Class III commodities are allowed to have a "limited amount" of Group A or B Plastics. A "limited amount" is defined as a maximum of 5% by weight or volume. Factory Mutual considers paper cups in compartmented cartons to be a benchmark Class III commodity. Other examples of Class III commodities include: Aerosols (Level 1) Baked Goods (cookies, cakes and pies packaged in cartons) Grains (packaged in cartons) Cereals (packaged in cartons) Charcoal (bagged) Diapers (cotton or linen) Frozen Foods (on plastic trays) Furniture, Wood (no plastic coverings or foam cushions) Leather Goods Photographic Film (35 mm in metal cartridges) Textiles (natural fibers) Textiles (synthetics- 50-50 blend or less, not rayon or nylon) 535

Class IV Commodities Class IV commodities are those Class I, II or III commodities with an "appreciable amount" of plastic or with plastic packaging. An "appreciable amount" of plastic is defined as between 5 and 15 percent by weight or between 5 and 25 percent by volume. Group B Plastics are also defined as Class IV commodities. Factory Mutual considers polystyrene and paper cups in compartmented cardboard cartons to bc a bcnchmark Class IV commodity. Examples of Class IV commodities include: Anununition (small arms or shotgun packaged in cartons) Bottles/Jars (empty PET plastic) Liquor (100 proof or less in glass or plastic bottles) Nail Polish (2 oz glass bottles, cartoned) Paints (Friction top cans, cartoned, oil based) Vinyl Floor (tiles in cartons) Plastic and Rubber Commodities Plastics and mbbers are divided into three categories (Group A, B and C) depending on their burning characteristics. NFPA 13 contains a list of common plastics and the group that they fall into. It is possible for the manufacturer to add fire retardant chemicals into the plastic, which will alter its burning characteristics and lower its category. If this is the case, make sure that all authorities having jurisdiction (AHJ's), including the insurance company agree to the Group designation before the design of the sprinkler system is complete. Factory Mutual considers Polystyrene cups in compartmented cardboard cartons to be a benchmark Group A plastic conunodity. Group A Plastics include: o Acrylic o Butyl Rubber o Natural Rubber (Expanded) o Polyethylene o Polypropylene PVC (Highly Plasticized) Examples of commodities that burn like Group A plastics are: Batteries (truck batteries empty or full) Candles (packaged in cartons) treat as expanded plastic Diapers (disposable with plastic and uncartoned) Margarine (between 50 and 80% oil) Mattresses (foam) Milk (in plastic crates) Nail Polish (2 oz plastic bottles in cartons) 536

## Page 543

Group B Plastics include: Fluoroplastics o Nylon o Silicone Rubber o Natural Rubber (Not Expanded) Group C Plastics include: PVC (Rigid or lightly plasticized like pipe and fittings) o Melamine (Melamine Formaldehyde) Urea (Urea Formaldehyde) Under two conditions, Group A plastics can be treated as Class IV commodities. The first is when the plastic is considered "free flowing." To be free flowing, the commodity must be small objects which will fall out of the box, fill the flue space and smother the fire. Examples of free flowing plastics are powder, pellets, flakes, and small randomly packed objects. The second condition under which Group A plastics can be considered as Class IV commodities is when there are multiple layers of cardboard or equivalent outer material which would significantly delay the involvement of plastics in the.fire, and where the arrangement and the amount of material within the carton would not significantly increase the fire hazard. This is obviously a judgment call and the AHJ should be consulted before making this decision. For the original work on Group classification, a number of plastics were burned and the heat release rates were collected. Plastics with peak heat release rates exceeding 1500 BTU/sq. ft./min were considered Group A. Plastics with peak heat release rates between 1000 and 1500 BTU/sq. ft./min were considered Group B. Plastics with peak heat release rates under 1000 BTU/sq. ft./min were considered Group C. Remember that the sprinkler rules for plastics only apply to Group A plastics. For Group B plastics, treat the commodity as if it were a Class IV commodity. For Group C plastics, treat the commodity as if it were a Class III commodity. What if the Commodity Can't be Classified? If the building owner is not sure what class or group a specific commodity falls under, it is possible to run a fire test to determine the proper protection. Factory Mutual and Underwriters Laboratories will both perform this test. The lab will burn 8 pallet loads of the unknown commodity under a fire products collector and measure the heat release rate during the fire. The test will be performed three times to make sure that the commodity burns similarly each time, so a total of 24 pallet loads of the commodity are necessary, The heat release rate from the tests will be compared to the performance of the benchmark fuel packages discussed above. The commodity will be given the classification of the Class or Plastic Group that it most closely resembles in its burning characteristics. See Figure 37-1 for the burning characteristics of the five benchmark commodities in the eight-pallet test. 537

o 500 450 400 350 300 250 200 150 100 o 2.5 15 17.5 A Plastic Class IV Class Ill Class II Class I 20 5 Time (Minutes) Figure 37-1 Performance of Benchmark Commodities in Product Collector Test Encapsulation Encapsulation is defined as, "A method of packing consisting of a plastic sheet completely enclosing the sides and top of a pallet load containing combustible comrnodity or combustible packages." Banding or stretch-wrapping around the sides (and not the top) is not considered encapsulation. The problem with encapsulation is that the plastic on top of the pallet load tends to act as a shield, keeping the packages near a fire dry when sprinklers activate, This makes it harder to control the fire since combustibles near the fire are not getting wet, allowing the fire access to dry fuel to grow and expand. Although encapsulation does affect the sprinkler system design, it does not affect the classification of a commodity. Encapsulation is taken into account in other ways during the design of a fire sprinkler system. Usually, a greater density (more flow) is required for the ceiling sprinklers. Therefore, when a commodity is encapsulated, it should be classified as the same commodity as it would have been without the encapsulation. The penalty for encapsulation will be taken later in the design. 538

Mixed Commodities There are a number of options when protecting a building with a mix of different commodities. The first option is to protect the entire building for the highest (or most demanding) of the commodities present. This gives the owner the maximum amount of flexibility to move stock around without worrying about the adequacy of the fire protection at any location in the building. Another option is for the building owner to confine the higher hazard material to a designated area with each area of the building having a fire sprinkler system designed and installed to protect the hazard in that area. The drawback to this type of design is that the owner/user of the building must make sure to keep the proper storage in the proper area. If an excess of higher hazard material needs to be stored, then the owner has a problem because there is nowhere to put the higher hazard commodity where the sprinkler system can protect it. Another problem occurs if the people making the decisions regarding where to put material when a delivery is being unloaded either don't know about the sprinkler system restrictions or don't pay close attention to what they are doing. There is a potential for higher hazard commodities to be placed in areas where the sprinkler system cannot handle the demand. NFPA 13 allows a third option for small quantities of higher hazard commodities in section 5.6.1.2.3. Up to 10 pallet loads in any 40,000 sq ft of a higher hazard commodity are allowed in most circumstances. The higher hazard commodity must be randomly spaced with no adjacent pallet loads in any direction, including diagonally. When the fire protection system is designed for Class I or Class II protection, the number of pallet loads of Class IV or Group A Plastics allowed is reduced to 5. Effect of Plastic Pallets The rules for commodity classification were written assuming that wooden pallets were going to be used. Plastic pallets are permitted, but the fire protection system is required to be increased to account for the extra fuel load of the plastics. The amount of the increase depends on the type of plastic pallet. Plastic pallets are made with either reinforced plastic or unreinforced plastic. Where umeinforced plastic pallets are used, the commodity classification needs to be increased one level. For example, if a building owner were to store a Class I conmodity on unreinforced plastic pallets, the fire protection system would have to be designed for Class II. Likewise, if a Class III commodity were to be stored on umeinforcéd plastic pallets, the fire protection system would have to be designed for Class IV. If Class IV commodities are stored on unreinforced plastic pallets, the sprinlder system needs to be designed for cartoned unexpanded Group A plastics. No increase is required for Group A plastics being stored on plastic pallets. Where reinforced plastic pallets are used, the commodity classification needs to be increased by two levels. For example, if a building owner were to store a Class I commodity on 539

## Page 546

reinforced plastic pallets, the fire protection system would have to be designed for Class III. Likewise, if a Class III commodity were to be stored on unreinforced plastic pallets, the fire protection system would have to be designed for cartoned unexpanded Group A plastics. No increase is required for Group A plastics being stored on plastic pallets. If specific fire test data is available that shows how a specific commodity burns on plastic pallets, or shows how certain types of plastic pallets burn, (hat fire Lest data is allowed to overrule any other classification scheme. Selecting Sprinklers for Use in Storage Occupancies Fires in storage occupancies tend to be classified as "high challenge fires." High challenge fires are those that give off large quantities of hot gasses (mass) at high velocities. The combination of mass and velocity produces a momentum of the fire plume (mathematically, mass times velocity equals momentum). The water droplet (from the sprinkler) must penetrate this fire plume with its own momentum. If the water droplet has enough mass and velocity it will penetrate the plume and help fight the fire. But if the droplet does not have enough mass or velocity, it will get carried away by the plume and will not contribute to control of the fire. There are sprinklers that are designed to produce water droplets with increased mass and velocity, which increases their momentum, which gives them the ability to suppress high challenge fires. Suppression Theory The theory behind the suppression oriented sprinkler was developed by Factory Mutual in the 1980's. In order to completely understand the theory, one must compare the concepts Of Fire Control and Fire Suppression as well as learn some new terminology. Fire Control is defined by NFPA 13 as, "Limiting the size of a fire by distribution of water so as to decrease the heat release rate and pre-wet adjacent combustibles, while controlling ceiling gas temperatures to avoid structural damage." Providing fire control is precisely what standard sprinklers have done well for more than 100 years. Many times, the sprinkler system controlled the fire by actually putting the fire out, but that was not a design objective of NFPA 13, Putting the fire out was a fortunate byproduct of the conservative concepts used in the design and the result of significant safety factors. Fire Suppression is defined by NFPA 13 as, ' 'Sharply reducing the heat release rate of a fire and preventing its regrowth by means of direct and sufficient application of water through the fire plume to the burning fuel surface." By radically changing the design of a sprinkler, it is possible to achieve a type of sprinkler where the design objective is to suppress the fire rather than just control it. 540

## Page 547

The difference between Fire Control and Fire Suppression can be seen with the two following figures where the heat release rate (HRR) of a fire is plotted as a function of lime. Figure 37-2 shows a generic fire control situation while Figure 37-3 shows a generic fire suppression situation. HRR Time Figure 37-2 Generic Fire Control Curve HRR Time Figure 37-3 Generic Fire Suppression Curve In both figures, the fire starts at time "0". The fire grows until it sets off a sprinkler. With the Fire Control curve (Figure 37-2), the sprinklers keep the fire from spreading until it burns itself out or the fire department (fire brigade) can finish off the job. For the generic situation shown in Figure 37-2, the heat release stays constant, but in some situations the heat release may go up or down after the sprinklers have opened depending on the commodity burning and the discharge rate of the sprinklers. With the Fire Suppression curve (shown in Figure 37-3), the heat release rate goes sharply down after the sprinkler(s) open. In each case, the area under the curve represents the total heat released by the fire into the building. This can be equated to the total damage done by the fire. The Fire Suppression curve 541

## Page 548

will always have a smaller area under the curve, and will always help the building owner minimize the damage done by fire. In order to explain how sprifiklers were redesigned to achieve fire suppression, two new terms need to be defined; Required Delivered Density (RDD) and Actual Delivered Density (ADD). The Required Delivered Density (RDD) is the amount of water necessary at the surface of a buming fuel to suppress a fire consisting of that fuel. The RDD is measured in temas of gpm per sq ft. The RDD is a function of the type of fuel burning and how that fuel is arranged. As the heat release rate (I-IRR) from a fire (measured in BTU's per minute) increases, the RDD increases. In other words, the larger the fire, the more water is needed to suppress that fire. Figure 37-4 shows a generic RDD curve where the density necessary to suppress a fire of this particular fuel increases as the heat release from the fire increases. RDD Density Heat Release Rate (HRR) Figure 37-4 Generic RDD Curve The Actual Delivered Density (ADD) is the amount of water that leaves the sprinkler and penetrates the fire plume to reach the surface of the burning fuel. The ADD is measured in terms of gpm per sq ft. The ADD is a ftnction of the sprinkler deflector (and the droplet sizes it produces) and the velocity of the water as it leaves the sprinkler (which is a ftmction of the water pressure and the orientation of the sprinkler). As the heat release rate (HRR) from a fire (measured in BTU's per minute) increases, the ADD decreases. In other words, the larger the fire, the more water is carried away by the fire plume, the less water makes it to the surface of the burning fuel to help suppress that fire. Figure 37-5 shows a generic ADD curve where the amount of water that arrives at the surface of a burning fuel decreases as the fire gets bigger. 542

## Page 549

Density ADD Heat Release Rate (HRR) Figure 37-5 Generic ADD Curve When the ADD and RDD curves are plotted for the same fuel on the same graph, there will hopefully be a place where the two curves cross. This point is known as the "Suppression Point". If the sprinkler system can react to a fire before this point is reached, the sprinkler system will achieve suppression because there is more water reaching the surface of the fuel than is needed to suppress the fire. However, if the sprinkler system does not react to the fire until after the Suppression Point has passed, then suppression will not occur because an insufficient amount of water is making it to the surface of the burning fuel. Figure 37-6 shows the suppression point for a generic fuel. RDD Suppression Point Density ADD Heat Release Rate (HRR) Not Suppression Suppression Figure 37-6 Generic Suppression Curve 543
