In order to determine the RDD of any given commodity, a number of fire tests have to be conducted with the water being applied directly to the surface of the burning fuel. In order to determine the ADD of any given sprinkler, a number of fire tests have to be run with a special apparatus that collects water under a cenain size fire plume. Then, sprinklers need to be developed with sufficient sensitivity [laal they will respond to Lhe fire prior Lo the Suppression Point being passed, Yet the sprinklers can't be too sensitive, or too many will open during a fire. ESFR sprinklers, specifically designed for high challenge storage fire situations, were the first to be designed using this expensive process. In the future, it is possible that other sprinklers will be available for light and ordinary hazard Occupancies with the same suppression concepts. But the expense of testing will need to be outweighed by the advantages of the sprinkler. Selecting a Sprinkler There are four types of sprinklers that can be used in storage occupancies, standard spray sprinklers, large drop sprinklers, specific application control mode sprinklers and ESFR sprinklers. Specific application control mode sprinklers are very similar to large drop sprinklers and will be discussed with large drop sprinklers. Spray sprinklers were developed in the mid- 1950's and have proven themselves to be excellent sprinklers when fire control is the design objective. Table 37-1 shows the different size spray sprinklers that can be used in storage occupancies and some of the terms that have been used to describe them over the years. In the 1994 (and previous) edition of NFPA 13, the sprinklers were referred to by name (standard orifice, large orifice, etc.). During the development of the 1996 edition of NFPA 13, it became apparent that there weren't enough names that could be used to describe the bigger and bigger orifices that were being developed, How do you describe something that is bigger than "very extra large?" So instead, the committee chose to use the nominal orifice size to describe the sprinkler (1/2 inch or 17/32 inch). Unfortunately, the nominal orifice size idea did not work well either. There is nothing actually on a h inch sprinkler that really measures to h inch. So that terminology was dropped as well. What the committee has landed on is just using the k-factor of the sprinkler in order to refer to any specific size of a sprinkler. Name (Used in 1994 and Prior) Standard Lar e Extra Lar e Ver Extra Lar 1<-17 Nominal Size (Used in 1996) 17/32 5/8 Nominal K-Factor (Now Used Exclusively) 5.6 8.0 11.2 14.0 16.8 Table 37-1 Spray Sprinkler Orifice Sizes 544

## Page 551

NFPA 13 does limit thc use of spray sprinklers. The smaller the orifice of the sprinkler, the greater the pressure that is needed to push water out of the sprinkler. When water is discharged from a sprinkler at a high pressure, it breaks up into smaller water droplets when it strikes the deflector and loses much of its momentum. As discussed earlier in this chapter, water droplets need momentum to fight a high challenge fire. Therefore, NFPA 13 does not allow the use of some of the spray sprinklers where higher pressure might be needed to push the water out of the sprinkler. 1<-5.6 sprinklers are only allowed to be used where the design density is 0.2 gpm per sq ft or less. K-8.0 sprinklers are only allowed to be uséd where thc design density is 0.34 gpm per sq ft or less. For any design circumstance where the density requirement is greater than 0.34 gpm per sq ft, K-11.2 or larger spray sprinklers are required. Where spray sprinklers are used to protect storage occupancies, they are generally standard response sprinklers. NFPA 13 allows quick response sprinklers to be used to protect storage only if they are specifically listed for storage. There are a few quick response sprinklers that have been specifically listed for storage, but the majority of sprinklers used to protect storage occupancies are standard response. Large Drop and Specific Application Control Mode Sprinklers A large drop sprinkler is defined by NFPA 13 as, "a type of specific application control mode sprinkler that is capable of producing characteristic large water droplets and that is listed for its capability to provide fire control of specific high challenge fire hazards" (section 3.6.2.3 of NFPA 13-2002). A specific application control mode sprinkler is defined as, "A type of spray sprinkler listed at a minimum operating pressure with a specific number of operating sprinklers for a given protection scheme" (section 3.6.2.12 of NFPA 13-2002). Both large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers increase the mass of the water droplets, thereby increasing their momentum and allowing them to protect higher challenge fires than standard spray sprinklers. While large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers offer the ability to protect more challenging fires than standard spray sprinklers, they are still considered control-mode sprinklers. Large drop sprinklers were actually developed in the 1980's while specific application control mode sprinklers first came into being in the late 1990's and were first recognized in the 2002 edition of NFPA 13. The design criteria in Chapter 12 of NFPA 13 for both large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers is provided in tables that tell the user for any given storage configuration how many sprinklers need to be in the design area and what minimum pressure to apply at the sprinklers. This is distinctly different from standard spray sprinklers which traditionally use density and area to eventually determine how many sprinklers will be in the design area and how much pressure needs to be applied at the sprinkler. In general, the large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers need higher pressures to operate than the standard spray sprinklers, but their design area is generally smaller (contains fewer sprinklers). The total flow demand for the large drop or the specific application control mode sprinklers is then not too different from that needed for standard spray sprinklers. 545

## Page 552

However, since the pressure demand is higher, the water supply sometimes needs to be augmented with a pump. The installation criteria for large drop sprinklers can be found in section 8.11 of NFPA 13. The large drop sprinklers have their own spacing and obstruction criteria which are very different from standard spray sprinklers. One of the differences between large drop sprinklers and standard spray sprinklcrs is thc concept of a minimum arca of protection. Large drop sprinklers are not allowed to be closer than 8 ft from each other and they are not allowed to cover less than 80 sq ft per sprinkler. This can make it extremely difficult to space large drop sprinklers. Specific application control mode sprinklers do not have installation criteria or specific spacing criteria in NFPA 13. Instead, the manufacturer's instructions need to be consulted in order to determine what the installation rules are, Many of the specific application control mode sprinkler instructions send the user back to the large drop installation rules in NFPA 13, but not all of them. The user must be careful to follow all of the special rules in the manufacturer's instructions when using these sprinklers. Large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers are also different from standard spray sprinklers in that they need more than 18 inches of clearance between the top of the storage and the sprirflcler. Large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers need a minimum of 36 inches of clearance. The extra room is necessary for the spray pattern of the sprinkler to develop. Large drop sprinklers are upright sprinklers and the branch line to the sprinkler becomes an obstruction. When the branch line is 2-inch or less in size, it is not considered a problem. But for larger branch lines, a large drop sprinkler needs to be elevated over the pipe or offset to the side. The amount of elevation depends on the size of the branch line. For 2-1/2 inch branch lines, the sprinkler deflector needs to be elevated at least 13 inches over the centerline of the pipe. For branch lines that are 3-inch in size, the sprinkler needs to be elevated at least 15 inches over the centerline of the pipe. During the fire testing of the large drop sprinkler, it was determined that the failure of a single sprinkler to open and discharge water could have devastating effects on the ability of the sprinkler system to control the fire. Therefore, care has to be taken to make sure that sprinklers don't get plugged by pipe scale or debris. Strainers may be needed for water supplies that are questionable in terms of water quality. NFPA 13 requires that steel pipe used in dry-pipe systems with large drop sprinklers be galvanized. Note that this is the only sprinkler system where NFPA 13 requires the use of galvanized pipe for dry-pipe systems, 546

## Page 553

Early Suppression Fast Response (ESFR) Sprinlders ESFR sprinklers are defined by NFPA 13 as, "A type of fast response sprinkler that ... is listed for its capability to provide fire suppression of specific high challenge fire hazards." as described earlier in this text, ESFR sprinklers have been specifically designed to provide fire suppression rather than just fire control. But in order to take advantage of this improvement in perfonnance, the user must be aware that there are a number of design considerations that make it much more difficult to fit ESFR sprinklers into many buildings. The limitations on thc use of ESFR sprinklers are as follows: o Wet pipe systems only o Limited to ceiling construction without deep solid structural members o Ceiling slope is not allowed to exceed 2 in 12 Maximum and minimum spacing mles may make it through to fit the sprinklers into a building o Obstruction mles are difficult to comply with for many ESFR sprinklers If you can handle all of the limitations of using the ESFR sprinklers, there are some distinct advantages. ESFR sprinklers offer fire suppression rather than fire control. The discharge requirements are basically the same regardless of the commodity being protected, so each time the building owner changes what they are storing the system does not have to be redesigned and recalculated. And one of the greatest advantages of the ESFR sprinkler is that it can protect a wide range of rack storage configurations without needing in-rack sprinklers, which makes a lot of building owners very happy. There are a number of different sizes and orientations of ESFR sprinklers in existence. Orifice sizes range from K-14 to K25.2 with many sizes in between. At one time, there was a K- 11.2 ESFR, but it has been withdrawn from the market and is no longer manufactured. Many of the ESFR sprinkler sizes are available in upright and pendent versions, although not all are available both ways and not always from the same manufacturer. ESFR sprinklers are limited to a maximum spacing of 100 sq ft of area per sprinkler and a minimum spacing of 80 sq ft per sprinkler under the 2002 edition of NFPA 13. As of the writing of this text, Factory Mutual has already approved the use of ESFR sprinklers to a minimum of 64 sq ft per sprinkler and NFPA 13 is taking steps to lower its requirement to 64 sq ft per sprinkler as well in its next edition (2007). For most storage configurations, sprinklers are allowed to be installed at a maximum of 12 sq ft and a minimum of 8 ft. However, when the storage height exceeds 25 ft or the building height exceeds 30 ft, the maximum spacing between sprinklers is 10 ft. There is a rule that allows ESFR sprinklers to occasionally be spaced at 11 ft between sprinklers and 110 sq ft per sprinkler, but it cannot be used flaroughout an entire system. This special rule only applies to a limited number of sprinklers in the building. Like the large drop and specific application control mode sprinklers, the ESFR sprinkler needs the extra clearance of 36 inches between the top of storage and the sprinkler deflector. It is extremely important to allow the spray pattern to develop or the sprinkler will not be able to suppress the fire. 547

## Page 554

With respect to obstructions, ESFR sprinklers have their own very stringent obstruction rules. One of the most important rules is that the sprinkler needs to be located at least 12 inches horizontally from the near edge of any bottom flange of any bar joist or truss. ESFR sprinklers are not allowed to be installed in the centerline of a bar joist or truss. Instead, the sprinklers must be offset to the side. The bottom flange of the bar joist or truss, even though it is only a few inches wide, disntpts thc downward momcntum of thc sprinldcr'g spray and causes the sprinkler to be incapable of providing fire suppression. It is very important to keep the sprinkler at least 12 inches away (horizontally) from any bar joist or truss or similar obstinction. Some Basic Definitions Before getting to the requirements and organization of NFPA 13, some basic tern-ns need to be defined. These terms will be used throughout this text and the NFPA standards and need to be understood in order for the documents to make sense. The definitions will be presented in their approximate order of introduction in this text with some commentary following the definitions where appropriate. o Array — Although NFPA 13 does not have a definition for this term, it is simply a vertical stack of a commodity. o Closed Array — A storage arrangement where air movement through the pile is restricted because of 6-inch or less vertical flues (section 3.9.1.1 of NFPA 13 2002). o Open Array — A storage arrangement where air movement through the pile is enhanced because of vertical flues larger than 6 inches (section 3.9.1.2 of NFPA 13-2002). In any storage warehouse where the commodities are stacked on the floor, it is extremely difficult for a building owner to meet the definition of Closed Array. While a closed array does prevent the development of a large fire, it is too difficult to keep all of the spaces between all of the piles as 6 inches or less all of the time. Most piles should be considered as open arrays unless there is some special circumstance that forces the piles to be extremely close together. Solid Piled Storage — Although NFPA 13 does not have a definition for this term, it is simply storage stacked up on the floor with no pallets or aides. Piles can be stable or unstable as defined below, o Stable Piles — Those arrays where collapse, spillage of content, or leaning of stacks across flue spaces is not likely to occur soon after initial fire development (section 3.9.14 of NFPA 13-2002) o Unstable Piles — Those arrays where collapse, spillage of content, or leaning of stacks across flue spaces occurs soon after initial fire development (section 3.9.15 of NFPA 13-2002). All piles of storage will eventually collapse during a fire. The decision as to whether the pile you are trying to protect is "stable" or not depends on a number of variables including the 548

## Page 555

thickness, integrity and combustibility of thc cartons or containers being stacked, the weight of the product in the cartons or containers, and the existence of bands around the outside of the canons or containers to help keep them together. The Icey to the stability definition is whether the piles will collapse "soon after initial fire development" which is fairly early in the fire. When faced with a decision in fire protection, it is always good to try and lean to the more conservative side, so the question should be asked, "Which is the more demanding fire scenario, stable or unstable piles?" The answer is that stable piles are [he more demanding scenario. When a fire occurs with an unstable pipe, the pile tends to collapse and smother the fire or scatter the fuel so it is harder to bum. Also, with fires in unstable piles, when the sprinklers activate, water that falls on top of the pile is directed down towards the fire because the pile always collapses towards the fire, With stable piles, the fuel is held up in the air and sits in a manner much easier for combustion to occur. When sprinklers activate, the water that falls on top of the pile does not get down to actually do anything about the burning surface lower down in the pile. It is much harder for a sprinkler system to control a fire in a stable pile or storage. o Palletized Storage - Storage of commodities on pallets or other storage aids that form horizontal spaces between tiers of storage (section 3.9.13 Of NFPA 13-2002). o Bin-Box Storage - Storage in 5 sided wood, metallic or cardboard boxes with an open face on the aisles. Boxes are self-supporting or supported by a structure with little or no horizontal or vertical space around boxes (section 3.9.3 of NFPA 13-2002). o Shelf Storage - Storage on structures less than 30 inches deep with shelves usually 2 feet apart vertically and separated by approximately 30 inch aisles (section 3.9.17 of NFPA 13-2002). Miscellaneous Storage — Storage that does not exceed 12 ft in height and is incidental to another occupancy use group. Such storage shall not constitute more than 10 percent of the building area or 4000 sq ft of the sprinklered area, whichever is greater. Such storage shall not exceed 1000 sq ft in one pile or area, and each such pile or area shall be separated from other storage areas by at least 25 ft. 549

History of Storage Rules Prior to the 1999 edition of NFPA 13, most of the rules for protection of storage occupancies with sprinklers were not in NFPA 13. The only rules in NFPA 13 regarding storage were some general installation rules (like sprinkler spacing in storage occupancies) and the discharge criteria for a type of storage called "Miscellaneous Storage". The other sprinkler protection rules for storage occupancies were scattered around a bunch of other documents in (he NFPA system includingthe following: •NFPA 231 General Storage •NFPA 23 IC Rack Storage •NFPA 23 ID Rubber Tire Storage •NFPA 23 IE Baled Cotton Storage •NFPA 23 IF Roll Paper Storage The NFPA found that there were a number of problems with having the sprinkler requirements scattered throughout so many documents, so for the 1999 edition of NFPA 13, the other documents were withdrawn and the sprinkler document (and committee såucture to produce the document) were expanded to take in all of the sprinkler requirements for protecting storage. In this 1999 edition of NFPA 13, the discharge criteria for the storage occupancies was added to the discharge criteria for other occupancies, making one very large Chapter 7 in the standard. For the 2002 edition, the discharge criteria was split with the rules for light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies in Chapter 11 and storage occupancies in Chapter 12. Organization of NFPA 13 The installation rules that apply to storage occupancies are scattered throughout the chapters of NFPA 13 and are organized by the subject material. For example, the rules for how many square feet of floor area that can be protected by a single sprinkler riser in a storage occupancy are found in section 8.2 with the rules for how many square feet of floor area that can be protected of light, ordinary and extra hazard occupancies. Likewise, the rules for sprinkler spacing of standard spray sprinklers in storage occupancies can be found in section 8.6 along with the other rules for sprinkler spacing in other occupancies. A short list of these rules is as follows: 08.2 System protection area limitations (high-piled storage only) •Table 8.6.2.2. I(d) Sprinkler spacing limitations (high-piled storage only) 08.11 Large drop sprinklers 08.12 ESFR 08.13 In-Rack Sprinklers 08.15.1,6 In-Rack Sprinkler Control Valves The discharge criteria rules for NFPA 13 can be found in Chapter 12. The chapter is then divided into seven sections that each covers a different aspect of storage. Section 12.1 contains 550

## Page 557

some general rules that apply to all kinds of storage. This section also contains some very specific rules for low piled storage and miscellaneous storage. Section 12.2 contains all of the discharge lilles for protecting solid piled, palletized, bin- box and shelf storage. These four types of storage used to be called "General Storage" by the NFPA and the lules for protecting these types of storage were in NFPA 231. Section 12.2 of 13 still looks a great deal like the old NFPA 231. Section 12.3 contains all of the discharge rules for protecting storage on racks. For some structures that hold up storage, it can be difficult to decide if you should follow the rules in section 12.2 for shelves or 12.3 for racks. Take a look at the definition of shelf storage. If you can meet the definition of shelf storage, then you can use section 12.2. Otherwise, you will probably have to consider the structure of a rack and use section 12.3. The remainder of Chapter 12 covers the following subjects: 012.4 Rubber Tire Storage 012.5 -- Baled Cotton Storage 012.6 — Roll Paper Storage 012.7 — Special Designs Section 12.1 of NFPA 13 — General Rules As stated above, section 12.1 has some general rules that apply to all storage configurations as well as some special rules that only apply to low piled storage and to miscellaneous storage. Our discussion in this text will begin with rules that apply to all sprinklers. Roof Vents and Draft Curtains NFPA 13 starts off with the assumption that roof vents and draft curtains will not be present in the building (see section 12.1.1 and C.6 in NFPA 13-2002). Full-scale fire tests have shown that when roof vents and/or draft curtains are present in a building, the number of sprinklers that will open in a fire can exceed the number of sprinklers in the design area, sometimes by more than 100%. The rules in NFPA 13, specifically the rules on the number of sprinklers that will open in a fire (design area or remote area) are based on full-scale fire testing without roof vents and draft stops. When such devices are present, the number of sprinklers that will open during a fire is unknown. The criteria in the standard are only valid for those situations where none of these devices are present. 551

## Page 558

Large Drop and ESER Sprinklers Interestingly, this is the place where we find that large drop and ESFR sprinklers are allowed to protect ordinary hazard occupancies. You might expect to find this information in Chapter 11 of NFPA 13 because that is where the ordinary hazard rules are, but actually, it is in section 12.1.2.3. This section is important because it is fairly common to find combination industrial/storage occupancies where there is some manufacturing or production process going on with storage of raw materials at one end of the process and storage of a finished product at the other end. ESFR sprinklers can obviously protect the storage at both ends of the facility, but plan review authorities frequently question whether or not the ESFR sprinklers can be used to protect the manufacturing process, which is typically ordinary hazard. The use of ESFR sprinklers tlu•oughout the facility is a good idea because it gives the building owner the flexibility to move their storage and manufacturing positions around without having to redesign the sprinkler system. And, according to this section, there is no problem with using the ESFR sprinklers in this manner. Hose Connections Section 12.1.3 of NFPA 13 states that all storage occupancies are to have small hose connections, The connections are intended to be 1-1/2 inch connections for basic first aid and mop-up operations. They are not intended to be standpipe systems, but just small hoses connected to the sprinkler system piping. Chapter 8 of NFPA 13 (section 8.16.5) contains details on how to make the connection to the sprinkler piping. But section 12.2.2.1.3 contradicts section 12.1.3 slightly. Section 12.2.2.1.3 states that hose connections are not required for solid piled, palletized, bin-box and shelf storage of Class I- IV commodities that are stored 12 ft or less in height. This kind of contradiction is not unusual in NFPA 13. Often, statements in general sections are contradicted by more specific statements in portions of the standard that apply to specific situations. While this is not optimum writing style, it is clear that in the specific case of low-piled storage in the specified configurations, hose connections are not intended to be required by NFPA 13. For wet pipe sprinkler systems, it is easy to just connect the hose station to the closest sprinkler main. But for dry-pipe sprinkler systems, it is a bit more difficult to connect the hose station to the sprinkler piping. Section 8.16.5 of NFPA 13 only allows the hose station piping to be connected to water-filled piping. For dry-pipe systems, the hose is not permitted to be connected to the air-filled piping because it is difficult to keep the air from leaking out the hose nozzle, which would cause frequent false trips of the dry-pipe valve. So, for cold storage areas, the hose stations are still required, but they have to be piped back to the water supply outside the cold area separate from the dry-pipe sprinkler system. Where hose stations are connected to the sprinkler system piping, the hydraulic calculations are effected. Each hose station is considered potentially responsible for taking 50 552

## Page 559

gpm of flow in addition to the sprinkler demand. For hydraulic calculation purposes, Table 11.2.3.1.1 of NFPA 13 requires that a maximum of two hose stations (100 gpm) be added to the sprinkler system flow with 50 gpm added at each of the two most demanding connections. It does not matter. how many hose stations are connected to the sprinkler system, the maximum amount of flow that we add to the hydraulic calculations is 50 gpm at the most remote connection and 50 gpm at the second most remote connection. Adiacent Hazards When two different commodities classifications or storage configurations are next to each other, NFPA 13 gives the user three options as to how to handle the sprinkler system. The first option is to design the entire fire protection system for the higher hazard, This gives the owner of the building the maximum flexibility in moving the storage piles wherever they want. The second option is to segregate the storage so that the higher hazard commodity or configuration is confined to one area while the lower hazard commodity is confined to a different area. The sprinkler system basically needs to be designed so that the sprinklers at the ceiling protect whatever is below them. However, for the sprinkler system over the higher hazard to be limited to just the ceiling directly over the higher hazard, there needs to be some physical separation between the two different hazards. NFPA 13 does not require any specific fire resistance rating, but does require a "barrier or partition capable of delaying heat from a fire in one area from fusing sprinklers in the adjacent area" if the sprinklers at the ceiling are to be limited to being just above the higher hazard. The type of partition or barrier necessary for this Lille is a judgment call based on the hazard being protected. The concern with using this option is that the higher hazard material needs to be kept in the segregated area, If any piles of the higher hazard commodity end up in the lower hazard area, a fire could get out of control. The third option is to segregate the storage areas without any kind of barrier or partition. For this option to work, NFPA 13 requires that the higher hazard sprinkler design be carried 15 ft into the perimeter of the lower hazard design to account for heat from the higher hazard from migrating into the lower hazard space and opening remote sprinklers, Design Area Increases For dry-pipe sprinkler systems, NFPA 13 requires that design areas (for standard spray sprinklers) protecting storage occupancies be increased by 30%. This is the same as dry-pipe systems for other hazards like light and ordinary hazard. While many of the fire tests that were performed to develop the criteria for protecting storage commodities were only done with wet- pipe systems, experience has shown that the 30% increase is sufficient for most configurations of storage. Preaction systems protecting storage are handled much differently than preaction systems protecting light or ordinary hazard occupancies. For light and ordinary hazard occupancies, the 30% increase only applies to double-interlock preaction systems, but for storage occupancies, the 553

## Page 560

30% increase applies equally to all preaction sprinkler systems including single-interlock systems and non-interlocking systems. There is an exception to the lille that will allow single- interlock systems to avoid the 30% increase to the design area. This exception requires the designer to calculate the time it takes for water to be delivered to the remote sprinkler. If water can get from the preaction valve to the remote sprinkler within the time lag between when the detector trips the preaction valve and when the sprinkler opens, then the design area does not need to be increased, In other words, if the detectors are much more sensitive than the sprinklers, the water will have the time to get to the sprinkler before it opens and the system will respond just like a wet pipe system and can be treated as such. Another common increase to design areas is for sloped systems. For light and ordinary hazards, NFPA 13 requires an increase of 30% to the design area to make up for extra sprinklers that open when the heat from a fire travels up the slope and openssprinklers remote from the fire. However for storage occupancies, there isn't enough data to know whether the 30% increase is sufficient to protect the commodity and configuration. It is entirely possible that even more sprinklers will open. Since there isn't enough information to determine how many sprinklers will open, section 12.1.7 warns the user that the design criteria from NFPA 13 is appropriate to use if the ceiling slope exceeds 2 in 12. What do you do if you encounter a storage commodity where the ceiling pitch exceeds 2 in 12? The answer is that you have two choices. Install a false ceiling that is level and put the sprinklers below the false ceiling, or find a fire protection engineer that is willing to provide design criteria without guidance from NFPA 13. Such criteria might come from fire tests, fire modeling or engineering experience. Idle Pallets There is an old saying that, "Idle hands are the devil's workshop." For fire protection, that phrase could be modified to say, "Idle pallets are the devil's workshop." It is hard to imagine a more efficient fuel source for a fire. If you were going to design an of fuel that maximizes the ability of fuel and oxygen to combine, and makes it most difficult to get water into the commodity, you would end up with an arrangement that looks exactly like a pile of pallets. Often, the most challenging situation from a fire protection perspective is not the storage commodity itself in a building, but the pile of empty pallets that are sitting around the warehouse. The rules for protecting pallets depend on what the pallets are made of. Pallets can be made of wood or plastic. If they are made from plastic they can be reinforced or unreinforced. The optimum place to store idle pallets is outside. If they have to be stored indoors, the next best option is in a building of their own. If they have to be stored in the same building as the rest of the storage, the following rules apply (only one of the options needs to be selected): o Idle wood pallets can be protected with standard spray sprinklers designed to discharge the density for the commodity and configuration they are protecting if the pallets are limited to 6 ft in height and the piles are limited to four stacks in a pile and each pile is separated by at least 8 ft of clear space or 25 ft of comrnodity. 554

Idle wood pallets can be protected with standard spray sprinklers designed to discharge in accordance with Table 12.1.9.1.2(a) Idle wood pallets can be protected with control mode specific application sprinklers in accordance with Table 12.1.9.1.2(b) Idle wood pallets can be protected with ESFR sprinklers in accordance with Table 12.1.9.1.2@) Idle plastic pallets can be protected in a cut-off room (separated by 3-hour fire walls from the rest of the building) in accordance with section 12.1.9.2.2(1) Idle plastic pallets can be protected without a cut-off room in accordance with 12.1.9.2.2(2) Idle plastic pallets can be protected with k-16.8 spray sprinklers (and no cut-off room) in accordance with section 12.1.9.2.1(5) Idle plastic pallets can be protected with ESFR sprinklers (and no cut-off room) in accordance with Table 12.1.9.2.1 High Expansion Foam For many storage occupancies, the ceiling sprinkler density can be dramatically reduced if a high expansion foam system is installed. Section 12.1.11 contains some 'general information that the foam system would have to meet. In general, the system would need to be designed to meet NFPA 1 IA. NFPA allows the ceiling sprinkler densities for many commodities to be reduced by 50% as long as the density does not go lower than 0.15 gpm per sq ft. For most commodities, the rules of NFPA IIA apply for submergence times, But for idle pallet protection, the foam system must fill the space in no morc than 4 minutes. Spray Sprinkler Limitations NFPA 13 limits the use of smaller orifice size spray sprinklers (section 12.1, 13) in order to assure that the water droplets discharging from the sprinkler have sufficient momentum to penetrate the fire plume. As the density that the sprinkler needs to discharge increases, the pressure that the sprinkler needs to operate at increases. At high pressures, the water leaves the orifice of the sprinkler and strikes the deflector with so much velocity that it breaks the water up into tiny little droplets. Since momentum is a product of mass times velocity, a sprinkler spray pattern with tiny little water droplets does not have much momentum because each of the droplets has little mass. The use of spray sprinklers with a k-factor of 5.6 is limited in new sprinkler systems to those systems that need a discharge density of 0.2 gpm per sq ft or less to protect the storage. At this low density, the pressure will be reasonable and the sprinkler will be able to produce water droplets with sufficient momentum. Existing systems (and modifications to existing systems) are allowed to keep their k-5.6 sprinklers even if the density required is greater than 0.2 gpm per sq ft. 555

## Page 562

Similarly, the use of k-8.0 spray sprinklers is limited in new sprinkler systems to those systems that need a discharge density of 0.34 gpm per sq ft or less to protect storage. As with the other types of sprinklers, existing systems (and modifications to existing systems) are allowed to remain in service even if the design discharge is required to be greater than 0.34 gpm per sq ft. if the discharge density for a new sprinkler system is required Io be greater than 0.34 gpm per sq ft, the sprinklers are required to have a k-factor of 11.2 or higher, Such sprinklers are also required to be specifically listed for storage occupancies. These are the types of sprinklers that have been specifically designed to create the momentum of the water droplets that will work best for storage. Jn addition to the orifice size, section 12.1.13 of NFPA 13 also restricts the use of quick response sprinklers for protecting storage. Quick response sprinklers can be used to protect storage only if they have been specifically tested and listed for storage protection. By referencing curves in Figure 12.1.10 rather than ordinary and extra hazard, the committee has set up a situation where many of the rules for protecting miscellaneous storage and low piled storage are no longer clear. While it appears that the committee was just trying to isolate Chapter 12 from Chapter 11, the decision had unintended consequences. Many of the other rules in NFPA rely on the determination of a hazard classification. For the correct combination of storage and ceiling heights, the table gives the user the minimum pressure for each type of ESFR sprinkler. Since the 2002 edition of NFPA 13 was published, there have been a few additional ESFR sprinklers manufactured that are not in the table. For these new ESFR sprinklers, use the manufacturer's special listing for design pressure. When ESFR sprinklers are used with Table 12.2.2.3.1, the design area is always 12 sprinklers. The design area will be 4 sprinklers on the tlu•ee most remote branch lines. The k- factor of the sprinkler times the square root of the pressure from the table will provide the minimum flow that needs to discharge from each sprinkler. For example, for the protection of a storage facility for palletized Class III commodity stored up to 20 ft in height in a 25 ft high building protected by a wet pipe sprinkler system with k-25.2 ESFR sprinklers, the minimum pressure will be 15 psi, the hose stream demand (total inside and outside) is 250 gpm and the water supply duration is 60 minutes (1 hr). The flow demand from the sprinklers will be a minimum of 97.6 gpm (25.2 times the square root of 15 psi) from each sprinkler. Protection of Group A Plastics Just like Class I through IV commodities, plastics can be protected with spray sprinklers, large drop sprinklers, specific application control mode sprinklers or ESFR sprinklers. The decision is up to the designer of the sprinkler system. Group A Plastics with Spray Sprinklers When protecting Group A plastics stored in solid piled or palletized arrays with spray sprinklers, the user gets the sprinkler discharge criteria from Table 12,2.3.1,6. Note that Table has five columns labeled A, B, C, D and E. In order to know which is the correct column to use, the designer needs to use the Plastics Decision Tree (Figure 12.2.3,1.1). By starting at the top and working down through the decision tree, the user arrives at the correct column to use. 560

## Page 567

When using Table 12.2.3.1.6, the user needs to find the combination of storage and ceiling heights that would routinely or periodically exist that cause the worse-case density and the sprinkler system needs to be able to provide this worse-case density. For many storage configurations, the worse-case density occurs with the highest pile of storage, but that is not true for Table 12.2.3.1.6. It is quite possible that lower storage heights actually need more water than taller storage arrays. This occurs because Group A plastics produce a plume (hot gasses rising from a fire) with significant vertical momentum. With 10 or 15 ft of clearance (distance from top of storage to the ceiling), the discharge from a sprinkler needs to fight down through that plume, whereas when the clearance is only 5 ft, the plume pushes against the ceiling and changes to a horizontal direction. The discharge from a sprinkler can make it through a horizontal plume easier than through a vertical plume. Consider palletized storage of non-expanded-stable-cartoned Group A plastics stored 25 ft high in a 30 ft building. According to Figure 12.2.3.1.1, this storage would have to be protected with Column C. According to Column C, the density for 25 ft high storage in a 30 ft high building would need to be protected with a density of 0.55 gpm per sq ft. However, wherever there is 25 ft high storage in a 30 ft high building, there is also the significant possibility that there will be 20 ft high storage in the same 30 ft high building. For 20 ft high storage in a 30 ft high building, the density needs to be 0.7 gpm per sq ft, significantly higher than the 0.55 for 25 ft storage. So, the sprinkler system should be designed with a density of 0.7, not 0.55. Once the density is known, the design area will be one of three possibilities. For closed arrays (less than 6 inches between piles), the design area is 2000 sq ft. For open arrays (more than 6 inches between piles) the design area is 2500 sq ft. Since it is very difficult to maintain closed an•ays, the open array rules (2500 sq ft) should be used unless the owner can guarantee that the closed atray can always be maintained. The third option for design area only exists where "Curve 3" is referenced by Table 12.2.3.1.6, in which case the design area is allowed to be any area that corresponds to the density selected from Figure 12.1. IO. Group A Plastics and Large Drop and Specific Application Sprinklers Where Group A plastics are protected with large drop or specific application control mode sprinklers, the rules are very similar to the rules discussed above for protection of Class I through IV commodities protected with these same kind of sprinklers. The only difference in protecting Group A plastics is that the table for design criteria is different. For large drop sprinklers, the correct table to use is Table 12.2.3.2.1(a). For specific application control mode sprinklers, 'the correct table to use is Table 12.2.3.2. I(b). 561

The only difference in protecting Group A plastics is that the table for design criteria is different. The correct table to use is Table 12.2.3.3.1. Rack Storage Section 12.3 of NFPA 13 applies to the protection of storage on racks. The section is broken up into subsections based on type of conmodity being protected and the maximum height of storage for that commodity as follows: 0 12.3.1 General rules for all rack storage facilities 0 12.3.2 Protection of Class I-IV Commodities up to 25 ft in height 0 12.3.3 Protection of Group A plastics stored up to 25 ft in height 0 12.3.4 Protection of Class I-IV commodities stored over 25 ft in height 0 12.3.5 Protection of Group A plastics stored over 25 ft in height Within each of the subsections, the rules for protection of single-row racks, double-row racks and multiple-row racks will be provided. Also, within each subsection, the rules for use of spray sprinklers, large drop sprinklers, specific application control mode sprinklers and ESFR sprinklers will be provided. General Criteria for Rack Storage The rules for thc protection of rack storage include a discussion of what to do with solid shelving in the racks. The basic rules of section 12.3 assume that the racks are open. If the racks have solid shelving that is 20 sq ft or less in area, they can be treated as open racks. Ifthe solid shelves exceed 20 sq ft, but are 64 sq ft or less in area, the rules of open shelf racks can be used, but additional in-rack sprinklers need to be installed 6 ft apart vertically. Where the shelving exceeds 64 sq ft in area, additional in-rack sprinklers need to be installed below every shelf, even if the shelves are very close together vertically. See section 12.3.1.9 for more information. Another of the rules covered in the General section applies to the protection of steel columns in the rack area. The designer needs to make sure that one of the following methods are used to protect the steel columns: Fireproof the columns Install sidewall sprinklers at the 15 ft level spraying at one side of the column Provide the minimum density from the ceiling sprinklers as indicated in Table 12.3.1.7.1. The design area in this case shall be 2000 sq ft. Use large drop, specific application control mode or ESFR sprinklers Use in-rack sprinklers (see section 12.4.1.2 in the rubber tire section) 562

Class I-IV Commodities and Spray Sprinklers For spray sprinklers that are protecting Class I through TV commodities stored on racks, there is a table in each section of the standard that provides information on the density and area to use for the discharge criteria. Each table also provides information on whether or not in-rack sprinklers are required. For storage 25 ft or less in height, the table directs the user to an arca/density curve. For storagc over 25 ft in height, the user is given an area/density directly in the table. The tables also give the user information on possible adjustments that need to be made to the density based on the storage height. Although not in the tables, the narrative in the sections includes changes to the discharge requirements based on certain conditions and increases in the design area for dry-pipe and preaction systems, Where additional in-rack sprinklers are installed over and above those required to protect the commodity, a reduction in the discharge requirements to the ceiling sprinklers is allowed, The reduction depends on how many additional in-rack sprinklers are installed. The reductions are based on the more efficient delivery of water directly to the fire through the in-rack sprinklers. The following tables contain the discharge criteria for each situation: o Table 12.3.2.1.2 for single and double row racks with storage up to 25 ft o Table 12.3.2.1.3 for easy to protect multiple row racks with storage up to 25 ft o Table 12,3.2.1.4 for harder to protect multiple row racks with storage up to 25 ft Table 12.3.4.1.1 for single and double row racks with storage over 25 ft Table 12.3.4.1.3 for multiple row racks with storage over 25 ft Group A Plastics with Spray Sprinklers For the protection of Group A plastics with spray sprinklers for storage up to 25 ft in height, there are a series of figures in section 12.3.3. The user needs to determine which of the figures 12.3.3.1.5(a) through 12.3.3.1.5(f) that most closely resembles the storage they are trying to protect. Each of the different figures represents a different combination of storage height and ceiling height in 5 ft increments. The user needs to pick the figure that gets as close as possible to the actual scenario. Each of the figures contains a plan view and an elevation view along with written information above the plan view and notes below the figure. The elevation view shows how many levels of in-rack sprinklers are required (if any). The plan view shows how far to place the in-rack sprinklers apart horizontally (if any). For many of the figures, the user is given several choices of options. In most of the options, there are single-row racks, double-row racks and two different configurations of multiple-row racks. For a few of the choices, multiple-row racks are not shown, because they are not permitted to be protected with that option. Above the plan view for each option is the information on the ceiling sprinkler design. The notes at the bottom of the figure give additional information and in some cases, additional options are presented. 563

For the protection of Group A plastics stored greater than 25 ft in height, the ceiling sprinkler density is given in Table 12,3.5.1.1 and depends on the height of storage above the highest level of in-rack sprinklers in the rack structure. When the storage is only 5 ft above the highest level of in-rack sprinklers, the ceiling density is 0.3 gpm per sq ft over 2000 sq ft. When the storage is up to 10 ft over the highest level of in-rack sprinklers, the density is 0.45 gpm per sq ft over 2000 sq ft. If there is more than 10 ft above the highest level of in-rack sprinklers, additional in-rack sprinklers need to be added until the storage is 10 ft or less above the highest level of in-racks. Section 12.3.5.4.1.4 contains a new option for protecting storage over 25 ft in height of Group A plastics on single and double-row racks with no solid shelves. In order to use this protection, the aisles cannot be less than 4 ft wide and the ceiling sprinklers need to be designed for a minimum of 0.45 gpm per sq ft over 2000 sq ft. A level of in-rack sprinklers needs to be installed in every other tier of storage at the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse flues (approximately 5 ft apart). The advantage to this option is that there are no face sprinklers required. This protection option is for a maximum storage height of 54 ft and a maximum building height of 60 ft. See the Formal Interpretation on this protection option explained in the January/February 2005 edition of Sprinkler TechNotes for more information on the dimensions in Figure 12.3.5.4.1.4. Additional special arrangements for protecting Group A plastics with spray sprinklers can be found in section 12.7. CHAPTER 38 RACK STORAGE Rack storage was discussed considerably in the last chapter of this text. In this chapter, the subject will be discussed specifically with the focus of making the dccision as to whether or not sprinklers should be installed in the racks. If the decision is made to put sprinklers in the racks, the spacing requirements along with the hydraulic calculation requirements will also be discussed. This chapter is an excellent study guide for NICET •Work element 14006 and good general information for anyone involved in providing fire protection for storage warehouses. More in-depth information can be found in the NFSA publication, Sprinkler Protection for Warehouse and Storage Occupancies. Definitions Some of these definitions were covered in the previous chapter in this text, but it is important that the user be familiar with these terms, so they are repeated here for ease of reference. All of these definitions come from NFPA 13-2002 edition. The section numbers at the end of each definition are the references to the section numbers in NFPA 13. Single-Row Racks: Racks that have no longitudinal flue space and that have a width up to 6 ft with aisles at least 3.5 ftfrom other storage (3.10.8.5). See Figure 38-1 for an example of single- row racks in the plan view of a warehouse. Double-Row Racks: Two single-row racks placed back to back having a combined width up to 12 ft with aisles at least 3.5 ft on each side (3.10.8.1). See Figure 33-2 for an example of double- row racks in the plan view of a warehouse. 575

Aisles less than 3.5 ft Figure 38-4 Multiple-Row Racks in Plan View (Aisles Less Than 3.5ft Wide) Longitudinal Flue Space: The space between rows of storage perpendicular to the direction of loading (3.10.7). Transverse Flue Space: The space between rows of storage parallel to the direction of loading (3.10.11). The longitudinal and transverse flue spaces run perpendicular to each other in the plan view of a rack structure. See Figure 38-5 for an example (in plan view) of longitudinal flue spaces between double-row racks and transverse flue spaces between loads on the racks. The longitudinally flue spaces are indicated with an "L" and the transverse flue spaces are indicated with a "T". The square in the rack structure represents a pallet load on the rack. 578

## Page 585

Direction of Loadin "L" = Longitudinal Flue Space "T" = Transverse Flue Space Figure 38-5 Longitudinal and Transverse Flue Spaces in Double-Row Racks (Plan View) Flue spaces represent challenges for fire protection systems. On the one hand, flue spaces provide a chimney for the hot gasses to escape from the fire and pre-heat combustibles on the way to the ceiling, allowing the fire to grow and spread. On the other hand, flue spaces allow water from the sprinklers that activate near the ceiling to get down through the rack structure and control the fire. Therefore, flue spaces are both helpful and hurtful to fire protection, which explains why NFPA 13 has a schizophrenic attitude when it comes to flue spaces. In some cases NFPA 13 tries to mandate the flue spaces be present, and in other cases, NFPA 13 requires barriers across the flue spaces to prevent the fire from moving up the rack structure. In general, flue spaces are required where ceiling sprinklers are expected to assist in providing fire control (where in-rack sprinklers are not installed or where in-rack sprinklers alone will not be able to control the fire). But in situations where the in-rack sprinklers are sufficient to deal with the fire in the rack structure, the barriers are required to prevent the spread of the fire above the activated in-rack sprinklers. Where solid shelves exist within the racks, blocking flue spaces, in-rack sprinklers need to be added beneath the solid shelves. Section 12.3.1.9 of NFPA 13 allows a solid shelf up to 20 sq ft in area (between flue spaces) to be treated as an open rack and the protection criteria is not required to have any additional sprinklers. If the solid shelf is between 20 and 64 sq ft in area, 579

## Page 586

then additional in-rack sprinklers need to be added to the rack structure at 6 ft intervals, but not necessarily under every shelf. For example, if 4 ft x 8 ft sheets of plywood (32 sq ft) were being installed on the racks at 2 ft vertical increments, in-rack sprinklers would only be required under each third shelf. Only when the area of the shelf exceeds 64 sq ft are sprinklers required under every shelf. pros and Cons of In-Rack Sprinklers There are advantages and disadvantages to installing in-rack sprinklers. The final decision as to whether or not in-rack sprinklers will be installed belongs to the designer of the sprinkler system. Some combinations of storage configurations and commodities are required to be protected with in-rack sprinklers, but many are not. Additional in-rack sprinklers may be installed beyond what is required by NFPA 13 (or another standard like NFPA 30). It will be up to the designer to decide if in-rack sprinklers are going to be installed in any given situation. The advantages of installing in-rack sprinklers include: In-rack sprinklers deliver water closer to where the fire is, The water droplets do not need to fight tlu•ough the fire plume (hot gasses from the fire) to get to the burning surface. In-rack sprinklers are less obstructed by the stored commodity above the fire than the ceiling sprinklers. In-rack sprinklers require less discharge to control the fire than ceiling sprinklers, allowing the discharge from the ceiling sprinklers to be reduced and making the overall fire protection system more efficient, In-rack sprinklers provide some redundancy so that if there is a problem with the ceiling sprinklers, there is still a mechanism to get water on a fire in the racks. Given all of the nice things discussed above regarding in-rack sprinklers you might wonder why they are not installed in every case. The reason is that there are a number of negative aspects to in-rack sprinklers as well, including: e In-rack sprinklers add cost to a system (materials and labor) o The existence of in-rack sprinklers makes it more difficult for a building owner (or operator) to move their racks around if they need to make changes to their rack configurations. In-rack sprinklers have the potential to be damaged if they are struck while products are being moved in or out of the racks. Such damage might be costly to maintain and possibly could lead to water damage if the in-rack sprinkler opens after being struck. When all of the pros and cons are weighed, most people agree that although in-rack sprinklers provide superior fire protection, they should be avoided if possible due to the problems discussed above. Building owners go to great lengths to avoid the installation of in- 580

## Page 587

rack sprinklers. However, there are some circumstances where it is just not possible to protect a given commodity in the configuration desired without in-rack sprinklers. In these cases) the building owner has no choice. One of the reasons that ESFR sprinklers were developed was to try and protect extremely challenging commodities and configurations without in-rack sprinklers. Group A Plastics stored very high in a building on multiple-row racks are one such example of a challenging commodity that can bc protcctcd with ESFR sprinklcrs and no in-rack sprinklers as long as the racks are open (no solid shelves) and the flue spaces are maintained. There are a few commodities and storage heights that do need in-rack sprinklers when ESFR sprinklers are used at the ceiling, but in these cases, fewer in-rack sprinklers are required as compared to ceiling protection with standard spray sprinklers. How Do You Know If In-Rack Sprinklers are Required? We have already discussed one situation where in-rack sprinklers are required, where solid shelves have an area greater than 20 sq ft between flue spaces. There are a number of other situations where NFPA 13 requires in-rack sprinklers to be installed. In addition to NFPA 13, there are other standards with sprinkler criteria including NFPA 30 (Flammable and Conibustible Liquids) and NFPA 30B (Aerosols) where in-rack sprinklers are required. This text will only deal with NFPA 13 since the other standards are more advanced. For sprinkler systems using standard spray sprinklers at the ceiling, there are a series of tables within NFPA 13 that tell the user where in-rack sprinklers are required. The requirement for in-rack sprinklers depends on the configuration of the storage (single, double or multiple-row racks), the height of the storage and the commodity being stored. Table 38-1 summarizes where NFPA 13 contains the requirement for in-rack sprinklers to be installed. 581

In order to answer this question, you need to consider two variables, the vertical spacing and the horizontal spacing. The vertical spacing will vary with the height of the rack structure, the commodity being stored and the number of levels of sprinklers required for the conditions or desired to maximize the efficiency of water delivery. The horizontal spacing will vary based on the length of the rack structure, the distance between the rack uprights and the commodity being protected. It should be noted that none •of the rules for spacing of ceiling sprinklers apply to the spacing and location of in-rack sprinklers, Therefore, the rule about keeping sprinklers at least 6 ft apart does not apply to in-rack sprinklers. In fact, in-rack sprinklers may need to be much 583

closer than 6 ft and this is not a problem because the spray from one in-rack sprinkler should not prevent the one next to it from activating if the fire is close enough to that sprinkler. Likewise, the obstruction criteria for spray sprinklers at the ceiling does not apply to in- rack sprinklers. The rules discussed below for vertical and horizontal placement of the sprinklers will outline what obstruction criteria does apply to in-rack sprinklers. In general, the rules are much more relaxed than what is required for ceiling sprinklers. Vertical Spacing of In-Rack Sprinklers The best place to start with vertical spacing is to review the requirements for a number of levels as discussed above. For many in-rack sprinkler situations, only one level of in-rack sprinklers is required. But in other situations, additional levels are required because of the commodity, the height of the rack or the presence of solid shelves. Tables 33-1 and 33-2 discussed above direct the user to the places in NFPA 13 that contain the basic requirements for the number of levels of in-rack sprinklers. Earlier in this chapter of this text, the concept of solid shelves was discussed. For some solid shelf situations, in-rack sprinklers are required every 6 ft veltically in the rack structure. For other solid shelf situations, in-rack sprinklers are required under every solid shelf. After detemining the number of levels of in-rack sprinklers that need to be installed, the user needs to decide if they want to add extra levels of in-rack sprinklers. While extra levels of in-rack sprinklers cost more to install, they increase the efficiency of the delivery of water to the fire and sometimes allow the decrease of the requirements for the ceiling sprinklers. See sections 12.3.2.1.5.3 through 12.3.2.1.5.6 and Table 12.3.2.1.5.3 in NFPA 13 for examples of situations where NFPA 13 permits the decrease of the ceiling sprinkler density requirements when extra (more than required) levels of in-rack sprinkler systems are installed. After determining the number of in-rack sprinklers that will be installed, the user then needs to decide exactly where the sprinklers will be located. When only one level of in-rack sprinklers is installed, the sprinklers should be approximately half-way up the rack structure (see Figure 33-6). When two levels of in-rack sprinklers are going to be installed, the sprinklers should be approximately one-third of the way up the rack and two-thirds of the way up the racks (see Figure 33-7). Where more than two levels of in-rack sprinklers are going to be installed, they are generally split evenly throughout the racks, or NFPA 13 will direct the user to a specific vertical spacing through tables or figures. See Table 12.3.4.1.1 in NFPA 13 for an example of in-I?Ck sprinkler placement for different protection scenarios where the second column of the table tells the user how to space in-rack sprinklers vertically. See Figures 12.3.5.4.1.3(a) through (f) for examples of in-rack placement being shown in the Elevation View of the figures. 584

There are three different sets of rules that need to be followed, and at times they appear to contradict each other. The first set of rules concerns maximum allowable distances between sprinklers. NFPA 13 states for most commodities what the maximum allowable horizontal distance is between sprinklers. For 586

## Page 593

example, Table 12.3,2.4.2.1 in NFPA 13 provides information on the maximum allowable horizontal distance between in-rack sprinklers where Class I through IV cornmodities are being stored under 25 ft in height, The maximum allowable distance is usually 12 ft, but goes down to 8 ft for Class III commodity where the racks are only separated by 4 ft aisles and for all protection of Class IV commodity. The second set of lilles that applies to the horizontal spacing of sprinklers discusses the maximum allowablc arca that any sihglc sprinkler is allowed to covcr. Similar to ceiling sprinklers, some commodities and storage anangements have a special rule that states that in- rack sprinklers are not allowed to cover more than a certain area within the rack, When calculating this area, it is only the area of the rack that is considered and not the floor area of the aisles. For example, section 12.3.2.4.2.2 requires that in-rack sprinklers for protection of Class I, II or III commodity on multiple-row racks are not permitted to cover more than 100 sq ft of rack structure. Likewise, for Class IV commodities on multiple-row racks, the same section in NFPA 13 states that in-rack sprinklers are not permitted to cover more than 80 sq ft. This means that even though Table 12.3.2.4.2.1 might allow 12 ft spacing horizontally between in-rack sprinklers protecting a Class II commodity in a multiple-row rack, the sprinklers are not allowed to be spaced 12 ft in both directions since that would constitute 144 sq ft of area protected by the sprinkler. The sprinklers would need to be closer than 12 ft in one or both directions in order to comply with the 100 sq ft maximum. The third set of rules that helps determine the horizontal spacing of in-rack sprinklers is in the figures of NFPA 13. For many storage configurations, NFPA 13 states that in-rack sprinklers need to be installed in the locations shown in the figures. The figures represent typical pallet loads which are usually squares about 4 ft wide. Leaving some room for flue spaces around the loads, the distance between flue spaces is usually 4.5 to 5 ft. When putting sprinklers in the flue spaces, the maximum spacing limitations discussed above are always met by just following the figures. See Figure 12.3.3.1.5(f) in NFPA 13 for an example of in-rack sprinkler placement by a figure. In the double-row rack scenario on this figure, two levels of in-rack sprinklers are provided, The top row (represented by the "o") is located in the longitudinal flue space and sprinklers are placed at the intersection with every other transverse flue, making them approximately 9 ft apart. The bottom row (represented by the "x") is also located in the longitudinal flue with sprinklers at the intersection with every other transverse flue (the opposite transverse flue as the top level), so those sprinklers are also approximately 9 ft apart. As long as the pallet loads are approximately 4 ft wide; this protection scheme works very well. The problem is trying [o decide what to do when the pallet loads arc more than 5 ft wide, Consider 25 ft storage of Group A plastics on double-row racks in a 35 ft high building with pallet loads that are approximately 6 ft wide. Figure 12.3.3.1.5(f) is still the correct figure to use to determine in-rack sprinkler location, but if the pallet loads are 6 ft wide, and if the in- rack sprinklers are located horizontally in every other transverse flue intersection, then the sprinkler will be slightly more than 12 ft apart. Which rule becomes the most important, the maximum spacing or getting sprinkler at the intersection of the transverse and longitudinal flue? The answer is that it depends on the commodity and configuration. Since fire moves to the flue spaces and then up through the racks, full-scale fire tests have shown that locating the in-rack sprinklers at the intersection of the transverse and longitudinal flues is the most effective placement of the sprinklers. But fire tests have also shown that if these sprinklers are placed too far apart, a fire in the middle can grow up the flue space without any direct water spray and never encounter an in-rack sprinkler. Different portions of NFPA 13 address this problem in different ways; there is no clear answer to the question. Judgment needs to be used when deciding to place the sprinklers. Future editions of NFPA 13 may state a maximum horizontal spacing for in-rack sprinklers and at the same time, may require that in-rack sprinklers be installed at the intersection of the flue spaces. If the flue spaces are too far apart to meet the maximum spaces, then the sprinklers will need to be installed at the intersection of the flue spaces and at locations in between the flue spaces to meet the maximum spacing criteria. One other item on horizontal spacing of in-rack sprinklers needs to be discussed. Earlier in this section, we used the double-row rack portion of Figure 12.3.3.1.5(f) as an example of how to locate two levels of in-rack sprinklers. We noted how the top level of sprinklers was located in every other transverse flue while the bottom level of in-rack sprinklers was also located in every other transverse flue, but that they were offset so that no flue had sprinklers from both levels. It also works out that every transverse flue has one sprinkler at some level. This concept of offsetting the placement of different levels of in-rack sprinklers so that every transverse flue is covered by some level is called "staggering" in-rack sprinklers. The concept of staggering was developed so that a fire could not burn all the way up a transverse flue space from the bottom to the top without eventually encountering an in-rack sprinkler. For storage over 25 ft in height, staggering takes place on multiple levels so that the fire cannot burn too far up the rack without encountering an in-rack sprinkler in every transverse flue space. 589

## Page 596

Installation Rules for In-Rack Sprinklers In general, the installation rules for in-rack sprinklers are similar to the rules for ceiling sprinklers. The pipe is joined in similar methods and supported from the rack structure rather than the ceiling. However, there are some special concerns and they will be addressed in this portion of the text. Water Shields In-rack sprinklers need to activate when the fire is near the sprinkler, yet there is no ceiling over the sprinkler to bank down the heat from the fire. This is not generally a problem since the combination of the radiant heat from the fire and the convection of a nearby fire is usually enough to open the in-rack sprinkler. However, if sprinklers above the in-rack sprinkler have already activated due to the fire, the in-rack sprinkler may have water on it, which would possibly delay the opening of the sprinkler or might even prevent it from opening at all, yet the sprinkler is necessary to achieve fire control, To avoid the problem of a sprinkler getting wet from the water spray of a sprinkler above it, in-rack sprinklers are usually required to have a water shield. The purpose of the water shield is to prevent the sprinkler from getting wet from sprinklers above it, not to collect the heat in order to activate the sprinkler. Sprinkler manufacturers make listed sprinklers with water shields already attached (generally called "intermediate level sprinklers") but these are not required by NFPA 13. The user is permitted to use any listed pendent or upright sprinkler and add their own water shield to protect the sprinkler from spray from a sprinkler above. In-rack sprinklers under barriers in racks are not required to have water shields because the barriers protect the sprinklers from water spray. Section 8,13.3 of NFPA 13 requires the in-rack sprinkler shields to be used to protect Class I tlrough IV commodities when there is more than one level of in-rack sprinklers. This section also requires shields to be used to protect in-rack sprinklers for plastic storage situations regardless of the number of levels of sprinklers. So, according to this section, if you have one level of in-rack sprinklers protecting Class I through IV storage, you do not need shiekis, but if you are protecting plastics with a single level of in-rack sprinklers, you do need shields. This may make some sense in that plastic protection rules are generally more stringent than Class I tlu•ough IV protection, but when it comes to water shields, you wouldn't think the difference would be that important. Control Valves Similar to ceiling sprinklers, there is a limit to the number of in-rack sprinklers that can be controlled by a single control valve. NFPA 13 only allows 40,000 sq ft of floor space with in- rack sprinklers to be controlled by any single valve, Note that the rule (section 8.13.1 in NFPA 13) is not to count the floor space of just the racks, but to count all of the floor space, including aisles, By counting floor space for in-rack sprinklers the same way you count for ceiling 590

## Page 597

sprinklers, the intent is to have the same number of systems for the in-rack sprinklers as well as the ceiling sprinklers. There is no requirement to line these systems up so that the dividing line between the in-rack sprinkler systems and lhe ceiling sprinkler systems is in the same place on the floor, but many sprinkler system designers do this out of convenience. The next question is whether or not the ceiling sprinklers and the in-rack sprinklers can share the same mains to deliver water to the branch lines. The answer is in section 8.15.1.6 of NFPA 13, which requires that if there are more than 20 in-rack sprinklers in the system, the ceiling sprinklers and in-rack sprinklers have to be controlled by separate valves. This means that the in-rack sprinklers are not allowed to be fed from the ceiling sprinkler mains unless there are 20 or fewer in-rack sprinklers. See Figure 38-9 for an example of 20 sprinklers being fed from the same mains as the ceiling sprinklers. See Figure 38-10 for an example of how more than 20 in-rack sprinklers can be fed from the same water supply with separate control valves from the ceiling sprinklers. Ceiling and In-Rack Sprinkler Control Valve Water Supply Figure 38-9 InuRack Sprinkler Control Valve Arrangement Permitted with 20 or Fewer Sprinklers 591

## Page 598

In-Rack Sprinkler Control Valve Figure 3&10 In-Rack Sprinkler Control Valve Arrangement with More than 20 Sprinklers Ceiling Sprinkler Control Valve Water Supply The intent of the requirement for separate control valves is to make sure that if the ceiling sprinklers are out of service for any reason that the in-rack sprinklers will still be able to provide some help in fighting a fire, so they should be kept in service if at all possible while the valve to the ceiling sprinklers is closed as repairs are being made. Likewise, if the in-rack sprinkler control valve needs to be turned off so that the in-rack system piping can be repaired, the ceiling sprinklers in the same area will not bc turned off at the same time. The in-rack sprinklers and ceiling sprinklers are allowed to be connected to the same water supply, even when they are serviced by separate control valves. The only requirement is that any single valve is not allowed to turn off both in-rack sprinklers and ceiling sprinklers if it is closed (unless the 20 sprinkler limit is used). Piping to In-Rack Sprinklers Since the valves in most cases are required to separate the in-rack sprinklers from the ceiling sprinklers, they are not allowed to share the same piping. Therefore, there needs to be a completely separate system of piping to get the water to the sprinklers in the racks. There are three options to getting the piping to the sprinklers in the racks: 1. Run the piping and the ceiling and drop down into the racks (as shown in Figures 33-9 and 33-10). 2. Run the piping along the wall at the elevation of the racks and when you get to the racks, put the pining straight over to the racks. 3. Run the piping in the floor and sprig up into each rack where the in-rack sprinklers need to go. 592

## Page 599

Running the piping along the wall at the elevation of the Wrack sprinklers and then lunning the piping directly over to the racks has major problems. When piping is installed in this manner it usually blocks aisles and presents problems for moving equipment tlu•ough the space. This method of running pipe is usually reserved for racks that are against walls. Running the piping in the floor also has its problems. This generally means trenching the floor slabi which is a major expense. Since most people do not want to actually embed the piping in the concrete floor, the piping is usually left exposed in the trench and some sort of grate is put over the pipe. Over time, water discharged on the floor and debris collect in the trench and tends to promote con•osion of the pipe faster than if it was installed in another location. Also, if portions of the grating get removed, the pipe is open to being damaged. The most popular method of running pipe to in-rack sprinklers is to run the pipe at the ceiling and then drop down into the racks to feed the in-rack sprinklers. While this pipe needs to be separate from the ceiling sprinkler pipe, it can be run alongside the sprinkler system pipe. Some building owners color code the pipe with different colors for mains feeding ceiling sprinklers and mains feeding in-rack sprinklers so that they can tell the difference as maintenance is conducted years after installation. Seismic Considerations The same basic seismic rules apply to piping feeding in-rack sprinklers that apply to piping feeding ceiling sprinklers. The piping needs both flexibility and rigidity. Flexibility is needed for vertical pieces of pipe that will move in different directions than the ceiling during an earthquake. Rigidity is needed to keep the piping at the ceiling moving with the ceiling and to keep the piping in the racks moving with the racks. Specifically, flexible couplings are required near the top and the bottom of drops supplying in-rack sprinklers (see section 9.3.2.3(5) of NFPA 13). The couplings need to be within 24 inches of the top of the drop and within 24 inches of the bottom of the drop, The flexible couplings each provide one degree of angular movement, which should be enough to absorb any differential movement between the ceiling and the racks during an earthquake, Bracing is required for mains of any size feeding the in-rack sprinklers. Note that this will usually only apply to the piping at the ceiling. The drops into the racks should not be braced to the ceiling because they will be expected to move with the racks. The horizontal pipes feeding the sprinlders in the racks should be treated as branch lines and will not require bracing mless they exceed 2 inches in size. If the branch lines in the racks to do not receive seismic braces, they do need to be restrained in accordance with section 9.3.6 of NFPA 13 because movement of the branch line might cause impact between the sprinklers and the racks, damaging the sprinklers. Restraint is a lesser level of making the piping rigid and generally consists of wrapping wire around the pipe from two different directions and attaching the other end of the wire to the rack at 30 ft intervals and at the end of each branch line. 593

## Page 600

Hydraulic Calculations with In-Rack Sprinklers When performing hydraulic calculations where in-rack sprinklers and ceiling sprinklers are separately controlled, the ceiling sprinklers are calculated back to the point of connection with the in-rack sprinklers under the control valve (as shown in Figure 38-10). The in-rack sprinklers are then hydraulically calculated back to the same point and then the two demands are added together (in most situations). Additional discussion on this topic will be included later in this section of this text. If a small number of in-rack sprinklers (20 or fewer) are connected directly to the ceiling sprinkler piping, the in-rack sprinkler demand needs to be calculated back to the connection to the ceiling sprinkler piping and added to the ceiling demand at that point. Number of Sprinklers to Calculate When in-rack sprinklers are installed, some of them will open during a fire, therefore some number needs to be added to the hydraulic calculations. The number of in-rack sprinklers that need to be added will depend on the number of levels of in-rack sprinklers and the commodity being protected. Table 33-5 summarizes the rules from sections 12.3.2.4.3.1, 12,3.3.4.3, 12.3.4.4.3 and 12.3.5.4.3 of NFPA 13. Commodity Class 1, Class 11 or Class 111 Class 1, Class 11 or Class 111 Class IV Class rv Grou A Grou A Number of Levels Number of In-Rack Sprinklers of In-Rack S rinlders Oni One Two or More Only One Two or More Oni One Two or More to Include in Hydraulic Calculations 6 10 (5 on each of the two to levels) 8 14 (7 on each of the two to levels) 8 14 (7 on each of the two to levels) Table 38-5 — Summary of In-Rack Sprinklers to Add to Hydraulic Calculations Where the rack structures are so short that the required number of in-rack sprinklers for the hydraulic calculations are not in a single rack, NFPA 13 allows the user to calculate the total number of sprinklers in the rack. Additional sprinklers from another rack across the aisle are not required to be added to make the total number of in-rack sprinklers for the calculations (see section 12.3.1.11.3). The rationale for this rule is that successful fire tests control the fire without allowing the fire to jump the aisle to the next rack. Therefore, sprinkler protection based on such successful fire tests should prevent the fire from jumping the aisle, so sprinklers in adjacent racks across the aisle should not need to be included in the hydraulic calculations. 594
