Flow from Open Sprinklers After determining the number of in-rack sprinklers that need to be added to the calculations, the next determination that needs to be made is the flow required for each sprinkler. Coupled to the information about the flow is the water pressure at the in-rack sprinkler. As discussed earlier in this text, the flow that discharges from a sprinkler is a function of the k-faclor of the sprinkler (related to the size of the orifice) and the pressure of the water at the sprinkler. In some circumstances, NFPA 13 requires a minimum pressure for the water discharging from the sprinkler. In other circumstances, NFPA 13 requires a minimum flow from the sprinkler. If the minimum pressure (p) is given, the minimum flow (Q) can be calculated using the formula: Q = KJF If the minimum flow (Q) is given, the minimum pressure can be calculated from the formula: 2 NFPA 13 generally allows k-5.6 or k-8.0 sprinklers to be used as in-rack sprinklers. Where NFPA 13 specifies a minimum pressure, it is advantageous to use k-5.6 sprinklers because these sprinklers will discharge less water than k-8.0 sprinklers at the same pressure. Likewise, where NFPA 13 specifies a minimum flow, it is advantageous to use k-8.0 sprinklers because these sprinklers can produce that flow at a lower pressure than k-5.6 sprinklers. Table 33-6 summarizes the rules from sections 12.3.2.4.4, 12.3.4.4,4 and 12.3.5.4.4, as well as the notes in Figures 12.3.3.1.5 (a) to (f) of NFPA 13. Commodity Class 1 to IV Class 1 to IV Group A Grou A Storage Height 25 ft or Less Over 25 ft 25 ft or Less Over 25 ft Minimum Flow or Pressure 15 si 30 m 15 psi or 30 psi depending on the notes to Figures 12.3.3.1.5 30 m Table 38-6 In-Rack Sprinkler Discharge Requirements Balancing Flows for Ceiling and In-Rack Sprinklers As noted earlier in this chapter, ceiling sprinkler flow demands and in-rack sprinkler flow demands can only be added together where the pressure demands are the same. If the calculation of the ceiling sprinkler system and the in-rack sprinkler system back to the same point end up at two different pressures (which they almost always will), the technician has .two choices for dealing with this situation: 595

## Page 602

l. Go back and change some of Lhe pipe sizes in either (or both) systems until the demand pressure is the same for both systems at the point of connection. 2. Balance the flow at the lower pressure situation to the higher pressure situation and account for the greater flow that will occur when the water supply operates at a higher pressure. Examples of this option have been performed in the hydraulic calculation poltion of this text and other examples will be given hcrc. For example, consider sprinkler protection for a rack stoiage facility where the in-rack sprinkler demand has been calculated back to where the connection is made to the water supply and has been found to be 150 gpm at 50 psi. If the ceiling sprinkler demand has been calculated to the same point and has been found to be 700 gpm at 60 psi, what is the total demand of the ceiling and in-rack sprinklers? In the example above, the ceiling sprinkler flow demand (700 gpm) cannot be added directly to the in-rack sprinkler flow demand (150 gpm) because the pressure demands are not the same, In order to add the flows, the pressure demands need to be equalized. In order to equalize the pressures, the conditions at the lower pressure •need to be brought up to the higher pressure. In this example, the in-rack sprinkler demand is the lower pressure, so it needs to be adjusted. In order to make the adjustment, we need to know the k-factor for the in-rack sprinkler an•angement, which can be calculated using the formula: For the in-rack sprinkler arrangement, the flow (Q) is equal to 150 gpm and the pressure (P) is equal to 50 psi, This makes the K-factor that describes the in-rack arrangement 21.21 calculated using to following formula: Q 150 K 21.21 Using the K-factor calculated above for the in-rack sprinkler arrangement, the determination can be made as to what the flow would be in the in-rack sprinkler system at any given water pressure. In this case, we want to know what the flow will be in the in-rack sprinkler system when the pressure is 60 psi, since this is the pressure needed for the ceiling system. We can calculate the flow into the in-rack sprinkler system with the formula: In the case of the example that we are currently working on, the K-factor has been found to be 21.21 and the pressure that we are interested in is 60 psi. The flow into the in-rack sprinkler system at this pressure would be 164 gpm using the following formula: Q = KUF = 21.21066 = 164 596

## Page 603

Now that we know that at 60 psi there will be 164 gpm going to the in-rack sprinklers and 700 gpm going to the ceiling sprinklers, so the two flows can be added. The total demand for the ceiling and in-rack sprinklers will be 864 gpm (700 + 164). As discussed earlier in this section, another option would be to go back to the in-rack sprinkler system and change the pipe size, increasing the friction loss so that the demand becomes 150 gpm at 60 psi at the point where it ties together with the ceiling sprinklers. If this were accomplished, the total demand for the ceiling and in-rack Sprinklers' would be 850 gprn (150 + 700) at 60 psi. For this example, PNI = 84 psi, QI = 968 gpm, Nl = 1700 rpm, N2 1870 rpm (1700 x 1.1 = 1870), Plugging into the affinity laws, (22 = 968(1870/1700) = 1065 gpm, PN2 = = 102 psi. 17) Note that pumps rated at 1000 gpm or less were not considered for this exercise because the flow demand exceeds 150% of the rating of the pump. The first pump considered is the one rated at 1250 gpm. The water supply will provide the following pressures at the following flows: 75 psi at 0 gpm, 45.7 psi at 1522 gpm, and 30.7 psi at 1875 gpm. Taking into account friction loss and elevation loss, the suction pressure at the pump will be the following pressure at the three flows that are interesting to us: 70.7 psi at 0 gpm, 38.4 psi at 1522 gpm, and 22.4 psi at 1875 gpm, Since all these suction pressures are positive, we can continue trying to use this pump. At the demand flow for the sprinkler system (1522 gpm) the pump produces a net pressure of 68 psi (see Figure 28-32), making the discharge pressure 106.4 psi (suction pressure of 38.4 plus net pressure of 68 = discharge pressure of 106.4). Since this exceeds the 102 psi that we needed for the sprinkler system to work, this pump is still acceptable. Next we look at the maximum pressure that the pump will produce, which is 145.7 psi (suction pressure of 70.7 psi added to net pressure of 75 psi = 145.7 psi). This is below the 175 psi pressure rating for fire protection equipment, making this an acceptable selection. Lastly, it is a good idea to look at the water supply. At the water main, the residual pressure will be 30.7 psi at maximum flow for the pump, this is well above the minimum required by water utilities, making this an acceptable pump all the way around. The same analysis needs to be performed for the 1500 gpm pump shown in Figure 28-33. When using this pump, the water supply pressures need to be analyzed at slightly different flows. The water supply will provide the following pressures and flows: 75 psi at 0 gpm, 45.7 psi at 1522 gpm, and 13 psi at 2250 gpm. Taking into account friction loss and elevation loss, the suction pressure at the pump will be the following pressure at the three flows that are interesting to us: 70.7 psi at 0 gpm, 38.4 psi at 1522 gpm, and 2.7 psi at 2250 gpm. Since all these suction pressures are positive, we can continue trying to use this pump (although one of those pressures is mighty low). At the demand flow for the sprinkler system (1522 gpm) the pump produces a net pressure of 59 psi (see Figure 28-33), making the discharge pressure 97.4 psi (suction pressure of 38.4 plus net pressure of 59 = discharge pressure of 97.4). Since this does not achieve the 102 psi that we needed for the sprinkler system to work, this pump is NOT acceptable. This pump also leaves a residual pressure of 13 psi at maximum flow for the pump, which is well below the minimum pressure usually allowed by, most water utilities, making this a difficult pump to use even if the system could be redesigned to accommodate it. The conclusion is that the 1250 gpm pump is the better pump to select given these two options. 34-1) e, a tank is not a useful tool for improving pressure problems by itself. 34-3) b, 75 x 0.433 = 32 psi 34-5) a, fiberglass cannot be used at the ground level, it must be buried. 622

Before adding the flows together, the system pressures need to be dealt with. At the point where the in-rack sprinkler supply is joining the ceiling sprinkler supply, there can only be one pressure. Therefore, if one system needs 49 psi to work, and the other system needs 57 psi, the water supply needs to deliver the higher pressure (57 psi). The system needing the lower pressure (in-rack system) needs to be balanced to account for the extra flow that will occur when 57 psi is provided to that system. The first step in balancing is to calculate the K-factor for the system with the lower pressure demand (in-rack sprinklers in this case). The ceiling sprinkler system (using lh inch pipe on the branch line except for the starter piece on each side of the main, which is 2 inch, and using 4 inch cross main and 6 inch riser) has a demand of 711 gpm at 54 psi at the point below the control valve on the ceiling sprinkler system riser. The in-rack sprinkler system (using Ih inch pipe on the branch lines, 2 inch pipe on the lower portion of the drop into the racks (Y to Z), 3 inch pipe on the upper portion of the drop into the racks (X to Y) and 4 inch cross main and riser) has a demand of 333 gpm at 36.9 psi at the point below the control valve on the ceiling sprinkler riser. The in-rack system has a lower pressure demand, so it needs to be adjusted to determine the flow that will go into the in-rack system when the higher pressure of 54 psi is provided to the ceiling sprinklers. The k-factor for the in-rack system comes out to be 54.84. Using this kefactor, we find that the in-rack sprinkler system will receive 403 gpm at 54 psio We can now add the ceiling sprinkler flow and the in-rack sprinkler flow together (because they are at the same pressure) to get a total flow demand for the sprinklers of 1114 gpm at 54 psi. We also need to add 100 gpm for inside hose (50 gpm for two hose stations, even 627

though there are more hose stations, we only need to add a maximum of two) making the total flow demand 1214 gpm at 54 psi. An alternate solution for this situation would be to replace some (or all) of the 4 inch pipe used on the cross main and riser for the in-rack system with 3 inch pipe. This would increase the friction loss and bring the in-rack pressure demand closer to the ceiling sprinkler demand, making the flow adjustment to the in-rack sprinklers less significant. If all of the 4 inch pipe from point X to the connection between the ceiling system and the in-rack system was replaced with 3 inch pipe, the new demand for the in-rack sprinkler system would be 333 gpm at 52.4 psi, much closer to the ceiling sprinkler demand. This situation has a k-factor of 46.02. Applying the k-factor at 54 psi, the new flow into the in- rack system is only 338 gpm (saving 65 gpm from the solution with 4 inch cross main and riser). ANNEX A WET PIPE SPRINKLER SYSTEM EXAMPLE The following information will be used to layout a wet pipe sprinkler system for an occupancy that is used to assemble wood products. This building is the set of plans accompanying this text with the large open area and the flat roof. The 146 ft x 82 ft steel frame building with 20 ft ceilings is located in Kansas City, Missouri. The office area walls have less than a one-hour fire rating. The Engineer of Record has determined that the occupancy hazard classification is ordinary hazard group 2. Use the materials included in this packet including the Victaulic V 2704 upright k-5.6 sprinkler (see cut Sheet). The local municipal authority has determined that a backflow preventer is required. (Assume a 4-inch DC VA requires 5 psi loss and 6-inch DCVA requires 6 psi friction loss). The specifications for the project indicate that the branch lines will consist of schedule 40 steel pipe with cast iron screw fittings and that the cross mains will consist of schedule 10 steel pipe with welded outlets to be assembled with mechanical couplings. The size of the pipe is be determined by hydraulic calculations. The alarm and OS&Y valves are grooved-end. The actual inside diameter of the 6-inch cement lined ductile iron pipe is 5.89 inches. The structural steel dimensions are included on the building plans. The underground pipe location has already been determined and is shown on the building plans. The water supply test was conducted at the fire hydrant as indicated on the building plans. The results of the test have been adjusted down for the reasonable worse-case accounting for daily and seasonal fluctuations of the water supply and after adjustment, the static pressure is considered to be 80 psi and the residual pressure is considered to be 50 psi at 839 gpm. Layout a wet pipe sprinkler system in this building using all of the rules of NFPA 13 including appropriate sprinkler spacing, pipe materials and size, hanger type and locations, seismic considerations, all appropriate connections and components. Perform hydraulic calculations for the sprinkler system that you lay out for the building and prove that the system will work with the water supply. 631

Bulletin 417 Rev.N Model E (I OO (150 mm) and 8" (200 mm) Alarm Check Valves with Model E3 Trim ...i .18 The Reliable Model E Alarm Check Valve acts as a Water Flow Alarm Device in wet pipe sprinkler systems. The de- sign allows for installation under both variable and con- stant supply pressure conditions. When water flows in the sprinkler system due to the operation of one or more Auto- matic Fire Sprinklers the Alarm Valve opens, allowing con- tinuous flow of water into the system and a transmition of an alarm, both electrically and mechanically. .01 lhe Reliable Automatic Sprinkler Co., Inc., 525 North MacQuesten Parkway, Mount Vernon, New York 10552 636

Operation Variable Pressure The Reliable Model E Alarm Check Valve in ils closed and open positions is shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2. The closed position is maintained as long as the water pressure in the sprinkler system piping above the Alarm Valve is greater than, or equal to, the supply pressure. A flow 01 water in the system piping, resulting from the discharge through one or more fused Automatic Sprinkler(s), causes the Clapper to rise off its Grooved Seal and permits water from the supply to enter the system for distribution on the fire. Virtually all sprinkler systems piping contain confined air. If a water hammer or pressure surge occurs in the supply line, the increased pressure will compress the confined air and cause the Alarm Valve Clapper to lift in- termittently which may result in false alarms. The Model E Alarm Check Valve prevents false alarms under these conditions using two features: a. The By-Pass connection with Check Valve (Figure 3 & 4) allows pressure surges from the supply to by-pass the Alarm Valve Clapper. An excess system pressure is thus created which steadies the Clapper. Should a heavy surge unseal the Clapper and permit water to flow into the alarm line, the Retard Chamber then co- mes into action. b. Drain Orifice Restriction from / Io the Retard Chamber al- lows intermittent flows to be drained before the Cham- ber fills and activates the Alarms. Constant Pressure The operation of the Model E Alarm Check Valve in instal- lations where the water pressure is constant, is the same as described above, with this exception: The Retard Chamber is not required and water passing through the Groove in the Alarm Check Valve Seat flows directly to and activates the Mechanical and Electrical Alarms. ANNEX B DRY PIPE SPRINKLER SYSTEM INFORMATION The building is a metal working facility. The building will be unheated most of the time. There is no incidental storage. The building is already complete, the sprinkler system will be a retrofit into this existing building. The water supply is already in place with the pump house to the north and east of the building. The pump is already in place and cannot be altered. The specifications call for the use of upright Tyco series TY-L sprinklers with a k-factor of 8.0. See the enclosed equipment cut sheet. The specifications call for the piping that is between 1 inch and 2 inch to be schedule 40 steel pipe and the fittings will be cast iron screw fittings. The piping 2h inch and larger is specified to be schedule 10 steel pipe with welded outlets. The fittings will be assembled with mechanical couplings. The underground comes into the building 3 feet inside the south wall and 1 foot inside the east wall. The underground piping will be lined ductile iron, Class 52 (See the cut sheet for detailed information for Thickness Class and diameter). Don't forget to subtract the lining thickness to determine the inside diameter of the pipe before performing hydraulic calculations. There is a 4 ft x 4 ft heated, lighted enclosure for the dry valve header assembly in the southeast comer of the building. The dry pipe valve will be a Viking Model F-1 (See equipment cut sheet). The control valve needs to be and OS&Y. The backflow preventer will be a Maxim Series M200/M200N (See equipment cut sheet). The results of the water supply test for the main north of the building, adjusted for daily and seasonal fluctuations, have been provided in this package (see Figure B-1). The test results of the fire pump have been plotted on a graph (see Figure B-2), Layout a dry-pipe sprinkler system in this building using all of the lilles of NFPA 13 including appropriate sprinkler spacing, pipe materials and size, hanger type and locations, all appropriate connections and components. Do not worry about seismic considerations (this is an unimportant building in an area where seismic issues are not a concern). Perform hydraulic calculations for the.sprinkler system that you lay out for the building and prove that the system will work with the water supply. 645

With reference to Figures I, 2, and 3, the W-Type 9 Sprinkler Wrench is to be applied to the wrench area, or as applicable, the adjustable Crescent wrench is to be applied to the wrenching flanges. When installing wax coated sprinklers with the adjustable Crescent wrench, additional care needs to be exercised to prevent damage to the wax coating on the sprinkler wrench flats or frame arms and, consequently, exposure of bare metal to the corrosive environ- ment. The jaws of the wrench should be opened sufficiently wide to pass over the wrench flats without damag- ing the wax coating. Before wrench tightening the sprinkler, the jaws of the wrench are to be adjusted to just con- tact the sprinkler wrench flats. After wrench tightening the sprinkler, loosen the wrench jaws before removing the wrench. After installation, the sprinkler wrench flats and frame arms must be in- spected and the wax coating re- touched (repaired) whenever the coat-

NOTES Only retouching of the wax coating ap- plied to the wrench flats and frame arms is permitted, and the retouching is to be performed only at the lime o/ the initial sprinkler installation, The steel rod should be heated only to the point at which it can begin to melt the wax, and appropriate precautions need Io be taken, when handling the heated rod, in order to prevent the installer from being burned. If attempts Io retouch the wax coating with complete coverage are Unsuc- cessful, additional wax can be ordered in the form of a wax stick (the end of which is color coded). PRODUCT DESCRIPTION Dry Systems 120a DRY VALVE MODEL F-1 The Viking Model F-I Dry Pipe Valve is a latching differential valve used to separate the water supply from the dry pipe sprink ler sys- tam. The valve combines a positive latching clapper and air plate assembly, with a differential alr to water seat design. The I atching clapper and air plate assembly provides a positive mechanical seal for the air pressure in the dry pipe system. The differentia I design allows an air supply of moderate pressure to control a higher water supply pressure. When the air pressure in the dty pipe system is lowered sufficiently to destroy the pressure differential, the valve opens allowing water to enter the dry pipe system. The valve is also designed to operate a water motor alarm and/or an electric pressure alarm switch. The Viking accelerator with external Anti-flood Device can be used to speed the operation of the valve on large capacity system s or where faster action Is required. 4. OPERATION (Refer to Figure 5) The clapper (5) and air plate (11) assemblies combine to form a floating member assembly. With the clapper assembly (5) latched closed, system air pressure forces the member assembly down, sealing the water seat (16) from the intermediate chamber. When a sprinkler operates, the system air pressure is reduced. When system air pressure is reduced to the differential tripping point of the valve, water supply pressure in the inlet chamber lifts the member assembly off the water seat (16) and flows into the intermed iate chamber, As the member assembly continues to rise, the latching hook (15) is forced against operating pin (23), which causes th e hook (15) to pivot on hook rod (6b) and unlatch the clapper. The clapper is spring loaded and swings to a full-open locked posi tion (See Figure 3A). When equipped with the optional Accelerator and external Anti-flood Device, a drop in system air pressure causes the Accelerato r to operate. Operation of the Accelerator causes the Anti-flood Device to open allowing system air pressure to enter the dry valve inter- mediate chamber. This immediately destroys the pressure differential, causing the member assembly to rise faster. The intermediate chamber is normally at atmospheric pressure and is connected to the alarm line. When the valve trips, the inte rmedi- ate chamber and alarm line are pressurized with system water pressure, activating alarms connected to the dry valve trim. 9. INSTALLATION For proper operation and approval, the valve must be trimmed in accordance with Viking Model Fel Dry Valve Trim Charts. The Model F-1 Dry Valve must be installed in the vertical position as shown in Figure 2. Air or nitrogen supply to the chy pipe system must be clean, dry, and oil free. Automatic air Supplies must be regulated, restricted, and from a continuous source. A Viking Air Maintenance Device should be i n- stalled on each system equipped with an automatic air supply. Never exceed 60 PSI (4.1 bar) pressure in the system piping with the dry valve clapper closed, The dry valve must be installed in an area not subject to freezing temperatures orphysical damage. If required, provide a valv e house (enclosure) with adequate heat around the dry valve and trim. Freezing temperatures and/or excessive pressure will damage the d ry valve member assembly. When corros[ve atmospheres and/or contaminated water supplies are present, il is the owner's responsibility to verify compatibi lily with the Model F-I Dry Valve and associated equipment. Consider installation Of the Viking Accelerator and Anti-flood Device. An accelerator (quick opening device) is recommended on all differential dry pipe valves and is required on dry pipe systems of certain capacities. Refer to Installation Standards and Aut horities

TRIP TESTS Partial Flow Trip Tests are conducted with the water supply main control valve partially closed to minlmize the amount of water enter- Ing the system during the test. Performance of a Partial Flow Trip Test is recommended during warm weather at least annually ex cept when a Full Flow Trip Test is conducted. Partial Flow Trip Tests may verify operation of equipment and devices but do not simul ate operation of the system in fire conditions. Full Flow Trip Tests are conducted with the water supply main control valve fully open. The dry valve Is operated by opening th e system test valve to simulate the opening of a sprinkler in fire conditions. When the dry valve operates, the sprinkler piping will be flooded with water. Performance ofa Full Flow Trip Test is recommended during warm weather at least once every three years. More frequent testing may be required by the Authority Having Jurisdiction. Consider replacing the clapper rubber. If the alr seat has beén pitted or damaged by debris, it may be necessary to r eplace the air plate assembly. b. Air leaking past the rubber diaphragm. Suggested action: Inspect the rubber diaphragm for deterioration. If necessary, replace the diaphragm. 4. Clapper will not latch, Possible causes: a: Incorrect resetting tool. Suggested action: Verify that the re-setting tool used is smooth and of the proper strength and diameter* to provide the required force at the appropriate angle to cause the latching hook to slide over the clapper arm when setting the dry valve. *The Viking Re-setting tool is a 3/4" (19mm) diameter cold rolled steel bar 15" (381 mm) long, chamfered at both ends. b. The hook not sliding on the re-setting tool. Suggested action: File or grind the re-setting tool. Remove any rough spots to provide a smooth sliding surface and proper clear- ance. c. Clapper rubber worn. Suggested action: Replace the clapper rubber. d. Internal parts damaged by accidental application of high pressure. Suggested action: Replace the valve member assembly. 5. The valve latches but will not remain set. Possible causes: a. Improper resetting procedure. Suggested action: See paragraph IO, PLACING DRY VALVE IN SERVICE. b, Inadequate air supply. Suggested action: See Paragraph 10, PLACING DRY VALVE IN SERVICE and Figure 5. c. Air pressure and priming water passing through the intermediate chamber and out of the drip check. Suggested action: Clean the air seat and the clapper rubber. Replace the clapper rubber, if worn.
